name: West Virginia Watch
title: Kanawha County Commission wants more information as WV DEP considers permit for Clean Seas
description: Members of the Kanawha County Commission sent a letter to the state Department of Environmental Protection this week urging it to refrain from issuing an air quality permit for a proposed “advanced recycling” plant until the company behind the project can provide more details to confront concerns raised by residents.
text:
Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who is concerned about the proposed Clean Seas project, speaks at the Kanawha County Commission meeting on July 23, 2026. Caruthers — along with several of his neighbors — delivered a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents opposing the pyrolysis plant to commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant. (Photo by Caity Coyne | West Virgina Watch)
Members of the Kanawha County Commission sent a letter to the state Department of Environmental Protection this week urging it to refrain from issuing an air quality permit for a proposed “advanced recycling” plant until the company behind the project can provide more details to confront concerns raised by residents.
A public comment period for the project — which, as proposed by company Clean-Seas West Virginia, would build a plastics pyrolysis facility at the old 84 Lumber building near Belle, in eastern Kanawha County — was closed on Monday. The DEP has already granted a draft permit for the facility, which would operate by burning plastic feedstock to create pyrolysis oil, synthetic gas and solid residue to be used and sold for petrochemical manufacturing purposes.
Residents in the region have been sounding the alarm on the project — and the company proposing it — for nearly a year. They worry about potential emissions particularly as the proposed location sits only a few hundred feet from Riverside High School, Midland Trail Elementary School, residential neighborhoods and a new offroad trail system meant to increase tourism opportunities in the region.
Last week, several residents appeared at the Kanawha County Commission meeting. Armed with a petition signed by nearly 1,000 residents, they asked commissioners Ben Salango and Natalie Tennant to hear their concerns and let Clean Seas know residents are not happy with the way they’ve operated and are deeply concerned about the potential health and community impacts, especially for vulnerable populations.
“My son is a combat veteran who suffers from COPD from his time in Iraq, and he lives right behind me. This is going to hurt him. It’s going to hurt me as an older person. It’s going to hurt little children,” said Laura Wellstead, who lives a few miles down the road from the proposed plant in London. “What we’re asking you is to stand up for those of us who do not have access to people who wield the levers of power and authority in this state. To stand up for us in Kanawha County, to stand up for the elderly and the children and the disenfranchised, so that we can be proud of our state and say, ‘Come here! It’s beautiful. The air is fresh, and we welcome you, as West Virginians, to our community.’”
Several residents made similar requests at that meeting. They spoke about how difficult it’s been to get answers from the company about the proposed project. They cited Clean Sea’s previous, mostly failed, attempts at building similar facilities in other places. They raised alarms about the company’s questionable financials and what impact such a project could have on a community that’s attempting to rebrand itself as part of the tourism “gateway” to the New River Gorge National Park.
Salango, president of the Kanawha County Commission, told members that while he shared their concerns, the powers of the commission were limited. He cited a policy implemented about 40 years ago that stops the county from enforcing zoning in unincorporated areas, which includes most of eastern Kanawha County.
“So we can’t zone. We can’t. Commissioner Tennant and I couldn’t come up with an ordinance right now that says no plastic emissions or no recycling plants in that zone if we wanted to,” Salango said. “They took that away from us. That was the voters.”
In the letter to the DEP, Salango and Tennant — the third position on the Kanawha County Commission is currently vacant — pushed the DEP to evaluate several factors before moving forward with permitting, including:

Whether the air dispersion modeling provided by Clean Seas reflects potential worst-case operating conditions
If emissions estimates included in the air quality permit application are based on reliable data that is comparable to other, similar facilities
Whether the pollution control measures touted by Clean Seas are sufficient enough to protect children at the nearby schools and those who live in neighboring communities
What enforcement measures exist to verify actual emissions after the plant begins operations

Eric Caruthers, a Belle resident who has taken the helm of organizing his community to seek these answers and more about the proposed plant, said it’s critical not only for those who live nearby but the region as a whole to ensure that Clean Seas would bring a net positive to the area.
Based on what they know so far, though, that doesn’t seem to be the case.
“We all want economic development. We want jobs, we want new industries and opportunities. We just aren’t convinced that this kind of development will be good for us — or anyone,” Caruthers said. “We’ve done our research and we have a lot of concerns. This isn’t the first time this company has tried to open something like this, and they don’t really have a track record with projects that we can trust. On top of that, what they’re proposing to bring here — it really could harm us. We don’t need more polluters in a place already known as ‘Chemical Valley’.”
A report published this week by the Ohio River Valley Institute lays out several of the concerns shared by Caruthers and his neighbors about previous ventures taken on by Clean Vision Corporation, which is Clean Seas’ parent company.
Per the report, Clean Vision has proposed opening at least 14 plastics pyrolysis facilities worldwide since 2020. As of December 2025, only two of those operations were functional. Filings indicate that the ones that were operational have also scaled back services due to infrastructure needs and a lack of interested funders.
In those projects and in West Virginia, Clean Vision has repeatedly realigned projects, walking back previously promised timelines, changing the proposed scopes of projects and, in many cases, abandoning them altogether, per the report.
Caruthers said this doesn’t inspire hope for how they would operate in Kanawha County if they’re given approval to move forward.
“We want stable jobs. If we’re going to bring new industries, new companies here, we want to make sure that they’re stable and coming from (a company) that has experience and knows what it’s doing and can handle its financials,” Caruthers said. “No one that I know has seen that kind of evidence or assurance come from Clean Seas.”
Clean Seas initially came to West Virginia in 2023, when then-Gov. Jim Justice entered the state into a memorandum of understanding with the company, which promised to invest $50 million to build up the pyrolysis plant. Around that time, the company was making similar agreements with governments in Massachusetts, Arizona, Michigan and Puerto Rico. 
None of those other projects appear to have advanced, per the ORVI report. 
In 2023, the company asserted that operations at the Belle facility would be running by 2024, where it would process 100 tons of plastic per a day with plans to eventually scale up to 500 tons per a day. 
By 2024, the plant was not yet operating. The company had yet to start the permitting process necessary to begin operations. That July, however, the West Virginia Economic Development Authority granted a $15 million bridge loan to Clean Seas to get the facility off the ground.
Throughout 2025 and into 2026, the project saw delay after delay announcement come from the company. The proposed scale of the project — as well as its predicted start date — changed almost quarterly.
Financially, the ORVI report paints an overall concerning picture for Clean Vision. The company currently has two operational pyrolysis facilities: one in India and another in Morocco. Since operations began at those locations in 2023, filings with the federal Securities and Exchange Commission show the company has generated less than $614,000 in revenue from pyrolysis activities, with the income shrinking year over year. Meanwhile, it’s accumulated nearly $58 million in deficits due to operational losses and other growing expenses.
Morgan King, the climate manager for West Virginia Citizen Action Group, said the company’s financials and the fact that taxpayer dollars have gone to this project raise grave concerns for residents in eastern Kanawha County.
“People don’t want their tax dollars going to a company that can’t even really prove it knows what it’s doing,” King said. “They’re really frustrated, and they do want to see new things come to the area but not like this, and not as some kind of experiment.”
And on top of being concerned over the financials, King said there are residents who — because of broken promises from numerous would-be developers in the past — don’t believe the pyrolysis plant will really happen.
“They’ve seen this before, so many times. Someone comes in promising jobs and a new industry, whatever that industry is, and it just never happens,” King said. “There are a lot of residents who don’t really believe this is real, but don’t want to see any more taxpayer dollars going toward it either way.”
For Caruthers, it’s difficult to ignore the history of Kanawha County’s “Chemical Valley.” The region was once thriving — nearly a metropolis in West Virginia terms. Chemical manufacturers like DuPont dominated the region, giving hundreds of locals good-paying jobs and contributing to building up the community through investing in local schools, roads and other amenities.
But over the years, Caruthers said, operations shrunk. Job opportunities dwindled. When the economic boons slowed, residents were left in communities with little else to show for that boom period other than poor air quality and manufacturing and chemical “eye sores.”
Now, he said, residents want to ensure they’re not watching history repeat itself. For the past few years, investments have come to the communities off the Midland Trail that gave residents hope.
The new Appalachian Outlaw Trails are paving the way for a new tourism-based economy. There are discussions occurring about how to capitalize on the region’s proximity to the New River Gorge and other tourist attractions. 
A pyrolysis plant, Caruthers said, puts the potential benefits of these investments at risk.
“No one wants to see something like that right off the road, next to two schools, when they come to enjoy outdoor tourism,” Caruthers said. “The company is not cleaning the area up, they’re just coming inside and adding equipment, so it’s going to be an eyesore. It’s going to be a smell sore. It’s going to be a chemically-induced emissions sore. You’re going to have people coming to the trails, getting exposed to this, and then not wanting to come back.”
And further, Caruthers doesn’t feel that his community should be used as an economic experiment for alleged recycling technology brought by a company that has a questionable background in successfully running such endeavors. 
“That’s not the kind of economy or investment that we’re asking for down here, and we deserve better than being guinea pigs for this company that hasn’t made any real effort to talk to us about our concerns or provide information that we can trust,” Caruthers, 45, said. “Since as long as I can remember, it’s felt like it’s just one bad thing after another for this portion of the county and we’re tired of it. We don’t want to live with the fallout of something we don’t support, so we need people to hear us and join this fight.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former state agency directors call new Medicaid fraud task force a ‘sham’
description: Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations said Friday that Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird’s newly formed fraud task force is “political theater.” Dean Lerner and Kevin Techau, who served as directors of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under Democratic governors Tom Vilsack and Chet Culver, said Bir[...]
text:
Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations are raising objections to a new Medicaid fraud task force led by Attorney General Brenna Bird. (Stock photo by zimmytws/Getty Images)Two former directors of the state agency that oversees Medicaid fraud investigations said Friday that Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird’s newly formed fraud task force is “political theater.”
Dean Lerner and Kevin Techau, who served as directors of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under Democratic governors Tom Vilsack and Chet Culver, said Bird, a Republican, is “leaving millions of dollars on the table” by not working to fully fund Iowa’s existing Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.
Bird, who is seeking reelection this year, heads the newly formed, 11-member Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force, which was created to develop recommendations on how to reduce fraud to stop incidents of fraud in the taxpayer supported healthcare program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed an executive order July 1 creating the task force, which is expected to produce a final report that will be submitted by Oct. 29, 2026.
Dean Lerner, left, and Kevin Techau have each served as director of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals. (Photo by Clark Kauffman/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Techau, who has served as the U.S. Attorney for Northern District of Iowa, and Lerner held a press conference Friday at which they described the task force as a “sham.” The two said Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, which was created in the 1970s and operates within the state agency they once headed, is best suited to address Medicaid fraud — in part because 75% of the cost of its operations is funded by the federal government.
Also, Techau said, for every dollar the unit spends, it generates $4 to $5 in revenue that’s collected through reimbursements and civil and criminal penalties.
Calls and emails to Bird’s office were not returned Friday.
Lerner said Friday that part of the problem is that Iowa has chosen not to fully staff its Medicaid Fraud Control Unit. That decision, he said, limits the number of cases that can be investigated and the amount of taxpayer dollars that can be recovered.
While each of the 50 states has its own Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, a 2024 report from the Office of Inspector General at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says that Iowa has a history of providing far less funding for its MFCU than states with comparable levels of Medicaid spending.
Data from the National Association of Medicaid Fraud Control Units indicates there were five states that in 2022 had Medicaid budgets within $1.5 billion of the $8 billion spent by Iowa Medicaid that year.
All five of those states had MFCUs with budgets that were two to four times that of Iowa’s unit. In fact, some states with far smaller Medicaid budgets than Iowa spent significantly more on their fraud control units.
The latest data from the national association is from 2025, and indicates Iowa still lags behind many states with similar or smaller levels of Medicaid spending:
Iowa: 10 MFCU staffers to oversee $8.3 billion in Medicaid spending.
Arkansas: 23 MFCU staffers to oversee $8.9 billion in Medicaid spending.
Kansas: 16 MFCU staffers to oversee $6.5 billion in Medicaid spending.
Mississippi: 35 MFCU staffers to oversee $7.7 billion in Medicaid spending.
Utah: 22 MFCU staffers to oversee $5.3 billion in Medicaid spending.
Kentucky: 16 MFCU staffers to oversee $6.4 billion in Medicaid spending.

Commentary: Don’t create political theater — fund the Medicaid fraud fighters

Techau: Better data analytics can uncover fraud 
In 2022, the inspector general reviewed the work of Iowa’s MFCU and praised it for operating effectively but noted the unit was leaving positions vacant and was not maintaining its own approved staffing levels.
The inspector general said adding more staff “would ultimately enhance the unit’s ability to protect the Medicaid program and its beneficiaries,” but state officials disagreed and argued current levels of staffing were adequate.
“Iowa doesn’t need another task force to tell us how to fight Medicaid fraud,” Techau said Friday. “We already have trained investigators, a Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, the Iowa False Claims Act, whistleblower protections and experienced federal, state and local law-enforcement partners. The question is whether Iowa is willing to adequately fund them and aggressively use the tools we already have.”
Lerner and Techau made several recommendations on how Iowa could better combat Medicaid fraud, including:
— Staffing: Fully fund Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit with the full number of authorized qualified investigators and staff.
— Analytics: Modernize investigative technology and data analytics to better detect suspicious billing patterns that point to Medicaid fraud.
— Hotline: Restore and actively promote a statewide Medicaid Fraud Hotline.
— Partnerships: Fully empower the Iowa Auditor of State and other independent agencies to investigate fraud.
Fraud investigations, Lerner said, are built by experienced investigators using whistleblower information, audits, referrals and sophisticated analysis of billing data. “Iowa should invest in the people and tools that actually do that work,” he said.
Techau and Lerner also questioned the “political” nature of the new task force, noting that Bird, whose office doesn’t handle Iowa’s Medicaid fraud investigations, heads the panel, while Auditor of State Rob Sand, a Democrat now running for governor, was not given a seat on the task force.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. Supreme Court rejects extension of stay in life without parole for second degree murder ruling
description: Roughly 1,100 people are currently serving life without parole for second degree murder. Now that the stay on the Supreme Court’s decision is lifted, they have an open door to challenge their sentences.
text:
SCI Somerset during a media tour on Wednesday, June 2, 2021. (photo by Commonwealth Media Services)The Pennsylvania Supreme Court denied a request for another 120 day stay of a landmark ruling that found mandatory life sentences for second degree murder unconstitutional.
The charge is brought when someone dies during the commission of a felony, even when the person charged never intended to kill.
The ruling stemmed from the case of Derek Lee, an Allegheny County man who was sentenced to life without parole for second degree murder. Lee took part in an armed robbery and, while he was in another room, his accomplice shot the victim, Leonard Butler. 
The Supreme Court ruled in March that, while a life sentence may sometimes be appropriate, requiring one for in all cases of second degree murder violated the state constitution’s ban on cruel and unusual punishments.
That decision could kick off the largest resentencing effort in the history of the state.

What happens when the clock runs out on felony murder legislation?


Roughly 1,100 people are currently serving life without parole for second degree murder. Now that the stay on the Supreme Court’s decision is lifted, they have an open door to challenge their sentences.
Initially, the court stayed its March ruling until July 24, effectively delaying Lee’s resentencing and giving the legislature time to create new sentencing guidelines that can hold up under judicial scrutiny.
Lawmakers also had the opportunity to address an issue that the court did not — what should happen to the those currently serving life without parole sentences on second degree murder charges.
However, the GOP-controlled Senate and Democratic-majority House were unable to agree on how long into their sentence detainees should become eligible for parole, or on what future sentencing guidelines for second degree murder should look like.
Allegheny County District Attorney Stephen Zappala made a last-minute request for an additional 120 day stay, but it was denied Friday.
Justices Kevin Dougherty wrote a dissent, with Justice Sallie Mundy joining, arguing the legislature should be given more time.
“While a final compromise has not yet been achieved, this does not appear to reflect an irreconcilable legislative impasse,” he wrote. “Rather, it seems the General Assembly’s focus was on the state budget, and then its summer recess arrived before a final agreement on these difficult and important issues could be reached.”
The Abolitionist Law Center, which represented Lee, welcomed Friday’s ruling denying the extension of the stay.

A specter of justice in Pennsylvania


“We’re ready and prepared to be moving forward for resentencing for Mr. Lee,” said staff attorney Quinn Cozzens. “And we hope that the process moving forward brings about a quick remedy for the over 1,000 people who are serving an unconstitutional sentence,” 
Now that the stay is over, Lee will appear before a lower court for resentencing. And advocates expect other inmates charged with second degree murder to similarly appeal their own sentences. That process, however, could take years. 
An alternative route would be for attorneys to file what’s known as a king’s bench petition, effectively bypassing lower courts and asking the Supreme Court to make a decision about what should be done for those serving life sentences.
The most likely outcome, according to Cozzens, is the state’s highest court allowing all those currently serving life sentences for second degree murder to go before a judge for resentencing.
The Public Defender Association of Pennsylvania says that approach could take years and cost between $34 million and $36 million.
Despite the deadline passing, the legislature could still approve  a bill allowing those affected to go before the parole board instead, which is considered a quicker and cheaper option. But that would require bridging a partisan divide.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Feds charge man with making threats in Nolan Xavier Wells’ death investigation
description: Jackson County Chancery Judge Ashlee Cole.
text:
Federal authorities have arrested a California man accused of sending a bomb and death threat to a Mississippi Gulf Coast judge, the parent of a friend who went with Nolan Xavier Wells on the Fourth of July to Horn Island, where the Black teenager’s body was found two days later. 
Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce, 27, of Sacramento, faces a federal charge of interstate transmission of threatening communication. Conviction on that felony carries a maximum sentence of five years, a maximum $250,000 fine and up to three years of post-release supervision. 
On July 11, a Facebook user “yaeyae962” sent a direct message to a Jackson County chancery judge who is not named in the criminal complaint and only identified by the initials “A.C.” in an indictment, which were both unsealed Thursday. 
That judge, Ashlee Cole, posted online about receiving the threat and others from the user. Cole is the stepmother of Warren Hudson, who was part of the friend group with Wells who traveled by boat to Horn Island on July 4. 
Wells did not return to Ocean Springs with Hudson and other friends. Instead, the friends told investigators that Wells wanted to stay on the island and would get a ride back to the mainland. On July 6, a National Parks Service ranger found Wells’ body off the northwest tip of Horn Island. 
Investigators linked the Facebook account to Dumarce by tracing an email, IP addresses and a phone number to a Sacramento address. The complaint states records from the number show the phone number called office numbers for the Jackson County Chancery Court on July 11 around 1:30 a.m.  
The screenshot of the message included in the complaint shows a string of nearly a dozen messages sent together telling the judge that a bomb would arrive at her office and “blow you away when you see it.” 
The sender wrote that the explosive would leave blood everywhere and lead to a quick death, and told the judge to “ask god for forgiveness.” 
Dumarce was booked into the Sacramento County Jail on Wednesday on a federal hold, according to jail records. It is unclear whether he will be transported to Mississippi. 
He is listed on the California sex offender’s registry for a 2019 conviction of annoying or molesting a child and a 2020 conviction of harmful matter sent with intent of seduction of a minor. Dumarce was released from prison on the recent charge in 2023, according to the registry. 
Cole posted a statement July 7 to deny that her family was not hindering Wells’ death investigation. 
The judge also posted about threats she had received on social media with screenshots of some allegedly sent by Dumarce under the username “yaeyae962.” That includes the messages cited in the court records and comments on photos on Instagram. 
The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department is investigating Wells’ death, and the sheriff reached out to the FBI to help investigate interstate threats that have been received by friends of Wells, their families, Wells’ parents and public officials working on the case. 
Elmore Wonsley, right, pauses from speaking as wife Christine Wonsley holds a photo of their deceased son, Nolan Wells, as they appear at the National Urban League’s annual conference, Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. Credit: AP Photo/John Amis
The day of Wells’ funeral, his estate began sending letters giving notice of an anticipated civil lawsuit. Recipients were directed to immediately preserve all evidence, including communications, photos, video, audio recordings, metadata and other types of records. 
Cole is one of the letter recipients, according to a copy of the letter addressed to her that was published by the Sun Herald. 
Wells’ parents, Christine and Elmore Wonsley, hired national civil rights attorney Ben Crump shortly after their son’s death. Crump  has called for an impartial investigation and has helped the family get an independent autopsy. 
On Thursday, the Wonsleys said the threats and character attacks against them will not stop them from advocating for Wells. 
The family of another friend who traveled to Horn Island with Wells is pursuing a defamation lawsuit against those spreading misinformation implicating Bart Edmiston Jr. in Wells’ death, which have come with safety threats, including death threats.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey sounds alarm on energy costs — but a legislative solution remains elusive for now
description: Healey’s decision to speak specifically on energy policy as the Legislature scrambled elsewhere in the State House to tackle other priorities is the latest sign of urgency from the governor to respond to Bay Staters’ angst around soaring utility bills — and of the political salience of the issue as the governor seeks reelection this fall.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY used her bully pulpit Friday to lambast the state’s utility companies amid an affordability crisis, but with the key decisions now in the hands of lawmakers who are often content to move at their own pace, she left the podium without outlining a tangible sense of when Beacon Hill may actually act to lower energy costs. 
Two days after lawmakers formally started negotiating an energy affordability bill and as the House and Senate rushed to tackle myriad other loose ends on the last day for new major legislative business, Healey laid out the squeeze in which Massachusetts residents now find themselves.  
She elevated her criticism of utilities like Eversource and National Grid for “repeatedly forcing ratepayers to pay even more” while they earn record profits for investors, and bashed President Donald Trump for his moves to crack down on new clean energy projects and for launching a war in the Middle East that has raised oil and gas prices worldwide.  
But finding consensus that spiraling gas and electric bills pose a problem hasn’t been an issue.  
It’s what to do about it that’s deeply divided the Democratic supermajority in the Legislature. 
“I talked to [lawmakers] as recently as yesterday, and we’re going to keep talking because I think we all recognize how important it is that we get this done and that we take the actions that we can take to lower people’s energy bills,” Healey said at a press conference. 
Healey’s decision to speak specifically on energy policy as the Legislature scrambled elsewhere in the State House to tackle other priorities is the latest sign of urgency from the governor to respond to Bay Staters’ angst around soaring utility bills — and of the political salience of the issue as she seeks reelection this fall.  
Massachusetts officials are juggling a complicated confluence of rising power demand, skyrocketing utility bills, and aggressive climate commitments that demand a swift move away from fossil fuels as a source for heating and electric generation. Electricity prices in Massachusetts have reached double the national average, turning the issue into a top household concern. 
Yet her remarks Friday offered few clues about what progress is now being made after the House and Senate advanced significantly different versions of legislation aimed at saving ratepayers money. A conference committee tasked with landing on a compromise bill met for the first time earlier this week, but indicated that a potentially monthslong slog awaits before they strike a final agreement, keeping Healey in waiting mode more than a year after she originally filed her legislation that kickstarted the whole process. 
Even amid all the other legislative business crammed into Friday, Healey is antsy for a deal on energy and urged members of the conference committee to get to “yes” in a new letter, writing that residents “urgently need relief” and speaking in harsher terms of the greed of utility executives as they “exponentially increase spending and squeeze out more and more profit.” Energy costs have dogged Healey throughout much of her term, prompting her to offer temporary reductions on residents’ gas and electric bills this past winter and ordering regulators to review “all charges.” 
Though the letter reiterated many of the same policy points intended to save ratepayers money that were included in her original legislation, she did tip-toe into some new territory, signaling potential areas for compromise where lawmakers remain far apart. 
Healey said that she wants to “cap the spending” on Mass Save, the state’s energy efficiency program that provides subsidies for home insulations and heat pump installments and is funded by a charge on customers’ bills.  
A major flash point in the debate over the legislation came when, after House Democrats sidelined a push to weaken the state’s 2030 climate commitments, the chamber voted to cut Mass Save by $1 billion and limit the program’s future budget. The Senate proposal includes no such Mass Save cuts. 
And Healey said that she’s “concerned about utility profits” earned through the contentious Gas System Enhancement Program, which allows gas companies to more quickly recover costs from customers for fixing leaky pipes. Spending under GSEP has ballooned since the program started in 2014. 
The Senate bill would end GSEP by 2030, while the House plan doesn’t do so. 
“The key here is there’s a lot of good things that we can do,” Healey said. “We know how to do it. We know what needs to happen, and we’ve got to get it done now.” 
It’s unclear exactly who the “we” is in her telling, though.  
A coalition of business groups and unions wrote to conference committee members on Thursday, warning them of the risks of failing to meaningfully lower energy costs in new escalatory terms: A bad deal, they said, is worse than no deal. 
Specifically, the groups urge greater government transparency about how much it will cost to achieve a transition to clean energy sources and oppose some of the main pillars of the Senate plan to save $14 billion over 10 years, including by ending GSEP and financing utility electric system upgrades through bonds.  
“Progress on affordability is within reach if the Commonwealth can make sensible choices,” reads the letter, which is signed by groups like the Associated Industries of Massachusetts, Retailers Association of Massachusetts, and the Laborers’ International Union of North America. “Should the product of this conference report fail to lower ratepayer bills or put the reliability and safety of our energy infrastructure at risk, we would urge conferees to table any energy legislation until next session.” 
The utilities, for their part, warned of well-intended legislation having the opposite effect.  
Brendan Moss, a spokesperson for National Grid, said in a statement that measures that simply “shift costs to future customers” will “not deliver meaningful affordability.” William Hinkle, a spokesperson for Eversource, said in a statement that not enough attention has been paid in the legislative debate to the “costs of the central proposals” and instead “focused solely on projected savings.” 
At the same time, Healey’s pledge to pursue an “all of the above” energy strategy is looking more and more likely to be put to the test. 
Enbridge, a major Canadian pipeline company, doubled down on its pursuit of a significant gas expansion in New England known as Project Beacon on an earnings call earlier Friday.  
If the company takes more concrete steps through the federal permitting process, it could inject new life into an already-volatile energy landscape in Massachusetts with the prospects of a resurgence of fossil fuels as the state stares down ambitious clean energy targets to halve greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels.  
Greg Ebel, the president and CEO of Enbridge, said that an effort to gauge interest in purchasing additional gas through an expanded pipeline from energy producers and suppliers that ended on July 1 “exceeded our initial expectations” and that more updates will come later this year. 
While details are still light, Matthew Akman, the company’s executive vice president and president of gas transmission, said that Project Beacon would be “multiple times” the size of a small gas expansion currently underway that Healey supported.   
“It’s very, very compelling, and we’re really pleased that our customers and all the stakeholders there are recognizing the importance of it,” Akman said. “So, it’s something we’re definitely going to pursue commercially here, as the need is very strong.” 
The Healey administration isn’t taking a formal position on the proposal yet. 
“We’re going to be looking at the Enbridge project like we would any other project,” said Rebecca Tepper, secretary of energy and environmental affairs. “Is it a good deal for customers?”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal’s bill, mental health grants, Electric Boat: CT politics news
description: Plus: A survey suggests support for schools sharing services, a summit addresses threats, and Connecticut Innovators reports a record year.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more news about the 2026 legislative session, campaigns, elections and more, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Blumenthal’s Russia sanctions bill gets boost
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal’s bill to ramp up economic pressure on Russia and its oil and natural gas exports got an initial victory this week.
On the same day as the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral, the Senate took a procedural vote to advance it. Graham was a main sponsor and worked closely on the bill with Blumenthal. Tuesday’s vote brought it closer to final passage.
With some hesitation from Democrats on granting President Donald Trump more power over tariffs, the overwhelming bipartisan vote came together after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with senators at the U.S. Capitol.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Judge grants temporary restraining order in mental health grants lawsuits
A federal judge has temporarily halted the Trump administration’s efforts to end certain school mental health grants, including $3 million awarded to Connecticut.
The administration tried canceling the grants last year, but a group of state attorneys general, including Connecticut’s William Tong, successfully sued to restore funding. The administration has continued trying to end the grants by other legal means, prompting Tong and others to file a second lawsuit in mid-July.
A temporary restraining order now prevents the administration from canceling grants until Aug. 24. A hearing on a longer-term preliminary injunction is expected before then.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Electric Boat secures massive sub contracts
Electric Boat got a major boost: a $76.6 billion contract from the U.S. Navy that’ll go toward the construction of nine Virginia-class submarines and five Columbia-class submarines.
The funding was authorized by Congress through annual defense policy bills that passed in 2023 and 2025. U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, the ranking member of the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, celebrated the news as the “biggest shipbuilding award in modern American history.”
He said they’ll help the Groton-based submarine manufacturer as it prepares for the sale of three Virginia-class subs as part of the Australia-United Kingdom-United States security pact known as AUKUS.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Survey suggests support for schools sharing services, with a caveat
Over 1,000 people have responded so far to a survey on how Connecticut could better support its public schools. The results will inform the Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability as it seeks to reimagine CT school funding.
One noteworthy stat for a state not known to favor regionalization: A majority of respondents agreed schools should share more services.
The survey will remain open through the summer. Some members of the commission expressed concerns that white respondents were overrepresented, suggesting the survey may be missing other perspectives.
The survey can be accessed here.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Summit addresses threat of swatting, violent extremism in schools
Connecticut’s Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection convened several public safety organizations Thursday to share resources and discuss threats to schools.
High on the list: nihilistic violent extremism, in which perpetrators pursue violence for the sake of violence. This often involves manipulating vulnerable youths into self-harming on camera, as well as swatting schools (calling in a fake emergency to draw a SWAT team to a target). The FBI is investigating nihilistic violent extremism cases across the United States.
Speakers warned that swatting incidents are expected to increase once schools are back in session in August.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Connecticut Innovations reports record year
The state’s venture capital arm is experiencing growth and record deals, arguing that its recently ended fiscal year shows the strength of Connecticut’s developing innovation economy.
In late July, Connecticut Innovations reported that it generated close to $70 million from recent portfolio exits in the state, while investing close to $60 million into early-stage startups and venture funds.
The quasi-public agency was involved in multiple projects in the 2026 fiscal year, including the launch of a $50 million AI/Q Fund dedicated to supporting artificial intelligence and quantum companies. The fund is expected to play a key role in the state’s growing quantum computing ecosystem.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Call for input on wetlands regulations should catch South Dakotans’ attention
description: Duck hunters know the difference between a bird passing overhead and one circling the decoys. The first may vanish. The second deserves your full attention. A notice published July 24 by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is beginning to circle South Dakota’s wetlands, and anyone who cares about birds, wildlife, flooding, water quality or […]
text:
A wetland sunset in South Dakota. (Unaltered photo courtesy of USDA NRCS South Dakota under a Creative Commons license)Duck hunters know the difference between a bird passing overhead and one circling the decoys. The first may vanish. The second deserves your full attention.
A notice published July 24 by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is beginning to circle South Dakota’s wetlands, and anyone who cares about birds, wildlife, flooding, water quality or the meaning of a permanent agreement ought to take notice.
The agency wants public input on setbacks for drain tile near federally protected wetland easements. Drain tile is buried, perforated pipe used to remove excess moisture from farm fields.
Comments are due Aug. 7, giving the public just 14 days to respond to a five-state question involving hydrology, private property rights and permanent conservation agreements.


How to learn more and comment
Read more about the federal request for information at federalregister.gov/d/2026-14995.
Public comments are open until Aug. 7 at regulations.gov/commenton/FWS-HQ-NWRS-2026-2641-0001.


That is an extraordinarily short window. It is the regulatory equivalent of shooting at a blue-winged teal with a stiff tailwind: You can take the shot, but no one pretends it’s a fair one.
Across northeastern South Dakota, thousands of small wetlands are protected by permanent federal easements. Landowners voluntarily sold those easements. The government made a one-time payment — much of it from federal Duck Stamp purchases — and the landowner agreed that wetlands would not be drained, filled, leveled or burned.
When they dry naturally, they can still be farmed, grazed or hayed.
Now the Fish and Wildlife Service is reconsidering how far underground tile must remain from wetlands to prevent drainage.
A tile line does not have to run through the middle of a wetland to drain it. Modern systems can intercept groundwater, snowmelt and rainfall before the water reaches the basin. The pothole can stay on the map while holding less water for shorter periods, or eventually almost none at all.
The current approach uses site-specific science — soil, slope, tile depth and groundwater conditions — to determine how close tile can be placed without harming the wetland. Water does not stop at a line on a map.
Ducks Unlimited, Delta Waterfowl and other conservation organizations are warning that weakening the system could diminish wetlands that hunters and taxpayers already paid to protect. A permanent easement should protect a functioning wetland, not a dry outline in a government file.
These shallow basins support shorebirds, cranes, grebes, herons, pelicans and migrating birds. They also support the insects and plants that sustain grassland birds. Temporary and seasonal wetlands may not hold water all year, but they are often among the most productive parts of the landscape during spring migration and nesting season.
When those wetlands disappear, the effects spread beyond the edge of the basin.
Farmers also have legitimate expectations. They deserve clear rules, timely decisions and calculations they can understand.
The agency should explain its methodology, establish timelines and provide meaningful technical review when a landowner believes a setback is excessive.
The current system also protects cooperating landowners. A landowner who requests a setback determination and installs tile according to the approved plan is protected if an unexpected wetland impact occurs. That is a reasonable balance.
But making the process clearer is different from making the easement weaker.
The agency says restrictions on tile outside the mapped wetland may allow it to regulate “a larger property interest than it acquired.”
‘Wild places are worth fighting for’: Concern grows for receding South Dakota wetlands

The government did not merely purchase an interest in the ground beneath the wetland’s visible boundary. It purchased the right to prevent the wetland from being drained. That right means little if a drainage system can be installed just outside the line and pull away the water that creates the wetland in the first place.
This matters far beyond bird populations.
Wetlands hold water on the landscape, slow runoff, reduce downstream flooding, filter nutrients and provide habitat for deer, amphibians, fish and pollinators. Northeastern South Dakota is already dealing with rising lakes, flooded roads, threatened homes and proposals to spend tens or hundreds of millions managing excess water after it moves downstream.
It makes little sense to weaken wetlands that store water upstream while taxpayers write checks to deal with that water later.
South Dakota’s wetlands have already lost layers of federal protection through recent court decisions and Clean Water Act policy. Wetland easements are different. They are not new regulations imposed on unwilling landowners. They are permanent property agreements voluntarily sold and publicly purchased.
The Fish and Wildlife Service should improve the process. It should provide landowners with speed, clarity and fairness. It should also extend the comment period and give South Dakotans a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
It should not move the decoys, silence the marsh and then tell us the Prairie Pothole Region is still functioning as nature intended.

text:
The Lowe's Foundation awarded Northeast Iowa Community college a grant for its electrical training program. (Photo courtesy of Northeast Iowa Community College)Northeast Iowa Community College will use grant funding from a corporate foundation to expand its electrical training capabilities.
The Lowe’s Foundation announced in a news release it has awarded $420,000 to the Calmar-based community college to bring electrical training space and equipment to its Peosta campus and help “meet growing regional demand for electricians.”
“We are grateful to the Lowe’s Foundation for its investment in our region’s workforce. This grant creates new opportunities for students while helping local employers address the growing demand for skilled electrical professionals,” said Northeast Iowa Community College President Dave Dahms in an emailed statement. “Expanding our electrician program to the Peosta Campus is another example of what’s possible when education and industry work together to strengthen our communities and build a skilled regional workforce.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the release, the community college will open a new electrical lab in Peosta with equipment for hands-on learning, providing greater access to the opportunity to earn credentials across Northeast Iowa Community College’s service area.
This grant, part of a combined nearly $8 million in grants provided to 10 community and technical colleges across the U.S., are part of a larger plan to invest $250 million by 2035 in training 250,000 people for skilled trades careers, the release stated. The foundation has invested more than $60 million in this area since 2023.
Janice Dupré, president and chair of the Lowe’s Foundation and the company’s executive vice president of human resources, said in the release the foundation has worked for three years to connect different stakeholders in skilled trades workforce development, including higher education and community organizations.
“Funding is just one part of the equation; our greatest impact comes from bringing the entire ecosystem together,” Dupré said in the release. “We are proud to help lead this collaborative model, to train and develop skills trade professionals to serve across multiple industries and companies.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: ‘What did we do wrong now?’: Rural Iowa schools weigh impact of ESA expansion
description: As Iowa’s Education Savings Account program continues to expand to include all K-12 families, rural public school districts are still trying to determine how the scholarships will affect their classrooms, budgets and enrollment. Supporters argue ESAs give families more educational choices, while critics say the program diverts money away from public schools[...]
text:
Rural public school districts are grappling with the effects of Iowa's funding of Education Savings Accounts, which cover tuition and other costs of private K-12 schools. (Photo by Ellen Schmidt/Minnesota Reformer)As Iowa’s Education Savings Account program continues to expand to include all K-12 families, rural public school districts are still trying to determine how the scholarships will affect their classrooms, budgets and enrollment.
Supporters argue ESAs give families more educational choices, while critics say the program diverts money away from public schools that remain the center of many rural communities.
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed the ESA program into law in 2023, allowing eligible families to use public funds toward private school tuition and other expenses. Eligibility for the program has expanded each year. For the 2026-27 school year, all Iowa K-12 families are eligible to receive ESAs.
Joshua Brown, president of Iowa State Education Association, said many public schools have had to make difficult financial decisions that include cutting elective programs or cutting core curriculum teachers.
“You have situations like what was happening in Boone, where they’re eliminating their 100‑year orchestra program to ensure that they can still offer the core curriculum,” Brown said. “Other schools are eliminating a second-grade classroom teacher and just combining classes, which is going to increase class size.”
Brown said in the most drastic cases, rural schools have had to merge with other districts to streamline resources and reduce costs, or choose to only have an elementary school and then their secondary programs go to another district.
Creston
Creston, a town of more than 7,500 people, has two private schools along with its public school district.
Deron Stender, superintendent of Creston Community Schools,  said Creston schools only lose a handful of students to private schools each year, but small changes still have a major financial and structural impact.
“Each year we see maybe three to five more kids go than in previous years,” Stender said. “In a district of my size, three to five kids is still a significant number. $8,000 is roughly what a student is worth when they go someplace else.”
Stender said the implementation and expansion of the ESA program has created new challenges for retaining staff and stabilizing the district’s finances.
“We’ve always been challenged with finding and retaining qualified employees, especially in rural communities,” Stender said. “Having two private schools in my community has increased that challenge for us. We lose some of our best teachers because they’re able to pay them the same or more.” 
Southeast Valley
Brian Johnson, superintendent of Southeast Valley School District in Webster County, said the “narrative” surrounding public school educators, and laws regarding public schools have led to staff losses for the district.
“The negative narrative that I believe is being spread really affects a lot of these people that have dedicated their lives to educating kids, and it just seems like some of the storylines or some of the laws that are being passed are tough for people to swallow,” Johnson said.
Johnson said most of the students that leave Southeast Valley end up being homeschooled, as there are no private schools in the Southeast Valley District.
Johnson said Iowa public and private schools “play by different rules,” despite both receiving public funding, and that’s “unfair.”
“I know there’s a lot of frustration every spring or winter when the legislative session meets because I get asked like, ‘What now? What did we do wrong now,’” Johnson said. “Why do private schools and public schools, if they’re getting the same amount of funding, not have to follow the same rules or laws or guidelines?”
Market-based competition
Shane Vander Hart, communications director for Iowa Alliance for Choice in Education, said the ESA program allows for competition between public and private schools, which encourages both to be better.
“Ultimately, I think school choice will help improve public schools because it’s forcing them to be competitive,” Vander Hart said. “The majority of Iowans will still send their kids to the public school, but public schools might have to rethink their approach and the legislators might have to rethink the approach to school finance. School districts and school boards, in particular, will have to look at how many, for instance, non-teaching staff they employ.”
Brown argued that the idea of market-based competition does not match what families are seeing in much of rural Iowa, saying there is no accountability for how private schools are using ESA funds.
“The issue with that logic is that we’re not playing by the same rules,” Brown said. “Private schools receiving ESAs have no accountability for how they’re using these funds, and no oversight to ensure that they are following all of the state laws.”
Brown added that in many rural school districts, parents have to make difficult decisions, saying public schools are not properly funded by the state.
“The only choice a parent has is to go to their public school that’s underfunded, or go to an online private school where their student doesn’t have the opportunity to connect with other students,” Brown said.
Vander Hart argued concerns about public school districts losing funding are overstated, saying public schools still receive approximately $1,600 in per pupil funding for ESA recipients who leave public schools.
“They’re still getting money for students they’re not even educating,” Vander Hart said. “This idea that public schools should get money for students that aren’t attending there anymore is something you could argue, but I’m not very sympathetic toward that view.”
Stender said Creston receives nearly $1,200 in per pupil funding for students who leave for private schools, but state laws lock that money into specific categorical funds, such as money for “gifted and talented” or supplemental teacher salaries.
“We could use those $200,000 to hire two or three people to help with our behavioral or mental health issues,” Stender said. “Right now, the way it’s categorical, we can’t do that.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Nudification law to go into effect Saturday after judge denies delay request from Musk’s AI company
description: A new Minnesota law banning the use of technology that creates sexually explicit images or videos of a person without their consent will go into effect Saturday after a federal judge rejected the request of an Elon Musk AI company to delay the law’s enforcement. U.S. District Court Judge Donovan Frank denied a request from […]
text:
Elon Musk arrives for a meeting with Senate Republicans at the U.S. Capitol on March 5, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)A new Minnesota law banning the use of technology that creates sexually explicit images or videos of a person without their consent will go into effect Saturday after a federal judge rejected the request of an Elon Musk AI company to delay the law’s enforcement.
U.S. District Court Judge Donovan Frank denied a request from xAI, which developed the Grok chatbot, to sign off on a temporary restraining order, citing the lawsuit’s timing.
“xAI filed the motion on July 29, 2026, nearly three months after the law was signed, and only three days before the law is set to take effect,” Frank wrote. “Such a delay in bringing the action and the motion suggests that harm is not immediate.”
xAI in its lawsuit requesting the judge to enjoin the law from being enforced argues that it is too broad as written and infringes on free speech rights guaranteed under the First Amendment.
Minnesota’s evenly divided Legislature was the first in the country to enact — by wide, bipartisan margins — the ban on accessing or using nudification technology, which is becoming an increasing trend in school cyberbullying. Young girls have been targeted by deepfake, sexually explicit images depicting their likeness.
The law punishes AI platforms for letting users depict a person’s “intimate part” using nudification technology. It also imposes a $500,000 fine on the AI company each time a person uses the technology to generate or alter an image to make it sexually explicit.
xAI said in its lawsuit that it doesn’t take issue with Minnesota outlawing the “dissemination of artificially generated nude images of real people without their consent. But the statute Minnesota enacted extends far beyond that goal.”
In a filing, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said xAI’s lawsuit shows the company didn’t do its due diligence before filing to stop the law’s enforcement.
“xAI is a sophisticated and well-resourced litigant yet chose to wait until just a few days before Minnesota’s Nudification Ban effective date to bring this lawsuit. xAI’s lack of diligence and unreasonable delay confirms that a (temporary restraining order) is unnecessary,” Ellison wrote.
Frank ordered a hearing on Aug. 19 to discuss xAI’s motion for an injunction against the nudification law.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC GOP will likely lose its case, judge says in keeping US Senate candidate in the race, for now
description: Another decertified candidate took issue with the rule disqualifying him for living in North Carolina instead of South Carolina.
text:
Danny Ford II can stay on the ballot for the U.S. Senate primary for the time being, a judge ruled Friday, July 31, 2026. (Stock photo by Yin Yang/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — A decertified candidate for U.S. Senate should stay a choice for voters for the time being, a Richland County judge ruled Friday, just five days before early voting starts.
The decision came one day before the state’s deadline for mailing absentee ballots in the special GOP primary.
Danny Ford II, one of a dozen people who filed to run in the Aug. 11 primary, sued the Republican Party on Thursday for disqualifying him as a candidate. The winner of the primary will replace U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November following his unexpected death July 11.

PIImageDisplay (3) 
Ford was one of three candidates the GOP party decertified, citing its rules. One candidate, Clark Neilson, was disqualified for living in North Carolina. The other two, Ford and self-named “hip-hop Republican” Darius Mitchell, were deemed ineligible for failing to meet a new rule requiring all candidates vote in two of the last three statewide GOP primaries.
That was unconstitutional, Ford argued in the lawsuit that asked for the ability to compete. Judge Daniel Coble barred the election commission from keeping him off ballots, saying he will likely win the case.
The party decertified the three as soon as filing ended, ahead of the ballot being made.
Coble will hear arguments from both sides Monday morning and make a final decision after that.
“The South Carolina Constitution declares that all elections shall be free and open and that every qualified inhabitant possessing the constitutional qualifications shall have an equal right to be elected to public office,” Coble wrote Friday.
Coble needed to act fast. The election commission must send absentee ballots to voters who requested them by Aug. 1, and early voting begins Wednesday.
Nearly 700 overseas and absentee ballots have already been mailed out without Ford’s name on them, and 21 had already come back as of Friday, according to court filings from the election commission. Coble’s ruling Friday didn’t address what might happen to those ballots.
Who should be on the ballot?
Ford argued the two-out-of-three rule, which the party added in June, violates the state constitution’s requirement that the Legislature decide how and when an election should take place. Political parties can decide only if a candidate meets the qualifications for office under state law, the lawsuit argued.
Ford argues he actually meets the requirements. He voted the Republican ballot in the June 9 primary and the June 23 runoff, in which he ran unsuccessfully for commissioner of agriculture.
The party counted those as a single election cycle. But Ford contends they should count as separate statewide elections, which would allow him to run.
US Senate candidate disqualified by new GOP rule sues to get on the ballot

Nothing in the rule specifies that those elections would count as a single primary, Coble said in his Friday order. The rule also requires candidates be a “registered Republican elector for at least 90 days,” which is impossible in a state that doesn’t require people register by party, Coble noted.
The Republican Party has long pushed unsuccessfully for legislation to change that. The party sued the state July 6 in an effort to close elections to only registered Republicans, but no decisions have been made in that federal lawsuit.
In response to Ford’s lawsuit in state court, the party made arguments similar to what’s in federal filing, saying the U.S. Constitution allows political parties to decide who they affiliate with, including who can run in their primaries. Deciding who’s qualified to run in a primary also falls squarely under the party’s duties in state law, the GOP party said in its response late Thursday.
“South Carolina law gives the Party the sole authority and duty to ensure the qualifications of its candidates and to certify those qualified candidates to run in partisan primaries,” the party’s response read. “So does the constitution.”
Before the most recent election, the last time Ford voted was in the 2012 general election, according to a voting record included with the party’s response. The only other primary he voted in was in 2004. He did vote the Republican ballot, according to the record.
Ford wasn’t interested in politics until recently, he told the Daily Gazette on Thursday. Life often got in the way of making it to the polls, and he didn’t know the importance of participating in primaries, he said.
Most people don’t participate in party primaries. In the June primary, 25% of registered voters cast a ballot.
SC GOP sues to close primaries to registered Republicans

Attorneys for the GOP party also argued Coble shouldn’t make any changes because absentee ballots have already gone out. In the past, courts have refused to touch cases filed after voting is already underway.
“When a court begins to tinker with an election on its eve, the potential for chaos arises,” the party’s response said. “That potential is only exacerbated when an election is already underway.”
In its response, the state Election Commission asked Coble to change his order, also pointing to the hundreds of ballots already sent. Any change in the schedule for overseas voters could bring the agency out of compliance with the deal it made with the Department of Justice, which allowed the commission to ignore the federally required 45-day window for overseas voters because state law required a much faster turnaround.
Questions about another rule
Neilson, a land surveyor who lives in Charlotte, also took issue with the party’s decision to decertify him.
The Republican Party removed Neilson’s name because he doesn’t live in South Carolina, violating another party rule requiring all candidates be a “bona fide resident of the State” and a registered South Carolina voter at the time of filing.
The state GOP decertified Clark Neilson for not living in South Carolina at the time of filing. (Photo courtesy of Clark Neilson)
The U.S. Constitution says otherwise, Neilson told the Daily Gazette.
To run for U.S. Senate, a person must live in the state “when elected.” If the 70-year-old won the primary, he planned to rent an apartment in South Carolina and become a resident, before eventually building a house on a plot of land he owns in Charleston County, making him a resident by the time of his election, he said.
His survey business operates in both Carolinas, and he planned to retire to South Carolina anyway, he said.
A spokeswoman for the Republican Party did not respond to a request for comment on Neilson’s arguments.
Neilson is not planning on suing, he said. He also noted the tight turnaround if he tried to file a lawsuit ahead of the election.
He is closely watching Ford’s case, he said.
“If that comes out that he’s successful, I should be successful,” Neilson said.
Neilson, who has no political experience, acknowledged he would be an unlikely winner, especially trying to run in a state where he doesn’t live. He would’ve been up against the likes of two sitting congressmen, a former governor and Graham’s sister, who has President Donald Trump’s endorsement.
But he would have liked the chance to try, he said.
“Anything’s possible with God,” he said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Pro-Israel donors fuel Onwenu in contentious Detroit-area state Senate primary
description: Michigan pro-Israel donors have mobilized to support Justin Onwenu against a Yemeni-American opponent in the Democratic state senate primary race for a district covering parts of Detroit and Downriver.   The donors, largely from Michigan, account for at least $117,000, or 33%, of the $353,000 in Onwenu’s reported fundraising haul, state campaign finance reco[...]
text:
Justin Onwenu. | Photo courtesy of Justin Onwenu for State Senate.Michigan pro-Israel donors have mobilized to support Justin Onwenu against a Yemeni-American opponent in the Democratic state senate primary race for a district covering parts of Detroit and Downriver.  
The donors, largely from Michigan, account for at least $117,000, or 33%, of the $353,000 in Onwenu’s reported fundraising haul, state campaign finance records show. The donations come from a range of powerful and sometimes controversial pro-Israel donors, including donors to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, Jewish Federation contributors, Republicans, a University of Michigan regent, a PAC that also supports Michigan GOP legislative leadership, a bank executive, and members of establishment Democrats’ campaigns. 
This level of spending is unusual in a state race, but not unprecedented. Many of the same donors also backed Democratic attorney general candidate Karen McDonald in her failed bid for the nomination earlier this year. The finding comes just after reports that Onwenu is backed by PACs that include DTE Energy and billionaire Matthew Moroun’s companies.
Onwenu is running against former Democratic State Rep. Abraham Aiyash (D-Hamtramck) in what has become among the most bitter fights of the cycle. Aiyash said he has likely drawn the attention of pro-Israel donors because he is an outspoken critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza, which Amnesty International and a United Nations independent commission have described as a genocide, as well as ongoing military operations in southern Lebanon in which more than 4,300 people have been killed. 
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Onwenu said, “The suggestion that there is something nefarious at play or conflation of support from Michigan’s vibrant Jewish community for my vision with support for the Netanyahu government is harmful, offensive, and divisive.” 
He said he has support of “Christian, Jewish, Muslim, and a range of faith communities that have a diverse set of views.”
 Aiyash, however, pointed to an interview in which Onwenu was asked if he took donations from any “AIPAC or AIPAC-aligned” donors. 
“I’m happy to say no,” Onwenu said. State records show he had received donations by then. 
“My opponent lied,” Aiyash told the Advance. “Gaza is a litmus test not because of the connection to the Middle East, but because it is a question about whether you have the moral clarity and courage to stand up to moneyed interests.
“He was willing to lie about this and now that is exposed his knee jerk reaction is to say that it is antisemitic or problematic.” 
Former state Rep. Abraham Aiyash (D-Hamtramck) speaks to students and activists at the Michigan Capitol following the Feb. 13, 2023 mass shooting at Michigan State University, Feb. 15, 2023 | Laina G. Stebbins
The 1st Senate District is located in Wayne County and includes part of Detroit, Ecorse, Lincoln Park, River Rouge and Wyandotte. It is considered a strong Democratic seat, though Lincoln Park and Wyandotte were split between President Donald Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.
Onwenu is a former 2020 Bernie Sanders delegate who left Michigan to attend Columbia Law School and returned to Detroit last year largely aligned with establishment politicians. FEC records show in 2019 he donated to progressive figures such as U.S. Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit). By 2025, he had donated to several AIPAC-backed officeholders, including McDonald and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), who is seeking the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, as well as state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield Township), who is running for Congress.
The Michigan Advance analysis only includes donors who have made donations to, or are part of, explicitly pro-Israel organizations. It does not include donors who are merely part of a communal Jewish organization, or who are Jewish and have no connections to pro-Israel groups.
Onwenu received nearly $5,000 from Detroit Pistons executive and AIPAC donor Arn Tellem and his wife, and a $500 contribution from former AIPAC president David Victor, who still sits on its national board.  
David Handleman, a former AIPAC Michigan president who once organized a Detroit pro-Israel event with the 2002 Iraq War architect and diplomat John Bolton as the featured speaker, also gave $1,000 to Onwenu.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Teller and Torgow did not respond to a request for comment. This story will be updated if a response is received.
Another nearly $5,000 came from U-M Regent Mark Bernstein and his wife, Rachel Bendit. Bernstein, who sits on the Executive Committee of the Jewish Federation of Metropolitan Detroit, helped lead the university’s controversial legal response to pro-Palestinian students’ protests. He also received donations from AIPAC-backed U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit).
Aiyash pointed to Onwenu refusing to state during a debate that Israel was committing a genocide in Gaza as evidence that the pro-Israel donations had influenced his positions.
Onwenu received $20,000 from Jewish Agency PAC, which also gave to Republican leader Matt Hall, who would oppose most of Democrats’ agenda in the next legislative session. 
Onwenu raised over $20,000 through a fundraiser at the residence of Joshua Opperer, a member of AIPAC’s National New Leaders Network who has donated $10,000 to AIPAC, and published a Substack article titled, “Fireworks in Rafah,” that includes a picture of Israeli soldiers celebrating Israel’s independence day by lighting off fireworks in Rafah, a city in Gaza. 
It appears Onwenu took steps to fundraise from these donors, as records show he paid pro-Israel Jewish National Fund staffer, Molly Goldberg, $2,000. 
Onwenu received $14,000 from Huntington Bank executive and Jewish Federation of North America executive director Gary Torgow and his family. While the Jewish Federation offers programs that combat antisemitism and promote Jewish culture, it has also been criticized for producing programs for schools and universities that critics say have a pro-Israel bias.
The Jewish Federation and one of its arms, the Jewish Community Relations Coalition, have also actively supported legal efforts opposing protests against Israel, including voicing support of Michigan Attorney General Nessel’s failed cases against pro-Palestinian protestors at the University of Michigan. 
Onwenu said his campaign “has been consistent about lowering utility and healthcare costs, standing up to corporate polluters, delivering for workers, and protecting our rights in the face of Trump and we’re proud to earn support from a range of people who agree with that vision.”
Aiyash said the pro-Israel donations show Onwenu cannot be trusted to take on corporations. 
“This is the cancer of our politics and if you allow your donors to control what you say now that is not going to change further down the line,” Aiyash said.
