title: Cortez Masto slams Trump immigration policies, and Biden’s too
description: Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto this week called President Trump’s immigration policies “extreme” and “un-American” and said former President Biden “placed too little emphasis on border security.” “I think I speak for everyone here when I say that we thoroughly understand the failures of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda,” Cort[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto at Center for American Progress event on July 29, 2026. (Photo courtesy Cortez Masto's office)Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto this week called President Trump’s immigration policies “extreme” and “un-American” and said former President Biden “placed too little emphasis on border security.”
“I think I speak for everyone here when I say that we thoroughly understand the failures of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda,” Cortez Masto said during a speech at a Center for American Progress event in Washington, D.C. Wednesday.
“Every day, we’re hearing about masked agents without identification coming into our neighborhoods with the intention of intimidating and attacking immigrants. ICE agents are attacking peaceful protestors and killing American citizens.” 
While Cortez Masto criticized the Trump administration, she said “the Biden administration did not handle immigration policy well either.” 
The Biden administration placed “too much emphasis on supporting the newly arriving asylum seekers,” she said, and overlooked undocumented immigrants who lived in the United States for decades.
Cortez Masto this week reintroduced the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act, which failed to pass in 2021. The bill would eliminate three- and 1o- year immigration bars, which block undocumented immigrants from reentering the United States after they leave or get deported for three or 10 years after residing in the country without legal status. 
Cortez Masto said the bill would reestablish the 245 (i) program, which allows undocumented immigrants to adjust their legal status by paying a penalty fee and is only eligible for those who filed for the program on or before April 30, 2001. The bill also promises to protect DACA recipients, parents of U.S. citizen children, and immigrants with pending applications from deportation, and crack down on fraudulent immigration services.
“The legislation pulls down some of the arbitrary barriers in our current immigration laws that keep people undocumented with no way of fixing their status,” she said. “It protects immigrant families from fraud. And it’s been updated to address the new threats we’re seeing under the second Trump administration.” 
Cortez Masto described her proposal as a way for the nation to learn from past mistakes and “offer pragmatic solutions to our country’s broken immigration system.”
But, with a Republican majority in the Senate and Trump still in office, the bill is not likely to pass. 
Cortez Masto did not directly condemn ICE in her comments, but she acknowledged the community fear surrounding the organization, stating detainment based on physical appearance “erodes all Americans’ civil liberties.” 
Cortez Masto also commented on the current administration’s intentional delay of DACA renewals and the fear immigrant families face daily, calling it “horrific” and “unacceptable.” 
Along with the emotional factors, she highlighted the positive economic impact of immigrants. Undocumented immigrants contributed over $37 billion in state and local taxes in 2022, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. In Nevada, undocumented immigrants accounted for over $500 million of that amount.

name: Nevada Current
title: Medicare & Medicaid’s 61st birthday not so happy thanks to Trump’s big bill, advocates warn
description: For 55-year-old Ivon Meneses, Medicaid has become a lifeline to afford treatments for her myriad of health problems including asthma and diabetes, which has come with a slew of medical complications for her.  The federally funded program, which was first signed into law 61 years ago as of Thursday, has been a safety net for […]
text:
Ivon Meneses speaking during a press conference in Las Vegas Thursday. (Photo courtesy Battle Born Progress)For 55-year-old Ivon Meneses, Medicaid has become a lifeline to afford treatments for her myriad of health problems including asthma and diabetes, which has come with a slew of medical complications for her. 
The federally funded program, which was first signed into law 61 years ago as of Thursday, has been a safety net for Meneses and many others who wouldn’t be able to pay for health care. 
“This program is not just a line item in the federal budget,” Meneses said. “It is absolutely the foundation to my daily survival. Medical coverage isn’t an option for me.”
Members of Battle Born Progress, Nevada Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, and SEIU 1107 gathered Thursday to condemn cuts to Medicaid as a result of Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
An estimated 70,000 Nevadans will lose medical coverage due to federal rule changes and spending cuts under the legislation, said Shelbie Swartz, executive director of Battle Born Progress, referencing the Nevada Medicaid administrator’s presentation to state legislators earlier this year.
“This isn’t an abstract policy,” Swartz said. “It’s a grandmother rationing insulin, it’s a mother watching her son’s disability coverage hang by a thread, it’s a rural clinic deciding whether it can keep its doors open.”
Health care providers and state legislators have been among those warning about the challenges ahead in Nevada next year when most of the Medicaid cuts in the Trump bill take effect.
Those challenges will likely be compounded as a result of the Trump administration announcing this week it was ending a subsidy designed to help Medicare recipients with out of pocket expenses. 
Of the many provisions of the climate, health care and tax law signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, known as the Inflation Reduction Act, capped out of pocket costs of the Medicare Part D prescription drug benefit at $2,000.
Nearly 470,000 Nevadans were enrolled in Medicare Part D in 2025, according to a KFF analysis.
All the changes and disruptions to access to health care show that “Republicans are doubling down on putting profits over people and making it harder for people to get health care,” Meneses said. 
Prior to being an organizer for Mi Familie Vota, Meneses worked as a casino porter and was able to get her health care costs covered through employment-related insurance. 
In an interview, she said health complications stemming from diabetes have left her disabled and unable to work full time. 
Like many working people who have trouble finding health insurance coverage, she turned to Medicaid. 
“Latinos are workers and we’ve given so much to this country,” she said during the press conference. “Unfortunately we know that Latinos are overrepresented in industries that do not offer employer-sponsored health insurance. We cannot afford any cuts to these critical important programs.”
The State of Nevada, Tesla, Walmart, and Amazon are among the state’s employers with the most Medicaid recipients, according to a 2026 report.
Meneses said it has become increasingly hard for her to walk, further cutting into her ability to work. As her vision began to fail, she also had surgery on her eyes last month.  
Without Medicaid coverage to pay for numerous prescriptions and procedures, “I would face impossible choices paying for housing and getting health care,” Meneses said.
Access to Medicaid for people like Meneses is going to become even more challenging. 
A new work requirement authorized under the Big Beautiful Bill and scheduled to start Jan. 1, 2027 will require adults to prove they are working, going to school, or volunteering for at least 80 hours a month to maintain their coverage.
The new rule applies to people aged 19-64 who gain Medicaid coverage through the Affordable Care Act expansion. Beneficiaries will also have to reapply every six months instead of once a year. 
An estimated 280,000 Nevadans who benefited from expanded Medicaid coverage are expected to be affected by the change. 
The rule is supposed to exempt those deemed “medically frail,” which could include pregnant people, foster youth up to age 26, veterans with total disability, Native Americans, incarcerated people, those in treatment for drug or alcohol use disorder, but state health officials have warned determining eligibility will be extremely complex.
Meneses said she has spoken to a social worker about the new requirements and was told she could also volunteer in lieu of finding work. But even that seems daunting as Meneses struggles to walk. 
“I fear I won’t be able to work because my complications are getting worse and worse and worse,” she said. “It’s scary. I still have a teen who is only 13. Imagine losing my vision. Who is going to take care of her?”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: BMW battery plant nears completion in Upstate SC
description: BMW will begin assembling battery packs for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles in December.
text:
BMW will begin assembling battery packs  at its Woodruff battery plant in December 2026 for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)WOODRUFF — BMW will begin assembling battery packs for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles in December.
The German automaker has already hired and begun training more than 300 people at the battery assembly plant near the town of Woodruff, 15 miles from its vehicle plant in nearby Greer.
Those employees will work alongside 250 robots to put together the batteries for the all-electric iX5, which the company unveiled in June.

BMW will begin assembling battery packs at its Woodruff battery plant in December 2026 for its new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)

BMW, in 2022, announced its electric vehicle plans for its Upstate South Carolina plant.
It has since invested $1.7 billion into both the existing, 10 million-square-foot factory in Greer, as well as a new, 1-million-square-foot, battery assembly plant on 314 acres in Woodruff.
In exchange for that investment, the state offered up a $52 million grant to purchase the land in Woodruff and pay for offsite environmental improvements to offset the loss of acreage to development, as well as grade the property, which BMW officials said used to be home to a peach farm, to get it ready for construction.
The company also received income tax credits for each of the roughly 300 new jobs, according to the state Department of Commerce. Those credits are worth $1,500 for each new job.
At the same time, BMW announced it would partner with Envision Automotive Energy Supply Co. (AESC), a Japanese-headquartered company, to make the cells for the battery packs.
Last year, however, AESC pressed pause indefinitely on its $1.6 billion battery cell plant under construction near Florence.
Electric vehicle battery company halts construction of SC manufacturing plant

AESC representatives said then that the company “fully intends to meet our commitments to invest $1.6 billion and create 1,600 jobs in the coming years,” but did not indicate what the new timeline might be.
Neither the company nor Florence County economic development officials responded to messages from the SC Daily Gazette about an updated restart.
In the meantime, AESC is expected to ship battery cells made in its China facilities to the BMW battery plant in Woodruff, said Rich Everly, vice president of production at BMW Group Plant Woodruff.
Inside the Woodruff plant, employees are getting ready for the start of production by training on a virtual reality platform that mimics the assembly work they’ll be doing on the production line.
And on a sneak peak tour of the plant last month, reporters from the SC Daily Gazette and other news outlets got a glimpse of how the factory will operate.
At the start of the assembly line, thousands of cylindrical battery cells will be glued together in clusters, which will give the iX5 the capacity to drive 435 miles per charge.
BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)BMW workers train on virtual reality stations at the company's Woodruff battery plant, preparing for production to start in December 2026. (Photo courtesy of BWM)
From there, the cell clusters are transferred to the next set of stations, where they’re cleaned by lasers, welded by robots and inspected using camera and artificial intelligence systems.
“In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality,” Raymond Wittman, a member of the Board of Management at BMW, said in a statement.
The clusters are then sealed inside a foam-filled battery pack, roughly the size of a queen mattress.
Thousands of cylindrical batter cells will be glued into clusters at BMW’s Woodruff battery plant to make packs for the company’s new, South Carolina-built electric vehicles. (Photo courtesy of BWM)
Some 50 trucks a day will enter and exit the Woodruff plant, Everly said, delivering supplies and sending finished battery packs to Greer to be installed in hybrid and all-electric vehicles.
The new iX5 will hit the market in early 2027, according to a June news release from the company.
The Greer vehicle plant, BMW’s largest in the world, produced more than 412,800 vehicles last year. Of those, around 200,000 were exported — a total value of $9 billion.
BMW has the capacity to make as many as 450,000 vehicles in Greer annually, Everly said, and updates to the plant allow it to shift seamlessly between gas, electric and hybrid vehicle production.
The Woodruff plant and Greer updates bring BMW’s total investment in South Carolina since 1992 to nearly $16 billion.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters weigh ending income tax. Here’s how other states replace the revenue
description: Voters have the opportunity Aug. 4 to put Missouri on track to be the 10th state without an individual income tax. Many of the states without an income tax have to get creative in the way they generate revenue to fund state operations. From property taxes and sales taxes to communication taxes and live entertainment […]
text:
(Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight).Voters have the opportunity Aug. 4 to put Missouri on track to be the 10th state without an individual income tax.
Many of the states without an income tax have to get creative in the way they generate revenue to fund state operations. From property taxes and sales taxes to communication taxes and live entertainment fees, revenue from these taxes is vital for providing essential services.
Individual income tax revenue made up 63% of the state’s general revenue in fiscal year 2025. The amendment asks voters to require the legislature to gradually reduce the individual income tax rate with the goal of eliminating it by 2032.
A yes vote will allow a broad sales tax on all goods and services to make up for the loss in revenue. This would repeal limits currently in place on such taxation. The state’s sales tax is 4.225%.
Gov. Mike Kehoe has suggested exemptions for healthcare, agriculture and real estate; the legislation passed by the House included no language for such exemptions.
The resolution’s sponsor, state Rep. Bishop Davidson, a Republican from Republic, noted the amendment that voters will consider does not mandate that the state make any changes to a sales tax. However, the Missouri budget must be balanced, so the loss in income tax revenue must be made up elsewhere.
Proponents of the resolution often compare Missouri to other states with no state income tax. Although a majority of these states rely on sales tax, their tax structures can vary drastically depending on different industries present, constitutional provisions or recent policy changes.
Here’s an overview of how the nine states without individual income tax generate state revenue:
Alaska became the first state to successfully repeal its income tax in 1980, thanks to the state’s oil boom. Almost all Alaskan oil production is on state-owned land, allowing the state to receive revenue in four different ways: production tax, property tax, royalties and corporate income tax.
According to the Resource Development Council, Alaska has made up to 90% of the state’s unrestricted general fund revenue from taxes related to oil in most years.
Roughly 30% of general fund revenue came from taxes on petroleum while 60% came from various investment returns. A majority of these investments came from Alaska’s permanent fund, which has received financial deposits used to invest in bonds, stocks and real estate.
Transfers from the fund make up a majority of investment revenues in Alaska’s unrestricted general and restricted designated general fund revenue.
Florida receives over 70% of its general revenue from sales tax with another 11% coming from corporate income tax. The state gets revenue from tourism through the Tourist Development Tax.
Nevada receives roughly 37% of its general revenue from a sales tax and use tax, including taxes on gaming fees, insurance premiums and a live entertainment tax.
The state’s base rate is 6.85%.
If Nevada were its own country, it would rank 10th in gold production, but tax revenue from natural resources only produces a small portion of revenue in taxes related to its natural resources. A state constitutional provision limits taxes on minerals.
New Hampshire phased out its individual income tax in 2025 and does not have a state sales tax either.
The state derives a little over a third of its budget from a business profits tax. New Hampshire has a meals and rooms tax, which serves as a form of tourism tax. This accounts for a little over one-tenth of its revenue.
New Hampshire makes up the remainder of its revenue from miscellaneous fees, such as its tobacco tax, Medicaid enhancement tax and its tax on real estate transfers.
South Dakota makes over 60% of its revenue from sales tax. The state has a base rate of 4.2% on general sales. The state also imposes a contractor’s excise tax, which is a 2% fee on the total cost of a construction project. This tax accounts for a little under one-tenth of the state’s budget.
Similar to Nevada, South Dakota has a strong mining industry but derives less than 1% of its revenue from its severance tax.
Tennessee makes up 60% of the state’s revenue from a general sales tax. Tennessee’s state sales tax is 7%. Tennessee employs a franchise and excise tax on corporations and businesses that contributes 16% of revenue.
In Texas, a 6.25% state sales and use tax is imposed on all retail sales, leases and rentals for most goods and certain services. The state first imposed a sales tax structure in 1961, and it provides over half of the state’s budget.
Texas fills the remainder of its budget with various taxes on motor vehicle sales, franchise taxes and taxes on the state’s natural resources.
Washington brings in about 45% of its budget from its sales and use tax. The state levies a fee of 6.5% on sales and transactions.
Washington makes almost a fifth of its budget from the state’s business and occupation tax, calculated based on the gross income of a business. The rate depends on which category of activity the business is classified as, with Washington having over 50 different classifications.
Washington also has a property tax that generates 13.4% of its revenue.
A massive reform to the state’s tax structure was approved in March when Senate Bill 6346 was signed into law: the first-ever “Millionaires Tax.” Beginning in 2028, a 9.9% income tax will be applied to taxable earnings above the $1 million standard deduction.
Wyoming makes a little under 40% of its revenue from its general and select sales tax structure.
Wyoming generates significant revenue from its mining industry. The state levies fees ranging from 1% to 6% for the various minerals and resources that are extracted.
Similar to Alaska’s permanent fund, the Permanent Wyoming Mineral Trust Fund receives revenue from its severance tax and is used by the state legislature to invest in various assets.
Investment income and severance taxes account for 47.51% of its general fund revenue, with miscellaneous revenue and tax sources filling the remainder of the budget.
Wyoming ranked ninth nationally for natural gas production and eighth in crude oil production in 2023. This allows the state to fund its entire budget reserve account just with federal mineral royalties or severance tax revenue.
State Rep. Steve Butz, a Democrat from St. Louis, argued that Missouri cannot replicate the similar success seen by other states that never had an income tax or repealed it.
“God bless Branson, but it’s not Orlando,” Butz said in a March committee hearing. “We are never going to be Texas, Texas has a huge percent of this nation’s energy in that state, and it’s just not below our ground.”
“You have to face the facts,” Butz added. “Tennessee hasn’t had an income tax; it’s not part of the way they fund their government, but their sales tax is dramatically higher.”
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Kratom alkaloids found in cat’s claw tablets linked to multiple overdoses, Utah agencies warn
description: A product labeled as cat’s claw is being removed from Utah shelves as Utah officials investigate a recent death and several severe health incidents that may be linked to it.  According to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food and the Utah Poison Control Center, multiple flavors of Buzzers’ cat’s claw tablets were found to […]
text:
Buzzers Cat's Claw tablet packets. (Photo courtesy of Utah Department of Agriculture and Food)A product labeled as cat’s claw is being removed from Utah shelves as Utah officials investigate a recent death and several severe health incidents that may be linked to it. 
According to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food and the Utah Poison Control Center, multiple flavors of Buzzers’ cat’s claw tablets were found to contain kratom alkaloids, a recently mostly-banned substance in the state. Additional details were not provided about the fatal overdose.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The agencies said in a new release they “warn all members of the public not to buy or consume Buzzers Cat’s Claw tablets and to safely destroy any existing product. Retailers should immediately remove products and contact UDAF’s Specialized Products Division.”
Cat’s claw, a woody vine, is considered to be a safe supplement promoted to treat joint pain and other conditions, so the Poison Control Center wouldn’t expect it to have opioid-like effects, said Amberly Johnson, director of the center. However, within the past several weeks, many calls made to the center have been related to cat’s claw tablets.
“Within 2026, we received around 40 calls related to kratom or kratom derivative products,” Johnson said, mentioning alkaloids like 7-OH, which occur naturally in kratom products but are often enhanced in labs. “Just within the past several weeks, we’ve seen an increase in about 19% of those cases have been related to these cat’s claw products that we suspected had a synthetic kratom derivative in them.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The state’s Department of Agriculture and Food confirmed those suspicions when officers tested the Buzzers products identified in overdose cases in recent weeks and found they contained mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15, two opioid-acting compounds derived from the kratom plant, the agency said. 
The compounds, Johnson said, can be more potent than morphine, and can have withdrawal effects among users.
“We’d expect to see profound sedation or drowsiness, sleepiness, leading to, like, coma. And then also to effects on breathing, so really slow, shallow breathing, even to the point of someone not breathing,” Johnson said.
Johnson recommends administering naloxone in suspected overdoses from these products, and calling 911 to ask for medical help. Those with concerns about the substance’s adverse effects can also call the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222 anytime for free, expert advice.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Trump cut Forest Service funding for wildfire mitigation — and then the Northland started burning
description: The U.S. Forest Service lost more than 100 Minnesota employees and delayed $10 million in grant funding for wildfire mitigation in the Superior National Forest during the chaotic first year of President Trump’s second term.  Democratic elected officials say those setbacks left Minnesota ill-equipped to face the fires that have burned more than 60,000 acres [[...]
text:
Smoke from wildfires in the Boundary Waters creates haze on Big Sandy Lake in McGregor on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Lorie Shaull/KAXE)The U.S. Forest Service lost more than 100 Minnesota employees and delayed $10 million in grant funding for wildfire mitigation in the Superior National Forest during the chaotic first year of President Trump’s second term. 
Democratic elected officials say those setbacks left Minnesota ill-equipped to face the fires that have burned more than 60,000 acres in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness since early July and repeatedly billowed smoke across the Great Lakes region and beyond. 
“The Forest Service diverted forest management funds that Congress provided through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the Inflation Reduction Act to pay for the Deferred Resignation Program,” DFL Rep. Angie Craig told U.S. Forest Service chief Tom Schultz at a July 22 congressional hearing. Craig is the highest-ranking Democrat on the House Agriculture Committee.
The move had “obvious consequences: the Forest Service treated 23% fewer hazardous fuels acres last year compared with 2024,” Craig added.
The Forest Service did not respond to a Reformer request for comment. 
The Boundary Waters have seen several major fires since a 1999 derecho left tens of millions of mature trees to decay — or burn — on the forest floor. Repeated droughts made worse by climate change have also encouraged the spread of spruce budworm, a native insect that can weaken or kill spruce and fir trees, leaving yet more fuel in the wilderness. These natural conditions exacerbated what some conservations say were decades of misguided forest management practices, which favored fire suppression at all costs over the beneficial, low-intensity fires that periodically sweep the northwoods. 
Forest management today is a more holistic practice that combines selective tree thinning and prescribed burns with efforts to boost ecological diversity and protect “keystone” species, which in northern Minnesota include the towering white and red pines that make the Boundary Waters so special.
The delayed Forest Service grants would have supported prescribed burns and other fuel-reduction efforts on thousands of acres near the Echo Trail, which has borne the brunt of this year’s fires. These “shovel-ready” projects “would have been effective in stopping or slowing down these fires,” a former Forest Service official who retired in December told the Washington Post last week.
Citing current and former Forest Service officials, some of whom spoke anonymously for fear of retaliation, the Post reported that the grants were among countless earmarks paused or canceled by Elon Musk’s DOGE, which aimed to cut federal spending and especially Biden-era programs connected to social justice or climate change. 
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the top Democrat on the committee that oversees the Forest Service, joined several high-ranking colleagues in signing a letter in February 2025 raising “significant concerns” about the funding pause and a separate hiring freeze that kept the agency from adding permanent and seasonal firefighters. 
Craig, who is running against Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the DFL primary to replace retiring Sen Tina Smith, said at the hearing last week that the agency lost about 16% of its workforce due to the DOGE cuts. Those losses put the agency on the back foot ahead of fire season, she said.
“‘We only have so many resources to go around,’” Craig said, repeating a July 17 warning from National Incident Management Organization official Jason Loomis, who said his teams would need to focus equipment and personnel on protecting nearby communities and public infrastructure over the wilderness itself. By then, the entire Boundary Waters had been evacuated and closed to new entry.
“That would certainly suggest that the lack of staffing was at least partially related to the closure,” Craig said.
The agency unfroze the two wildfire mitigation grants in December after state and local officials went to Washington to advocate for the funding, but not before requiring modifications to allow more of the thinned vegetation to be marketed for timber, the Post reported.
On a webpage touting “2025 Forest Service Accomplishments,” the agency said it “strengthened America’s timber supply and forest industry and exceeded timber targets” while launching a “long-term strategy for forest productivity and rural economic growth” that would see timber volume grow 25% by 2028 to 4 million board-feet, a level not reached since 1993.
State Sen.Grant Hauschild, a Hermantown Democrat whose sprawling district covers the Boundary Waters and surrounding state and national forest lands, told the Reformer in an interview that reducing wildfire risk requires a “multifaceted approach” that includes fuel reduction in vulnerable forests.
“One of the things we could have done is supported the federal grant to help clear the fuel around the Echo Trail,” he said. “That’s not to say we couldn’t have done more than that…(but) we can’t just have across-the-board cuts to Forest Service staff and we can’t have cuts to grants that help with wildfire mitigation.”
In last week’s hearing, Craig accused Schultz of the Forest Service of redirecting large chunks of wildfire mitigation funding and reassigning hundreds of Forest Service staff without receiving congressional approval, which she said the law required. 
Schultz pushed back, saying the agency was well within its rights.
“We did not receive approval because we did not think it was required by law,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: 43,000 fewer Mississippians are on SNAP after Congress and President Trump slashed funding
description: Bagged lunches await stapling before being distributed to students on March 3, 2021 in Fayette, Miss.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi and the U.S. are experiencing the steepest drop-off of participation in the nation’s largest anti-hunger program in nearly 30 years following federal cuts made last summer by Congress and President Donald Trump, experts say. 
In April, 43,000 fewer Mississippians had access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program than nine months earlier. Mississippi’s decline of 12% in the program previously known as food stamps is slightly higher than the national average of 11%, according to recent data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
“And it’s not because the need is any lower,” said Ty Jones Cox, vice president for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, during a July 22 press conference.
President Donald Trump speaks at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach Fla., Friday, May 1, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Matt Rourke
In fact, food insecurity in the U.S. is the highest it’s been in a decade, according to the most recent data. 
Regulations that Congress passed through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and that Trump signed into law last July have changed the face of SNAP. Stricter work requirements subjected previously-exempt older adults and caregivers to more paperwork. An already burdened system became more strained, at a time when the same federal law posed new fines for states with high error rates in eligibility determinations. 
A payment error rate measures how accurately each state determines the number of SNAP dollars an eligible person receives. In May, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves praised the Mississippi Department of Human Services for lowering the state’s error rate and qualifying for a lower penalty. 
MDHS Communications Director Mark Jones previously told Mississippi Today the department was able to achieve this by providing more training for staff who determine if people are eligible to receive SNAP and by reminding recipients about the importance of updating income changes to ensure their paperwork is accurate. 
However, experts say it’s problematic that delaying or denying benefits to an eligible family does not count as an error.
“That creates an enormous incentive for states to slash their error rates by any means necessary,” Jones Cox said. “And that’s what we’re seeing.”
The decline is outpacing even the government’s predictions. Shortly after Congress passed Trump’s megabill last year, the Congressional Budget Office predicted SNAP enrollment would decrease by 2.4 million people nationwide. To date, enrollment has decreased by 4.5 million people. 
Dr. Patricia Tibbs.
At least a third of those people are children, according to data from 19 states. Mississippi does not track data on children. 
Dr. Patricia Tibbs, president of the Mississippi chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said she worries about the effect that the decrease in enrollment will have on the next generation. Nutrition is one of the most influential determinants of health – and children are the most vulnerable.
“It’s children we’re talking about,” Tibbs told Mississippi Today. “They don’t choose their families’ income.”
Politicians should look at SNAP as a return on investment, Tibbs said. Access to healthy foods helps Mississippi children grow into productive citizens, saving the state millions of dollars on more complex issues that arise from inadequate nutrition. Tibbs also said increased investment in SNAP could boost the state’s workforce participation rate, currently the second-lowest in the country. 
“Hospitalizations, developmental services, special education, mental care, chronic disease treatment – those are all down the road, if we don’t focus on nutrition,” Tibbs said.
‘It’s a lose-lose situation’
In 2019, Debra Expose of Jackson, a single mother of five children ages 2 through 12, began facing severe financial hardship after divorcing the father of her eldest daughter. Expose said she doesn’t receive child support for any of her children, despite being their primary caregiver and picking up most of the costs of child rearing. 
Over the years, Expose has worked at Walmart, Kroger, Xerox and for the city of Jackson as a crossing guard. Most recently, she worked for the United States Postal Service. She resigned last year due to the lack of family leave, flexible hours and affordable childcare. 
SNAP has been a lifeline for Expose as she looks for a more family-friendly job. Now, she said she worries that federal cuts and pressure on states to lower error rates will mean increased red tape that could put food out of reach for her family. 
Expose said paperwork delays are already commonplace. Every six months at her recertification appointments, she routinely gets kicked off the program for one to three months, she said. Even when she submits her paperwork early, caseworkers do not get to her case in time to prevent her from losing coverage, she said. That has meant making difficult decisions, such as whether to put food on the table or keep the lights on. 
And sometimes, losing one means losing the other. 
“Am I gonna lose my power that’s gonna help me keep the food fresh and able to be eaten? It’s a lose-lose situation,” Expose said. 
Food is stored on pantry shelves at Johnson Elementary School in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 5, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Safia Malin is policy director for the nonprofit One Voice, a Jackson-based civic engagement group. She said hearing from people such as Expose should be a central part of how lawmakers develop public policies. In Mississippi, it’s not. Formal opportunities for constituents to provide testimony do not exist in the state Legislature. 
“There is so much we can learn from data and numbers, but also from real live human beings who are withstanding the impacts and figuring out how to make ends meet,” Malin said. “We know that the unfortunate reality for so many folks is that a reduction in benefits for them just means they’ll be forced to go without.”
Although the Mississippi Legislature doesn’t have the power to reverse or delay federal cuts to social safety net programs, Malin urged the Mississippi Department of Human Services to make sure it is not lowering its error rate by cutting eligible people. 
Malin also recommended the Legislature adopt a system called “simplified reporting,” as every other state has done, to administer SNAP. Malin believes it would reduce the number of errors – without cutting eligible families – and save the state money that could go back into the program. 
As situations such as Expose’s become more common, repercussions will be felt for decades, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. 
He said that includes not only the long-term health conditions resulting from inadequate nutrition but also the effects of chronic stress on children living in food-insecure homes. Studies show that toxic stress, including prolonged and extreme economic hardship, can impair cognitive development and leave children more vulnerable to physical disorders such as cardiovascular diseases and diabetes, as well as mental health issues such as depression and alcoholism. 
“To the extent that we are making policy decisions today about foregoing the opportunity to feed hungry children, we are having consequences that will haunt us going forward a generation from now,” Racine said. “And it’s entirely avoidable.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Women allege Mercer County doctor sexually abused them
description: A Mercer County doctor sexually abused dozens of women over more than a decade, according to a new lawsuit that also blames the clinic where he worked.
text:
A Mercer County doctor sexually abused dozens of women over more than a decade, according to a new lawsuit that also blames the clinic where he worked. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)A Mercer County doctor sexually abused dozens of women over a decade, according to a new civil lawsuit that describes a pattern of inappropriate touching, unnecessary procedures, and painful treatments that spanned more than a decade.
Attorneys with a Philadelphia-based law firm filed a complaint Wednesday in state Superior Court in Mercer County on behalf of 31 New Jersey residents alleging former physician Bruce Pierce abused his position of trust and that Delaware Valley OBGYN, his employer, should have done more to protect patients. Many of the women had been under Pierce’s care for years.
The lawsuit comes nearly two years after the New Jersey State Board of Medical Examiners announced it had suspended Pierce’s medical license, saying it found “credible evidence he baselessly sexually exploited two patients under the cloak of providing routine medical care.”
According to the lawsuit, patient complaints date to 2012. Women reported Pierce’s behavior to the clinic or other physicians at least eight times, and in two cases chaperones were in the exam room when the abuse is alleged to have occurred, it notes.
“Defendant Pierce’s conduct went far beyond the bounds of decency and would be regarded as atrocious and utterly intolerable in a civilized society. Pierce intentionally targeted Plaintiffs at times when they were vulnerable, unclothed, or in private medical settings, exploiting their trust in Delaware Valley and its providers,” the lawsuit says.
Nathaniel Foote, attorney for the plaintiffs, told the New Jersey Monitor some of the plaintiffs have also reported the abuse to police. He said he is not aware of any criminal charges filed against Pierce.
The New Jersey Monitor was unable to reach Pierce, who joined Delaware Valley in the early 1990s. Calls to attorneys who represented him in the medical licensing dispute were not returned. A message with Delaware Valley OBGYN was also not returned.
Multiple plaintiffs said they have since shunned regular gynecological wellness exams, annual visits designed to spot breast, cervical, and other cancers and address reproductive health concerns. One has now gone six years without such a check-up, according to the lawsuit.
“Plaintiffs experienced immediate terror, humiliation, and shame during Pierces’ assaults. Plaintiffs have since suffered severe and ongoing emotional distress, including depression, anxiety, nightmares, fear of medical providers, hypervigilance, and post-traumatic stress symptoms,” the complaint says.
The suit faults Pierce for abusing his position and taking advantage of vulnerable women and blames Delaware Valley for failing to ensure patients were safe. It claims the clinic was grossly negligent in how it failed to establish and enforce sex abuse prevention policies; how it hired, trained, monitored and supervised staff; and in failing to report Pierce to the authorities.
Delaware Valley should have known or discovered that Pierce was conducting improper, abusive exams and using force on their patients, the complaint says.
The complaint alleges 13 claims including assault and battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, invasion of privacy, discrimination against women, medical malpractice, corporate negligence, and more. The claim does not specify an award the plaintiffs are seeking, something Foote said is not required in New Jersey.
The state medical board said it suspended Pierce’s license in 2024 based on the testimony of two witnesses who claimed he touched them inappropriately, one a longtime patient whose child was delivered by Pierce. The board found both women credible and the vote was unanimous, the board said then.
“No patient should ever have to fear being sexually exploited on a physician’s exam table,” Cari Fais, the then-director of the state consumer affairs division, which oversees the board, said in 2024. Fais is now a magistrate in the federal court system.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State finalizes deal to buy rights to Preakness for $85 million
description: Maryland got deeper into the horse-racing business Thursday, announcing it has finalized its purchase of the rights to the Preakness Stakes and the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes for $85 million.
text:
Horses on the track at Laurel Park, where the Preakness was run in 2026. (Photo by Joe Andrucyk/Patrick Siebert/Office of the Governor)Maryland got deeper into the horse-racing business Thursday, announcing it has finalized its purchase of the rights to the Preakness Stakes and the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes for $85 million.
The purchase keeps those properties out of the hands of Churchill Downs Inc., the owners of the Kentucky Derby, who announced plans this spring to buy rights to those races from 1/ST Maryland LLC for that amount. But  !/ST’s previous deal with the state gave it the right to match any offer for the sale of rights to those races, which it said in June it would do.
State officials were quick to note Thursday that no tax dollars will be used for the purchase. Funds for the deal will come from notes issued by the Maryland Economic Development Corp. (MEDCO). which will be repaid with funds generated by the two races.
In a statement released by the goveror’s office, MEDCO CEO Tom Sadowski says the organization is “proud to have had the opportunity to conceive and execute a financial transaction that secures ownership of the Preakness and Black-eyed Susan IP and cements the success of horse racing in Maryland for generations to come.”
By buying the Preakness, the state not only guarantees that the race remains in Maryland, but it ends regular licensing fee payments to 1/ST Racing, that would have risen over time.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) said in the statement that horse racing is “a cornerstone of Maryland’s history, culture and economy,” which is why it’s important to own the rights to the Preakness.
“With this final acquisition we are not only leveraging the Preakness’s iconic status and uplifting our horse racing industry, we are revitalizing the communities that directly benefit from the economic opportunities of the race,” Moore’s statement said.
The Preakness is the second leg of racing’s storied Triple Crown, which begins in May with the Kentucky Derby and ends five weeks later with the Belmont Stakes.
The state’s purchase of intellectual property rights to the two races is the latest in a string of investments in the horse racing industry. The Maryland Stadium Authority owns Pimlico, the historic track where the Preakness has been run for more than a century, and it is spending about $400 million for a complete teardown and rebuild of the facility, which is going on now.
The state is also in the process of buying the only other thoroughbred track in the state, Laurel Park, which hosted this year’s Preakness while Pimlico is under construction. Plans call for Laurel Park to be converted to a state-owned training facility.
The state also owns Shamrock Farms in Carroll County, which it has planned to turn into the state training facility, but abandoned those plans recently when it encountered financial and logistical problems with the site. It is currently deciding what to do with that property.
As the owner of the Preakness and Black-Eyed Susan, the state will be responsible for running those races every year. All other racing days will be run by the Maryland Jockey Club, a nonprofit established under state law.
The state said in its announcement that the Maryland Jockey Club has secured partnerships with Oak View Group for sponsorship growth and KO Productions for event production. It also said that while it owns the intellectual property rights to the races, the state “remains open to identifying areas of mutual interest with Churchill Downs and other industry partners to benefit the broader Triple Crown and the sport of horseracing.
“With all assets now residing with the State, we will work closely with the Maryland, Baltimore and Park Heights business communities to showcase the Preakness on the national stage,” said Bill Knauf, president and general Manager of the Maryland Jockey Club, in the statement.

name: WyoFile
title: Central Wyoming anglers, boaters and recreationists got the low water blues
description:
Fishing “is on fire” at Pathfinder Reservoir, one angler reports. But that's partly due to the reservoir shrinking to just 18.7% capacity.
The post Central Wyoming anglers, boaters and recreationists got the low water blues appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
“The fishing is on fire” at Pathfinder Reservoir, says Casper resident Chris Bobo, who shares his enthusiasm for “tight lines” via his YouTube channel, Bobo’s Fishing Adventures.
Unfortunately, the frenzy of taut lines reeling in fish is partially due to water in the reservoir retreating to just 18.7% capacity. “It’s the same amount of fish and a lot less water,” Bobo told WyoFile. “So it’s packing them all down, and it’s concentrating them into a hole.”
As he trolls around what’s left of the reservoir, Bobo can spot fish everywhere — and not just sun-basking carp. If you look carefully, he says, you can see the shadowy movement of walleye, kokanee salmon, as well as rainbow and brown trout. Tempering the glee over the windfall of fish though is the fact that spawning beds are out of the water. Bobo worries that, unless there’s stellar snowpack this winter to make up for a huge water deficit, this fishery — and hundreds of others in the region — may suffer long-term losses.
Chris Bobo shows off a pair of walleye harvested at Pathfinder Reservoir. (Chris Bobo)
“They’ve been dropping it and dropping it more and more over the years,” Bobo said. “If they keep at it, we won’t have a reservoir in two years. That’s my favorite lake in the world. I don’t want it to disappear.”
A searing, lingering heat wave is making matters worse. Trout, a cold-water species, get stressed as water temperatures surpass 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Beyond 75 degrees can be deadly. The water temperature at Pathfinder this week was 71 degrees, according to Lake Monster, a website with fishing intel.
Upstream from Pathfinder on the North Platte River system, Seminoe Reservoir was 31.8% full earlier this week, with a water temp of 71 degrees. Below Seminoe, the prized Miracle Mile trout fishery measured 72 degrees.
The reservoir side of the Pathfinder Dam in central Wyoming was mostly dry on July 29, 2026. (Chris Bobo)
The effects of climate change-driven drought and heat at Seminoe and Miracle Mile are a primary concern among opponents of a controversial pumped-water storage hydroelectric project. Federal officials recommend greenlighting rPlus Hydro’s plans to build a $4 billion facility at Seminoe. It would pump water uphill during daytime “off-peak demand” hours for electricity then in the evening release the water to drive hydroelectric turbines.
That daily churn threatens to exacerbate high water temperatures during unusually hot and dry conditions, opponents have said.
Meantime, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department is imploring anglers to adjust practices, noting, “as water temperatures approach 70 degrees, the chance for any fish species to survive being caught and released is reduced.” For those planning to release what they catch, early morning fishing hours are best. “If water temperatures are too high, consider escaping the heat with a trip to a top-notch, high-country fishery where it’s cooler,” Game and Fish Deputy Chief of Fisheries Dave Zafft said in a statement.
Click here for more warm water fishing advice from the agency.

name: WyoFile
title: Why Wyoming needs healthcare professionals in the Legislature
description:
When every policy decision has downstream effects, practical, on-the-job knowledge must inform legislation, writes guest columnist Stacey Zeidler.
The post Why Wyoming needs healthcare professionals in the Legislature appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
For the past 15 years, I’ve had the privilege of working alongside hospitals, physicians, nurses, EMS agencies and communities across Wyoming to improve access to specialty healthcare. Traveling our state’s rural frontier has given me a firsthand look at the unique challenges facing patients and providers alike. It has also convinced me that healthcare is one of the most complex policy issues our Legislature addresses — and those decisions are strengthened when informed by people who understand how healthcare actually works.

Opinion

Wyoming stands at a pivotal moment.
The Rural Health Transformation Program provides Wyoming with an extraordinary opportunity to improve healthcare across the state. The first installment of approximately $205 million is already being put to work, with organizations across Wyoming developing proposals that could reshape healthcare delivery for years to come. Over the next four years, this investment has the potential to approach $1 billion if implemented successfully. This funding arrives at a critical time.
Healthcare in Wyoming faces challenges unlike almost anywhere else in the country. We are a frontier state with long travel distances, aging infrastructure, workforce shortages and a low population spread across a vast geographic area. Providing high-quality healthcare in this environment requires experience and creative solutions from someone with a deep understanding of how hospitals, clinics, emergency medical services, insurers and providers all work together.
Perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in women’s healthcare.
Across Wyoming, hospitals and health systems are struggling to recruit and retain obstetricians and gynecologists. Many communities have limited or no local access to obstetrical care, forcing expectant mothers to travel hours for prenatal appointments or to deliver their babies. For rural families, that can mean repeated trips over mountain passes, missed work, additional childcare expenses and increased risks when emergencies arise.
Recruiting OB-GYN physicians is extraordinarily difficult. Wyoming competes nationally for a limited pool of specialists, and these physicians weigh numerous factors when deciding where to practice — including call schedules, hospital resources, malpractice insurance costs, professional support, educational opportunities for their children, employment options for spouses and quality of life.
Johnna French, a maternal child health nurse with Albany County, weighs and measures babies during home visits. (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile) 
The physician shortage extends far beyond obstetrics. Primary care physicians, psychiatrists, general surgeons, cardiologists and many other specialists remain in short supply. Recruitment often takes years, requires significant financial investment and offers no guarantee of success. Even after a physician is recruited, retaining them presents another challenge entirely.
Simply wanting more physicians in Wyoming does not make them available.
Rural hospitals, meanwhile, are operating under enormous pressure.
Many face rising labor costs, inflation, increasing technology demands, declining reimbursement and the financial realities of caring for Medicare and Medicaid populations. Several rural hospitals across the country have already closed, and many others remain financially vulnerable. Every hospital closure means more than losing a building — it means losing emergency care, labor and delivery services, outpatient clinics, local jobs and an essential pillar of the community.
Emergency medical services face similar pressures. Many EMS agencies struggle with inadequate reimbursement while responding to increasing call volumes across vast geographic areas. They remain an essential part of Wyoming’s healthcare system, yet many operate under tremendous financial strain.
These are not problems that can be solved with a resolution or a talking point.
Healthcare policy is extraordinarily complicated. It involves reimbursement systems, workforce development, hospital finance, electronic medical records, quality reporting, insurance regulations, licensing, technology and countless federal and state requirements. Every policy decision has downstream effects that impact patients, providers, hospitals and communities.
The Wyoming Capitol during the 2026 legislative budget session. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
That is why having real-world healthcare experience matters in the Legislature. Physicians, nurses, hospital administrators, EMS leaders, therapists, pharmacists and other healthcare professionals bring practical knowledge that cannot be learned solely through reading reports or attending committee meetings. They understand what happens when reimbursement changes, when workforce shortages worsen, when regulations increase administrative burdens or when a rural hospital struggles to keep essential services available.
The Rural Health Transformation Program represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen Wyoming’s healthcare system. Success won’t happen by accident. It will require thoughtful leadership, collaboration and informed decision-making grounded in the real-life experience of delivering care in our frontier communities. The people who have worked on the front lines of healthcare deserve a voice in shaping what comes next — and we cannot afford to move forward without them.
Every Wyoming resident deserves access to quality healthcare close to home. As our state navigates this critical moment, the decisions made in the Legislature will shape healthcare delivery for years to come. The challenges facing rural and frontier communities are too significant — and the opportunity too important — to risk getting it wrong.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Brink, Maasdam trade barbs amid vote-splitting concerns in Michigan’s 7th District race
description: Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam show no signs of backing down in the race to take on U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in November, even as some strategists fear moderates splitting between the two could create an opening for progressive challenger William Lawrence to win the Democratic nomination. […]
text:
Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, right, speaks during a campaign event in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. She was joined by U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, left, and Michigan state Rep. Joe Tate, center. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam show no signs of backing down in the race to take on U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in November, even as some strategists fear moderates splitting between the two could create an opening for progressive challenger William Lawrence to win the Democratic nomination.
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who held the U.S. House seat before being elected to the Senate in 2024, endorsed Maasdam earlier this month, saying he “knows what it means to fight.”
Slotkin’s endorsement came as Maasdam was running third in both polling and fundraising.
It represented a break from many party officials, including former Govs. Jennifer Granholm and Jim Blanchard, and some major labor unions, such as the Michigan Education Association, who had endorsed Brink.
Michigan State University political scientist Matt Grossman said Slotkin’s endorsement could undermine efforts to defeat Lawrence by preventing consolidation of support behind one candidate.
Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink speaks during a campaign event in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, left, speaks at a campaign event for former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, right, in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. Michigan state Rep. Joe Tate, center, moderated the conversation. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, left, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, center, and Michigan state Rep. Joe Tate, right, at a campaign event in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett greets voters during a campaign event for former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, left, and Michigan state Rep. Joe Tate, right, at a campaign event in Lansing, Mich., on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
A spokesperson for Lawrence’s campaign declined to comment, saying the infighting “isn’t something we’re focused on right now.”
If Lawrence does win, Grossman said Slotkin could face criticism over the strategic implications of her endorsement.
Brink pointed to the range of endorsements her campaign boasts during an interview with Michigan Advance ahead of a campaign event featuring U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) in Lansing on Thursday.
“I’m really proud of the coalition I built,” Brink said. “Because what I think is, this is going to be a team effort, and we’ve got to work together to stand up to Trump and be able to deliver for the people of mid-Michigan, and that’s exactly what I’m focused on.”
Maasdam has called for Brink to end her campaign, telling the Advance during an interview earlier Thursday that she “has a tough decision to make in front of her.”
“It would be tough to be third in the race and know that you’re taking votes from other people,” Maasdam said. “I think there’s more votes against Will Lawrence than there is for him in this district. So that’s a choice for her to make. I think that choice is a big one because it affects the direction of this race and potentially the House.”
 Michigan Democratic 7th Congressional District Matt Maasdam (center) during a canvassing kickoff event in Lansing, Mich. July 30, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceVolunteers for Michigan Democratic 7th Congressional District Matt Maasdam bundle literature ahead of a canvassing kickoff event in Lansing, Mich. July 30, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Maasdam argues he is the strongest candidate to face Barrett in November’s general election. He said Slotkin’s endorsement wasn’t the only reason he gained momentum in the race, but it certainly helped.
“It was like jet fuel,” Maasdam said.
While Maasdam campaigned Thursday with End Citizens United, which has endorsed him, Brink criticized the amount of outside spending in the race, much of which benefits Maasdam by attacking her and Lawrence.
“I can’t trust someone saying one thing and doing another, and I think this is what the voters are sick and tired of,” Brink said.
Michigan Advance Senior Reporter Ben Solis contributed to this report.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: An Idaho law penalizes people sleeping in public spaces. Advocates say it harms more than it helps.
description: On the afternoon of June 22, Neil “Lee” Spring was sitting in Rhodes Skate Park with a friend when officers from the Boise Police Department approached him. “We’re going to give you a ticket for sitting here everyday,” Spring said officers told him. He was issued a $10 citation for camping on public property — […]
text:
Public camping became illegal in Boise last summer after Gov. Brad Little signed Senate Bill 1141, which forces cities with populations over 100,000 people to police the issue or face financial penalties. (Photo by Getty Images)On the afternoon of June 22, Neil “Lee” Spring was sitting in Rhodes Skate Park with a friend when officers from the Boise Police Department approached him.
“We’re going to give you a ticket for sitting here everyday,” Spring said officers told him. He was issued a $10 citation for camping on public property — a violation of Boise’s city ordinances.
Public camping became illegal in Boise last summer after Gov. Brad Little signed Senate Bill 1141, which forces cities with populations over 100,000 people to police the issue or face financial penalties. 
The law applies to just three of Idaho’s cities: Boise, Nampa and Meridian. Sponsored by Sen. Codi Galloway, R-Boise, Sen. Kelly Anthon, R-Rupert, and Rep. Bruce Skaug, R-Nampa, the “Galloway law,” so named after its main sponsor, was promoted as a remedy to what many saw as a growing homelessness issue in Idaho.
A year after its implementation, critics say the law makes it harder to serve homeless populations and targets the unhoused. 
The legislation received renewed interest this month when House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, and Skaug tied a July homicide on the Greenbelt to a lack of enforcement of the Galloway law. The suspect was “unlawfully camping regularly in the area where the attack occurred,” according to a press release from Skaug and Moyle. 
2 years after Grants Pass, 14 states, 350 cities have tougher laws on street homelessness

“Idahoans who use the Boise greenbelt, float the Boise River or visit a downtown restaurant should not have to fear for their safety because Boise Mayor Lauren McLean won’t follow the law,” Moyle said. “It is sad and infuriating to see a possibly preventable crime occur because Boise won’t enforce the law.”
Public records show that the Boise Police Department has issued more than 100 tickets under the public camping statute since it was adopted into the city code a little over a year ago. More than 45 of those citations were issued either on the Greenbelt or one of its neighboring parks.
The effectiveness of the law also remains unclear as records also show that almost 50% of tickets were issued to repeat offenders — often in the same location on different days. One offender accrued six tickets between November and May, all of which were issued on the Greenbelt. 
Boise Mayor Lauren McLean pushed back on the state representatives’ characterization of the city’s enforcement.
“We adopted the state’s criminal camping ban once it became law and enforced it on day one,” she wrote in a statement.
The mayor also pointed to city efforts aiming to help residents who are unhoused. 
“We’ve reduced unsheltered homelessness 25 percent this year compared to last,” she said. ”We’re building 250 homes for folks exiting homelessness and raised $15 million to provide the wrap around services they need to stay housed.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
What has enforcement of Idaho’s public camping law looked like in Meridian, Nampa and Boise?
When Spring arrived at court to handle his $10 citation, he found that he was out more than 5 times that original amount once he had paid the court’s processing fees for a total of $66.50. For those already struggling financially, the cost can be crippling. 
But Spring’s citation could have been a different story had he been in Nampa or Meridian — the two other cities compelled to follow the public camping ban. 
Estimates of homeless populations in the three cities are opaque. The Point-In-Time count is a once yearly survey of people who are sheltered and unsheltered across the country. The survey takes place on a single day in January, meaning it can miss those who are seeking shelter from the cold, and it struggles to account for those staying with friends or in other kinds of temporary shelter. 
Additionally, the count is done by region. Because Meridian and Boise are both in Ada County, their tally of close to 687 homeless individuals in January 2026 does not give insight into how they are spread across the two cities. Nampa’s survey is combined with the residents of Adams, Washington, Payette, Canyon, Elmore, Gem, Owyhee, Valley, and Boise counties for a total of 754.
Residents who are unsheltered in the region that includes Nampa outnumber those counted in Ada by more than 7 to 1, with 686 unsheltered residents tallied in the nine counties compared to 95 in Ada. The relationship, however, flips for sheltered unhoused residents with Ada counting 592 compared to 68 across the nine counties.
The variation reflects different access to resources across the state.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“You don’t have overnight shelters in Meridian, so all the resources are mostly down in the Boise area,” said Jess Abbott, executive director at Boise homeless shelter Corpus Commons. “It’s just something that hasn’t affected Meridian and Nampa as much.”
While over 100 citations have been given out for public camping in Boise, Meridian and Nampa have seen far less documented policing. 
Since July 2025, the Meridian Police Department has only issued three warnings for public camping. Two of the three warnings appear to be issued to individuals residing in vehicles, and all three were issued in April of this year. The total charge for a public camping ticket in Meridian is $156.50. 
In Nampa, a public records request found no citations or tickets issued for public camping either by the Nampa Police Department or the Parks and Recreation Department. The police department’s deputy chief, Curt Shankel, said the law had caused greater attention to areas where camping is common but it had no large impact on enforcement.
“We haven’t really changed how we’ve enforced our ordinances,” said Shankel. “We’re just going out and watching these areas more than we ever did prior to this law.”
Advocates say law pushes people facing homelessness to the fringes
In Boise, however, residents who are unhoused say the law’s enforcement makes them feel vulnerable as they have to scatter apart to remain hidden from police.
“The Galloway law makes us hide, and we shouldn’t have to hide,” said Marquita Burgess, who has been unhoused for three years. “We should be able to sleep in a group, so that we’re safer.”
Scattering has also made it more difficult to connect the homeless population with resources, according to Jodi Peterson-Stigers, who runs the Interfaith Sanctuary shelter. 
“Our most vulnerable unhoused are moving further and further away from resources, so that they’re not able to be seen or ticketed,” Peterson said. “It’s harder to find people who are on our waitlists.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Guests at Corpus Commons also say police have told them to disperse as they wait outside for the shelter to open. 
“There’s people that call on file and complain if you have a backpack on,” said Spring. “A cop wants to talk to you like ‘What are you up to? What are you doing?’ — It’s like I’m just walking down the street.”
Still, some business owners believe that the city is not doing enough to combat crime and enforce the ordinances. 
“As a building owner we’ve had buildings broken into, automobiles stolen, telephone lines cut, and we’ve had public nudity during the day time,” said Bill Ilett who owns multiple properties in Boise. While Ilett could not definitively tie offenses to unhoused populations, he said the instances were examples of how police had allowed those acting in “bad faith” to remain a threat. 
For Spring, the policing is a new, frustrating experience for a person who otherwise adheres to the law.
“I’ve never been in trouble with the cops before I became homeless,” he said.

title: President Ulysses S. Grant proclaimed Colorado a state 150 years ago this week
description: The telegraphic dispatch, dated Aug. 1 and sent from Washington, D.C., appeared in newspapers across Colorado and the nation the following day. “The President, in accordance with the provisions of an act of Congress, approved March 3, 1875, has issued his proclamation declaring and proclaiming the fact that the fundamental conditions imposed by Congress on [[...]
text:
A west-facing view of central Denver in the 1870s. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-18618)The telegraphic dispatch, dated Aug. 1 and sent from Washington, D.C., appeared in newspapers across Colorado and the nation the following day.



← July 23–29
July 30–Aug. 5 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

“The President, in accordance with the provisions of an act of Congress, approved March 3, 1875, has issued his proclamation declaring and proclaiming the fact that the fundamental conditions imposed by Congress on the state of Colorado to entitle that state to admission to the Union have been ratified and accepted,” the message said, “and the admission of said state into the Union is now complete.”
Though the Rocky Mountain News in Denver reported that “our people are now in the state of Colorado and the state of beatitude,” President Ulysses S. Grant’s proclamation of statehood wasn’t greeted with much pomp and circumstance by the residents of the new Centennial State, compared to the grand parades and fireworks shows the Colorado Territory had held for the nation’s 100th birthday a month earlier.
Colorado was the first state in nine years, after Nebraska in 1867, to be admitted to the union, but the occasion was overshadowed nationally by major developments elsewhere in the centennial summer. Other headlines leading the Rocky Mountain News on Aug. 2 reported the latest news on the aftermath of the Battle of the Little Bighorn, which had shocked the nation just after the Fourth of July, along with impeachment trial of Secretary of War William Belknap and the prosecution of the Whiskey Ring — two of the many corruption scandals that plagued Grant’s administration in its final days.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Plenty of local matters, too, like the descent of the latest swarm of Rocky Mountain locusts in the Platte River farmland surrounding Denver, were more urgent than the news of statehood.
“Those who thought state admission would end the grasshopper plague slipped up on it,” quipped the News.
Public officials, meanwhile, went to work dealing with the legal quirks and complexities of transitioning from territorial to state government — like the fact that the state would temporarily comprise a single judicial district. As provided for by the constitution approved on July 1, the Centennial State’s inaugural elections were to be held on the first Tuesday in October.
“The year is an important political one, and we are early called upon to take part in the events connected therewith,” said the Denver Times. “There are to be elected one Representative to Congress, Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Auditor of Slate, State Treasurer, Attorney General, Superintendent of Public Instruction, three Supreme Judges, and six Regents of the State University,” along with four district attorneys, four district judges, 26 state senators and 49 state representatives.
(Courtesy of the Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection, Colorado State Library)
Most importantly of all, a pivotal presidential election loomed in the near future. Colorado’s admission to the union ahead of the 1876 election had been a political ploy by Republicans, who had also inserted into the new state constitution a clause giving the inaugural Colorado General Assembly the power to cast its three electoral votes.
It had been two years since Democrats won control of the House of Representatives for the first time since the Civil War. The Colorado Territory, long a Republican stronghold, had even been swept up in the Democratic wave, electing Democrat Thomas Patterson, an Irish-born Denver lawyer, as the territory’s non-voting delegate to Congress.
With Grant’s popularity souring amid corruption scandals and much of the country still reeling from the Panic of 1873, the opposition party now hoped to return to the White House in the 1876 presidential election. That was a grim prospect for Republicans and northerners to whom the Democratic Party still stood as a symbol of slavery and rebellion. The fate of Reconstruction, under which the federal government had acted to secure Black civil rights in the South, hung in the balance.
Though it judged such a scenario to be “not probable,” the Denver Times presciently raised the possibility that Colorado’s three electoral votes could be decisive in the contest between Republican Ohio Gov. Rutherford B. Hayes and Democratic New York Gov. Samuel Tilden.
“In view of such possible contingency, the two parties will strive their utmost to curry the young State,” said the Times. “It is an extraordinary situation that a people should be called upon so early to decide, by their votes, matters of so great interest, and matters which may exert an overwhelming influence in the country.”

The Denver Times, Aug. 2, 1876
