name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A CT sheep farmer’s view from the solar field
description: A well-managed flock keeps vegetation under solar panels trimmed naturally, with minimal machinery, without pollution or the risk of damaged panels.
text:
Hillview Farm began in Ellington in 2014, built on a lifelong passion for animal agriculture. Sheep proved to be the most sustainable livestock we raised, but growing the operation meant finding affordable pasture, and that proved to be the central challenge.
We quickly outgrew the resources we had to make our farm profitable. Sheep, being a ruminant; thrive on pasture as they were born to graze all day and convert that grass into energy – not be fed grain and hay inside barns or on dry lots. Finding access to affordable pasture was cost prohibitive. Larger farms typically control the available farmland, and pastures we could access were often overgrown and in poor condition. Small farms simply cannot compete with larger entities.

Hillview Farm sheep grazing at a CT solar installation

Like many small farmers in this state, we spent nearly as much time worrying about margins as we did caring for our flock. Without access to pasture it made no sense to keep the flock, let alone expand. Even though demand for lamb and breeding stock continued, we couldn’t keep absorbing costs of production and expansion.
That started to change when we began working with solar developers to graze our sheep on land hosting photovoltaic arrays. Today, more than a decade into running Hillview Farm, our operation has grown dramatically, from starting out with just shy of a dozen sheep to the more than 130 in our flock today and plans to expand to over 300 head seasonally. This arrangement has proven valuable not just for us, but for Connecticut agriculture as a whole.
How solar grazing works, and why it works well 
The concept is straightforward. Ground-mounted solar panels require vegetation management beneath and between them. Uncontrolled grass and brush can shade panels, reduce efficiency, and increase maintenance costs. Traditionally, developers hired mowing crews, which is both expensive and pollution-generating. Flying rocks and debris can also crack panels, creating costly damage.
Sheep solve many of these issues. A well-managed flock keeps vegetation trimmed naturally, with minimal machinery, without pollution, and without the risk of damaged panels. The sheep graze, preferring the shaded panels which traditionally are the most difficult area to manage vegetation; the developer gets reliable, low-cost vegetation management; and we receive a per-acre fee for the service on top of what we earn from our animals, reinvested each year in equipment and improved management.
There are benefits for the sheep too. The shade provided by solar panels reduces heat stress on the flock during summer months, which supports better weight gain and animal welfare. Forage quality under the panels is often superior to open-field forage, with research showing significantly higher protein content in grass grown beneath arrays. Each site has a forage blend planted that is specifically selected for its nutritional value, added plant species that also support pollinators and improve soil structure. Our animals are thriving, and Hillview Farm is more financially stable than it has ever been.
The partnership with landowners matters
Some of the solar sites we work on are leased by developers from farm families who have worked the land for generations. These are landowners who embraced solar because they needed economic breathing room.  A 25- or 30-year solar lease provides reliable income during a period when commodity prices are volatile and input costs keep rising. But many of these families want to know that their land is still producing something and is still connected to agriculture.
Our presence on these properties gives them that. When a landowner sees our flock grazing where their grandparents once hayed, that means something. It is not a compromise. It is a continuation. We take seriously the responsibility of being good stewards on those sites, and the landowners we work with appreciate knowing that the land is not simply sitting under panels collecting dust.
The land comes back healthier 
People should understand what happens to farmland at the end of a solar project. Most arrays have a useful life of 25 to 30 years, after which the land is returned. The question is: returned to what condition?
Research conducted at commercial solar sites across the Northeast found that grazed solar sites showed significantly higher soil organic matter, soil protein, and active carbon than non-grazed sites. Sheep improve soil through natural fertilization and rotational grazing practices. When these projects conclude, land that has been carefully grazed throughout the solar lease should be well-positioned to support row crops, hay production, or other agricultural uses, potentially in better condition than when the panels went in. Connecticut-specific data remains limited, which is why the agrivoltaics study now mandated by state law matters so much.
House Bill 5340, passed by the legislature this spring, includes an agrivoltaics feasibility study to be completed by January 1, 2027. How many acres, how many farmers, what the economic impact looks like: none of that exists in organized form for Connecticut yet. The study aims to change that, and we are grateful that state leaders are investing the time to better understand this growing dimension of Connecticut agriculture.
Agriculture does not look the same as it did 50 years ago, and it should not have to. Embracing new models, including grazing sheep under solar panels, does not diminish farming, it sustains it. Our thriving flock, and the growth of Hillview Farm, are proof of that.
Natalie Cohen is the owner of Hillview Farm in Ellington.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Before you vote, learn Duverger’s Law
description: Democrats and Republicans both benefit from a structure that enables their duopoly by disadvantaging emerging competitors.
text:
Do you consider yourself an informed voter? If so, understanding Duverger’s Law can empower you to make strategic choices in upcoming elections, including the November midterms, regardless of your party affiliation.
In many undergraduate American Politics 101 courses, students learn that the United States has a “two-party system.” They study the histories of the Democratic and Republican parties, the shifting coalitions each has represented, their partisans’ general policy preferences, and the ideological differences between them. Yet considerably less attention is given to the electoral mechanics that preserve the dominance of these two large parties.
So-called “third parties,” of course, are not outlawed from participating in the democratic processes of our constitutional republic. They may nominate candidates, organize supporters, appear on ballots, and compete for public office. Why, then, have third parties so consistently remained minor parties?
The obdurate U.S. party “duopoly” does not endure because the electorate naturally sorts itself into two tidy political camps. On the contrary, the national motto, e pluribus unum (“out of many, one”), describes a nation forged in the crucible of profound social, cultural, and political diversity —not one whose individual citizens have ever fit squarely into two partisan categories. 
This diversity is currently reflected, at least partly, in Americans’ growing reluctance to identify with either major party. Gallup reported in January that a record-high 45% of American adults identified as political independents in 2025, including 56% of Gen Z (born between 1997 and 2007) and 54% of Millennials (born between 1981 and 1996). Although many of these self-identified independents still lean toward one of the two major parties, these figures hardly suggest widespread attachment to the existing partisan choices.
The continued dominance of only two nationally viable parties, then, cannot be explained solely by voter satisfaction, tradition, political culture, or media coverage. Instead, it is sustained and continually reinforced by the rules under which U.S. voters elect their public officials.
This is where Duverger’s Law, named for the French political scientist Maurice Duverger (1917–2014), offers valuable insight into one of the most durable patterns in electoral politics: single-member districts using plurality voting tend to produce competition between two major parties.
Let us begin unpacking this claim because, in its compressed form, it sounds much more complicated and perhaps less intuitive than it actually is.
Duverger developed his principle during the mid-20th century, most famously in his 1951 book Les Partis Politiques, published in English in 1954 as Political Parties. Under plurality voting in single-member districts (also called first-past-the-post or choose-one voting), the candidate who receives more votes than any other candidate wins, even without securing an absolute majority. In a four-candidate race, for instance, a candidate could win with only 35% of the vote if their opponents received 30%, 20%, and 15%, respectively.
At this point, the word “law” may still create some confusion. Duverger’s Law is not a legal rule enacted by a legislature or an electoral management body, nor is it an exceptionless iron command comparable to a mathematical certainty. Rather, it is a scientific law in the social-scientific sense: a concise statement describing a repeatedly observed relationship between particular conditions and a likely result.
Scientific laws identify regular patterns, but they do not necessarily imply that every individual case will unfold identically. Newton’s law of gravitation, for example, continues to describe the gravitational attraction between objects even when other forces, such as air resistance, affect their motion. Duverger’s Law likewise identifies a persistent tendency in certain electoral systems while allowing for exceptions arising from regional parties, unusual political divisions, electoral alliances, or other institutional arrangements.
Duverger’s central prediction thus remains remarkably useful for understanding U.S. electoral politics and the two-party system. Within this system, we have the following conditions: a) only one candidate can win a district, and b) victory requires only a plurality of votes (as described above, despite our majoritarian intuitions about electoral fairness, a candidate need not receive more than 50% of the vote to win). The result: political competition usually consolidates around two viable choices.
The logic hinges on two related forces.
The first is a mechanical effect. In “winner-take-all” elections, such as the presidential contests in nearly every state under the Electoral College, finishing second, even by a slim margin, yields no electoral votes from that state. Similarly, a political party could receive 40% of the vote in every single-member congressional district and still win no seats. Its support would be substantial but insufficient to secure office, as it never finished first.
Proportional representation, one of the most widely used electoral systems among democratic nations today, works differently. If a party receives 15% of the vote under a genuinely proportional system, it may receive approximately 15% of the seats, typically through multi-member districts. Winner-take-all elections in single-member districts provide no comparable reward or representation.
The second force is a psychological effect. Voters, candidates, donors, and political organizations anticipate the mechanical effect and adjust their behavior accordingly. For example, voters may strategically vote for a major-party candidate to avoid “wasting their vote,” and candidates may align with one of the two major parties to increase their chances of winning, thereby reinforcing the two-party system.
For this reason, promising candidates often join one of the two major parties rather than build a new one. Donors follow suit, hesitating to support campaigns regarded as incapable of winning from the get-go. Journalists concentrate on the two leading candidates. Voters may even abandon a preferred third candidate in favor of a less-preferred but more viable alternative.
The result becomes a self-reinforcing dialectic. Third parties struggle because voters doubt their viability, while voters doubt their viability because third parties struggle.
The 2000 presidential election provides the most famous example of Duverger’s Law at work in the United States. George W. Bush’s certified margin over Al Gore in Florida was just 537 votes (roughly 0.009%) of the nearly six million votes cast in the state. Because Bush finished first under Florida’s winner-take-all rules, he received all 25 of the state’s electoral votes.
Meanwhile, Green Party candidate Ralph Nader received 97,488 votes (1.64%) of the statewide total —far more than Bush’s margin of victory. If one assumes that most Green Party voters were ideologically to the left of the Democratic Party and hence preferred Gore to Bush, their votes for Nader may have helped elect the candidate they preferred least. In other words, voting for their first choice may have actually contributed to their least-preferred outcome. This is commonly known as the “spoiler effect,” in which support for a candidate with little to no chance of winning changes the outcome between the leading candidates.
Nevertheless, it would be inaccurate to claim that every Nader voter would otherwise have supported Gore. Some would have voted for Bush, chosen another candidate, or simply stayed home. The election also notoriously involved ballot-design problems, disputed recount procedures, voter-access controversies, and the Supreme Court’s consequential 5–4 decision in Bush v. Gore (2000).
Still, Florida demonstrates the strategic risk created by plurality voting. When only a few hundred votes separate two leading candidates, support for a third candidate can help determine which of the leading candidates wins —even when that third candidate has no realistic path to victory. Moreover, the ultimate victor may be further removed from third-party voters’ political preferences than the major-party candidate they chose not to support.
The 2016 election supplied another example. Donald Trump defeated Hillary Clinton in the swing state of Michigan by a margin of 10,704 votes (0.23%). Green Party candidate Jill Stein received 51,463 votes (1.07%) of the nearly 5 million votes cast in the state, while Libertarian Party candidate Gary Johnson received 172,136 votes (3.59%). The Michigan ballot also included candidates from the U.S. Taxpayers’ Party and Michigan’s Natural Law Party, who together received less than 0.40% of the statewide vote.
Those third-party voters by no means belonged to Clinton. Nor can analysts assign all the possibly right-leaning Libertarian votes to Trump. The figures instead reveal the razor’s edge upon which presidential elections may be decided.
Of course, the strategic problem can affect either major party.
In 2020, Joe Biden defeated Trump by 10,457 votes (0.3%) in Arizona, 11,779 votes (0.23%) in Georgia, and 20,682 votes (0.63%) in Wisconsin. Libertarian Party candidate Jo Jorgensen received more votes than Biden’s margin in each of those states.
Again, one cannot assume that every Libertarian voter would have chosen Trump in a two-candidate race. Yet a voter deciding among a favored third-party candidate, an acceptable major-party candidate, and an unacceptable major-party candidate should understand the possible consequences. The worst consequence is helping elect the candidate the voter opposes most.
Be that as it may, Duverger’s Law does not prove that third-party voting is foolish, immoral, or illegitimate. In a political system animated by deliberation, third-party campaigns can introduce neglected ideas, pressure major parties, provide political homes for dissatisfied citizens, and build organizations for future elections.
A protest vote can also serve a defensible purpose. Some voters use the ballot not merely to select an officeholder but to register opposition to the available choices. In a state or district where the outcome is virtually certain, the immediate risk of a “spoiler candidate” may be small. However, in a closely contested election, such a vote may be criticized as politically reckless or insufficiently attentive to its likely consequences. Indeed, some political scientists might call this sort of sincere voting behavior “naive” rather than “strategic.”
Therefore, voters should distinguish between two different uses of a ballot.
An expressive vote says, “This candidate most closely represents my beliefs.”
A strategic vote asks, “Which available choice gives me the best chance of producing an acceptable outcome or preventing an unacceptable one?”
Sometimes the same candidate satisfies both purposes. Sometimes the voter must choose between them.
Someone whose highest priority is building a third party may rationally vote for a candidate who is unlikely to win. Someone whose highest priority is defeating a particular major-party candidate, however, is better off voting for the most viable alternative.
This argument offers no defense of either major party. But it does explain why many voters feel as though they are stuck choosing between “the lesser of two evils.” Democrats and Republicans both benefit from a structure that enables their duopoly by disadvantaging emerging competitors. Yet both have also lost close elections in which minor-party candidates attracted potentially pivotal votes.
Now, Connecticut voters reading this in anticipation of August 11 should note that Duverger’s classic model does not apply as neatly to party primaries. Plurality primaries may encourage strategic voting: a voter may support a second-choice candidate if the preferred candidate appears unlikely to defeat a disliked rival. At the same time, crowded primaries may sustain several competing ideological or regional factions within the same party, making the outcome much harder to predict.
Americans who want more than two viable parties in general elections, however, need not wait for millions of partisan voters to become more adventurous. They can change the electoral rules that sustain the two-party structure.
Ranked-choice voting allows citizens to rank candidates in order of preference. A voter can support a third-party candidate first while identifying an acceptable major-party candidate as a backup. If the first-choice candidate is eliminated, the ballot transfers to the next-ranked candidate. This approach can reduce the spoiler problem, although it does not guarantee the development of a multiparty system.
Proportional representation offers a more direct route. Legislators may be elected from multi-member districts, with seats distributed according to each party’s share of the vote. A party winning 40% or 15% of the vote could then gain meaningful representation rather than repeatedly finishing second or third and receiving no representation at all.
Other reforms could include runoff elections, easier ballot access, more inclusive debates, fusion voting, and public financing to support competitive campaigns by political outsiders.
Connecticut already has experience with one alternative, namely “cross-endorsement” or “fusion voting.” Under this system, a minor party may endorse the same candidate as a major party while maintaining its own ballot line. For example, a voter can support the Working Families Party, the Independent Party, or another qualifying organization without splitting the total vote received by the endorsed candidate. The Connecticut State Elections Enforcement Commission (SEEC) also administers the Citizens’ Election Program, “allowing candidates to compete without reliance on special interest money.” That said, while such arrangements demonstrate that the current system is neither natural nor inevitable, they do little to create a genuinely competitive multiparty democracy in which third-party candidates have a realistic chance of winning office and their supporters have a meaningful chance of gaining representation.
In a word, electoral systems shape political behavior. Winner-take-all plurality elections reward large coalitions capable of finishing first and punish smaller organizations whose support is widely dispersed. Voters respond to those incentives whether they recognize Duverger’s Law or not.
Still, before entering the voting booth, voters should ask more than, “Which candidate do I like best?” They should also ask, “What am I trying to accomplish with this vote, and how do the rules translate my choice into political power?”
Duverger’s Law cannot answer that question for them. But it can help them understand the decision they are making.
Robert T.F. Downes is a PhD candidate in the Department of Political Science at the University of Connecticut, specializing in political theory and public law. He is also an Adjunct Professor at Rhode Island College.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Harford County residents fight back against battery storage proposal
description: Officials in Maryland’s Harford County say they’re concerned by a proposal to add a battery storage to a hillside along the “pristine” Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River.
text:
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) speaks during a news conference Thursday encouraging the state to advance battery storage projects. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Harford County officials and residents say they’re concerned by a proposal to add a utility-scale battery storage facility to a hillside along the “pristine” Deer Creek, a tributary to the Susquehanna River.
Their testimony came Thursday as regulators at the Maryland Public Service Commission reviewed four battery storage projects for eligibility for a new credit, created by state lawmakers in 2025. The other projects are planned on the site of a solar project near Westernport in Garrett County, at the Chalk Point power plant in Prince George’s County and at the former Dickerson coal-fired power station in Montgomery County.
But only the Harford project, a 500-megawatt proposal called the Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project, drew opposition Thursday, with critics citing concerns about fire risk and related environmental contamination.
“Environmentally, you would struggle to find a worse site for this project,” said Jennifer Wilson, a resident who said her children attend the nearby Norrisville Elementary School.
The mostly forested site already hosts Baltimore Gas & Electric’s Conastone Substation, located in the northwestern corner of Harford County. A representative from Tenaska, the company developing the project, said Thursday that the facility would be located at least 600 feet from the waterway, and that most of the 70 acres would remain forested.
Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly (R) also opposes the project, he said in an interview with Maryland Matters, particularly given that the beloved creek — a favorite kayaking spot for him and his family — is located downhill. He worried that firefighters would have trouble fighting any blazes at the site nestled behind the substation, and that any chemicals used for firefighting, or contained within the battery facility itself, would flow down into the river.
Harford County Executive Robert Cassilly (R). (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“If anything goes wrong with this thing, it goes right down into the Deer Creek,” Cassilly said in an interview. “This is a cherished waterway that feeds the water supply.”
In testimony to the commission, Matthew Kropp, director of Harford County’s planning and zoning department, expressed worries that “toxic heavy metals and chemicals” in the battery infrastructure could leach into the soil or water, and that local fire departments lacked “the training, knowledge and resources to deal with a potential emergency.” He worried that the proposal did not contain sufficient measures to contain a fire or other emergency.
A representative for Del. Lauren Arikan (R-Harford) also said at Thursday’s hearing that her office has gathered 1,300 signatures opposing the project near Deer Creek.
Lee Hine, who lives about a half mile from the proposed project, said he was surprised by its location, given the hilly terrain in a prized natural area.
“The watershed is a prime aspect of why we all moved to this area. It’s a natural preserve here,” Hine said. “I’m trying to understand why we’re not looking for ‘brown ground’ facility areas — or at least flatter areas. This is a mountain. We live on a mountain.”
Keith Latham, who leads battery storage development at Tenaska, said the company plans to use lithium-ion-phosphate batteries, a safer alternative to lithium-ion batteries, and house them in purpose-built enclosures complete with cooling systems.
“Additionally, code standards and best practices have also greatly reduced risk of issues in newer battery storage projects. As we move forward through the development process, we’ll also collaborate with local fire departments and the fire marshal. We’ll work with the first responders on an emergency response plan,” Latham said.
But residents also questioned the project’s cost-effectiveness. A study performed for the PSC found that the Oystercatcher project, the largest by megawatts, did not produce quite enough ratepayer benefit to equal the cost, using two different estimation models.
“I ask the commission to reject this project based on the fact that it doesn’t provide economic relief to BGE ratepayers, and it’s certainly going to put the ecosystem of Harford County at great risk,” Patti Hankins said at the meeting.
Even if one of the projects considered Thursday receives the credits, it still must receive construction approvals from the commission, according to a news release from the commission.
The PSC hearing came hours after a Baltimore news conference, during which environmental groups, unions and a few Democratic politicians extolled the benefits of battery storage technology, which can store extra power for four hours or more and release it to the grid later on. They argued, too, that some safety concerns may be overstated.
Adam Dubitsky, state director for the Maryland Land & Liberty coalition, speaks in support of battery energy storage projects during a news conference Thursday. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Adam Dubitsky, state director for the Maryland Land & Liberty coalition, a conservative nonprofit supporting renewable energy development, said much of the opposition is based on “outdated information about these systems.”
“They are safe when done right, and when firefighters know how to fight these fires — which is very possible — in the rare times when there is an incident,” Dubitsky said.
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) said any approved project must adhere to the National Fire Protection Association standards, which require separation between battery units to prevent fires from spreading between batteries.
“I understand that when new technology is coming to communities, people are asking questions — totally appropriate for folks to do that,” Charkoudian said during Thursday’s news conference. “It’s just really important that we don’t add to fear-mongering, and we make sure people have the accurate information about the things that keep batteries 100% safe.”
During Thursday’s PSC hearing, John Walser, a fire protection consultant at Fire & Risk Alliance, argued that fires at battery energy sites have become increasingly rare as safety standards have improved.
“This reduction is due to the lessons learned from early failures,” he said, including fires at other battery storage facilities.
At Thursday’s news conference, environmentalists largely focused on the overall benefits of battery storage. It’s particularly important now, they said, as residents face high power bills and the grid faces high demand from data centers and electrification, amid reductions in supply due to the retirement of some fossil fuel generators.
“For most of the history of the electrical grid, if someone flipped on a light switch, a power plant somewhere had to produce those electrons at virtually the same time. But battery storage is changing that,” said Rico Albacarys, political director for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 24. “It allows us to store electricity when it’s plentiful and the costs are less, and then deliver it back to the grid when demand is highest.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Maryland possesses very little utility-scale, battery storage connected to the transmission grid, Charkoudian said. That’s why the General Assembly stepped in last year with the Next Generation Energy Act, requiring the PSC to open a battery storage procurement for up to 1,600 megawatts. This year, the legislature extended the megawatt limit, as long as cost effectiveness requirements are met.
The facilities can also reduce emissions during high-demand situations, by avoiding the need for fossil fuel “peaker” plants to come online, said Rebecca Rehr of the Maryland League of Conservation Voters.
“Storage reduces reliance on the most expensive, most polluting, and harmful peaker plants that run only during the periods of highest demand,” Rehr said.
Still, the risks concern residents of Norrisville, the small town closest to the Oystercatcher project. Nancy Gladden, who said Thursday she moved to the “blink and you miss it” town in 1984, is concerned that battery projects are unproven, and their safety for the community “highly questionable.”
“We are surrounded by hills and beautiful rolling cornfields and meadows,” Gladden said. “It’s an idyllic place full of homes, happy kids, and wonderful outdoors for them to explore and grow up in. I’m commenting tonight because I’m concerned for the community — for my community.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore offers late admission, $800 credit for students disenrolled at Howard University
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Thursday the state would provide an $800 credit and expedited admission processing for any of the hundreds of incoming Howard University freshmen who were abruptly told last week that they no longer had a place at the school.
text:
The "M Circle" on the University of Maryland, College Park's campus. (Photo by Sam Gauntt/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Thursday the state would provide an $800 credit and expedited admission processing for any of the hundreds of incoming Howard University freshmen who were abruptly told last week that they no longer had a place at the school.
The governor said in a statement that he directed the Maryland Higher Education Commission and the University System of Maryland to expedite the admission process for any of the affected students for the fall semester. The process will include identifying available programs, navigating financial aid and expediting late admissions available at the more than dozen colleges, universities and higher education centers in the state’s system.
First day of classes for schools in the state system start next month.
The offer is aimed at 502 incoming freshmen in Howard’s first-time-in-college program who were told last week that because they had not met payment or other financial reporting requirements for classes that start Aug. 17, they had been disenrolled.
“Students who did not meet the established payment, payment arrangement, or scholarship and other financial aid reporting deadlines have been notified that the University can no longer hold their place in the incoming class,” the school said in a statement July 23. “As Howard finalizes enrollment for the Fall 2026 semester … confirming enrollment is essential to planning academic programs, housing, financial aid, and student support services.”
State workers union sues Moore, university system for withheld raises

The notice left students, many of whom said they were waiting on scholarships or financial aid to clear, scrambling for options. As of Wednesday, more than 200 students had been reenrolled after they provided documentation, or the university reevaluated their paperwork, Howard President Wayne Frederick said to WTOP.
In the meantime, the University of the District of Columbia said Monday that it had extended its application deadline to Aug. 7.
On Tuesday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said the state would provide affected Howard students an $800 credit, and she directed the State University of New York (SUNY) and the City University of New York (CUNY) to expedite the late admissions review process for those students.
Moore on Thursday posted a message on social media telling the “hundreds of student disenrolled from Howard University just weeks before move-in, I want you to know this: Maryland, we’ve got your back.”
“These students worked hard, earned admission to college, and were preparing to begin the next chapter of their lives,” Moore said in the statement released by his office. “Maryland is moving with urgency to give them a clear path forward — with hands-on support, expedited admissions assistance, and financial relief – so they can stay on track toward earning their degree.”
Moore said the $800 credit was meant to offset a nonrefundable deposit the students made to Howard. If at least 250 students chose to accept the $800 credit, it would cost the state about $200,000.
A Moore spokesperson said in a text message Thursday information about the funding could come from the higher education commission Friday.
The affected students interested in applying to a college or university in Maryland can contact the Office of Student Financial Assistance (OFSA) at osfamail.mhec@maryland.gov.
“The University System of Maryland is committed to helping these displaced students,” University System of Maryland Chancellor Jay Perman said in a statement. “Our goal is to help these students continue with their education with as little interruption as possible.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: NorthWestern Energy’s resource plan gets criticisms for ignoring data centers
description: Members of the public and a coalition of advocacy groups want NorthWestern Energy’s long-term plan for power to include more renewable energy and account for data centers’ impacts on their pocketbooks. They also want the utility’s Integrated Resource Plan, a projection of how it will meet energy needs the next 20 years, to address climate […]
text:
Solar panels illustration by Getty Images.Members of the public and a coalition of advocacy groups want NorthWestern Energy’s long-term plan for power to include more renewable energy and account for data centers’ impacts on their pocketbooks.
They also want the utility’s Integrated Resource Plan, a projection of how it will meet energy needs the next 20 years, to address climate change head on.
Montanans and the group of advocates and a business represented by Earthjustice shared those concerns with the Montana Public Service Commission at a recent public meeting and in a 134-page review of the plan filed with the agency.
At a recent meeting, PSC chief legal counsel Amanda Webster said the agency does not have authority to approve or reject the plan, but it may identify deficiencies.
Commissioner Annie Bukacek said the PSC anticipates taking up the plan in mid August.
At a meeting, Amy Cilimburg, with Climate Smart Missoula, said the plan mentions climate change just once as a response to a stakeholder comment even though the planet is facing “the hottest conditions ever.”
She said a heat wave in Europe in June led to the deaths of 10,000 people — France counted an excess mortality rate of 36%, according to the Guardian.
Cilimburg said scientists associate  burning of fossil fuels with extreme weather, but the plan continues to call for fossil fuels.
“Can we please listen to the climate experts?” Climiburg said.
Many people worry data centers will increase their power bills, which are already going up.
Ashley Fisher, of Helena, said a study by the University of Michigan shows examples of the way data centers drive up costs and places where “prices have doubled.”
“We need to take a really serious look about how this is going to affect Montanans who are already having a hard time being able to afford the places that they live,” Fisher said.
The report from Michigan says residential electricity rates increased by 25% since the construction of one data center in the state in 2017. It said rates in one city in Louisiana jumped 39% for residential customers.
The report says utility companies often pass on infrastructure costs to residents and small businesses.
NorthWestern Energy has said data centers “must pay their fair share of the transmission, generation and distribution upgrades they require.”
The filing from Earthjustice said NorthWestern Energy is under negotiations to at least double and potentially increase by tenfold its daily retail load to serve data centers.
But the groups said NorthWestern doesn’t accurately project the demand in its plan, and it also doesn’t disclose enough information about its agreements with data center developers.
The coalition is made up of 16 parties including Bridger Bowl Ski Area, Helena Interfaith Climate Advocates, NW Energy Coalition, 350 Montana, and others.
Energy watchdog Montana Environmental Information Center has said ensuring Montanans aren’t picking up the tab for data centers requires guarantees by the PSC and consumer protection legislation — draft bills are in the works for the 2027 session.
Shannon James, with MEIC, raised concerns about the process, not just the plan. MEIC is part of the coalition with Earthjustice.
James said the PSC chose to have only two public meetings, both in Helena, “limiting public participation in a process that will shape Montana’s energy future for decades.”
A PSC spokesperson earlier said the commission is facing a shortened period to review the utility’s plan this year, and staff weren’t able to travel to multiple districts this year due to increased workloads.
As for the plan, James said it presents nuclear power as “a cornerstone of Montana’s energy future” even though small modular reactors remain “commercially unproven.”
“NorthWestern’s planning choices appear driven less by what is most affordable for Montana families and businesses than by investments that expand the company’s rate base and increase returns for shareholders,” James said.
The filing from Earthjustice noted a similar concern.
It said NorthWestern Energy’s plan suppresses clean energy alternatives, such as by putting arbitrary limits on battery storage, used to store electricity from renewable sources.
“NorthWestern’s decision to arbitrarily cap these resources is yet another way the utility is putting its finger on the scale in favor of fossil fuels at the expense of Montana’s environment,” the filing says.
The filing also said the plan ignores NorthWestern Energy’s proposed merger with Black Hills Corp.
The proposal is pending with the PSC, but the filing notes the merger could accelerate the utility’s capacity, which has implications for customers if data centers come onto the grid.
“This pending merger has the potential to dramatically influence NorthWestern’s future resource adequacy and load forecasts,” the groups said. “As a result, the utility’s failure to account for the possibility of a merger when drafting the 2026 IRP is a significant oversight.”
NorthWestern Energy could not be reached for additional comment in time for this story.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Egg facility inspections in WA still falling short of state requirements
description: Washington’s Department of Agriculture did not complete hundreds of mandated inspections at egg production and packing plants for the past two years, posing health risks to consumers, according to a new state audit.  The agency says it lacks the staff to meet the requirements and is drafting language to update state inspection regulations for egg […]
text:
(Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Washington’s Department of Agriculture did not complete hundreds of mandated inspections at egg production and packing plants for the past two years, posing health risks to consumers, according to a new state audit. 
The agency says it lacks the staff to meet the requirements and is drafting language to update state inspection regulations for egg facilities.
The department failed to complete 97% of required quarterly inspections of egg packing plants between state fiscal years 2024 and 2025, the state auditor’s office reported. 
It also failed to meet its own annual inspection frequency targets for egg production plants, which are generally on the same site as packing plants.
“By not performing inspections required by state law, there is an increased risk that eggs unfit for human consumption may reach the consumer, posing serious health and safety risks,” the report notes. 
In 2024, the department completed 13 of 165 required inspections. And in 2025, it completed just two of 294 required inspections, according to the audit. 
It’s not the first time this has happened. The state auditor reached a similar conclusion when it released its first audit on egg facility inspections in 2024. Between fiscal years 2022 and 2023, that report found, the department only completed 2% of required inspections. 
For at least four years, the Department of Agriculture has severely underinspected egg facilities.
“We do not believe quarterly inspections are necessary,” the department said in 2024 in response to the first audit. 
Since then, the department has met with federal and other state egg regulators and is working on draft language to update Washington’s egg inspection guidelines, which are stricter than federal inspection requirements, according to the agency’s response to the most recent audit.
The department contends that state law allows exemptions, specifically for egg packers with less than 3,000 laying hens. If those smaller facilities were exempted, as they are under federal regulations, the Department of Agriculture would only be required to inspect fewer than 10 Washington egg packing plants.
“We believe that the legislature did not necessarily intend for the program to conduct that number of inspections ad infinitum,” the agency said in its response. 
When the state law was created in 1975, the Department of Agriculture had its own egg inspection unit, the department said. Today, its Food Safety Program regulates many more facilities and “does not have sufficient staff to visit egg facilities quarterly,” according to the agency.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds turn over Alaska hazardous waste management to state
description: Alaska is now in charge of hazardous waste regulation in the state, a task that can be made more challenging by geographic remoteness. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Wednesday officially transferred authority for hazardous waste regulation to the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation. That makes Alaska the 49th state to be granted haza[...]
text:
The hazardous waste collection site at Anchorage's Solid Waste Services Central Transfer Station is seen on July 29, 2026. In the background, a worker documents materials that have been collected. The Midtown Anchorage facility is a site where residents can drop off hazardous materials like old paint, solvents and lithium batteries. Alaska is now the 49th state to be granted prime responsibility from the federal government for hazardous waste regulation and management. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska is now in charge of hazardous waste regulation in the state, a task that can be made more challenging by geographic remoteness.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Wednesday officially transferred authority for hazardous waste regulation to the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation. That makes Alaska the 49th state to be granted hazardous waste primacy — the term for primary responsibility for management and enforcement — over the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA.
The applicable federal law is the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA.
Before Wednesday, the last state to be granted RCRA primacy was Hawaii in 2001, according to EPA records. Now the only state without RCRA primacy is Iowa, according to the EPA.
The transfer of authority, completed with a signature ceremony, was several years in the making, said Emma Pokon, EPA’s Pacific Northwest regional administrator and a former DEC commissioner.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

DEC has assembled a hazardous waste program and team and has created state regulations that became effective a year ago. The Alaska Legislature has made regular appropriations in budgets for the hazardous waste program, which is part of DEC’s Division of Environmental Health.
“The good news is that the state has been implementing the program hand-in-hand with the EPA for the last several years,” Pokon said in a brief interview. “This moment isn’t a new imposition of costs. . . They are up and running. They’re staffed up. They’re trained up.”
Lori Aldrich, the DEC staffer managing the program, is “a gem of a public servant,” Pokon added.
 

Emma Pokon, the Environmental Protection Agency’s regional administrator, stands amid work stations at the federal agency’s Anchorage office on July 29, 2026. Pokon was previously commissioner of the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Hazardous waste, as defined by RCRA, include a variety of substances like solvents, petroleum refinery sludges and dioxin-containing materials. Sources range from large industrial and military facilities to individual households.
Alaska in 2023 reported 2,729 tons of RCRA-classified hazardous waste, a total that ranked 48th among states, according to the EPA. The top sources that year, which is the most recent year with data available publicly, were the Petro Star Valdez Refinery, Eielson Air Force Base and a Palmer-based environmental services company that manages such wastes as part of its operations, according to the EPA.
For Alaska, distance poses a major challenge to hazardous waste management, Pokon said.
There are no hazardous-waste disposal facilities in the state, so almost all of the collected materials have to be shipped out for proper disposal, she said. And the shipping has to be timely, she said.
“There are limitations on holding times because of the risks presented by those materials,” she said. “The logistics involved with — once you get something into the community — getting it out, pose specific special challenges.”
Challenges are exacerbated when communities are especially remote or when there are natural disasters, she said. For that reason, hazardous waste management is part of preparation for and response to events like the Mendenhall Glacier outburst floods that now affect Juneau on a nearly annual basis or the Western Alaska floods from ex-Typhoons Halong and Merbok.
The newly formed program at DEC has already been addressing those emergency response tasks, Pokon said.
“One of the great things about DEC having the program is that really it’s been their teams that have been closer to the on-the-ground issues,” she said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: New federal Medicaid rule threatens more coverage on top of Congress’ cuts, Utah advocates say
description: A substitute teacher who doesn’t want her healthcare coverage to lapse while school’s out in the summer.  A single mother of five who almost permanently lost her eyesight from tears in her retinas.  A mother who left an abusive relationship, but the stress of a custody battle took a toll on her daughters’ physical and […]
text:
Lorena Horse, CEO of Sacred Circle Healthcare, speaks during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare's offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)A substitute teacher who doesn’t want her healthcare coverage to lapse while school’s out in the summer. 
A single mother of five who almost permanently lost her eyesight from tears in her retinas. 
A mother who left an abusive relationship, but the stress of a custody battle took a toll on her daughters’ physical and mental health. 
All three of these women have something in common: they know firsthand the importance of Medicaid, the publicly funded health insurance program for people with low incomes — and how detrimental any additional barriers to get or maintain its coverage can be. 
States face tight timeline as feds unveil new Medicaid work requirement rules

Stephanie Foster, a substitute teacher from Farmington, Brenda Oluwalana of West Valley City, and Ronni Batement, a child welfare advocate from Logan, all told their stories at a news conference in Salt Lake City on Thursday. 
“I’ve been getting notices saying that you only have three months to find a job, or you’re terminated from Medicaid,” Foster, the substitute teacher, said. “So it’s just been kind of a struggle.”
They and healthcare advocates gathered at the offices of Sacred Circle Healthcare — a clinic owned by the Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation that serves many patients who rely on Medicaid — to mark the 61st anniversary of Medicaid’s federal creation and to call on state leaders to stand against looming federal cuts and new requirements on the program. 
“I’m not a statistic,” said Oluwalana, who credited Medicaid and doctors for saving her from blindness. “I’m a person who kept my eyesight because Medicaid was there, appointment after appointment for years. I’m asking you to think about who is on the other end of these cuts.” 
Brenda Oluwalana, a West Valley City resident who relied on Medicaid coverage for eye surgery, speaks during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
The cuts and how they’re impacting Utah
When Congress passed HR1, or the “big, beautiful” law last year, it enacted the largest ever cuts to Medicaid, with most of those cuts and new work requirements set to take effect at the end of the year, by January 2027. 
Last month, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services also issued a new interim rule giving states more details on how they’re supposed to verify the work status for about 20 million adults enrolled in Medicaid. 
That new rule “goes further than Congress did in HR1, adding more red tape that will raise costs and kick more Utahns off their healthcare,” said Rachel Craig, government affairs manager for the Association for Utah Community Health and a leading member of the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition, which organized Thursday’s news conference. 
States gird for new Medicaid ‘medically frail’ rule

The new reporting requirements will “cut tens of thousands of Utahns off of healthcare,” even though “the vast majority of Utahns on Medicaid either already work or … otherwise qualify for exemptions due to a disability or other reasons,” she said. 
“We gather here today to urge CMS to reconsider its draconian rules … and implore our elected officials in Utah to fight to preserve the progress we’ve made to make Medicaid a strong and effective program,” Craig said. 
Faced with the looming end-of-year deadline, state officials across the nation, including in Utah, are grappling with how to implement the new administrative requirements. Earlier this year, the Utah Legislature budgeted nearly $16.5 million to administer HR1’s new Medicaid eligibility requirements, but they’re still working through the details of how to put them into practice. 
In response to Thursday’s news conference, Utah Medicaid Director Julie Ewing issued a prepared statement. 
“At the heart of Utah Medicaid are the more than 330,000 Utahns who rely on these services for their health and well being,” Ewing said. “As federal requirements under HR1 deploy, our core commitment remains unchanged: supporting our members every step of the way. We are dedicated to transparent, straightforward communication so eligible adults keep their coverage without unnecessary hurdles, all while ensuring every dollar is managed responsibly to keep this safety net strong.”
New eligibility requirements
Advocates worry the new requirements — including eligibility checks every six months and proof of employment paperwork — will inevitably result in lost coverage, even for those who should be eligible, because of the new administrative burdens. 
To Bateman, the new administrative obstacles can threaten healthcare coverage for victims of domestic violence — adding another barrier that prevents them from leaving their abusers.
Ronni Bateman, a child welfare advocate and survivor of domestic abuse, speaks during a news conference held by he Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“More frequent eligibility checks make us feel like criminals and increase the labor required to keep our benefits, which we already have so little time and resources to shoulder,” Bateman said. “Every time we complete one of these, we are consumed with fear that somehow we will not pass.” 
While HR1 created a work requirement exemption for people who are “medically frail,” the new interim rule created an additional requirement that in order to qualify for that “medically frail” designation, a person must have a significant health condition and be significantly impaired in their ability to work. 
Advocates including Nate Crippes with the Disability Law Center worry healthcare providers will have a hard time determining whether their patients fit that definition, and it will make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to stay on Medicaid. 
Nate Crippes with the Disability Law Center speaks during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“Too often, public debates around Medicaid focus on stereotypes and misconceptions. The reality is that the people most affected by these cuts are our neighbors, friends, family members, and fellow Utahns living with disabilities,” Crippes said. “These are people striving to work, contribute to their communities, and live independently.”
Crippes said that proponents of HR1 argued that its cuts would not impact people with disabilities, “but the latest interim final rule makes clear that people with disabilities will disproportionately be impacted.”
“If we are serious about addressing the needs of people with disabilities, mental illness, and substance use disorders, then Utah policymakers must stand up against an interim final rule that goes too far and threatens the independence and dignity and health of people with disabilities,” Crippes said. 
A special program specifically for Utah’s homeless slated to end
Another Medicaid program unique to Utah — created more than a decade ago by the state’s Republican-controlled Legislature — is on the cusp of ending because federal officials recently signaled they won’t allow it to continue. 
Utah’s Targeted Adult Medicaid Program, known as TAM, has provided 12 months of continuous Medicaid coverage for Utah adults earning up to 5% of the federal poverty level who are chronically homeless, involved in the justice system or need substance abuse or mental health treatment. 
Sheriffs, police, mayors rally to save Utah Medicaid program for the homeless, parolees

Local leaders, sheriffs and police have sent letters to state leaders urging them to keep TAM alive as crucial for helping Utahns stop revolving in and out of homeless shelters and jails — but federal officials haven’t budged on their position against programs that allow continuous eligibility. TAM is still slated to end in July 2027, after which eligible TAM members will transition to adult expansion Medicaid, according to state officials. 
Salt Lake County Council member Suzanne Harrison — who is also a medical doctor — said at Thursday’s news conference that the loss of TAM, combined with the cuts from HR1, will set state leaders’ efforts to end chronic homelessness “backwards” while also “shifting costs to local governments and ultimately local taxpayers.” 
“Cuts to such programs only increase burdens on our local law enforcement, our ER, our emergency rooms, and our jails,” Harrison said. “All told, cuts to Medicaid saddle local governments and taxpayers with more costs, while making our citizens less healthy and our streets less safe. These harsh federal cuts will limit our state’s ability to design our Medicaid program in a way that best supports Utahns.”
Salt Lake County Council member Suzanne Harrison speaks during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Impacts to tribal-owned clinics
Lorena Horse, CEO of Sacred Circle Healthcare and a member of the Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation, said the cuts to Medicaid will also have cascading impacts on clinics like hers, where many of their patients rely on Medicaid coverage. 
“Weakening Utah’s programs will undermine years of investment and progress in this healthcare system,” Horse said. “Reductions in Medicaid funding does not eliminate healthcare needs. It simply shifts costs to emergency rooms, hospitals, and taxpayers in other areas.”
Horse said Sacred Circle has already had to reassign staff to administrative tasks related to Medicaid eligibility rather than working directly with patient care, and those “administrative burdens will only increase once Medicaid changes go into effect,” she said.
“Ultimately, the long-term consequences of these changes may result in clinic operation decisions that directly affect patient care,” Horse said, “such as longer wait times for appointments, reduced clinic hours, and fewer specialty and ancillary care services.”
A poster board advocating for Medicaid is displayed during a news conference held by the Protect Medicaid Utah Coalition at Sacred Circle Healthcare’s offices in Salt Lake City on July 30, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ole Miss sues 2 ex-players who transferred to LSU, alleging they did not comply with financial deals
description: LSU head football coach Lane Kiffin waves to the crowd in the first half of an NCAA college basketball game against Kentucky in Baton Rouge, La., Thursday, Jan. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The University of Mississippi is suing two former football players who transferred to LSU, alleging they failed to compensate the school for their departure as required by revenue-sharing agreements they had signed in early January.
The lawsuits were filed against edge rusher Princewill Umanmielen and offensive lineman Devin Harper. Ole Miss seeks $550,000 from Umanmielen and $400,000 from Harper, according to the lawsuits filed Monday in Lafayette County Circuit Court in Oxford, Mississippi.
The lawsuit stems in part from former Ole Miss coach Lane Kiffin’s high-profile departure for LSU late last season. LSU declined comment on Wednesday.
College athletes have been able to transfer far more freely in recent years without having to sit out a year, as was once required by the NCAA. There have been scattered disputes between players and their former schools over compensation agreements; earlier this year, Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. said he would return to the Huskies after his school was reportedly prepared to pursue legal options to enforce his lucrative name, image and likeness contract.
In a statement released to reporters, Ole Miss said it “values its student-athletes and is committed to honoring all obligations made to them.
“In return, the university expects that same commitment from its student-athletes and their representatives in upholding their contracts,” the school said.
Ole Miss said revenue-sharing agreements signed by both players included a provision requiring them to compensate the university with a predetermined amount if they departed before fulfilling their commitment.
“The University of Mississippi has a responsibility to enforce its contractual terms, and this position is consistent with the actions of other institutions in the current landscape of college athletics,” the Ole Miss statement said. “The university attempted to amicably resolve this matter prior to filing.”
Kiffin left Ole Miss following its regular-season finale against Mississippi State in late November. Kiffin initially asked to continue coaching the Rebels in the College Football Playoff after he’d accepted the position at LSU, but Ole Miss declined and appointed then-defensive coordinator Pete Golding as Kiffin’s replacement. Golding coached Ole Miss to the national semifinals.
After the Rebels’ playoff run ended, Umanmielen and Harper transferred to LSU.
Umanmielen had nine sacks and 13 tackles for loss as a junior last season for the Rebels. Harper was a freshman reserve in 2025, appearing in six games.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana modernizes access to WIC food assistance benefits
description: Louisiana’s extra food assistance program for women, infants and children will come with a new benefits card that can be used at grocery stores starting Aug. 1.
text:
Louisiana’s extra food assistance program for women, infants and children will come with a new benefits card that can be used at grocery stores starting Aug. 1.Louisiana’s extra food assistance program for women, infants and children will come with a new benefits card that can be used at grocery stores starting Aug. 1. 

The new card allows state officials to upload the program’s benefits remotely. Previously, WIC enrollees had to report to an office every three months to have their benefits replenished in person. 

“This long-awaited modernization makes the program more convenient, accessible and responsive to the needs of today’s families,” Louisiana Health Secretary Bruce Greenstein said in a news release. 

The WIC special supplemental nutrition program is available to low-income people who are pregnant, nursing a child up to 1 year-old and postpartum without nursing up to six months after giving birth. Low-income families can also use it to buy food for infants and children until they are five years-old. Families who already qualify for Medicaid or other government food assistance typically also qualify for WIC.

The benefits can only be applied to certain types of food purchases such as formula, baby food, fruit, vegetables, eggs, milk, breakfast cereals, peanut butter, tuna fish and canned salmon. 
People enrolled in the WIC program began receiving their new cards at in-person meetings in June, and they can be used at grocery stores starting Saturday.

Participants will also have to set up a numeric passcode on the card before shopping with it.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Ten selected for ‘Gallery of Outstanding Montanans’
description: Ten candidates have been selected for inclusion into the “Gallery of Outstanding Montanans,” which honors citizens who have made significant contributions to the state or nation. The Montana Historical Society manages the program, which will honor the 10 Montanans – two at a time– during the next decade. The honorees will have an eight-year display […]
text:
The Gallery of Outstanding Montanans is pictured. (Montana Historical Society photo)Ten candidates have been selected for inclusion into the “Gallery of Outstanding Montanans,” which honors citizens who have made significant contributions to the state or nation.
The Montana Historical Society manages the program, which will honor the 10 Montanans – two at a time– during the next decade. The honorees will have an eight-year display at the Montana State Capitol.
“Each of these 10 individuals contributed to Montana, and in some cases, changed the nation,” Martha Kohl, a program manager with the Montana Historical Society, said in a press release. “Their stories span a remarkable range of lives, fields, and eras, and together they reflect the full breadth of what it means to be an Outstanding Montanan.”
The program was established in 1979, and the historical society puts out a call every 10 years for honorees — the next round will take place in 2036.
Candidates for induction into the Gallery are:
Charles Bovey (1907–1978) and Sue Bovey (1907–1988)
The Boveys were historic preservationists who were key in preserving Virginia City and Nevada City. Both of those towns are deeply important to the state’s early gold-rush history.
Frances Senska (1914–2009)
Senska was a potter and longtime Montana State University professor who helped found the Archie Bray Foundation for the Ceramic Arts. Colloquially known as “The Bray,” it’s a large ceramic facility outside Helena that’s helped contribute to a strong tradition of pottery in parts of the state.
Carmen Louise Cross (1919–2014)
Cross was one of 19 women elected to the 1972 Montana Constitutional Convention and was the only woman to lead a committee. She was critical in helping enshrine the state citizens’ right to a clean and healthful environment, the release says. She also helped found Glendive’s Frontier Gateway Museum and was a longtime curator there.
Dr. Huie Pock (1849–1927)
Dr. Pock was a Butte doctor, herbalist, acupuncturist and merchant who practiced medicine in the Mining City from around 1895 until his death. He notably treated patients from all backgrounds and helped defend the rights of Chinese Montanans “during a period of intense anti-Chinese discrimination” with the release saying he built a distinguished professional life in the face of racial prejudice. 
Elouise Pepion Cobell (1945–2011)
Cobell helped found the nation’s first tribally owned bank during her time as treasurer for the Blackfeet Nation. She was also the lead plaintiff in a lawsuit — Cobell v. Salazar — over mismanagement of federal funds that impacted nearly a half million American Indians. That case resulted in a $3.4 billion settlement. She was also honored with warrior status by the Blackfeet Nation in 2000.
Cornelius Hedges (1831–1907)
Hedges was critical in helping establish Yellowstone National Park and also founded the Masonic Order in Montana. He additionally was the territory’s first Superintendent of Public Instruction.
George Horse Capture (1937–2013) 
George Paul Horse Capture was one of the first Native Americans to be a museum curator and was a Gros Ventre scholar, curator and activist. He was also critical in creating the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C. The release quoted him as saying that such a museum should be “for Native peoples, not just about them.”
Emma Ingalls (1860–1940)
Ingalls was one of the first two women elected to the Montana Legislature and introduced the 19th Amendment in the Montana House for ratification. She also introduced legislation creating the Mountain View Vocational School for Girls and was a newspaper publisher.
Harriette Cushman (1890–1978)
Cushman is credited with helping to drastically expand Montana’s poultry industry and worked for the Montana Extension Service from 1922 to 1954. She was one of the few women of her time to pursue agricultural science, the release said, adding that she was instrumental in making the state’s turkey industry the most profitable in the nation during the Great Depression.
Benjamin Steele (1917–2016)
Steele was an artist and survivor of the Bataan Death March during World War II, helping document the march through art. He spent decades at Eastern Montana College in Billings as an educator, continuing his art while teaching.

name: National
title: As fires rage in the Pacific Northwest, leaders call all hands on deck
description: With dozens of large fires burning across the Pacific Northwest, and nearly 2 million acres burned already, state leaders are calling for firefighting reinforcements and bracing for a grueling August.  “We’re going to have a long year ahead,” said Washington state forester George Geissler. “I keep getting depressed every time I listen to the meteorologists.[...]
text:
The Ptarmigan Fire burning in Washington’s Pasayten Wilderness, as seen in this aerial photo taken by smokejumpers July 20, has crossed the Canadian border and burned at least 18,000 acres so far. State leaders in Oregon and Washington have called for reinforcements and expect a grueling August. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service)With dozens of large fires burning across the Pacific Northwest, and nearly 2 million acres burned already, state leaders are calling for firefighting reinforcements and bracing for a grueling August. 
“We’re going to have a long year ahead,” said Washington state forester George Geissler. “I keep getting depressed every time I listen to the meteorologists. There’s really not any relief we can see.” 
Across Washington and Oregon, wildland fire crews are battling 45 large fires that have burned more than 1.8 million acres so far, an area larger than the state of Delaware. Roughly 2.6 million acres have burned nationwide this year. 
Trump’s new conditions on DEI, immigration could cut off states’ wildfire funding

In Oregon, Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek issued an executive order in June making all wildfire qualified staffers at various state agencies available to fight fires. State forester Kacey KC said teams from 35 different states are currently fighting fires in the Northwest, and Oregon is No. 1 on the national priority list as new resources become available. 
“It’s not an award you want to win,” KC said. “It’s all hands on deck everywhere. We’ve seen some very aggressive fire runs this year.”
In Washington, Geissler has issued a more targeted call for reinforcements. His “ready reserve” message, sent Tuesday, called for employees with qualifications to serve as strike team leaders, task force leaders, division supervisors, aviation positions, engine bosses, heavy equipment bosses and dispatch positions. 
“We are in a bad fire year,” Geissler said, speaking Wednesday. “We are at a straining point. We’re in the third or fourth week of August (in terms of fire activity), and it’s not even August yet. We are out of the gate earlier than we have been in years and years and years.”
Geissler said he had just finalized a plan to deploy 100 National Guard troops to help fight fires in Washington. 
Idaho Gov. Brad Little, a Republican, signed a wildfire disaster emergency Tuesday and ordered the Idaho National Guard to help fight a fire along the border of Oregon and Idaho, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. 
And crews from Utah have deployed to help fight fires in Oregon. 
Across the West, record heat and drought this winter left mountains bare of snow, forests parched and rivers dwindling. Leaders have been preparing for a brutal fire season, one that has now arrived in the Northwest. Washington state has brought in crews from the South, Southwest and California, Geissler said, along with teams from Australia and New Zealand.
Unlike in previous years, Canada has been unable to send help since massive wildfires there have commanded all available resources. 
While other U.S. regions have seen less fire activity so far, experts say there’s a long way to go. 
“It’s pretty dry,” said Riva Duncan, a former wildland fire chief who served more than 30 years with the U.S. Forest Service. “One lightning (storm) would put the northern Rockies into play, and that’s gonna be more competition for resources.” 
Duncan serves as president of Grassroots Wildland Firefighters, a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of wildfire professionals.
While the current situation in Washington is intense, Geissler said, the state Department of Natural Resources is playing the long game and planning out work and rest cycles for crews in the field. 
“You don’t want to burn everybody out all at one time,” he said. 
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Here’s when to expect results in Alaska’s 2026 statewide primary election
description: Early, in-person voting begins Monday for Alaska’s Aug. 18 state primary election, and thousands of voters have already cast absentee ballots by mail. Regardless of when — or how — Alaskans vote, ballots will be counted starting on election day, according to a preliminary schedule provided by the Alaska Division of Elections.  Polls close at […]
text:
Elections workers double-check the results of Alaska's Aug. 16, 2022, primary election during a meeting of the state review board on Tuesday, Aug. 30, 2022, at the Alaska Division of Elections in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Early, in-person voting begins Monday for Alaska’s Aug. 18 state primary election, and thousands of voters have already cast absentee ballots by mail.
Regardless of when — or how — Alaskans vote, ballots will be counted starting on election day, according to a preliminary schedule provided by the Alaska Division of Elections. 
Polls close at 8 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time, and the division expects to have the first preliminary results “between 8:45 p.m. and 9 p.m.”
“There are additional results updates that follow but how many or at what time they will be published will vary,” the division said in an information packet given to reporters.
The final unofficial tally will take place Aug. 28, 10 days after election day, and the division expects to certify official results by Aug. 31.
Any recounts must be requested by Sept. 5, and any lawsuit challenging a result must be filed by Sept. 10.


Timeline of the 2026 primary election

Aug. 3 – Early voting begins in person.
Aug. 11 – Elections officials begin ID checks on absentee ballot envelopes. Absentee votes in those envelopes are not counted until at least Aug. 18.
Aug. 18 – Election day. Polls open across the state. 
Late Aug. 18 – Absentee ballots begin to be counted, in-person votes are counted.
9 p.m. Aug. 18 – First results expected online.
Early morning Aug. 19 – final election day results expected online.
Aug. 25 – Absentee votes counted to this point are added to the unofficial tally.
Aug. 28 – Final unofficial results available online.
Aug. 31 – Official results certified. Deadline for final four candidates to withdraw from the November election. 
Sept. 5 – Deadline to request recounts.
Sept. 10 – Deadline to challenge election results in court.



Under Alaska’s election system, voters pick one candidate for each race in the primary election. The top four vote-getters, regardless of political party, advance to the general election in November. If there are four or fewer candidates in a race, all advance to the general election.
In practice since 2022, lower-finishing Republican candidates have preferred to withdraw after the primary rather than compete against another Republican.
The Valley Republican Women, a notable group from the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, are running ads this year to promote the strategy. Those ads urge Republicans to “consolidate the vote” and “don’t split the field.”
In races with many competitors, a withdrawn candidate will be replaced by another until there are four options on the ballot or no more replacements are available. Any replacements may themselves withdraw.
The deadline to withdraw after the primary is Aug. 31. 
Normally, ballots cast in person are counted on election day itself. Since 2020, votes cast in person have leaned Republican. 
It’s common for some rural Alaska precincts to not report results on election night itself.
Two years ago, for example, only 387 of 403 precincts had reported results by 1 a.m. Wednesday, the day after election day. Four years ago, four precincts needed more than four days to report results from election day.
Historically, some rural precincts have had staffing problems that prevented them from opening on election day. In 2024’s primary, two precincts failed to open, and one opened only in the afternoon. In 2022, two precincts failed to open. In both 2024 and 2022, voters in the affected places were able to cast absentee ballots instead.
Absentee ballots are counted starting on election day, but that counting process extends until Aug. 28. Under Alaska law, absentee ballots — if they are postmarked on or before Aug. 18 — can reach the Division of Elections up to 10 days after election day and still be counted.
Counting an absentee ballot requires the division to first verify the identity information on the outside of the ballot envelope. That verification process starts Aug. 11, the division said, though the ballot inside the envelope won’t be counted until at least election day.
The verification process continues after election day, with ballots added to the tally in batches. The division expects to update results on Aug. 25 and again on Aug. 28, with additional updates possible between those two dates.
