name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The Dean of Massachusetts mayors
description: After more than 32 years in office, Dean Mazzarella has become the longest serving mayor in Massachusetts history, managing to transform the city, limit his list of enemies, and remain an ever-present, zealous leader. Despite an electoral touch other officials would die for, he comes off far more as affable everyman than calculating politician, which could b[...]
text:
DEAN MAZZARELLA’S day starts at 3 a.m. when he hops out of bed and promptly posts a good morning message on Facebook to his fellow “3 o’clockers.” Despite the early hour, dozens of Leominster residents, some working the third shift, greet him in the comments.
“Good morning Mr. Dean!”
“Mornin’ captain!”
Before he was elected mayor of this sleepy city in North-Central Massachusetts, Mazzarella worked nights as a Leominster police officer. Decades later, he still hasn’t been able to fix his sleep schedule. His days are long, but he doesn’t mind. The constantly-in-motion 68-year-old has plenty of energy to spare for someone who hardly sleeps five hours a night.
“I like to watch the city wake up in the morning,” he said.
Mazzarella uses the early hours to prepare for meetings, plan his schedule, or respond to residents who message him directly about potholes, parades, or taxes. He lives by a rule he calls his “sunset clause,” making sure to call back every person who reaches out to his office before the end of the day.
“People count on us,” he said. “We’re going to work hard like they do, and we’re going to be responsive.”
When he gets to his office, he will host his near-daily “morning briefing” live online, where he chats about anything he sees fit, which is most often politics, gas prices, and things going on around the city. Every Thursday, Mazzarella also hosts his public access TV show “Inside Leominster” during which he can be found doing anything from giving a budget presentation to interviewing Santa Claus.
It’s hardly surprising that after more than three decades in office, Mazzarella seems recognized by virtually everyone he passes by on Main Street as he walks through the city he’s lived in all his life. Perhaps more remarkable for the leader of a city of more than 40,000 residents is that the recognition often seems to cut both ways.  
“Dean! What’s happening?” a construction worker shouted at him from across the street on a sunny afternoon in May. Mazzarella shouted his name back and stopped to talk.
Mazzarella, the longest serving mayor in Massachusetts, standing on the steps of Leominster City Hall. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
There’s no gimmick that is beneath Mazzarella. On any given day, he might hand out a free coffee voucher to a resident that reports a pothole to City Hall or give someone a ride on the Flamingo Express – a free, golf cart-style shuttle service named after the city’s iconic manufacturing symbol that Mazzarella rolled out to help transport people to and from downtown businesses that have been affected by parking changes and street closures around an ongoing brook stabilization project.
In many ways, he is the quintessential mayor seen in movies – accessible to all and everywhere at once. Most people agree that he makes the city of 44,000 feel much more like a small town.
He’s even been compared to George Bailey – the ever-selfless protagonist in Frank Capra’s beloved 1946 film “It’s a Wonderful Life” – who sacrifices his dreams to help his community. Mazzarella doesn’t think of himself like that, although it’s one of his favorite movies, he said. But a longtime friend said the shoe fits.
“George Bailey believed in his community, and Dean believes in his,” said former state senator Bob Antonioni. “His passion is Leominster.”
Mazzarella pictured in the Flamingo Express – a free, golf cart-style shuttle service that the mayor rolled out to help transport people to and from downtown businesses. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
That passion has fueled him through more than 32 years in office, making Mazzarella the longest-serving mayor in Massachusetts history, quietly surpassing former mayor Michael McGlynn of Medford, who served for 28 years before stepping down in 2015.
Gateway Cities like Leominster are not easy places to lead. These former industrial hubs suffered from the long-term decline in manufacturing following World War II. The hollowing out of those economic anchors and the poverty and blight that have often followed defy quick fixes. But that doesn’t keep impatient voters from voicing frustration at the polls, with Gateway City mayors thrown out of office with some regularity.
Mazzarella’s immediate predecessor, Jack Mahan, served just one term as mayor before the then-first-time candidate sent him packing. Before that, Steve Perla served just two terms. Fitchburg, a neighboring Gateway City, has seen six mayors in the time that Leominster has seen one.
Mazzarella has defied the odds, managing to transform the city, limit his list of enemies, and remain an ever-present, zealous leader on his way to completing 17 two-year terms. One key to that is his ability to be defined by his successes rather than his failures, as Leominster voters have chosen him time and time again, notwithstanding a handful of controversies in City Hall over his years in office.
“People pay a lot of money for government, especially in this state. They’re all my customers, no matter who they are. If it’s important to them, it’s important to me.”Mayor Dean Mazzarella
Despite an electoral touch other officials would die for, Mazzarella comes off far more as affable everyman than calculating politician – a quality that some say is exactly why he has endured politically for so many years.
“I think the art of being successful at politics is not appearing to be a politician,” City Councilor Mark Bodanza said.
Local leaders and residents marvel at his staying power, but “Mayor Mazz” – known for his practical solutions, fiscal conservatism, and relentless energy – suggests the secret to it is not that complicated.
“Government is a lot simpler than people think,” he said, explaining that he runs the city like a business.
It’s a line often invoked by elected officials, but for Mazzarella, the quip is backed by plenty of first-hand experience: He owns not one, but three, local businesses in Leominster. Like any successful business owner who must keep customers satisfied while not giving away the store, he seems to have mastered the tricky balance of keeping Leominster residents happy while also keeping the city fiscally sound.
“People pay a lot of money for government, especially in this state,” he said. “They’re all my customers, no matter who they are. If it’s important to them, it’s important to me.”
Mazzarella’s campaign website says Leominster is “a city on the move,” yet its residents haven’t elected a new leader in over 30 years. Many others in city government roles, including city councilors, have been serving for years if not decades.
“There’s a little bit of a trend in Leominster,” said Peter Bovenzi, a local housing developer who grew up in the city. “If it’s not broke, we don’t fix it.”
Leominster is the birthplace of Johnny Appleseed, who was born there two years before the signing of the Declaration of Independence, in 1774. Its more recent identity has been shaped by its standing as a major plastics manufacturing hub. Nicknamed the “Pioneer Plastics City” and the “Comb City,” Leominster’s plastic manufacturing began in the late 19th century during the Industrial Revolution, and a handful of plastic manufacturers still remain in the city today. The ever-popular plastic pink flamingo, first produced in the city by Union Products in 1957, has become a symbol of Leominster – and American suburban kitsch.
Downtown Leominster. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
While taking his responsibilities seriously, Mazzarella also exudes an unselfconscious goofiness that made it perhaps inevitable that he would found an annual Pink Flamingo Day to celebrate the city’s connection to the iconic lawn ornament. Next year, will be its 20th observance.
While it’s not a city of great wealth, Leominster is a stable, blue-collar community where people, for the most part, are able to get by. Its median household income sits at $84,000, a full $20,000 below the statewide figure of $104,000, but the share of Leominster residents who live below the poverty line – about 9 percent – is one point below the statewide average.
The city’s once vacant and blighted downtown is now at nearly 100 percent capacity with dozens of vibrant storefronts on Main Street, from hair salons and cafes to Allen’s Department Store. Leominster also enjoys one of the highest homeownership rates among the 26 Gateway Cities at 63 percent – mirroring the statewide homeownership rate.
“To me, this is America right here. Hard work, pride, family, whatever religion you want to believe,” Mazzarella said. “Most people here will give you a chance, because they’ve been given one.”
Mazzarella was born and raised in Leominster alongside his two brothers. His father was a factory worker while his mother worked retail at a department store. His grandparents on both sides were immigrants from Italy, and both of his parents were born in Boston. Shortly before he was born, the family moved to Leominster to settle down outside of the big city. His parents made ends meet, meaning there were no luxuries, he said, but he was “the happiest kid in the world.”
His grandfather bought a home on Leominster’s east side where many other Italian immigrants lived and later made additions to it so his children could live with him. Four generations of Mazzarellas have since moved in and out of the house, which Mazzarella owns.
“It’s like a starter home for everyone in our family,” he said. “I don’t have the heart to sell it.”
Mazzarella stands in front of the house his grandfather owned in Leominster. Four generations of Mazzarellas have since moved in and out of the house, which the mayor owns. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
After graduating from Leominster High School, he attended Mount Wachusett Community College where he studied criminal justice before taking the civil service exam. Mazzarella always knew he wanted to be a police officer, though he mostly enjoyed taking business classes in school and briefly considered doing construction or becoming an electrician.  
“We had cops that crossed us every day at school. They were the law enforcers, but also the community people,” he said. “Everybody knew their names, and I looked up to them.”
For 10 years, he worked from midnight to 8 a.m. for the Leominster Police Department. He is still a certified police officer, though he is on what he calls the “longest leave of absence in the state.”
“You have to have honest people around you. You can’t have ‘yes’ people. You need people that tell you you have broccoli stuck in your tooth and nobody wears those ties anymore.”Dean Mazzarella
While he loved being an officer, he also possessed an entrepreneurial spirit that led him in 1984 to start a commercial flagpole company – Central Discount Flag & Flagpole – that is still in business today.
“Some people go on vacation. I go dig holes, mix concrete, and put up flagpoles,” he said, adding that he has donated and installed some of those flagpoles around the city. “There’s a beginning, middle, and end to it, which I like.”
Mazzarella also owns Main Street Gift and Cafe downtown, as well as a local shed business called He Sheds She Sheds. He previously owned real estate and worked as a DJ in nightclubs under the name “Disco Dino” in the late 1970s.
“I just like to work. I like to be busy,” he said. “I wish I could start 50 businesses – all downtown or something.”
The long days he spent in City Hall when he was first elected meant he couldn’t always be present at home. His daughter Stephanie and son Dean were 12 and nine years old when Mazzarella entered office.
“Family suffers from it. Your kids suffer from it. I made it to their games and everything, but I certainly wasn’t dad of the year,” he said. “They learned at an early age, even when I was a cop, that you didn’t celebrate your birthday on your birthday.”
Neither of his children, now adults, has any interest in city government, Mazzarella said.
Mazzarella walking into Main Street Gift and Cafe, a downtown business he owns. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
But when it comes to family, nobody goes far. Mazzarella, who is divorced, lives with his partner, Tara. His 70-year-old brother, who has Parkinson’s disease, lives with them, and until she passed away in June, so did his 97-year-old mother. Their modest home is in the same neighborhood where the mayor grew up, and his daughter lives just down the street with her two children, while his son currently lives in the old house Mazzarella’s grandfather owned. His second brother also still lives in Leominster.
By 1993, Mazzarella, 36 at the time, had grown frustrated with the city’s lack of resources. The police department’s funding was limited, their equipment was dated, crime was high in some parts of the city, and the department had entered a sporadic period of hiring and firing, which was “the worst thing for morale,” he said.    
“I saw people working really hard with the resources they had. We had cars that were inadequate, radios that didn’t work, mace that was handed down for generations, and drug dealers everywhere,” he said. “I was young and had some good ideas, so I thought I’d put them out there and see whether they resonated with people.”
Mazzarella, a political outsider, announced his run for mayor in February 1993 and later that year defeated Jack Mahan, a first-term incumbent, with more than 60 percent of the vote.  
“Dean was definitely an underdog,” said Steve Perla, who served as mayor from 1988 to 1992 and graduated high school with Mazzarella. “He ran a very good grassroots campaign. People wanted a change, and Leominster was at a crossroads. They were looking for someone that was on the younger side that had a different approach.”

An old photo of Mazzarella when he was a Leominster police officer. (Photo courtesy of Dean Mazzarella) 

Mazzarella recalled the weeks that followed his election. As he drove back into Leominster from a meeting one night, he had a moment of reflection he said he’ll never forget.
“I realized that I’m now the mayor of that whole city, and everybody has a pamphlet or a brochure that says what I’m going to do as mayor,” he said. “They elected me, they’re counting on me, and then there’s the 40 percent that didn’t, and I have to make them believers.”
He entered a decades-long quest to do just that.
The city’s strong-mayor charter gave him plenty of running room. The mayor oversees every department, appoints most department heads and board members, builds the budget that the city council then votes on, and serves as chair of the school committee.
Mazzarella said his immediate priority was hiring a strong financial team and department heads who would keep him on his toes.
“You have to have honest people around you. You can’t have ‘yes’ people,” he said. “You need people that tell you you have broccoli stuck in your tooth and nobody wears those ties anymore.”
But coming in from the outside wasn’t easy, Mazzarella said, and the start of his tenure was tumultuous given the city’s financial state. He expected to serve just one term – maybe two.
“It wasn’t looking good for me, because the council wasn’t on my side,” he said of Leominster’s nine-person city council.
It’s a far cry from his relationship with City Council today, which he and other councilors describe as respectful and cooperative, despite occasional disagreements.
Mazzarella said he avoids the petty part of politics when he can.
“I like getting stuff done, and I think [politics] slows things down and gobbles stuff up,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what section of the city you live in, it doesn’t matter who you voted for – it doesn’t even matter if you don’t like me, because you might be my friend one day.”
Mazzarella stands in the pews of St. Cecilia Parish, a Catholic church in Leominster. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Mazzarella has long described himself as an independent, although he has supported moderate Republicans like former governors Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker.
And when it comes to the city’s finances, his conservative leanings are clear.
Mazzarella is most credited for transforming the city’s budget during his tenure. As sluggish state aid growth and rising costs continue to trap many local governments between a rock and a hard place, Leominster boasts a staggering rainy-day fund totaling more than $20 million. And Mazzarella has overseen that without maxxing out the city’s ability to raise property taxes: Leominister has an excess levy capacity of nearly six percent at a time when debt exclusions and Proposition 2½ overrides are polarizing other Massachusetts communities and making headlines.
“Go find a community right now that has $20 million in a stabilization fund. Go find a community right now that isn’t having layoffs,” said David Cormier, a Leominster city councilor. “When you look at what’s going on in other communities, I don’t know what more you could ask from your local government.”
During his first year in office, Mazzarella developed a fiscal plan to fully fund the city’s pension liability. And in 2019, Leominster became the first community in the Commonwealth to reach 100 percent funding status, meaning it has enough to make all current and future retirement benefit payments.
“He transformed Leominster from a place that had some really significant financial problems to the envy of the state in terms of finances,” Bodanza said.
When Mazzarella took office in 1994, state aid had been sharply declining, and the city had just over $40,000 in “free cash” – funds not already reserved for capital and operating expenses – and nearly $190,000 in unpaid debt.
“I remember what it was like to have no money in this community, and he pulled us out of that,” said longtime city councilor Claire Freda, who was elected the same year as Mazzarella. “We were looking at how much we had to do, and we had no money to do it. I don’t ever want to go back to that.”
Mazzarella stands in front of the old police station in downtown Leominster where he used to work as an officer prior to being elected mayor in 1993. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Mazzarella said he takes an aggressive approach to paying off the city’s debts – often clearing them early – and relies on his grant writer, who has been widely credited for securing millions for city projects and initiatives. He also initiated Leominster’s climb to a strong bond rating, which allows the city to borrow for new buildings and projects at lower costs. The city is currently building a new elementary school and recently completed a new police station downtown.
“During times of prosperity, you plan for the bad days,” Mazzarella said. “When things are good, people get carried away. They don’t put money aside. But I’ve been around long enough to see the bad days come, and we have to be ready for them.”
In September 2023, one of those bad days arrived when nearly a foot of torrential rain was dumped on the city, topping a dam and causing roads to collapse into a number of sinkholes.
In a drone video of the damage, the mayor could be seen pacing on a flooded bridge while making phone calls.
“That’s when people look to see that you’re strong,” he said. “Maybe you’re wearing the same clothes you’ve been wearing for the last four days, but you’re determined.”
The devastating 1,000-year flood caused nearly $30 million worth of damage to the city’s infrastructure, and approximately 1,400 homeowners sent claims to the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
The agency initially deemed that the repair costs fell below its threshold for aid, but the city, along with Gov. Maura Healey, successfully appealed the decision. That year, Mazzarella said the city dipped into its stabilization account to fund large amounts of overtime pay for firefighters and other city employees, cleanup equipment, and other operations.
Mazzarella driving the Flamingo Express downtown. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
It’s not easy to find Mazzarella detractors. One of the few is former city councilor David Rowlands. He said the mayor’s frugal ways have had drawbacks, particularly when it comes to school funding, which he called Mazzarella’s “Achilles heel.” The city has always funded its schools at the minimum level required by state law.
“Schools are a competitive business,” Rowlands said. “I don’t think we’ve made the investment over the years to be as competitive as we could have been.”
In 2017, school funding was at the center of the one close reelection race Mazzarella has faced. Even more remarkable, his opponent came close to toppling the mayor with a write-in campaign. In the end, Mazzarella beat Kenneth Ricker, who had been a dean at the city’s Samoset Middle School, by just over 100 votes.
Ricker, who could not be reached for comment, launched his campaign in the wake of a $5 million budget deficit facing the school district. He was one of roughly 90 employees who were laid off due to programming and staff reductions, although he and others were later rehired.
“As mayor, it’s always going to come back to you, and it came back to me,” Mazzarella said of his reelection near-miss.  
Though he’s largely led a charmed life throughout his more than 30 years in office, Mazzarella hasn’t escaped controversy entirely.
In 2010, the Sentinel & Enterprise reported on his romantic relationships with the city’s former economic development coordinator, as well as his former secretary after obtaining hundreds of emails from City Hall.
At the time he claimed he hadn’t done anything wrong and told the newspaper his “typical 18-hour days leave him no time for a personal life outside of work.” But 16 years later, Mazzarella acknowledges that the relationships were inappropriate.
“It’s nothing you want to be remembered for,” he told CommonWealth Beacon. “If it meant I wasn’t reelected, then that would have been self-inflicted.”
But the following year, Mazzarella ran unopposed as he had done since 2005.
Then, in 2012, he was cited by the State Ethics Commission and paid a $4,000 fine for violating Massachusetts’s conflict of interest law by directing the city’s housing rehabilitation program coordinator at the time to use Community Development Block Grant money to renovate the dilapidated home of his elderly neighbor, Mario Cavaioli.
The program was meant to bring substandard housing into compliance with applicable codes, but the commission stated that Mazzarella violated the law by having the 81-year-old’s home renovated ahead of other waiting applicants.
Mazzarella said he wanted to appeal, but his lawyer advised him to pay the fine and move on in order to avoid an ugly, expensive court battle. He knew Cavaioli well and had taken care of him over the years because he lived alone. But he claims he never directed any city employee to put Cavaioli at the top of the list, and said he was simply prioritized for the funds because he qualified for the program and demonstrated a high level of need for the services.
Despite the ethics ruling, Mazzarella rolled to yet another reelection victory the following year.
“If people generally like you, they’ll forgive things. We’re all imperfect,” Bodanza said. “When they don’t like you, then those things are your downfall.”
In 1999, Mazzarella led efforts to buy and preserve the city’s last, beloved apple orchard after the land was listed for sale. Sholan Farms (pictured) became one of only two city-owned apple orchards in Massachusetts. Though it is managed by a nonprofit organization today, Mazzarella and city staff spent the first year picking apples and selling them at City Hall. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
The mayor’s go-getter attitude hasn’t always been met with praise. During the 2005 mayoral election, Mazzarella’s opponent, Peter Angelini – who outraised and outspent him by more than a two-to-one margin – accused him of “falling in love with every development he sees.” Though Mazzarella won that election by 30 points, some residents and city leaders still share that sentiment today.
His support for certain projects has led to citywide controversy – most recently over a plan to construct more than 300 multifamily residential units on wooded land next to a major shopping plaza.
During a planning board meeting last summer, the development drew the usual litany of opposition from residents citing the added traffic and strain on local school enrollment. But others, including Susan Chalifoux-Zephir – the only city councilor to vote against the zoning change that made the project possible – raised concerns about the affordability of the housing units, which would rent for approximately $2,500 to $3,000 a month. Chalifoux-Zephir, one of the only councilors who regularly tangles with the mayor, said “all growth isn’t the best kind of growth,” and told CommonWealth Beacon she wishes others in city government would question the 32-year incumbent more often.
Mazzarella said Leominster needs all types of housing, from high-end to low- and moderate-cost – diving into the debate over development and market-rate housing that has landed in many Gateway Cities.
“If the city doesn’t grow, it will die,” Mazzarella said.  
In 2025, a proposed horse racetrack and sports gambling bar that would have been built on a capped landfill in Leominster drew intense scrutiny from local residents and leaders. They raised environmental and traffic concerns and argued that gambling would invite a host of negative activities to the family-oriented city. The city council ultimately voted 9-0 against the proposal, which Mazzarella initially supported but later took a neutral stance on.  
“It’s a nice city, and people like it the way it is. They don’t want to see it change,” Mazzarella said. “But I have to look for all the revenue sources, and when somebody comes to me and says the city can get up to $3 million a year, I have to take a look.”
Mazzarella walks into Allen’s Department Store on Main Street in Leominster where he said he buys his shirts. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Leominster hosts nearly 40 annual celebrations, events, and family-friendly festivals – many of which have been championed by Mazzarella over the years. During the city’s Winter Stroll, he roasts chestnuts over a fire while dressed in a top hat and coat reminiscent of a bygone era. On Groundhog Day, he stands in the snow with a pink flamingo ornament – which replaces Punxsutawney Phil – and declares whether the city will see six more weeks of winter. And at the city’s annual Italian Festival, he can be found enjoying a cannoli or two.
“Some people tell me I spend too much time on flowers and festivals, but that’s the fabric. That’s what brings people here, and that’s what they’re proud of,” he said.
Mazzarella stands outside of his old junior high in Leominster. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Though a Mazzarella reelection run every two years now seems like a reliable way to mark time in Leominster, the mayor insists that he goes through a deliberative decision-making process toward the end of every term. “Each time around, I do the whole self-evaluation thing. Am I holding the city back? Can I still do the job? Can I get to all these events? Am I still in touch?” Mazzarella said. “As of right now, I still think I am.”
Bodanza, the longtime city councilor, recalled a time in 2015 when he and the mayor dug up a time capsule that was buried in Leominster in 1915. When they finished, they replaced it with a new capsule to be opened in 2115.
“Dean said it was too bad we wouldn’t be around in 100 years when they open it,” Bodanza said. “I told him not to worry – he’d probably still be mayor.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska providers say childcare gap is growing
description: In Alaska, the gap between the need for childcare and the availability of services is growing, according to providers and national data. Some sources estimate it’s costing the state millions each year.  An estimated 55% of Alaska children lack reasonable access to child care, according to data compiled by the national non-profit advocacy group First […]
text:
Palmer Head Start teacher Moriah Morris sits with children. (Photo courtesy of Mark Lackey)In Alaska, the gap between the need for childcare and the availability of services is growing, according to providers and national data. Some sources estimate it’s costing the state millions each year. 
An estimated 55% of Alaska children lack reasonable access to child care, according to data compiled by the national non-profit advocacy group First Five Years Fund. Alaska childcare providers say state and federal funding to support programs is insufficient — and that rising costs mean they are able to offer less and less.
In Alaska, 60% of children have all available parents in the workforce. The cost of center-based childcare is an estimated $12,425 and over $11,000 for home-based childcare each year. 
Federal and state programs provide funding for childcare and early education, but there is only enough funding to serve a fraction of eligible families in Alaska — and cost and availability of providers range widely across rural and urban regions of the state.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough region, Head Start programs that serve children from infancy to age five have had to decrease the number of children served by 38% in the last five years due to insufficient funding, said Mark Lackey, executive director of CSS Early Learning, which operates four sites in Palmer, Wasilla and Fairview. 
“Because funding was not sufficient to cover inflation, from federal and state, and so our only option has been to ask the feds permission to serve fewer children while keeping our same amount of dollars,” he said. 
“We are in the fastest-growing area of Alaska,” he added. “And we have been for many, many years. We have had waiting lists that entire time.”
Lackey estimates 40% to 50% of children in his Head Start programs are in foster care or unhoused. Those children are bumped to the top of the waitlist, followed by children with disabilities and from low income families. He said it’s well-known that the need for childcare in the region far outweighs the combined 230 slots they have available. 
Statewide, an estimated 21% of eligible Alaska children from infancy to age three are served by Early Head Start, and 52% of eligible children from ages three to five are served by Head Start statewide in 2025, according to data from the national Office of Head Start. 
Alaska’s 17 Head Start programs are funded through various state and federal funding sources. Lackey said Head Start received a 1% cost of living increase in federal funding this year. Federal funds for Head Start totalled $68.6 million this year, plus $13 million in state grants provided through the Alaska Department of Education and Early Development. 
Lackey said federal and state funding have remained flat while costs have increased, including prices for food, utilities, fuel, employee salaries and health insurance. 
“The cost of health insurance is just staggering,” he said. “So we’ve had to slowly give our employees less quality health insurance, you know, higher deductibles. Just like every business in Alaska, we have to make those same sacrifices, which makes recruiting and retaining our workforce even harder.”
This fiscal year, Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed $6.4 million for childcare provider recruitment and retention grants that was approved by the Legislature. He approved a total of $20.4 million for child care assistance. He also vetoed $3.7 million in additional funding for Head Start programs, retaining $16.75 million this year. 
In his veto summary, the governor cited the need to preserve funds to support long-term fiscal stability. A spokesperson for Dunleavy’s office said on Wednesday that a bill the governor introduced, but that failed to advance in the Senate would have boosted the unemployment insurance trust fund, which supports grants for training and workforce development. 
“The bill could have easily funded childcare services using surplus UI trust funds but for some reason the Legislature passed on this opportunity,” said Jeff Turner, communications director for Dunleavy, by email. 
“That funding was crucial,” Lackey said of the vetoed money. “We can’t charge parents any more because they have all of these same inflationary pressures, and childcare already is expensive just to make the bottom lines work out.”
On the Kenai Peninsula, Laurie Mead has been working in early childcare for over 40 years and operates a licensed home-based child care business, Kyrie N’ Friends, serving 12 children.
“Right now, it’s just gotten harder and harder to find anyone that wants to work in the field of early childhood. It can be very rewarding, but at the same time, it’s high stress, low pay,” she said.
Mead said on average children are in her care for 10 hours a day, and while she wants to keep employees long term to maintain consistency for the children and families she has to compete with other employers who can offer higher wages and better benefits.
“It’s just a hard, hard thing to navigate. And you know, unfortunately, I would love to do it just because I love the kids, but I also need to make a wage as well,” she said.
Mead said she has a long waitlist, particularly for infants and toddlers, and some families have signed on to her waitlist as soon as they get pregnant. She said the cost of her daycare — $1,100 for an infant per month — is above what families receive in childcare assistance. 
Mead said she wants to see more state investment because childcare is essential for families. 
“It’s huge for them because they couldn’t put food on their table if they had one income. They just can’t do it,” she said. “It’s unfortunate, with inflation and things the way they are in America, not just Alaska. It takes two working parents now.”
Lost wages, tax revenue 
The economic burden of the childcare gap is felt by households in lost wages, lost revenue for businesses and lost tax revenue. 
According to a 2025 analysis from the non-profit advocacy group Child Care Trust, the earnings loss for households in Alaska over ten years is an estimated $1.1 billion. 
For Joanne Glaves, a 29-year old single mother based in Wasilla, state childcare assistance and enrolling her two-year-old at Meadow Lakes Head Start operated by CSS Early Learning was crucial for her to be able to work and support her family. But she is one of a diminishing number of parents who have access to care.
“My mom had been caring for him while I was going to work, and she got sick suddenly and had to go to the hospital. And so, I lost childcare, and I ended up losing my job. And I had no idea that Head Start even existed until I started doing my own research, and I found them, and reached out,” she said. 
Glaves said with state assistance, she pays $71 per month, and works full time as a peer support specialist for homeless youth at MY House in Wasilla. 
“It meant the world to me, and you can’t really put a number on it when you’re under such high stress,” she said. “And just knowing he was in a safe place and really getting, I think, the best care there is at Head Start because they have developmental check-ins and things like that, and they also connect you to community resources. So they really changed my life.”
Glaves said she was inspired to get involved with Head Start and now volunteers on several parent advisory boards and this year traveled to Juneau and to Washington D.C. to advocate for more support for Head Start programs.
“It’s the foundation of our society and our communities,” she said. “If we don’t take care of the children, then what does that future look like?”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Immigrant protection accord includes state, local enforcement rules
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: The compromise bill takes a broader approach to "sensitive locations," expanding protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests from courthouses to include public schools, child care centers, and health care facilities.
text:
LEGISLATIVE NEGOTIATORS ON Wednesday unveiled a compromise on the closely watched bill that would broaden protections against federal immigration enforcement, while preserving one key area of cooperation with federal authorities. 
The conference committee agreement (H 5620) was filed Wednesday after 4 p.m., and earlier in the day lawmakers described its contents at a State House press conference ahead of expected House and Senate votes later this week. 
Conferees said the compromise adopts the Senate’s broader approach to “sensitive locations,” expanding protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests from courthouses to include public schools, child care centers, and health care facilities. 
It also codifies the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court’s 2017 Lunn v. Commonwealth decision; bars new agreements allowing state and local officials to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions; and preserves the Department of Correction’s existing partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“This bill prioritizes the safety of immigrants and all Massachusetts residents from the weaponization of the federal immigration enforcement by the Trump administration,” Senate conference chair Cindy Friedman said, describing a lengthy list of provisions included in the compromise. 
Among them, she said, are new protections at “sensitive community locations,” a prohibition on new 287(g) agreements, restrictions on questioning people about immigration status during routine policing, new civil liability for Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, oversight of immigration detention agreements, protections for victims of crime, and expanded safeguards for people held in state custody. 
The conference committee was tasked with reconciling differences between bills the House and Senate approved this spring. 
One of the most significant centered on where ICE officers could conduct warrantless civil immigration arrests. The House bill protected state courthouses, while the Senate extended those protections to additional settings. 
Asked how legislators landed on the broader Senate approach, House conference chair Rep. Dan Cahill joked, “I lost.” 
Friedman said evolving reports of immigration enforcement activity drove negotiators to expand the bill. 
“The House created a bill that was very, very – it was real solid”, she said. “Once that was passed, though, lots of other information started to come out.” 
“We started to see and hear about people going to pick up their kids in school and being taken off the streets, things happening in courthouses where ICE was coming into a courthouse and just picking somebody up while they were in the middle of a trial or there to be a victim,” she continued. “We started to look at how can we ensure protections in all the places that we have some control over.” 
Responding to concerns about whether child care or health care providers would realistically be able to enforce those protections, Friedman said the compromise provides additional clarity. 
“The concern is, if you’re faced with an ICE agent, you’re a childcare worker, what do you do?” she said. “I think the language has helped to clarify that and detail what happens in those situations.” 
Negotiators also settled another divide over 287(g) agreements which authorize state or local law enforcement agencies to perform certain federal immigration enforcement actions. 
The House bill would have allowed a limited pathway for new criminal-purpose agreements with state approval. The Senate version prohibited all new, expanded or renewed agreements.
According to the conferees, the compromise adopts the Senate’s approach by prohibiting new agreements while preserving the Department of Correction’s longstanding 287(g) partnership with ICE. 
Asked why the existing DOC agreement remains intact, Cahill said lawmakers thought it reduced the likelihood that ICE would conduct enforcement operations in neighborhoods while searching for people already facing deportation after serving felony sentences. 
“Those folks, there’s not much protection, if any, under any immigration laws to prevent ICE from deporting them,” Cahill said. Rather than requiring federal agents to locate those individuals after release, he said the existing agreement “allows a safe transfer of folks who are going to be faced with imminent deportation.”
He added that conferees were concerned about the broader enforcement tactics they said they observed. 
“We don’t want ICE having to search for these folks in our communities… and we certainly don’t want them using it as an excuse to go and not only seek that individual, but anyone who happens to be around,” Cahill said. 
Rep. Andy Vargas said preserving the DOC agreement was consistent with the original proposal developed by the Black and Latino Caucus after hearing concerns from immigrant communities. 
“We heard feedback that, hey, they were coming to look for some guy that we knew committed a serious crime, but in looking for him, they picked up all these other people that just happened to be in the vicinity,” Vargas said.
The compromise also writes into statute principles established by the Supreme Judicial Court in Lunn v. Commonwealth, which held that Massachusetts officers lack the authority to detain someone solely based on a federal civil immigration detainer unless state law authorizes it. 
Friedman said the bill goes beyond relying on court precedent by placing those limits directly in statute. 
“Lunn was a court decision, and it basically clarified that it is not the role of state or local government to engage in immigration enforcement,” she said. “That is a federal responsibility.”
The legislation would also expressly prohibit officers from asking about a person’s immigration or citizenship status during routine traffic stops solely for immigration enforcement purposes. 
Asked how that provision would be enforced, Friedman replied simply, “By law.”
The agreement requires formal acceptance by both branches before it can be sent to Gov. Maura Healey, who earlier Wednesday said the measure was “top of mind” and expressed hope it would reach her desk before the Legislature concludes scheduled formal sessions this week.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Democrats may be unable to rank presidential primary under proposed DNC rule
description: Maine Democratic leaders are raising alarms after a national party committee gave initial approval to a rule that would prevent the state from using ranked choice voting in presidential primaries.  Ahead of the full Democratic National Committee meeting Aug. 13-15, the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee has met several times to finalize the 2028 presidential [[...]
text:
During the March 2024 primary election, Democratic voters in Maine were asked to rank the presidential candidates. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Maine Democratic leaders are raising alarms after a national party committee gave initial approval to a rule that would prevent the state from using ranked choice voting in presidential primaries. 
Ahead of the full Democratic National Committee meeting Aug. 13-15, the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee has met several times to finalize the 2028 presidential primary delegate selection process. 
That included a meeting in May where the committee voted 28-14 to add new language to the section governing “Fair Reflection of Presidential Preference” that states: “No ballot used for purposes of allocation of delegates among presidential preference shall permit voters to express more than one presidential preference. Where state law provides for multiple presidential preferences in a primary, only the first round will be considered for delegate allocation purposes.”
That means that for a state like Maine that uses ranked choice voting for presidential primaries, the party will not count the full results — instead it will determine delegates based solely on voters’ first round selections. 
Kyle Bailey, former state representative and advocate for ranked choice voting, said that despite state law allowing ranked choice voting, the DNC is trying to pressure Maine Democrats to ignore it.
“That’s problematic to me,” Bailey said. “That a national private organization would try to steamroll the Maine people, Maine Legislature and ignore the will of the people.”
In a statement, committee co-chair Jim Roosevelt said ranked choice voting is incompatible with the party’s delegate allocation process. 
“However, the Rules and Bylaws Committee respects the right of every state to make their own decisions on important voting procedures, which is why the rules include clear guidance for states with statutory requirements like Maine,” Roosevelt said. “We look forward to working with the Maine Democratic Party to ensure every Mainer’s voice is heard in the 2028 presidential primary.”
The Maine Legislature passed a bill in January 2020 to expand ranked choice voting to presidential elections and primaries. That bill passed into law without Gov. Janet Mills’ signature, which meant the law did not take effect until after the March presidential primary, in which former President Joe Biden won with 34.1%, defeating U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders by less than 3,000 votes.
The law was in full effect for the state’s 2024 Democratic presidential primary, but only two candidates were on the ballot: Biden and Dean Phillips. And in that case Biden — who ended up being replaced by Vice President Kamala Harris on the ticket — won more than 80% of the vote, so the primary did not have to go to a ranked choice tabulation. 
Bailey said that under the DNC proposal, Maine Democrats would still have a ranked choice ballot for the presidential primary — because it’s required under state law — which would likely confuse voters. 
“If I go to the polls and I pick a candidate — I will have a ranked choice ballot, because the law of Maine uses the ranked choice ballot, that’s not going to change — but I rank my choices one through whatever. What the DNC is saying is that only my first choice will count,” Bailey said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
DNC rules dictate that a state assigns delegates to presidential candidates in proportion to the percentage of votes a candidate won in the primary — as long as a candidate received at least 15% of the vote. Any candidate that doesn’t meet the 15% threshold will not be awarded any delegates at the nominating convention. 
The party says that 15% threshold is the main conflict with ranked choice voting. Under ranked choice voting, the winner of an election must get more than 50% of the votes. After counting all first round votes, if no candidate reaches 50%, the candidate in last place is eliminated and those votes are reallocated to each voters’ second choice. That process continues until someone surpasses 50%. 
At the May committee meeting, Frank Leone, the committee member who proposed the language for the rule change, said his goal was to give states clear guidance on the role of ranked choice voting. 
“Now, personally, I’m not really a fan of ranked choice voting, but this motion doesn’t address ranked choice voting in general,” Leone said. “There may be times when ranked choice voting is appropriate, and in fact, if we had a winner-take-all system, where you had to reduce a field to one person, it might make sense. Where it doesn’t make sense is in our delegate selection process, and there’s been a national effort to get states to adopt ranked choice voting for presidential primaries, as well as everything else.”
But Bailey said there are other ways to align ranked choice voting with the party rules. He suggested that after the first round calculations, all candidates that fall under 15% could be eliminated in one batch, and their votes reallocated. Once that is done, the count could stop without requiring tabulations to reach the 50% marker. 
That would preserve the DNC rules and keep all the benefits of ranked choice voting, Bailey said.
“It makes sure their voice is heard, their vote’s never wasted,” Bailey said. “And allows candidates to run who might otherwise be told that they’re not viable. Because there’s no worry about wasting your vote or having to vote strategically. It just all goes away, and it gives voters the freedom to vote their hopes and not their fears.” 
Leone said during the May meeting that the proposed rule change wouldn’t prevent states from using ranked choice voting in other elections.
“Everybody who’s doing ranked choice voting can continue to do it, except for when it comes to our delegate selection process,” Leone said. “The state law has to be consistent with our rules, or else our rules govern.”
At that meeting, committee members also discussed the importance of having consistent rules and a uniform system across states for the presidential primary. 
But Bailey said that’s simply not realistic, regardless of how ranked choice voting factors in. 
“I think there’s 50 different states and at least 50 different ways of running elections,” Bailey said. “So the sort of glossing over the reality that states have control over elections and that we have local control of elections, it’s just how we do elections in the United States, and I don’t think that a national organization should try to prescribe to individual states and voters and legislatures to tell them how they can and can’t run elections.”
Some committee members agreed, including Michael Kapp, a representative from California.
“To sit here and tell these state parties that they can’t use a system their own voters chose — that’s not party rule,” Kapp said. “That’s a veto over the democratic will of millions of people.”
Bailey said the national party should instead be working to involve voters and encourage changes like ranked choice voting. 
“The DNC in particular should embrace reforms like ranked choice voting that bring more people into the primary process, that excite voters, that electrify the base of the party and bring more people into the process to have more voices heard,” Bailey said. “That’s what political parties should be aiming to achieve, is to have a more vibrant, exciting democracy and ranked choice voting enables that.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Northeast Kansas education board candidates share ideas for funding, local control, technology
description: TOPEKA — While the Democrat running for the Kansas State Board of Education’s northeast district wants the state to fully fund special education, the Republican candidate says the board should investigate spending first. The Legislature has not met its obligation to fund 92% of special education costs since the 2010-2011 school year, according to the […]
text:
Democrat Jennifer Lloyd, left, and Republican Amy Cawvey will oppose each other in the November general election to represent Kansas' northeastern corner on the Kansas State Board of Education. (Kansas Reflector composite from photos submitted by the candidates)TOPEKA — While the Democrat running for the Kansas State Board of Education’s northeast district wants the state to fully fund special education, the Republican candidate says the board should investigate spending first.
The Legislature has not met its obligation to fund 92% of special education costs since the 2010-2011 school year, according to the Kansas State Department of Education, which estimated the state fell short of its obligation this current fiscal year by $226 million. In May, four Johnson County school districts announced plans to sue the state for the deficit.
Democrat Jennifer Lloyd, of Ozawkie, and Republican Amy Cawvey, of Lansing, disagree about funding plans. But they both hope to support local control and limit digital technology — in different ways.
Lloyd said fully funding special education is vital.
“Not funding the special ed is what is causing so much crisis in all of the schools, in public schools right now,” she said. “We’re having to use general funds to cover special ed, and then that’s pulling away from all of the kids.”
Cawvey said she has seen schools throw the budget “out the window” and wants to audit special education spending records.
“Yes, it will cost taxpayer dollars,” she said. “But I think it would be well worth it before we just say we need more money.”
 
The candidates
Lloyd, a librarian at Jefferson West School District, grew up attending Jefferson County public schools and earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in education and library science at Emporia State University. Before becoming a librarian, she taught special education and fifth grade in the same northeast state board district.
Financially supporting teachers is central to her candidacy.
“Our teachers are spending so much money, their own money,” and then not getting the pay raises that they need to be able to keep doing this,” she said.
Jennifer Lloyd, right, campaigns at a community event in Oskaloosa. (Photo submitted by Jennifer Lloyd)
Cawvey volunteers as the Kansas chair of the National School Boards Coalition and previously served on the Lansing school board. Years ago, her husband’s role in the military moved their family to several states across the country, including Hawaii. Wherever they went, she said, she volunteered at her children’s schools as a substitute teacher or in parent-teacher organizations.
She said her experiences in diverse school districts gave her insight into school systems.
“We were in some poor school districts and some districts that had more money,” she said. “We just did the best with what we had and got to know the staff and everyone.”
Amy Cawvey, right, campaigns at a Republican convention. (Photo submitted by Amy Cawvey)
The northeast district Lloyd and Cawvey aim to represent is one of the state board’s 10 districts. Five seats are up for reelection this year. All five Republican incumbents declined to seek reelection. Because Democrats hold the majority of the other five seats, Kansas voters could switch the board’s GOP majority.
 
Local control
The state board oversees Kansas K-12 public schools while working with local school districts — responsible for applying the state board’s standards — and the Legislature — responsible for state funding.
Both candidates said they want to maintain local control by improving the state board’s coordination with the Legislature, which considered bills in the 2026 session to impose certain curricula, such as lessons on communism and an annual fitness test.
Gov. Laura Kelly vetoed those bills, but she signed one to bar students from using their cellphones at school. The law requires districts to securely store students’ phones without providing funding for a storage method.
While both candidates said cellphone policies work best under local control, they disagree about the ban.
Cawvey said lawmakers got involved because local districts and the state board failed to set effective rules.
“It was implemented some at a local level, but then it wasn’t consistent,” she said. “The state board in the middle also needs to work. And they didn’t issue a lot of guidance on that either. They didn’t do as much as I felt they could.”
Lloyd said the Legislature’s ban prevented the state board from setting a cellphone standard.
“Instead of letting the schools, the state board having a recommendation and coming down to the local level, the local levels are now having to react,” she said. “So it’s causing some financial burdens on some of the districts to handle the cellphone ban.”
 
Digital technology
Both candidates want to address technology in the classroom if elected by limiting young students’ access to screens and making recommendations to schools soon.
Specifically, Lloyd said the state board should set standards regarding the one to one student device ratio schools implemented during COVID-19 and have continued.
“The local levels are spending money on technology, and so we need to get ahead of that and make sure the local boards see where the state board is,” Lloyd said.
Those recommendations by the state board, she said, should limit younger students’ access to technology in a way that transitions into greater access as students get older.
Cawvey wants to limit screens for all students. And, she said, local districts and state board should address technology soon before the state does.
“I would suggest,” Cawvey said, “if I was on a local board now, to go ahead and start implementing that now, because that’s kind of what happened with the cellphones.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Caregiver criminally charged with dependent adult abuse of autistic teenager
description: A central Iowa caregiver accused of kicking and punching an autistic teenager is now facing criminal charges of dependent adult abuse. State records indicate Falisha Turner, 47, of Des Moines was employed by as a care professional by Home Instead, an in-home care provider, earlier this year. The company provides daily living assistance for people […]
text:
Iowa Workforce Development manages unemployment claims filed on behalf of Iowans. (Photo by Getty Images, logo courtesy the State of Iowa)A central Iowa caregiver accused of kicking and punching an autistic teenager is now facing criminal charges of dependent adult abuse.
State records indicate Falisha Turner, 47, of Des Moines was employed by as a care professional by Home Instead, an in-home care provider, earlier this year. The company provides daily living assistance for people with disabilities, usually in residential settings.
According to court and state unemployment records, Turner was driving a home-care client on March 14, 2026, when she was pulled over by police, who informed her there was an arrest warrant for her related to an incident that had occurred days earlier when Turner was working for a different company. She was then charged with dependent adult abuse.
Court records indicate Turner was accused by police of punching an 18-year-old autistic woman in the face “multiple times in the face, and kicking her in the chest, causing physical injury.” The incident allegedly happened at a Waukee residence owned by Watchtower Investment Group, a company that provides affordable housing for people with disabilities.
Two days after her arrest, Turner was fired from Home Instead after being placed on the state’s adult abuse registry, which made it impossible for her maintain employment as a caregiver for that or any other Iowa company. A judge later denied Turner’s application for unemployment benefits, citing her placement on the registry.
Turner has pleaded not guilty to the charge of dependent adult abuse and a pretrial conference is scheduled for Sept. 11, 2026.
Turner told the Iowa Capital Dispatch that a state abuse investigator told her there was video of her attacking the alleged victim and that a supervisor had also witnessed the incident. Turner said she was never shown any video and that she suspects the supervisor fabricated the allegations to cover up her own role in the matter.
“I never punched that lady. I never punched her, I never choked her, I never chased her,” Turner said, adding that there had been a physical altercation that resulted in her trying to “break free” of the teenager who was grabbing at her clothes, neck and hair.
“The only thing I tried to do was run out the door,” Turner said.



Other recent unemployment cases
Other Iowans recently accused of workplace misconduct include:
— Haley Sly, who worked as a certified medication aide for Accura Healthcare of Cascade, a nursing home, until she was fired on May 1, 2026. State records show the facility alleged Sly had asked a resident of the home to come to the dining room to eat dinner, and that the resident declined. A certified nursing aide later alleged Sly grabbed the resident and pulled them up out of their chair and forcibly transported them to the dining table. The home’s administration investigated the matter and found that the resident had sustained “substantial bruising” due to Sly’s rough handling.
Sly was fired and applied for unemployment benefits, which led to a recent hearing before Administrative Law Judge Elizabeth Johnson. In ruling that Sly was ineligible for benefits, Johnson stated that Sly’s conduct amounted to abuse and a violation of workplace rules. She also ordered Sly to repay the $3,570 in unemployment benefits already collected.
— Alexander Gully, who worked as a full-time paraeducator at Butler Elementary School in the Fort Dodge Community School District from August 2023 through May 2026, when he was fired. The district alleged that while removing a fifth-grade student with special needs from the classroom due to misbehavior, Gully hoisted the 10-year-old child off the floor by one of the child’s arms, then carried the child in that manner while exiting the room and placing the child in a hallway chair. Gully’s alleged handling of the child left marks on the child’s arm, which triggered a complaint by the child’s mother.
Administrative Law Judge James Timberland recently ruled Gully was ineligible for unemployment benefits due to workplace misconduct. Gully, Timberland ruled, had chosen to disregard the district’s deescalation protocols “and elected instead to handle a 10-year-old student in a physically abusive manner in violation of district policy. There was no excuse or justification for (his) conduct.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Monitoring and curbing West Nile virus takes more than a mosquito truck
description: Mosquito trucks and equipment from Harrison County.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Wendy Varnado still remembers running behind the mosquito trucks. When she was a child in Edwards, in western Hinds County, in the 1980s, the trucks sprayed a haze of chemicals that mixed with engine smoke to create a dense fog the neighborhood children played in.
These days, mosquito trucks spray an ultra low volume mist that is nearly invisible, and Varnado, the Mississippi state public health entomologist, sees them in a different light. They’re now a tool she can harness against mosquito-borne diseases, including the most common one in Mississippi, West Nile virus.
There are now five confirmed human cases of West Nile virus in Mississippi this year in Hancock, Lincoln and Madison counties. This number is an undercount, Varnado said, because only a small percentage of cases are severe enough to send patients to the hospital where they can be tested. 
While people can be infected with West Nile throughout the mosquito season, human diagnoses peak in August and early September. As Mississippi reports more positive cases of West Nile virus in mosquitoes, an early indicator of impending human infections, experts emphasize the importance of local surveillance and reducing mosquito breeding grounds.
The majority of people who get infected with West Nile virus don’t show any symptoms, said Santos Portugal, an urban entomologist at Mississippi State University. About one in five will develop symptoms like a fever, headaches and body aches. Less than one in a 100 may develop a severe disease that spreads into the nervous system and can cause swelling in the brain. Elderly and immunocompromised people are at higher risk for complications, including chronic fatigue, memory loss and in rare cases, death.
“Mississippians should recognize that West Nile virus is very serious,” Portugal said. “(It’s) not something people should necessarily be afraid of, just something to be understood and do what you can to protect yourself.”
Surveillance and control
Having up-to-date counts of where mosquitoes are infected with West Nile virus is one of the most powerful tools for disease prevention, Varnado told Mississippi Today.
“The mosquitoes tell you everything,” she said. “You can have at least a two week lead time on human cases by monitoring mosquito population, and two weeks is a long time to be able to do some intervention work.”
Out of 82 counties in Mississippi, only 11 have programs to routinely trap mosquitoes and send samples to the Mississippi Department of Health for testing. Nine have reported mosquitoes with West Nile virus.
The patchwork surveillance effort all goes back to funding, Varnado said. Some states have special “mosquito control districts” and raise money through local taxes for their mosquito programs, but Mississippi does not. Many counties contract with an external pest management company for their mosquito control. 
Gravid traps collect female egg-bearing mosquitoes, which can then be tested for West Nile virus. Credit: Courtesy of Wendy Varnado
Harrison County is one of the few counties with a dedicated mosquito control program that includes surveillance, mosquito control and education efforts. Director Gene Fayard has a seven person team, including someone dedicated to setting up traps across the county. 
Every week, his team sorts through the collected mosquitoes and sends vials with female mosquitos to the Mississippi Department of Health, which has equipment to test for West Nile and the less common Zika and Chikungunya diseases.
Other personnel handle mosquito management. Mosquito trucks break up a liquid “adulticide” into micron sized droplets that kills adult mosquitoes upon contact. Another option is “larvacide,” which attacks mosquitoes in their juvenile stage. Many larvicides, including the ones found in stores, are based on naturally occurring bacteria that specifically target mosquitoes. 
Of the two methods, larvicide is cheaper, more efficient and often better for the environment, Varnado said. Mosquitoes breed in or around standing water, and in their active months of roughly April to October, a ditch by the side of the road can contain thousands of larvae. 
“It’s just easier to kill a million when they’re in a pothole,” she said.
But, she added, people like to see the mosquito truck, a tangible sign that mosquito control efforts are taking place. 
“The spray truck isn’t the end all be all,” she cautioned. “It’s the surveillance and it’s the larviciding and it’s those prevention and source reduction activities. That’s where you’re gonna get all the bang for your buck.”
Be aware, but ‘don’t be a hermit’
The mosquito species that carries West Nile in Mississippi is Culex quinquefasciatus, also known as the southern house mosquito. As the name suggests, this species is commonly found around human dwellings. 
“This is an urban breeder,” Varnado said. “Things you do around your home make a difference with this mosquito.”
Vials of mosquito samples ready for disease testing. Each pooled sample has up to 50 mosquitoes from one mosquito trap.  Credit: Courtesy of Wendy Varnado
Portugal, who has a focus on mosquito education, said he encourages people to clean up potential breeding grounds around their home. 
He’s met people who didn’t realize the ‘wiggly things in the bucket of water behind the shed’ are actually mosquito larvae, and that dumping the bucket could reduce the presence of mosquitoes around their home. Other common culprits are clogged gutters and storm drains filled with organic matter such as grass clippings. 
The southern house mosquito likes “stinky water” and like most mosquitoes, doesn’t fly far.
“If you go outside and you’re just getting pelted by mosquitoes, depending on the species, there’s a good chance that the breeding source is actually pretty close to where you are,” he said. 
The Harrison County mosquito program also does outreach, including at local schools and community events. They got their first positive mosquito samples in late July, although no human cases yet. As much as he wants people to be aware of the mosquito-borne illnesses, Fayard keeps the danger in perspective. Because there is a relatively small chance of developing a severe case, he doesn’t want to discourage people from spending time outside.
“Use repellent, try not to be outdoors at dusk and dawn. That’s the most active time,” he said. “Long pants when possible, but don’t panic, don’t stay inside and be a hermit.”

title: How does Delaware operate without a sales tax? The state’s corporate franchise has it covered
