name: Missouri Independent
title: What Missouri officials didn’t explain about an LGBTQ+ library story time
description: Denny Hoskins wants to cut a library’s funding over two books he has not read. He Googled them, saw excerpts and looked at some pictures. For Missouri’s secretary of state, that was enough. The books are “Rainbowsaurus,” the tale of a family searching for a rainbow dinosaur, and “Big Wig,” about a child who wins […]
text:
State Sen. Rick Brattin, a Republican from Harrisonville, and Secretary of State Denny Hoskins speak to reporters outside Hoskins's office in the Missouri State Capitol Tuesday. The press conference also drew in LGBTQ+ advocates who criticized the two officials for attacks on a "rainbow story time" held in Columbia Saturday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Denny Hoskins wants to cut a library’s funding over two books he has not read.
He Googled them, saw excerpts and looked at some pictures. For Missouri’s secretary of state, that was enough.
The books are “Rainbowsaurus,” the tale of a family searching for a rainbow dinosaur, and “Big Wig,” about a child who wins a costume contest in drag. Staff at a Columbia library read them aloud to toddlers and preschoolers during a “rainbow story time” attended by families who chose to be there.
The additional cost to Daniel Boone Regional Library for the event was $26 — $18 for a prop wig and $8 for contact paper. Everything else came from resources the public already owns.
When Hoskins learned of the event, he warned the library that if the “inappropriate endeavor” went forward, he would use his authority over the Missouri State Library to block every dollar of state and federal funding he could from future events.
The library read the books anyway.
Missouri Republicans threaten library funding over ‘rainbow story time’

And thus, a press conference was quickly convened.
Hoskins stood beside Rick Brattin, a state senator running for Congress, with a warning letter from Attorney General Catherine Hanaway providing the legal backdrop. Together, they brought the machinery of state government to bear on a Saturday morning story time for preschoolers.
The accusations were stark.
They described the story time as an effort to groom children. Hoskins called the event “unconscionable, if not criminal.”
But grooming is not even the standard in the criminal laws Hanaway cited in her letter to the library. The attorney general acknowledged the library’s right to determine its own programming and said she was prepared to act only if a program broke the law — pointing to statutes against giving minors pornography or displaying explicit sexual material in public.
So reporters asked Hoskins and Brattin the obvious question: Did these two books meet that bar?
Neither would say they did. Brattin argued the books carried “a message that’s meant to sexualize” and were intended to normalize a “lifestyle” and lower children’s defenses.
But the local prosecutor Hanaway copied on her letter to the library had already explained where the legal line lies. Roger Johnson, the Boone County prosecutor, told KOMU it is not a crime to talk about LGBTQ+ issues. The state laws concern depictions of sexual activity, not gender identity.
Told of the prosecutor’s view at the press conference, Hoskins responded that by that logic, “pornography is OK to be talked about because it’s a First Amendment right.”
If the story time is legal, he said, he will work with the legislature “to ensure this is illegal in the future.”
Politicians propose restrictions on legal conduct all the time. That’s not the notable part. The sequence is.
An attorney general’s warning, a secretary of state’s threat to the library’s funding and repeated accusations of grooming and criminality — all without anyone identifying conduct that violated the laws they invoked.
Tuesday’s press conference wasn’t an announcement that the library had violated the law. It was an announcement that officials wanted the law to prohibit what the library had done.
And rewriting the statute would not necessarily settle the matter. If government funding were withheld because officials objected to the viewpoint expressed in the library’s programming, that would raise a separate First Amendment question.
So here is where it stands.
Hoskins and Brattin have elected offices and the megaphone that comes with them. What they don’t have, at least according to the local prosecutor, is a crime.
The library’s side of the ledger is simpler.
Two books, one wig, some contact paper.
Twenty-six dollars.

name: Michigan Advance
title: What juvenile defense means for Michigan
authors: Jason Smith, Kristen Staley, Peter Cunningham
description: In 2023, a landmark legislative package passed, introducing significant reforms to Michigan’s juvenile justice system. The Justice for Kids and Communities Act initially contained 20 bills based on the recommendations of the Task Force on Juvenile Justice Reform. In the end, 19 bills passed the state legislature with bipartisan support, leaving legislation t[...]
text:
luoman/Getty ImagesIn 2023, a landmark legislative package passed, introducing significant reforms to Michigan’s juvenile justice system. The Justice for Kids and Communities Act initially contained 20 bills based on the recommendations of the Task Force on Juvenile Justice Reform. In the end, 19 bills passed the state legislature with bipartisan support, leaving legislation that would protect youths’ right to counsel behind.
Three years later, after relentless advocacy for advocates, attorneys, policymakers, and the community, that 20th bill was just signed into law by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, introducing new reforms to Michigan juvenile defense services. The Michigan Indigent Defense Commission (MIDC) now has the authority to establish statewide standards for juvenile defense services, bringing oversight, quality improvement, and support to defense attorneys.
For our justice-impacted children, this isn’t just a policy victory.
 Kids deserve experienced counsel
Juvenile court and the laws specific to juveniles are not the same as adult court. There are differences in language, circumstance, intention, and outcomes that matter, especially to the child facing court. Michigan’s children are entitled to a vigorous defense from the attorneys that represent them.
With the passage of this bill, the MIDC will be empowered to establish standards that mean that lawyers will have the time, resources and training to ensure the best possible defense for their young clients.
 Kids deserve a future
Legal involvement can have a devastating impact on the futures of Michigan’s kids. There are a wide range of offenses that can result in a kid facing court. Many youth who end up in detention or residential facilities committed low-level, non-violent offenses. Court involvement and placement into detention or residential facilities can affect their graduation rates, mental health, and employment outcomes.
A defense attorney with proper support can effectively advocate for their clients’ needs, whether that is a diversion program, substance use treatment, or mental health care. Kids who get in trouble are still kids, and deserve the chance to be rehabilitated.
 Kids deserve protected rights 
The passage of juvenile defense will help ensure that children’s constitutional right to due process is preserved.
In In re Gault (1967), the United States Supreme Court held that children have a constitutional right to counsel in delinquency proceedings that may result in a loss of liberty, noting that young people need “the guiding hand of counsel at every step in the proceedings against” them. Since youth are particularly vulnerable and often lack the capacity to understand legal proceedings, legal representation is essential to protecting their constitutional rights and safeguarding them against unjust outcomes.
 A more just Michigan
Our state has made strides to improve the juvenile justice system through the 2023 Justice for Kids and Communities Act. With the signing of Public Act 70, Michigan has taken a historic step forward to protecting the rights of our children, moving our state to a more fair and effective justice system for all of Michigan’s youth.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Advocates ask NJ to enforce state moratorium on horseshoe crab harvesting
description: Limuli Laboratories of Cape May County harvests thousands of horseshoe crabs a year for biomedical testing. Environmentalists demand a review.
text:
Limuli Laboratories of Cape May County harvests thousands of horseshoe crabs a year for biomedical testing. Environmentalists demand a review. (Photo courtesy of New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection)A nonprofit that advocates for endangered species wants New Jersey environmental officials to declare a Cape May County biomedical company in violation of a longstanding moratorium on harvesting horseshoe crabs.
In a petition filed Tuesday, the Center for Biological Diversity accuses Limuli Laboratories of flouting a 2008 state law that generally prohibits all collection of horseshoe crabs, except for those captured for the purpose of blood-harvesting for biomedical purposes. Horseshoe crabs’ blue blood contains an extract called Limulus amebocyte lysate that detects bacterial and fungal contamination and is used to test whether vaccines and other injectables are safe for humans.
The law requires biomedical collectors to release the creatures after harvesting their blood “otherwise unharmed to the same waters from which they were collected.” But the petition says Limuli ignores that requirement by injuring or killing thousands of the horseshoe crabs it plucks out of the Atlantic Ocean each year and returning the survivors to the Delaware Bay instead of the stretch of the sea between Ocean City and Cape May where trawlers got them.
The petition comes as the population of horseshoe crabs, a hardy, prehistoric species considered living fossils because they predate dinosaurs, has plummeted globally partly due to overharvesting. A million get harvested each year for biomedical research even though a synthetic alternative to the test has been available about 20 years, the nonprofit environmental news outlet Sentient recently reported.
New Jersey lawmakers enacted the state moratorium to protect migrating shorebirds that feed on horseshoe crab eggs, especially the federally protected red knot. That has helped horseshoe crabs recover at least in this region, but Limuli Labs’ practices threaten that progress, said Danny Waltz, a senior attorney at the Arizona-based center.
“A law is only as good as its enforcement, and we have some serious questions about the public records we received that show that a biomedical company is harvesting horseshoe crabs in New Jersey waters and killing and injuring the horseshoe crabs, which interferes with their ability to rebound,” Waltz said.
The New Jersey Monitor couldn’t reach Limuli Labs or owner Benjie Swan for comment. The company’s website is down and one phone number listed on its state permit documents is no longer in service, while a second number rings to an automated message that says: “The machine is off.”
State Department of Environmental Protection spokespeople did not answer questions the New Jersey Monitor sent Tuesday and Wednesday, and an automated email reply said they were in a staff retreat Wednesday.
The center has pushed for protections for horseshoe crabs federally, asking the Secretary of Commerce and National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration in 2024 to declare them an endangered or threatened species. But NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service rejected the request in February, and the center sued in May to challenge the denial as unlawful. The case remains pending.
Most horseshoe crab harvesting in the U.S. is done by four companies: Charles River Laboratories and Associates of Cape Cod that both are based in Massachusetts, the Swiss company Lonza Bioscience, and FujiFilm Wako Chemicals of Japan, Waltz said.

Limuli might be capturing about 100,000 horseshoe crabs annually, Waltz said.
“When there are all sorts of regulatory schemes that are trying to minimize the depletion of horseshoe crabs and actually rebound the horseshoe crabs, removing 100,000 of them really is impactful. And that’s just one company,” Waltz said.
Limuli also reports to the state how many horseshoe crabs it catches but rejects for testing due to injury or death, and those numbers averaged 315 dead and 4,270 injured horseshoe crabs a year over the past three years, according to the center’s petition.
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission estimates 15% of horseshoe crabs die during bleeding, although some researchers put that figure closer to 30%. Adding those in, Waltz’s group estimates 15,000 to 30,000 horseshoe crabs die a year as a result of Limuli’s operations.
The center wants state environmental officials to review Limuli’s activity and issue a declaratory ruling on whether the company is violating the 2008 law. Violators face permit revocation, denial of future permit applications, and prosecution under state law.
More than a dozen advocacy groups signed on as supporters of the center’s petition, including the Delaware Riverkeeper Network, NY/NJ Baykeeper, New Jersey Audubon Society, and New Jersey Conservation Foundation.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: TSET to continue contract with Georgia university despite Oklahoma lawmaker concerns
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A state governing body will allocate up to $150,000 to a private Georgia university despite concerns from some lawmakers that Oklahomans intended for the funding to remain in state.  The Oklahoma Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust’s decision could bring the total money paid to Emory University since August 2022 to nearly $1 million, […]
text:
Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia, is pictured. (Photo by John McCosh/Georgia Recorder)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state governing body will allocate up to $150,000 to a private Georgia university despite concerns from some lawmakers that Oklahomans intended for the funding to remain in state. 
The Oklahoma Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust’s decision could bring the total money paid to Emory University since August 2022 to nearly $1 million, according to an Oklahoma Voice analysis of the agency’s spending.   
Records obtained through open records requests show TSET, which oversees a $2.2 billion public trust endowment, has allocated Emory Centers for Public Health Training and Technical Assistance over $930,000 to provide technical assistance and training services, including creating and maintaining an online learning community for public health information.
The most recent allocation, which could reach $150,000, will enable Emory to provide other grantees of tobacco settlement dollars technical assistance and training support in the current budget year, said TSET spokesperson Thomas Larson.
TSET, which was created by voters in 2000, is responsible for overseeing the spending of proceeds from Oklahoma’s portion of a multi-state settlement with the tobacco industry. A state board allocates the interest from the fund toward priorities designed to improve public health. 
Much of TSET’s expenditures — which totaled nearly $82 million last fiscal year — remained in Oklahoma and were allocated to local nonprofits, counties and public universities, making the Emory expenditures an outlier, Oklahoma Voice’s analysis found.
Larson said nothing prohibits the agency from allocating money to out-of-state entities as long as it benefits the health of Oklahomans.
He said the agency first chose Emory to provide services in 2011 as part of a joint initiative between TSET, the State Department of Health and the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services.
Emory University had a reputation nationally as a “premier knowledge expert and technical assistance provider for comprehensive tobacco control services and strategies,” he said.
Beginning in 2015, Larson said TSET began sending additional money to Emory to create and maintain the OK In The Know training portal, a website that contains public health training and networking information.
A screenshot of the Tobacco Settlement Endowment Trust training portal, OK In The Know. The portal was created and maintained by Emory University, a private institution in Georgia.
TSET on Friday is discontinuing the training portal that Emory developed following a decline in use, Larson said. However, he said the agency is still contracting Emory’s training services because its “deep experience and expertise benefits Oklahomans through TSET’s partners and grantees.”
Larson said the agency did not go out for bids before awarding Emory the contract to build the website. He said the university was already under contract for training services and offered two learning system options for TSET to choose between. 
The agency did not select an in-state university because Oklahoma’s institutions of higher learning lacked the expertise to create the training resource, he said.
TSET does contract with the University of Oklahoma’s Hudson College of Public Health to operate the Oklahoma Tobacco Helpline, which helps Oklahomans quit smoking, and to evaluate ongoing TSET programs, Larson said.
State Rep. John Pfeiffer, the House deputy floor leader, said he believes OU or Oklahoma State University, which are both nationally recognized academic research institutions, had the expertise to build and operate the training portals.
“If all that it is is a collaborative website with resource sharing, there’s no reason that any university with a public health division shouldn’t be able to do that,” Pfeiffer said.
Pfeiffer, R-Mulhall, believes TSET has been successful at curtailing tobacco use, but he said some of the agency’s other expenses are questionable. For instance, he said the money allocated to Emory would be better spent supporting programs, including Oklahoma’s 211 helpline, that assists in connecting Oklahomans to services, including health care access.
Pfeiffer said he hopes TSET prioritizes keeping its spending in Oklahoma.
“If there’s something that isn’t offered in the state of Oklahoma that they absolutely need, then yeah, sure,” Pfeiffer said, “but if it’s something that could be done just as easily through our partners here in the state, there’s no reason why they shouldn’t do it here.”
House Appropriations Chair Trey Caldwell, R-Faxon, said the money going to Emory was “a little bit concerning.”
He said he could understand if TSET sent money out of state if there was not a local entity that could complete the services, but he said in-state medical groups like OU Health, OSU Medicine and the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation are capable local options.
“The University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State University are both flagships and are world class when it comes to not only public health, but also when it comes to technology, when it comes to websites,” Caldwell said. “Basically, there’s nothing that they can’t do on a world-class level, in my opinion. So I do find it troubling when we’re choosing to send almost a million dollars of an Oklahoma asset and not continuing to reinforce our local institutions.”
Caldwell has recently led efforts to broaden the Legislature’s influence over TSET and its spending. Last year, the Oklahoma Supreme Court found unconstitutional a measure he authored that would have term-limited the agency’s governing board.
During the most recent session, Caldwell authored legislation to consolidate the agency’s governing structure and move a billion dollars of TSET’s money into a fund the Legislature could spend. Both measures failed to advance out of the Legislature.
Sen. Mary Boren, D-Norman, said she was not worried about the Emory contract, and said TSET’s decision to outsource it was likely a consequence of “political backlash” to certain types of research in Oklahoma. She said behavioral health research, like addiction recovery, does not see as much state investment as other areas she says are less political, like cancer research or diabetes.
“In that environment, I’m not surprised that our folks who are charged with tobacco cessation and healthy living have to pay a lot of money and have to go outside of Oklahoma for the help that they need,” Boren said.

name: WyoFile
title: Here’s where the Republican candidates for Wyoming governor diverge on policy
description:
The top Wyoming gubernatorial candidates in 2026 differ on healthcare, data centers, abortion and library book bans. 
The post Here’s where the Republican candidates for Wyoming governor diverge on policy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In less than three weeks, Wyoming voters will cast their ballots in the Aug. 18 primary election and effectively decide who will be the state’s next governor. 
Four candidates are seeking the Republican nomination including Sen. Eric Barlow, Col. Brent Bien, Curt Blake of Centennial and Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder. Because of Wyoming’s Republican dominance, the primary election winner is expected to prevail in November’s general election. (Gov. Mark Gordon collected nearly 75% of the vote in the 2022 general election.)
The four Republicans overlap on several policy issues, but distinctions between them have emerged. Degenfelder is largely running on President Donald Trump’s endorsement, while Barlow is concentrating on protecting public lands and Bien is championing a property tax initiative he worked to get on November’s ballot. Blake, who has opted out of traditional campaigning, is the one Republican in the race who opposes abortion bans.
For many months now, the gubernatorial hopefuls have traveled the far corners of state for parade-day appearances, meet and greets with voters, as well as forums, debates and gatherings with local business owners, industry leaders and community organizers. But for the average voter, parsing out candidates’ policy positions from campaign platitudes is not always an easy task.
WyoFile identified several policy areas where the candidates diverge by comparing their responses in our election guide, comments at forums and other reporting. 
Healthcare
In the spring, WyoFile asked readers to rank issues that are important to them, and healthcare costs and access topped the list. As part of WyoFile’s 2026 election guide, candidates were asked what they would do as governor to make healthcare more affordable and accessible to Wyomingites. 

Republican gubernatorial candidate for Wyoming Megan Degenfelder talks during a primary election candidate forum organized with fellow contender Eric Barlow organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming at Casper College on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

In her answer, Degenfelder said her top priorities would include 1) focusing on the workforce pipeline and incentivizing providers to be in Wyoming; 2) creating greater regional coordination, including special services, community care coordination, EMS and electronic records streamlining; 3) expanding telehealth; and 4) working to reduce the overall cost in healthcare while bringing down premiums.
“As a cancer survivor with a husband in the medical field and a mother who was lost far too soon due to access to necessary care, this is something I care about deeply,” Degenfelder wrote. 
In his answer, Barlow wrote, “beginning the day after the primary, I will use the relationships I have built across Wyoming to assemble a healthcare strike team so we can act on day one to get results.”
“There are many dedicated folks to take this on, and I welcome their ideas,” he said. 
Barlow also said he would start “with clear policy goals,” including working to “attract and support more providers; strengthen rural hospitals and clinics; support EMS; expand behavioral health capacity; improve telehealth; maintain price transparency; and invest in training pathways for healthcare professionals.”  
Bien wrote in his response that he would “focus on the needs of the patient and the patient/doctor relationship” and that he would consider several things like supporting all levels of healthcare education in the community college system, reducing “the bureaucracy (red tape) where able,” and pursuing “tort reform in an effort to reduce malpractice premiums that are typically passed on to the patient.” 
Bien, who spearheaded a ballot initiative to cut property taxes that voters will decide on in November, also wrote that he would “prioritize meaningful tax relief for Wyoming families, and the sustainability of our critical local healthcare infrastructure.” 
“Any relief must be paired with efficiency, accountability, and smart funding strategies,” Bien wrote. 
Property taxes fund 14 hospital districts across the state and were among the hundreds of entities that experienced tax revenue declines last year after the Legislature created a 25% exemption on certain residential properties. 
Blake did not provide responses for WyoFile’s election guide. 
In June, Bien, Barlow and Degenfelder participated in a panel as part of a healthcare policy summit in Laramie. 
Moderator Samin Dadelahi, president and CEO of the Wyoming Community Foundation, asked the trio about Rural Health Transformation Program funds. As part of President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the large infusion of federal dollars over the next five years is intended to bolster healthcare in rural states like Wyoming where adequate emergency care, hospital viability and workforce development are challenges. 
In its application to the feds, the state had proposed establishing a perpetuity fund via a system of investments intended to generate revenue for Wyoming healthcare programs indefinitely. However, the perpetuity fund was struck from the final plan. 
“Without a long-term funding mechanism, any improvements we make with this investment will likely disappear when the federal dollars run out,” Dadelahi told candidates during the panel. “Would you commit as governor to championing a state-funded sustainability mechanism, such as a perpetuity fund, to preserve those gains?”
Degenfelder said she favors public-private partnerships “and how we bring all of these different funding mechanisms together.”
“That’s how our most successful start, and so I think that is absolutely the discussion we need to have — is how do we actually make this long-term funding?” she said. “And so yes, I’m committed to that discussion.” 
Wyoming Governor candidate Brent Bien, left, laughs with a delegate during the Wyoming Republican State Convention on Saturday, April 25, 2026, in Douglas. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Bien said he would consider both its “effectiveness and suitability” and pointed to the state’s rainy day fund, which is consistently ranked as the nation’s largest state reserve as a share of its operating costs. 
“If there’s a way to do it to where we can diversify some of the funds we already have, because we do. I mean, we do a pretty good job at actually setting things up and then earning interest over time to pay for certain things. And I don’t have a problem with that,” Bien said. “But you know, it does come down to the tax burden on everyday Wyoming Americans.”
Barlow gave the most direct answer to the question. 
“Yes,” he said. 
Data centers
Wyoming is home to dozens of data center proposals. As part of WyoFile’s 2026 election guide, candidates were asked who should decide on the fate of such proposals and what role the governor should play. 
“The people and the free market should decide,” Bien wrote in his answer, adding that a state tax cut for data centers should be repealed.
“Large corporations should not receive tax cuts that are unavailable to small businesses,” Bien wrote. 
In 2021, former lawmaker Clark Stith brought a bill to repeal data center tax exemptions, but it died in committee when then Reps. Chuck Gray, Tim Hallinan, Mark Jennings, Pat Sweeney and Mike Yin voted it down. 
As a member of the State Loan and Investment Board, Bien wrote that he would “oppose the further development of AI data centers in Wyoming particularly on state And [sic] agricultural lands.” 
More recently, Bien said in a statement on his Facebook that his campaign was being targeted for criticism because he’s “the only candidate against data centers running for Governor of Wyoming.” 
In his answer, Barlow wrote “data center proposals should be decided locally by the communities that will live with them.” 

Republican gubernatorial candidate for Wyoming Eric Barlow speaks during a primary election candidate forum with fellow contender Megan Degenfelder organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming at Casper College on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

“The state’s role is to protect water resources from misuse, prevent higher electricity rates, and help communities get truthful information if needed to make those decisions,” Barlow wrote. 
“Wyoming knows how to do hard things,” he wrote. “We have spent generations balancing development with land, water, private property, and local concerns. The same industries where we have learned that balance can help power data centers.”
In her answer, Degenfelder also wrote “the governor has a responsibility to protect our lands, water, ratepayers, personal property rights, and communities.” 
She also outlined “rules” that data centers would “have to play by” in Wyoming, including supplying or paying for its own electricity, operating on a closed-loop cooling system, not drawing from the state’s water supply, prioritizing local workers and contributing to the workforce-education pipeline. 
“You must be welcomed by your host community. Period,” she wrote.
Abortion 
Blake told WyoFile earlier this month that he does not support bans on abortion, which remains legal in Wyoming despite several legislative attempts to curtail or prohibit it. 
“I’ve never known or understood why it was anybody’s business except for the person making the decision,” Blake said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, I don’t think that that’s for me to judge. We’re supposed to live in a country where you have free choice. 
Barlow, Bien and Degenfelder, meanwhile, are opposed to abortion but split when it comes to making exceptions, such as in cases of rape, incest or the health of the mother. 
In June, the three candidates participated in a forum hosted by the Wyoming Family Alliance, a Christian advocacy group based in Cheyenne. 
Moderator Nathan Winters, a former lawmaker and president of the alliance, asked the candidates if they agreed that “abortion is the intentional act of ending the life of another human being while in the womb” and whether they “support any exceptions to legal protection for unborn children.” 
“Absolutely this is accurate, and that’s why I can’t accept any exception when it comes to life,” Degenfelder said, adding that “this is spiritual warfare that we have going on right now.” 
Barlow said he “absolutely” agreed with Winters’ statement but noted the times as a legislator he has supported abortion ban legislation that included exceptions. 
“Since 2022, the Wyoming Legislature has taken up numerous efforts and I’ve been a part of those to advance this absolute viewpoint,” he said. “Now, in some of those were exceptions because in the legislative process you actually have to bring people on board.” 
Barlow pointed back to 2025, when Sen. Larry Hicks accused Barlow of not being sufficiently opposed to abortion. He brought a motion to strip Barlow of his committee chairmanship. After 28 of the Senate’s 31 members rejected Hicks’ motion, Hicks made a Senate-floor apology. 
“And folks that have questioned my record, even on the Senate floor, have found themselves having to say, ‘Oop, not so fast,’” Barlow said. 
Earlier this year, Barlow voted in favor of Sen. Tim Salazar’s bill that would have put the question of abortion in the hands of voters. It failed an introductory vote. 
Bien says he doesn’t support making certain exceptions to an abortion ban. 
“I completely agree with the statement and I unequivocally support zero, no exceptions all the way across the board for this,” Bien said at the forum. 
Bien, a retired Marine Corps colonel, said his view was shaped by an experience he had while serving overseas. 
“It was a 6-year-old child. You know, this kid gets shot in the head. I was over in Iraq at the time. We were trying to get this kid down to Baghdad in the middle of the night and he bled out,” Bien said. 
“And there was something about that that made me absolutely resolute,” he said. 
Public libraries 
At a debate in Dubois hosted by the Wyoming Republican Party in June, Barlow, Bien and Degenfelder were asked about public library book policies. 
Joining a nationwide movement of social conservatives who say sexually explicit content, mostly in books written for young LGBTQ+ readers, is inappropriate, some Republican lawmakers have sought out statewide policies to regulate the children’s section of public libraries. The most recent effort stalled in March in the Wyoming Senate.
Republican gubernatorial canidates Megan Degenfelder,, Eric Barlow and Brent Bien address the audience Thursday, June 18, 2026, during a debate in Dubois. (Andrew Berger/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
“A lot of discussion has been had about inappropriate books in libraries,” John Birbari with the Fremont County GOP told candidates. “What do you intend to do to make sure age-appropriate material is located in its appropriate places?”
Barlow described recent legislative attempts as “big government telling local communities and parents what their kids and children have access to.”
“Look, I have no interest. I don’t even like — I don’t even like pornography. I don’t look at that stuff. No interest in it. I sure as hell don’t want young people having access to it,” he said. “But I also think that parents and local governments can take that up at the local level and have those conversations.” 
Degenfelder, who has served as superintendent of public instruction since 2022, highlighted the book policy she worked with stakeholders to develop to guide school districts in shaping their own policies for producing or restricting books. However, Degenfelder expressed support for a top-down approach at the forum. 
“It is unacceptable to have sexually explicit materials in taxpayer-funded libraries. Period,” she said. 
Bien said he supports a statewide policy “because it is completely unsatisfactory to have these kinds of things in our schools,” and argued that people, not entities like libraries, have freedom of speech.” 
While the primary election is Aug. 18, early voting is already underway.

title: Bright colors and bold stripes: Meet the lesser known denizens of Wyoming’s prairie streams
description:
Wyoming’s creeks still hold many of its native fish species, and they’re wilder than you think.
The post Bright colors and bold stripes: Meet the lesser known denizens of Wyoming’s prairie streams appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In a state with clean, cold waters that rush over boulders and through canyons, the adjectives warm, calm and muddy rarely elicit a positive reaction from anglers. 
When people think about fishing in Wyoming, they imagine feisty 4- and 5-pound rainbow trout, spotted brown trout with hooked jaws or prehistoric-looking walleye and whiskered catfish. It’s unlikely that many, if any, recreational anglers have listed the orangethroat darter as their favorite fish, or the brassy minnow or striped northern plains killifish. 
But maybe they should. 
While none of these native fish weigh more than a few ounces or measure longer than 3 inches, their beauty and pizazz should count for something. 
Hidden in the depths — or shallows — of Wyoming’s prairie streams swims a dazzling array of biodiversity that keeps the waters humming with life. And as our environment continues to warm, and creeks dry up, these lesser-known species are the ones that evolved to survive. They may prefer cold, clear water, but they hunker down in puddles that reach a trout-killing 90 degrees. Many can wait years to spawn and then lay bumper crops of eggs when conditions improve. Some males turn bright shades of turquoise and fiery orange to impress females, and others, like the hornyhead chub, build towers out of pebbles upon which females lay eggs.
Some of them are on the state’s list of species of greatest conservation need, which means they, too, could use some love as waters dry and habitat changes.
“And if the ecosystem isn’t fit for the little fish, then at some point in time it’s not fit for the fish everyone is excited about,” said Nick Hogberg, a Wyoming Game and Fish Department fisheries biologist in the Casper region. “If you don’t have water for minnows, you don’t have water for sportfish either.”
So in honor of this summer’s heat, meet a handful of Wyoming’s plains fish. Some are glacial relics. All are survivors. Consider them the understudies to Wyoming’s trophy rainbows and walleye and the indicators of the health of our waters. And next time you drive over one of these prairie streams, consider just how much life is hanging on. 
Orangethroat darter
The orangethroat darter is a member of the perch family, a diminuitive relative of walleye. (Christine Peterson)
If a fish went to a rave it might dress like an orangethroat darter. The orangethroat, along with its cousins the Iowa and Johnny darters, belong to the perch family, diminutive relatives of walleye. While most anglers are familiar with yellow perch, an introduced fish to the state, some darter species like the Iowa darter have been here since the glaciers receded, said Kye Dean Catlin, a University of Wyoming graduate student studying prairie fishes and how to improve their habitat. 
And when the males spawn, their colors are fit for any rock concert. The orangethroat darter has bright blue and orange striped dorsal fins with similarly colored bars running up and down its body.
They also evolved without swim bladders, which means they can stay put on the bottom of streams eating insect larvae instead of floating around in the midcurrent.
Northern plains killifish
Killifish at Bed Tick Creek in Converse County. (Christine Peterson)
If you cross a zebra with a minnow, a categorically impossible task, you might get something like a killifish. The northern plains killifish has vertical black and white stripes that give a distinct zebra flavor. 
The curious species not only lives in and can tolerate high-salinity waters like those in the slow-moving streams of eastern Wyoming, they thrive in them, said Matt Hahn, Wyoming Game and Fish’s fisheries supervisor in the Casper region. Their upturned mouths are perfectly adapted to suck oxygen from the top millimeter of water in a pond or puddle, allowing them to live in places no other fish could survive.
Sand shiner 
The sand shiner thrives in the warm, salty Powder River, along with other eastern Wyoming streams and rivers. (Christine Peterson)
In the warm and salty Powder River lives the sand shiner. It reflects with an intoxicating silver that glints in the sun. Each scale, no larger than the tip of a pencil, is intricately lined in black. 
It thrives in the Powder River alongside prehistoric shovelnose sturgeon, squishy stonecat, and behemoth channel catfish. But they’re also common across the eastern side of the state in small streams and big rivers.
“They’re doing really well even as other species struggle,” Hahn said.
Brassy minnow
The brassy minnow is an indicator species that, when found, usually signals good water. (Christine Peterson)
Coat a sleek little fish in 24-carat gold, throw in a few dark spots, and you have a brassy minnow. 
They don’t live in many streams in Wyoming, but they can be common in the ones they still occupy, Compton said. They’re also one of those indicator species. 
Brassy minnows, along with the plains and silvery minnow, swim great lengths to spawn. The females then lay eggs somewhere in the water column, which then slowly tumble and sink to the bottom where they stick ever so slightly to rocks or vegetation. 
“When you find a brassy minnow in Wyoming usually it’s because you have good water quality,” said Bobby Compton, Game and Fish’s Laramie regional fisheries supervisor.
Creek chub
The creek chub is active, abundant, and willing to bite just about anything on the hook. (Christine Peterson)
Anyone who wandered down to an eastern Wyoming creek as a child and caught a fish, likely hooked a creek chub. The species are active, abundant and willing to bite just about anything on a hook. A dark racing stripe runs down each side, and they can grow to 8 or even 10 inches long, a veritable monster among its prairie stream peers.
“They have a big mouth like a bass,” Compton said. “And they’re aggressive, the king of the creek and top predator.”
Creek chubs are not only abundant but also widespread, native to every drainage east of the Continental Divide. They deserve our respect because, if nothing else, they’re so often the fish that gives our imagination a taste of what else could live beneath the surface.

title: Wyoming archaeologists take BLM to court over Native sites, human remains
description:
The lawsuit argues that the boundaries of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act have been expanded far beyond what Congress had intended. The case revolves around six particular sites.
The post Wyoming archaeologists take BLM to court over Native sites, human remains appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—As often-White researchers dig up ancient Native sites, the archaeology of the West can be fraught with tension. A group of Wyoming archaeologists claims that the BLM has overstepped its authority.
Wyoming enjoys a rich archaeological heritage, but the question of who can lay claim to that heritage is now making its way through the courts. 
On July 24, the Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists filed a lawsuit against Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, the U.S. Department of the Interior and the Bureau of Land Management’s Wyoming and Colorado offices. The lawsuit argues that the boundaries of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act had been expanded far beyond what Congress had intended.
The case revolves around six particular sites: Shute Creek, Wardell Bison Trap, Upper Muddy Creek Village, Studhorse Butte, 48UT920 and Eagle Rock Shelter. 
Although the collection of material found at Eagle Rock Shelter is currently housed at the Fort Bridger State Historic Site in Uinta County, the site itself is located in Colorado; all five of the other sites are in Wyoming.
The plaintiffs claim that in 2010 and 2024 rulemaking, the BLM changed how it goes about implementing the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act in a way that oversteps its authority and potentially conflicts with the Archaeological Resources Protections Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
In January 2025, the University of Wyoming Archaeological Repository notified BLM Wyoming that it had in its custody collections from seven BLM archaeological sites where human remains had been discovered, and that the human remains and related items were not included in its collections, according to the filing.
In June 2025, the BLM published a Notice of Inventory Completion and a Notice of Intended Disposition regarding the human remains in question and thousands of items within the UW repository’s possession claimed to be associated funerary objects. 
Then, in July 2025, the BLM sent a letter stating that in consultation with 15 tribes it had determined that the entirety of the archaeological collections from seven sites, including four sites named in the lawsuit, are funerary objects associated with NAGPRA human remains housed in the University of Wyoming Human Remains Repository. The BLM stated that it intended to repatriate the objects and human remains to claimant tribes and asked that the items identified be moved to the Human Remains Repository.
This sparked a back-and-forth between the Office of the Wyoming State Archaeologist and the BLM over whether the items identified within the UW Archaeological Repository’s possession were items subject to the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act. 
The Office of the Wyoming State Archaeologist also conveyed that it did not believe the Human Remains Repository had the physical space to house the over 200,000 artifacts.
Additional items were identified by the BLM as associated funerary objects in April 2026. Neither set of items has changed hands yet, but the case states that the BLM has notified the University of Wyoming that it plans to take possession of the items in the near future.
The Eagle Rock Shelter Site went through a somewhat similar process. 
At this site, the case outlines, the human remains of a single individual were found near the back of the shelter, with no artifacts found to be associated with it by archaeologists. The remains were transferred to the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe and reburied. 
Now, the other items found at the site are being claimed as funerary objects, sacred objects, and/or objects of cultural patrimony, a claim which the Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists believes to be founded on physical proximity and traditional knowledge rather than archaeological evidence linking the items with the remains.
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, framed at the time of its passage as a compromise between the interests of Native American tribes and researchers, requires that human remains as well as cultural items such as funerary objects and ceremonial objects, which can be shown to be linked to a tribe within the United States, be repatriated to the tribe in question. 
The Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists argues that the BLM unlawfully expanded both the definition of cultural items covered under the act and the ways in which it can be determined that these items fall under the federal law.
One of these rule changes is the shift in language regarding the discovery of material. Previously, the standard was that items found with a burial were regarded as funerary objects. Now, the requirement is that items found with or near a burial are to be regarded as funerary objects. The archaeologists claim that results in items — clearly not associated with a burial but which are physically nearby — being caught up in federal repatriation claims.
The Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists gave as an example the Wardell Bison Trap site, an archaeologically important communal buffalo hunting site in Sublette County. 
“Among the thousands of bison bones and other artifacts recovered from the bonebed, records identify a single fragment of a human proximal femur recovered from one of the stratified bone beds. In reliance on the challenged regulations, BLM Wyoming has claimed that the presence of a single human bone fragment in this massive bison bonebed transforms it into a burial and thereby makes the entire contents of the bonebed … into associated funerary objects subject to repatriation.”
Some of the other changes the Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists is challenging include deference to traditional knowledge and the requirement of informed, ongoing, affirmative assent from tribes.
The filing makes the case that under current regulations, tribal traditional knowledge is broadly defined and can include safeguarded or confidential knowledge, making it difficult to independently assess. 
The Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists argues that traditional knowledge is meant to be a factor within decisions about whether the federal law applies, not the sole determining factor. Additionally, it continues, federal law does not require obtaining consent from tribes before exhibiting or allowing research on human remains and/or cultural items.
The Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists also argues that the federal law requires that a clear association be shown between remains or cultural items and a present-day tribe, either through direct cultural affiliation or lineal descent. In its case, it states that “Congress addressed culturally unidentifiable human remains in 25 U.S.C. 3006(c)(5), which directs the review committee to compile and inventory and ‘recommend specific actions for developing a process for disposition.'” 
The lawsuit argues that the decision of what to do with these remains still rests with Congress, and that the review committee in question is meant to serve in a purely advisory role.
In its filing, the Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists states its belief that these regulations detrimentally impact both individual researchers and education, learning, and research more broadly. The lawsuit argues that the repatriation of these items in some cases may remove the ability to study them from the scientific community forever, based on a regulatory interpretation of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act different from the one that archaeologists had been operating under prior to these rule changes.
The Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists is clear that its objections do not have to do with either BLM Wyoming or BLM Colorado’s application of the regulations, but rather the regulatory changes in 2010 and 2024 that BLM is basing its determinations on.
The group asks that the court halt the transfer until the case has been decided, enjoin the BLM and Department of Interior from “enforcing, applying, or relying on the challenged regulations” and award the Wyoming Association of Professional Archaeologists the cost of its suit and reasonable attorney’s fees.

title: Is anyone here Greek?
description:
Amid a new wave of culture clashing over casting for “The Odyssey,” columnist David Romtvedt wonders who gets to decide who or what is beautiful? Based on what criteria? Why do we care?
The post Is anyone here Greek? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The late writer Marvin Bell wrote a poem for his wife, titled simply, “To Dorothy.” It begins:


You are not beautiful, exactly.You are beautiful, inexactly.You let a weed grow by the mulberryand a mulberry grow by the house.So close, in the personal quietof a windy night, it brushes the walland sweeps away the day till we sleep.


To be beautiful inexactly — how beautiful. It makes me think of the complexity of this notion we have of the beautiful. Some things are beautiful and some are not. Some of us are beautiful and some of us are not. Who gets to decide? Based on what criteria? Why do we care?

Opinion

I’m writing this while sitting outside with the sky above and the earth below. I stand and walk up and down the alley, breathing as I move, inhaling the world around me. It’s as if the Earth were made for us, or perhaps more accurately, as if we were made for the Earth.
Recently, I’ve been reading about the new $250 million, 172-minute-long Hollywood blockbuster that is bringing Homer’s Greek epic “The Odyssey” to IMAX screens across the planet. This is the kind of thing Hollywood loves — swords, helmets, chariots, sandals, men and women in long robes, beauty queens and testosterone-fueled soldiers, betrayal, jealousy, degradation, petulant heroes, the victorious and the vanquished, the human experience in Wyoming or in Indonesia or Southern Chile or northern Finland somehow the same.
Such films are commonly romanticized versions of imagined histories fueled by our periodic need to escape the present, the lives we are actually living. But with the new “Odyssey,” current political and social discord has leaked in as a result of director Christopher Nolan’s decision to cast Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen, the Greek beauty queen kidnapped or maybe run away to Troy only to later regret her impetuous flight. Lupita Nyong’o was born in Mexico City of Kenyan parents. She considers herself to be Mexican-Kenyan. She’s Black.
Casting Nyong’o to play Helen has driven some in the blogosphere to apoplectic heights. We’re told the casting is a “woke” gesture meant to destroy Western civilization and everything upon which that civilization has been built. Elon Musk has said that in casting Nyong’o, Nolan was stomping on Homer’s grave. In some reports, Mr. Musk said it was pissing on Homer’s grave. Matt Walsh, a Daily Wire podcast host, said there’s not a single person on Earth who thinks Lupita Nyong’o is the most beautiful woman in the world. Imagine how much trouble Mr. Walsh must have gone to in order to check with each person on Earth about Ms. Nyong’o’s beauty.
The conservative influencer Tanya Bass complained that Helen is a “historically white character” and that casting Nyong’o is “racism against White people.” It’s a funny complaint for a couple of reasons, one being that the Greeks of Homer’s time — about 2,800 years ago — had no concept of race analogous to that of ours.
Another important detail in any examination of Helen’s racial makeup is that Homer’s Helen was born from the union of the god Zeus in the form of a swan and the Spartan queen Leda who may — or may not — have been of human parentage. Following her assignation with Zeus as a swan, Leda laid a clutch of eggs. It was from one of these eggs that Helen was born. Well, hatched. It makes the question of skin tone at best murky.  Better said, irrelevant. Was Helen Black or white?  Maybe she was covered in feathers. Has anyone measured the length of her neck?
The last big-screen depiction of Helen was in the 2004 film “Troy” in which the world’s most beautiful woman was played by the German actress Diane Kruger. Kruger is a blue-eyed, blonde-haired white woman. Those “Aryan” features were idealized by the Nazis. And yet, while “Troy” director Wolfgang Petersen was born in 1941 in Germany, I can’t recall anyone accusing him of being a Nazi for casting Ms. Kruger as Helen.
Let’s end with another poem on beauty, this one written by Frank O’Hara, who claimed it was a literary autobiography:


When I was a childI played by myself in acorner of the schoolyardall alone.
I hated dolls and Ihated games, animals werenot friendly and birdsflew away.
If anyone was lookingfor me, I hid behind a tree and cried out, “I aman orphan.
And here I am, thecenter of all beauty!writing these poems!Imagine!

title: Idaho to submit ‘Opportunity Zone’ proposals seeking tax breaks for economic development
description: A state advisory council has submitted its top recommendations for Idaho communities to be considered for a revamped federal tax incentive program meant to drive development.  The Idaho Economic Advisory Council submitted to Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s Office its 25 recommended areas to be designated as federal Opportunity Zones. Once an area receives that desi[...]
text:
A construction crew works outside a new development in Boise. A recommendation to the governor's office for areas in Idaho to receive a federal designation that allows for tax breaks on certain developments included multiple in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)A state advisory council has submitted its top recommendations for Idaho communities to be considered for a revamped federal tax incentive program meant to drive development. 
The Idaho Economic Advisory Council submitted to Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s Office its 25 recommended areas to be designated as federal Opportunity Zones. Once an area receives that designation, certain investments in housing and projects to spur economic growth there would be eligible for tax breaks. 
Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough.

Little will make a final decision on recommended areas for the program, which must be submitted to the U.S. Department of Treasury by Sept. 28. 
The Opportunity Zone program was created under the first Trump administration through the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Congress last year made the program permanent through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. There were 36 tracts submitted to the advisory council by Idaho cities and counties, state Department of Commerce Rural Services Manager Jerry Miller told members July 23.
The council’s recommendations were largely ranked by likelihood to see investment with the incentives based on data from the Urban Institute.  
The top three recommendations are all in Boise. 
“A number of the nominations mentioned downtown and Main Street revitalization as one of their goals for having an Opportunity Zone,” Miller said at the meeting. “… A few others mention housing as their primary goal or hope for having an opportunity zone nomination, and then third priority listed by the nominations were commercial and industrial growth corridors.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What areas are included in the top recommendations? 

Boise: 

West Main Street and downtown: The top recommendation includes much of west downtown Boise and the city’s downtown urban center. The city’s application summary said the position would put the zone “at the heart of the city’s economic activity and future growth.” The area includes Fairview Park, the Idaho State Capitol and Boise City Hall. 


West Boise corridor: This tract includes Boise Towne Square mall, Milwaukee Street, and Fairview Avenue. This area is Idaho’s largest employment center, according to the application. The area also includes “significant capacity for additional housing growth.”  




South Broadway Avenue: This proposal would focus on “incremental housing growth.” The area includes Manitou Park, the Federal Way Bikeway and sits along Valley Regional Transit’s Broadway bus line. 




Boise State University and West University Drive: The state university anchors this tract with its generation of $2.2 billion annually of economic impact, according to the application summary. 
South of downtown Boise and Shoreline Drive: Listed lower on the council’s recommendation is the southside of Boise’s urban center, which includes Ann Morrison Park, Julia Davis Park, Rhodes Skate Park, the zoo, Boise Art Museum and Idaho State Museum.

Burley: 

Overland Avenue and Main Street corridor: This tract includes Burley City Hall, the courthouse, jail, fairgrounds, airport, schools and parks. The tract is “largely undeveloped or underdeveloped,” according to the summary. 

Caldwell: 

The city of Caldwell: Much of the city is included in this tract, which includes Indian Creek Plaza, the College of Idaho, and the Canyon County Fairgrounds. The city isn’t “landlocked,” according to the summary, “enabling purposeful future development in employment, housing, commercial, industrial and mixed-use sectors.” 

Emmett: 

The city of Emmett and parts of Gem County: The city includes the Gem County courthouse and is served by the county’s only K-12 school district. Highway expansion projects position the city “to absorb investment priced out of Ada County,” the summary said. 

Garden City: 

The city of Garden City: The city is adjacent to downtown Boise and within biking distance of Boise State University and the new College of Western Idaho campus, the application summary said. “It contains significant urban infill and redevelopment opportunities, ready to provide supportive housing and relieve commuter routes,” the summary said.

Kootenai County: 

City of Coeur d’Alene: The county and Coeur d’Alene Tribe both submitted an application for this tract, which includes parts of the city, to be designated as an opportunity zone. “Significant vacant land owned by the Coeur d’Alene Tribe within the tract offers a rare opportunity for partnership, catalyzing projects that generate employment, diversify the economy, increase the tax base, and strengthen collaboration between the Tribe, Kootenai County, Coeur d’Alene, and private investors,” the summary said. 


City of Post Falls: The city submitted the application for Post Falls along the North Pleasant View Road and West Seltice Way corridor. The tract is located at the intersection of Interstate 90 and Highway 53. 

Nampa: 

Downtown, 12th Avenue South and First Street South: This area includes City Hall, the public library, Canyon County government buildings and parks. “Home values and rental rates have increased sharply, supporting the viability of new residential investment,” the summary said.   
11th Avenue North corridor: This tract serves as the “primary gateway” to downtown, the summary said. The area includes infrastructure such as sidewalks, parks and “and numerous underutilized commercial and industrial properties, presenting exceptional opportunities for adaptive reuse, mixed-use development, workforce housing, neighborhood-serving retail, and employment-generating investment,” the application summary said. 

Pocatello: 

Downtown, Main Street corridor, Portneuf River area: This area includes the historic downtown, river greenway, public schools, parks, and the Marshall Public Library. “The area is seen as a future hub for economic development,” the application said. 


Yellowstone Avenue, Pole Line Road, Garrett Way, West Quinn Road: This area includes public schools, the mall, and major retailers such as Fred Meyers, Winco and Costco. 

Shoshone County: 

I-90 corridor, Silver Valley: The tract includes a medical center, Kellogg public schools, Silver Mountain Resort, Bunker Hill Mine, and the Downtown Kellogg commercial district. The application summary said that “years of cleanup” from the mine “have now made redevelopment fundable, feasible, and lower-risk.” 

Twin Falls:  

Downtown, Main Avenue and Shoshone Street: The city is the county seat and “primary urban center” for the Magic Valley. The area is also home to Idaho’s first Opportunity Zone project, a food hall. 

There are other communities, including Rexburg, Moscow, Blanchard, Jerome and Power County that were included in recommendations but ranked lower based on lower likelihood of attracting Opportunity Zone investments. 
 Opportunity zones have been sold as a housing solution. Results have been mixed. 

Last year, U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner traveled to Idaho with U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, to discuss housing issues in the state, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Turner, who led the first iteration of the program, said it would be a continued focus for developing more housing to meet the needs. 
He said at the time 700 new housing units had been built inside Idaho Opportunity Zones and 4,000 new jobs had been created. 
A 2021 Brookings Institution analysis of the program nationally found some increased economic activity in urban areas, but not in rural areas, Stateline reported. However, that study’s data was limited by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Data is also limited from the first version of the program, because there was no reporting requirement associated with it, Miller of the Idaho Department of Commerce, told council members last week. 
The updated program, called Opportunity Zones 2.0, provides larger incentives for rural investments compared to urban ones and has a reporting requirement.

title: Tennessee named finalist for federal partnership involving nuclear energy sites
description: The United States Department of Energy announced Tuesday that Tennessee was one of the five states under consideration for a federal partnership as part of the Trump administration’s attempt to boost nuclear energy production.  The program, called the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, would allow Tennessee to build an industrial-like zone that could sup[...]
text:
The Tennessee Valley Authority's Sequoyah Nuclear Plant in Chattanooga, one of three nuclear facilities the energy giant operates. Tennessee is under consideration for a U.S. Department of Energy program to increase the state's nuclear capacity. (Photo: Facebook)The United States Department of Energy announced Tuesday that Tennessee was one of the five states under consideration for a federal partnership as part of the Trump administration’s attempt to boost nuclear energy production. 
The program, called the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, would allow Tennessee to build an industrial-like zone that could support “the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and disposition of waste.”
“Depending on state priorities and regional capabilities, the sites could also host advanced reactor deployment, power generation, advanced manufacturing, and co-located data centers,” the department’s news release said. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Tennessee has long been at the forefront of nuclear energy because Oak Ridge served as a federal research site for the atomic bomb during World War 2. The Tennessee Valley Authority, TVA, then steadily grew its nuclear energy production starting in 1966, and today operates three plants, two of which are in Tennessee. 
The state also was approved to take in low levels of nuclear waste, but tracking how much of it makes its way to Tennessee has been shrouded in secrecy. 
In 2000, the last year the federal government reported on collections, Tennessee took in 75% of the nation’s low-level radioactive waste, according to a report from Nuclear Information and Resource Service, a nonprofit that opposes nuclear energy production.
Then in 2017, the state Department of Environment and Conservation abruptly stopped reporting on where the low-level nuclear waste was ending up.
In recent years, Gov. Bill Lee has been a strong advocate for revitalizing Tennessee’s nuclear energy. He created a state investment fund that, as of 2025, was offering $70 million in incentives.
Part of the reason for the lifecycle campus program is that currently there is no place approved that can store high levels of radioactive waste.



Quotation







This isn’t just about today’s waste. It’s about committing Tennessee to an energy future that includes more reactors, more spent fuel, and more radioactive waste.


– Sen. Heidi Campbell, D-Nashville


The Trump administration has been trying to find a way around the ban on states taking in nuclear waste by enticing them with incentives, Politico reported after obtaining an internal White House memo. 
Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, said in a social media post that she had concerns about the program. 
“This isn’t just about today’s waste,” Campbell said. “It’s about committing Tennessee to an energy future that includes more reactors, more spent fuel, and more radioactive waste. We deserve transparency before irreversible decisions are made.”
Lee said in a news release he was “honored” that Tennessee was selected as a finalist. 
“Our state answered the call during the Manhattan Project and helped shape the course of history, and Tennessee stands ready once again to advance the safe, reliable energy solutions our nation depends on,” Lee said.
