name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Barbecue and Kentucky campaign previews are on the menu for Saturday’s Fancy Farm Picnic
description:
On the first Saturday in August, thousands of political spectators flock to a far West Kentucky town with a population of about 300 people. 

They are always ready to loudly cheer, boo and wave campaign signs during a church picnic that annually brings together Kentucky Republicans and Democrats vying for office. 

The Fancy Farm Picnic, a barbecue fundraise[...]
text:
Democrat and Republican supporters cheer on Saturday, Aug. 3, 2024, during St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Kentucky. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)On the first Saturday in August, thousands of political spectators flock to a far West Kentucky town with a population of about 300 people. 
They are always ready to loudly cheer, boo and wave campaign signs during a church picnic that annually brings together Kentucky Republicans and Democrats vying for office. 
The Fancy Farm Picnic, a barbecue fundraiser for the St. Jerome Catholic Church in Graves County, is where Kentucky politicians go if they want to get a boost ahead of an upcoming election — whether they are on stage flinging zingers at their opponents or in the crowd making connections with party faithful and trying to get a slice of the media attention.  
Governor Andy Beshear shakes hands with Senator Mitch McConnell during the 143rd Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
This year, Kentucky’s top Republican, U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, and top Democrat, Gov. Andy Beshear, will not be in attendance, but the line-up of speeches, starting at 2 p.m. Central, will feature candidates hoping to succeed McConnell this fall and set the stage for primary races in the 2027 governor’s race. In addition to the speeches, Republicans and Democrats hold dinners, breakfasts and more events ahead of the picnic. For both, it’s a way to connect candidates with organizers, voters and more during the unofficial start of fall campaign season in the commonwealth. 
Will Carle, a Democratic political strategist, said that McConnell’s and Beshear’s absence is a “passing of the torch” for both political parties. McConnell said last year that he wouldn’t seek reelection, opening the seat. In recent weeks, McConnell has been embroiled in the national spotlight as he was hospitalized in June and has not since been voting in the Senate. Beshear, who some see as a possible 2028 candidate for president, has become the Democratic face of criticizing McConnell, recently penning him a letter to ask for “proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.” 
“I think the party is always stronger when we have our best messenger there, which is Andy Beshear. But you’re going to get to see the next generation of leaders for the party emerge this year at Fancy Farm, and Gov. Beshear will be passing the torch on to one of them to lead our party into the future,” Carle said. 
As for McConnell, Carle added: “I think that this is another passing of the torch for the Republican Party, which is someone that’s been there almost as long as I’ve been alive passing a torch to another person, who both don’t seem to have the best interests of Kentuckians at heart.”
McConnell said in a Monday statement that he remained undergoing “intense physical therapy,” meaning that he would not attend Fancy Farm, which has become a favorite tradition of since his 1984 election. He said there was “no place I’d rather be on the first Saturday in August than with the good people of western Kentucky, feasting on pork and mutton.”
Abby Piper, a Republican who is a co-host of Kentucky Politics Weekly, said that while she believed McConnell “will be with his fellow Kentuckians in spirit this weekend,” she was “grateful he is taking care of his health.” 
“Democrats looking to score political points would be wise to remember the months-long absence of Democratic Senator Diane Feinstein before taking shots in this case or any other,” Piper said, referring to the California senator who died in office as the oldest serving senator at the time. 
On Beshear’s absence, Piper said she wasn’t surprised. Beshear last spoke at the picnic when he was running for reelection in 2023. 
“It’s pretty hard to make time to go out west when you’re running for president,” Piper said. 
Beshear recently told reporters this year’s picnic conflicts with his son’s final travel baseball tournament of his high school career.
Lt. Governor Jacqueline Coleman during the 143rd Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Governor’s race
Fancy Farm organizers are continuing a change from last year — allowing primary candidates on the stage. The change in rules, which typically allowed only office holders and general election candidates for the region, means that the crowd will get a preview of the Democratic primary for governor. Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman, who has been regularly invited to speak as an elected official, will speak, as well as Rocky Adkins, former Democratic leader in the Kentucky House and senior adviser to Beshear, who launched his campaign earlier this month.
Rocky Adkins, senior advisor to Governor Beshear, speaks to Congressman James Comer fist pumps to the crowd during the 143rd Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Carle said Saturday is a change for both Coleman and Adkins to give “introductions” for their campaigns. 
“I do think it’s a great way for them to demonstrate their very accomplished careers in public service,” he added. He also thinks Democratic speakers would be best suited to contrast themselves with Republicans nationally and statewide, particularly on affordability issues, such as tariffs enacted by President Donald Trump and Medicaid access. 
“There is a different agenda for the two parties, and I’d be looking for the Democrats to make sure that the voters of West Kentucky are acutely aware of those differences,” Carle said. 
There may be some movement for Republicans hoping to get in the governor’s race, too. Secretary of State Michael Adams, a McCracken County native who confirmed this week he accepted the speaking invitation, told the Lexington Herald-Leader he was considering launching a gubernatorial bid at Fancy Farm. Another rumored GOP candidate, U.S. Rep. James Comer, is a regular at the event and usually brings some of the loudest supporters to the crowd. 
Secretary of State Michael Adams speaks during the St. Jerome’s Church picnic in Fancy Farm, August 3, 2024. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Piper said going to Fancy Farm before launching a campaign is a way for a candidate to get their name out there. She pointed to 2018 when Stephanie Horne attended the picnic and later joined Adkins’ 2019 bid for governor as his running mate. 
“I think Mike Adams could certainly use the stage to his advantage, but Comer is going to be … an intimidating candidate to go against,” Piper said. “I’m not sure I would want to face Comer on a Republican ticket statewide in Kentucky, but it’s early.
Barr and Booker return
Both of the senate nominees have previously addressed the raucous crowd in years past. The Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr was on stage the first time last August with other GOP candidates. Democratic former state Rep. Charles Booker was at the picnic in 2022 when running against U.S. Sen. Rand Paul. While he hasn’t been a regular attendee of the picnic throughout his tenure in office, Paul will be on the stage this week. 
Barr and Booker “both of them are phenomenal speakers,” Piper said, but Barr has “the chops to back it up.” He’s a central Kentucky congressman who was first elected in 2012.
Pro-Palestine protesters hold up signs alongside supporters of U.S. Rep. Andy Barr and Senate candidate Nate Morris during the Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug 2, 2025. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)
“I think for Barr, the opportunity is to showcase what he can do for parts of the state that he hasn’t represented before now,” Piper said. “It’s going to be interesting to see how those talking points get shifted around for both candidates, quite frankly, to address a more broad audience. Kentucky is a very rural state, a very red state, but Western Kentucky gets left out a lot, and so I think that’s going to be one of those things that has to be balanced in his work.”
However, Carle argued that tenure in Congress means that Barr “has been in a bubble in Washington, D.C. for a long time.” Booker, who also served in Beshear’s administration after a previous run for Senate, grew up in Louisville’s West End and has frequently discussed growing up in poverty. 
“Charles Booker has a unique life experience that allows him to relate to people on a visceral level. He knows what it’s like to struggle, and Kentucky families are struggling,” Carle said. “And I think it’ll be a great opportunity for him to make the case that someone like them should go to the U.S. Senate instead of someone that’s out of touch.”
‘Shoe leather politics’
Saturday will mark the 146th year of the Fancy Farm Picnic. Brian Clardy, a history professor at nearby Murray State University, said that even though the political speaking tends to be a big draw, the picnic provides “a really family-friendly atmosphere” with live music, games for kids, and, of course, the barbecue — ”everything from pork shoulder to mutton.”
“It’s a really wonderful gathering, and anyone who has a passing interest in campaigns and politics and political history should check it out. It’s a historical event in its own right,” he said. 
 

If You Go
The annual Fancy Farm Picnic will be at the St. Jerome Church at 20 State Route 339 North, Fancy Farm, KY 42039. Political speeches start at 2 p.m. Central time, or 3 p.m. Eastern. 
KET will broadcast speeches statewide on television and online at KET.org. 


	Fancy Farm is rooted in early American campaigning traditions, Clardy said. When the country was founded, churches and other community organizations would provide spaces for political candidates to give speeches and hold debates. For those seeking office they needed to be out with the people and face their opponents directly, or as Clardy calls it, engage in “shoe leather politics.”
Clardy said he hopes that tradition continues for years to come. 
“I know that it’s very easy now to do a Zoom call, to do a podcast, to send out an email, to go on social media sites, and that’s well good and dandy, and that’s great, but democracy is a contact sport,” Clardy said. “And I want to see that continue where you have the give and take of ideas and raucous debates, so that voters can be informed because democracy, in large part, depends on that.”
Carle said the picnic “will always be a relevant and political event in Kentucky.” 
“I hope that people continue to invest the time that it takes to go there because it’s usually a three-to-four day trip because of all the events that surround it and the energy to go through the gauntlet that it is,” he said. 
Candidates that go and do well “all come out on the better side of it,” Carle added. Fancy Farm “creates the kind of character you want in a candidate to continue down in the home stretch of a campaign.”
Piper said the candidates who have  guts to go out west, whether they’re from there or not,” are doing something “courageous.” The crowd, full of Republicans and Democrats, are not shy when it comes to booing those they disagree with and cheering for what they support. 
The Fancy Farm Picnic’s role in today’s world is a reminder “to get off the screens, to get out in person, to be part of a community,” Piper said. 
“At the end of the day, it’s a church fundraiser, and it’s a place for community. It’s a place for bingo and a place for barbecue and Sun Drop and a little bit of fun — the roasting,” she added. “But also, it’s a time for us all to connect on what we have in common, and it’s not something that happens a lot in the echo chambers online.”
Men prepare barbecue pork and mutton at the St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky., on Saturday, Aug 2, 2025. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)

name: National
title: When families question a death investigation, getting a second autopsy can be complicated
description: After investigators ruled 31-year-old high school counselor and coach Kelsey Harris’ death a suicide in 2021, her mother, Kellee, said she was not convinced the inquiry had answered the most important questions. About a week before Kelsey died, police had arrested her boyfriend on a strangulation charge after Kelsey reported he attacked her, according to […]
text:
Nolan Xavier Wells, center, with his parents, Christine Wells-Wonsley and Elmore Wonsley. After Nolan’s death in early July during a boat trip with a group of white friends, his parents commissioned an independent investigation with the help of civil rights attorney Ben Crump. (Photo courtesy of Ben Crump Law)After investigators ruled 31-year-old high school counselor and coach Kelsey Harris’ death a suicide in 2021, her mother, Kellee, said she was not convinced the inquiry had answered the most important questions.
About a week before Kelsey died, police had arrested her boyfriend on a strangulation charge after Kelsey reported he attacked her, according to her mother and police records. After Kelsey was found dead of a gunshot wound to the head, the county medical examiner  ruled her death a suicide.
“I just couldn’t even believe that,” Kellee Harris said.
Kellee Harris has since questioned whether investigators fully considered the assault report and other circumstances surrounding her daughter’s death, including the bullet’s entry and exit points and the authenticity of Kelsey’s final text message to loved ones.  She has spent years seeking additional information about the case and has joined other Oregon families in advocating for changes to how suspicious deaths are investigated.
Forensic crime labs are buckling as new technology increases demand

“It’s been the most aggravating, challenging thing I’ve ever done in my life, you know, is to try and get to the bottom of what happened,” Harris said. “The system failed us every single step along the way.”
For families who question an official determination about how a loved one died — whether from suicide, an accident, natural causes, during an encounter with law enforcement or while incarcerated or detained — the next step is often unclear. Independent autopsies have become a familiar part of some of the nation’s highest-profile death investigations, most recently with the death of 18-year-old Nolan Xavier Wells, who died in Mississippi in early July.
Independent autopsies have often emerged from a deep distrust of official systems — particularly in cases involving Black victims killed by law enforcement, where families have questioned whether investigators treated their loved ones’ deaths with the scrutiny they deserved. For some, an outside review represents a way to seek answers when they believe the initial investigation overlooked key evidence, moved too quickly or failed to account for their concerns. 
But these reviews are not limited to police encounters; families have also sought independent examinations in cases involving domestic violence, disputed evidence and other circumstances where the official explanation remains contested.
Other high-profile cases include the deaths of Kendrick Johnson in 2013, Michael Brown in 2014, Tamla Horsford in 2018, George Floyd in 2020 and Patrick Lyoya in 2022. In some cases, the second autopsies reached conclusions that differed from or expanded on the initial investigation, while in others they provided additional medical evidence that became part of the public record. 
Some families hire independent forensic pathologists. Others seek outside investigators, ask prosecutors to reopen cases or turn to advocacy groups for help understanding what happened. 
Harris pursued nearly every avenue she could find. She consulted multiple independent experts to review the case, requested investigative records, including crime scene photos and other materials, repeatedly asked local investigators and prosecutors to take another look at the evidence, and ultimately became an advocate for changes to Oregon’s death investigation laws.
Linn County Sheriff Michelle Duncan told Stateline that investigators stand by their determination that Harris died by suicide. Duncan said she and the county district attorney have met with Kellee Harris and outside experts who have questioned the investigation and believe the crime scene was staged, but said those experts did not visit the scene in person.
“All of the evidence points to, unfortunately, a suicide,” Duncan said. “I feel really awful for the mother who is probably wanting to hang on that her daughter would not do that, but there is no evidence of anything but a suicide.”
The United States has no single death investigation system, and the options available to families can vary widely depending on where a death occurs.
A Stateline analysis of state death investigation systems found that 20 states and Washington, D.C., use centralized medical examiner systems, while nine states rely primarily on local coroners. The rest use a mix of state and local officials. In most places, death investigations are handled at the county level, where families may encounter different officials, including sheriffs and justices of the peace, procedures and resources.
A 2025 report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine found that the nation’s medicolegal death investigation system is fragmented and lacks the resources, uniform standards and oversight needed to ensure consistent cause- and manner-of-death determinations. 
Independent autopsies may provide another expert interpretation of evidence, identify unanswered questions or help families understand how investigators reached a conclusion. But they are not guaranteed to produce a different answer, and they can be expensive or difficult to obtain.
Death investigations, explained
Death investigations in the United States do not follow one national model. States rely on a mix of medical examiner systems, coroner systems and hybrid models that can vary significantly in structure, resources and oversight.
In a medical examiner system, deaths are investigated by physicians, typically forensic pathologists, who are trained to determine a person’s cause and manner of death. Medical examiner offices often employ investigators, forensic technicians and other specialists.
Coroner systems operate differently. Coroners are often elected officials, and the qualifications required for the position vary by state. In some jurisdictions, coroners are physicians with medical training; in others, they may not have a medical background and may rely on forensic pathologists or outside experts to perform autopsies and help determine the cause of death.
“When you have so many systems that are varied across the country, there’s going to be some nuances in those systems,” said Dr. Michelle Jorden, the president of the National Association of Medical Examiners. Jorden also is a practicing chief medical examiner in northern California.
Why ‘clearance rates’ don’t tell the whole story about solving crimes

Those differences can affect everything from who examines a body to what resources are available when families have questions about an official finding.
For families, the system can feel opaque. A death certificate may list a cause and manner of death, but relatives may not understand what evidence was considered, who made the final determination or whether there is a process for requesting another review.
“All you want is answers and information,” said Iva Rody, the chief operating officer at the National Center for Victims of Crime. “The system itself just kind of sets us up for not being able to truly be transparent and communicate well.”
Rody said some of that difficulty stems from the way investigations are structured. Law enforcement agencies often limit what they share while an investigation is ongoing to protect evidence, witnesses and the integrity of the case. 
Policing experts say investigations can also take months or years to complete depending on the complexity of the case, available evidence and the need for additional forensic testing or interviews. But those delays can leave families feeling shut out of a process that directly affects them.
“They want answers, and they want them based on the way they’ve been conditioned to expect them. That’s just not consistent with the reality of how investigations roll out,” said Matt Irvine, a retired detective and law enforcement instructor with 29 years of experience.
Irvine said public expectations are often shaped by TV shows and movies that portray forensic results and case resolutions as happening much faster than they do in real life.
For some families, a lack of information or communication with local authorities can become a reason to commission independent investigations.
Second autopsies
Independent investigations, which might include a second autopsy, may confirm the initial findings, identify information that was overlooked or provide families with a better understanding of how investigators reached a conclusion.
But forensic experts caution that a second autopsy is not designed to automatically replace an official investigation or prove that an initial finding was wrong. In many cases, the first examination provides the most complete opportunity to document evidence before it is altered or no longer available.
“The first autopsy is more than likely going to be the most valuable autopsy,” Jorden said. “That’s where the autopsy exam is most complete.”
Black homicide victims’ families most likely to be denied compensation

The goal of an independent investigation or autopsy is not always to produce a different conclusion, but to provide another examination of the evidence. In some cases, that review can still leave families with unanswered questions.
That was the case this summer for Nolan Xavier Wells.
The 18-year-old Mississippi college student’s family’s legal team commissioned an independent forensic review after questioning the circumstances surrounding his death. Wells, who is Black, was found dead two days after he disappeared during a July Fourth boat trip to Horn Island off the coast of Mississippi with a group of mostly white friends.
Roger Mitchell, an independent pathologist and former chief medical examiner for the District of Columbia, conducted a second autopsy and classified the cause and manner of death as “undetermined” pending further investigation.
This means that Mitchell determined there was not enough evidence to confidently classify the death as natural, accidental, a suicide or a homicide.
Mitchell wrote that the most significant limitation of the independent review was the inability to directly examine the airway and lungs for evidence of water or the stomach for gastric contents, in part because internal organs had been “rightfully” removed in the first autopsy and that the trachea was missing. Mitchell wrote that he “cannot rule out injury to the neck as a contributor or a cause of death.” He added, however, that a toxicology report hadn’t come back yet, and that questions remained about the circumstances that led to Wells entering the water. 
The Mississippi State Medical Examiner’s Office conducted its own autopsy but has not yet released the results.
“We have more questions than answers at this time,” said civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing Wells’ family, when announcing the results of the independent autopsy. Wells’ family and legal team declined Stateline’s interview requests.
Trust, transparency and accountability
Some researchers who study public trust in institutions say confidence in an official death investigation is shaped not only by outcomes, but also by whether people believe the process was transparent, whether they were treated fairly and whether they had a meaningful opportunity to understand how decisions were made.
Brandon Garrett, a Duke University law professor and leading scholar on forensic evidence reliability, criminal justice outcomes and constitutional rights, said the concerns families raise about death investigations reflect deeper problems in forensic science — not only that many labs are closely tied to law enforcement, but also that some of the judgments medical examiners are asked to make aren’t backed by strong research or clear scientific standards.
“The two biggest needs are for labs to be independent and have scientific oversight, and for the basic scientific research to be done, so that experts can reach more reliable conclusions,” Garrett said.
Jorden, of the National Association of Medical Examiners, echoed that point. She told Stateline that while forensic pathologists often rely on information from law enforcement as part of an autopsy, they must maintain independence when interpreting the evidence and reaching conclusions about a person’s death.
But confidence in those conclusions is also shaped by the history of the institutions making them. In Mississippi, civil rights advocates have long pointed to the state’s history of unsolved killings of Black residents and allegations of inadequate death investigations, contributing to skepticism when official conclusions are announced in more recent cases.
“There’s valid historical reasons for people to distrust the police in this country,” said Irvine, the retired detective. Irvine served in California and Oregon. 
That history has resurfaced in public discussions of several recent deaths in the state, including the death last year of 21-year-old Demartravion “Trey” Reed, who was found hanging from a tree on the campus of Delta State University. His death was ruled a suicide, and Crump’s legal team arranged an independent autopsy, though the results have not been publicly released, according to the Mississippi Clarion Ledger.
But some experts and advocates say past failures, or what community members view as failures, can influence how people respond when authorities announce conclusions in new cases.
Misinformation and speculation can further complicate efforts to build trust. Incomplete information, rumors and unverified claims can spread quickly online, as seen in the public discourse surrounding the deaths of Wells and Reed.

“(Families and victims) may not be able to be privy to investigative information, but (investigators) need to stay in touch with them to make sure that they understand that the investigation is really happening,” Garrett said. “And they should receive news first before the public does.” 
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH child advocate’s final report on Sununu Center could take weeks, or months, to be released
description: Jason Taylor, one of New Hampshire’s two assistant child advocates, said the Office of the Child Advocate’s final report on its investigation into potential abuse and neglect at the Sununu Youth Services Center could take “certainly weeks but maybe months” to complete.  “Really, what I hope our report will talk about is the impacts of […]
text:
An investigation began in March after a child being held at the Sununu Youth Services Center, the state’s juvenile detention facility in Manchester, called the Office of the Child Advocate. (Photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)Jason Taylor, one of New Hampshire’s two assistant child advocates, said the Office of the Child Advocate’s final report on its investigation into potential abuse and neglect at the Sununu Youth Services Center could take “certainly weeks but maybe months” to complete. 
“Really, what I hope our report will talk about is the impacts of isolation and a lack of activity on children’s health,” Taylor said in an interview this week. “I think that’s the story. I really, honestly do.”
Taylor was second-in-command at the office to Cassandra Sanchez, who served as child advocate from 2022 until she was forced out of the job last week. He now serves under Sanchez’s replacement, Allen Aldenberg, a former Manchester police chief who was appointed to serve as acting child advocate. Taylor said he doesn’t know how the leadership transition will affect the progress of the report.
For her part, Sanchez said in an interview: “The long and the short of it is that leadership has failed that facility. The children have not been safe, and what has gone on in that facility is extremely harmful and dangerous to these children, both physically and mentally.”
The investigation began in March after a child being held at the Sununu Youth Services Center, the state’s juvenile detention facility in Manchester, called the Office of the Child Advocate.
“Anytime a child calls we drop what we’re doing and we go meet with the child,” Taylor said.
Taylor was the employee who first visited the facility, he said. After interviewing the child, he returned a few days later with Sanchez and the other assistant child advocate, Jennifer Jones. The office sent a letter to lawmakers on March 30 alleging staff had been potentially abusive and neglectful. The office then continued its investigation and monitoring of the facility.
The Disability Rights Center-NH, the Attorney General’s Office, and a state Senate ad-hoc committee also launched their own parallel investigations. Several allegations, including an overly restrictive lockdown, children being forced to urinate on the floor of their cells, illegal restraints resulting in at least one broken bone, unnecessary strip searches, and dried blood found on the walls, have emerged as a result of the several investigations. The investigations also revealed that staff members’ aggressive approach to managing the children was a response to the kids’ violent behavior.
In early July, the Attorney General’s Office released its report, which concluded that there were staffing problems and general leadership failures but no evidence of physical abuse of youth by staff.
Sanchez was critical of the report. She said the Attorney General’s Office “put the blame on the children almost completely” and “very minimal blame elsewhere.” 
“That’s just not accurate,” she said. Sanchez said the staff experiences are important, but should be balanced with what children at the facility are saying. She hopes her team’s final report, which is no longer in her control, centers the experience of the children more.
Sanchez said she aligns closer with the ad-hoc state Senate committee’s report, released in May, which calls for sweeping changes to leadership, a ban on strip searches of children (except in “narrowly defined emergency circumstances”), increased training, upgraded cameras in the facility, and separating the Division for Children, Youth, and Families from its parent organization, the Department of Health and Human Services. She hopes her office’s report is closer to the Senate committee’s.
Taylor said he visited the facility Friday and “the kids are ripping that place apart right now.” He said there were broken windows, fire sprinklers, door handles, and more. He argues the aggression is a response to the kids’ deteriorating mental health. 
“Every journal you can find on juvenile incarceration is very clear” that isolating children has negative effects, he said. Children had never done that kind of damage to the facility before, he noted, even at times when the detainee population at the facility was much higher.
“The argument is, the staff did what they thought they needed to do to keep themselves safe,” he said. “No argument there. The next question is, how did that impact kids?”
Specifically, he believes the facility violates laws enacted in 2023 through House Bill 49, which requires “trauma-informed care” and “evidence-based practices.”
Taylor, who worked at both the Sununu Youth Services Center and DCYF before joining the Office of the Child Advocate, doesn’t put the blame on any individual staff members. In his view, the problems within the facility are systemic. The education programming the kids are getting is insufficient, the facility is understaffed, and the program is underfunded, he said.
“The staff have been made to be the scapegoats for what’s going wrong,” he said. “I think people want an easy way out of this discussion, and that’s not really how we got here.”
Meanwhile, Sanchez called it “so extremely frustrating” to be forced to leave in the middle of the investigation. She said the office was not yet drafting the report by the time she left.
“Particularly because the reason why we couldn’t get to the point of drafting the report is we were waiting on specific information from DCYF (the Division for Children, Youth, and Families) and the facility itself that we needed to review to capture in the investigation,” she said. “And that had been dragged out for so many months, and dragged out beyond the point of me being able to be available to assist in the drafting of the report.”
In January, Gov. Kelly Ayotte announced she wouldn’t be renominating Sanchez for another term. Instead, she picked Diana Fenton, a former prosecutor and attorney for the Education Department, but Fenton ultimately withdrew from consideration amid criticisms that she had a conflict of interest by being a foster parent with an active case before DCYF. 
Sanchez left the role Friday after serving six months in holdover status, which the state’s human resources department said was the longest state law allowed her to stay without being renominated. Ayotte announced Friday she was tapping Aldenberg to replace her in the interim while the search for a permanent replacement continues.
Sanchez fears that in her absence, the office will be pressured to be “more aligned with” the attorney general’s report on the subject “because I’ve seen the governor’s coverage of supporting that report and I am not sure that the state wants the facts to show otherwise.”
She worries  there could be outside pressure to downplay certain elements of its final report.
“These are children, and they may have made poor decisions, but they are children who need help,” Sanchez said. “And the system and the way it’s working right now is not helping them. It’s harming them further, and I do worry that that aspect is going to be either not allowed to get out public or downplayed completely.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Delivering bold leadership for Hoosier affordability
description: In a time when every extra dollar on a utility bill hurts working families, seniors and all Hoosiers, Gov. Mike Braun has shown exactly the kind of decisive, ratepayer-first leadership Indiana needs. His swift decision to change leadership at the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission sends an unmistakable message: utility companies must tighten their own bel[...]
text:
Utility bills have taken center stage in a fight between regulators and Gov. Mike Braun. (Getty Images)

In a time when every extra dollar on a utility bill hurts working families, seniors and all Hoosiers, Gov. Mike Braun has shown exactly the kind of decisive, ratepayer-first leadership Indiana needs. His swift decision to change leadership at the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission sends an unmistakable message: utility companies must tighten their own belts before asking Hoosiers to dig deeper into their pocketbooks.


Just days after the IURC approved a $71 million annual rate increase for AES Indiana, Braun acted. He replaced the commission’s chairman and installed Commissioner Anthony Swinger, a veteran with more than 25 years of experience at the Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, as the new leader. This wasn’t political theater. It was a direct response to a decision that disappointed ratepayers and fell short of the governor’s clear standard for protecting affordability.
Braun has been consistent on this issue: “My top priority is affordability, which is why I am deeply disappointed by the IURC’s approval of another AES rate increase. Hoosiers have spent years tightening their belts and making tough financial decisions. It’s time for utility companies to do the same.”
That single sentence captures the frustration felt across Indiana. Families are already navigating higher costs for groceries, housing, and fuel. Another increase on electric bills — on top of previous hikes — adds real pressure, especially for seniors on fixed incomes and households stretching every paycheck. The governor’s mandate is straightforward and fair: utilities should pursue genuine efficiencies, cost controls, and operational discipline first. Only after demonstrating that discipline should they come to regulators asking customers to pay more.
Braun appoints his 4th new member to Indiana utility commission since December

By moving quickly to install new leadership at the IURC, the governor is holding the regulatory process itself accountable. The commission exists to ensure just and reasonable rates while maintaining reliable service. When a decision appears to give too much ground too easily, the governor has both the authority and the responsibility to refocus it. Naming Swinger—who brings deep expertise from the consumer advocate’s office — reinforces that focus. Swinger understands the real-world impact of rate cases from the ratepayer side, and his elevation signals that consumer protection will be a core priority moving forward.
This action fits a broader pattern. Since taking office, Braun has made utility affordability a centerpiece of his agenda. He has appointed commissioners aligned with protecting families and businesses from excessive increases and has repeatedly called out the need for utilities to control costs rather than simply pass them along. The recent leadership change at the IURC is the latest and clearest demonstration that these words carry consequences.
Critics may call the move political. In reality, it reflects accountability. When regulators approve rate relief for a major utility while affordability remains a top concern for millions of Hoosiers, the governor is right to demand better. Leadership changes are a legitimate tool to realign an agency with the public interest it serves.
Indiana families deserve electric service that is reliable and affordable. Braun’s quick, bold response to the AES rate decision shows he is willing to use the tools of his office to fight for that balance. By insisting that utilities tighten their belts first, he is standing up for the very people who keep our state running every day.
Hoosiers are watching. They appreciate leaders who act decisively when costs threaten family budgets. Braun has earned that appreciation with this move—and he has set a clear expectation for the IURC going forward: protect affordability first.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: PTSD and torture claims by Salah Sarsour put under microscope in federal hearing
description: On the second day of federal immigration court hearings for Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, federal prosecutors attempted to cast doubt on Sarsour’s claims that he’d been tortured by Israeli authorities in the 1980s, when he was a teenager living in the occupied West Bank during the First Intifada uprising, and […]
text:
Salah Sarsour being released from immigration detention. (Photo courtesy of Yaseen Najeed)On the second day of federal immigration court hearings for Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, federal prosecutors attempted to cast doubt on Sarsour’s claims that he’d been tortured by Israeli authorities in the 1980s, when he was a teenager living in the occupied West Bank during the First Intifada uprising, and that he suffers from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder as a result. 
Sarsour, a legal permanent resident of the U.S., was targeted for deportation earlier this year, after the Trump administration accused him of having lied on his green card application when he came to the United States more than 30 years ago. 
Attorneys also argued over the results of a polygraph test Sarsour took while he was asked whether he knowingly voted in an election in 2004 as a non-citizen. Mark Robel, an FBI polygraph examiner, conducted the test which he said Sarsour passed. “If he had tried to register to vote in any election, he would not have passed that test,” Robel testified. Robel charged Sarsour’s attorneys $800 to conduct the test, plus $250 an hour for his court appearance, prosecutors pointed out. 
Community members call for the release of Salah Sarsour after his arrest in late March. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Robel said that the test did not assess Sarsour’s claims of being tortured while being held in Israeli detention, because polygraph tests need to focus on a single topic at a time, and there would be subsequent charges for each test. Robel testified that Sarsour’s attorneys chose to only focus on the voting question, allegations which had not previously come up publicly after Sarsour was arrested in late March and detained in an Indiana detention facility until his release in mid-June. 
Defense attorneys also called Amahl Bishara to the stand, a professor at Tufts University where she serves as chair of the Department of Anthropology. Bishara testified as an expert on Palestinian political expression and resistance in the context of Israeli occupation. Bishara described the West Bank in the late 1980s as a place under full military occupation. Soldiers were often the focus of protests and acts of resistance during the First Intifada, Bishara said. Many children also participated in the act of stone throwing, which Bishara framed as a form of political expression rather than a direct act of violence. 
Groups of children threw pebbles or stones at fully equipped soldiers in armored trucks parked dozens of meters away, Bishara said. She cited a human rights report, using data from the Israeli Defense Forces, which found that 60% of stone throwing was done by children 13 or younger. 
In this environment, Sarsour was detained by Israeli military authorities in 1988, when he was 15. The Department of Homeland Security has said that Israeli officials convicted Sarsour of throwing a Molotov cocktail at the homes of Israeli soldiers. This conviction in an Israeli military court, is what the federal government accuses Sarsour of omitting from his green card application.
Bishara testified that Israeli authorities treated children harshly for throwing stones in the late 1980s. Children were often tortured to give false confessions or implicate other children, she said. Prosecutors attempted to challenge Bishara, asking whether the political assassinations of leaders in Egypt were also political expression, but the judge struck down that line of questioning as not relevant. Prosecutors also brought up Bishara’s participation in protests calling for the release of Palestinian students of her university who were arrested by federal immigration agents after writing opinion pieces for the school newspaper. 
Community members gather to support Sarsour after his arrest. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Jackie Bashkoff, a forensic psychologist who met with Sarsour twice testified for the defense about her  evaluations she said showed that Sarsour suffers from PTSD, which she attributed to his torture by Israeli forces as a boy in the 1980s and another stint in detention in the 1990s. “He met all the criteria” for PTSD, Bashkoff said. She said Israeli authorities beat Sarsour daily, threatened him with rape, hit him so hard in the chest that he heard something snap and tied him to bars and a chair in stress positions. “He wasn’t given proper food, water,” said Bashkoff, adding that Sarsour described having flashbacks, nightmares, and that he displayed startle responses to guards walking in unexpectedly as they talked. 
“He anticipates that if he is deported then he’s likely to be killed by the Israelis if he is sent back to the West Bank,” said Bashkoff. 
Prosecutors attempted to discredit Bashkoff by  noting that she had charged Sarsour’s attorneys $4,000 so far, not including for her testimony Wednesday. They also pressed her on why Sarsour wouldn’t state on his green card applications that he had been tortured or convicted by Israeli authorities, something about which Bashkoff was unable to offer an opinion. At one point, prosecutors suggested that Sarsour’s diabetes could cause the psychological symptoms Bashkoff attributed to  PTSD, or that Sarsour could be faking it. Bashkoff dismissed these suggestions in  tense exchanges with the prosecution. 
Another hearing is scheduled for Tuesday morning. Defense attorneys say they are still waiting on documents to be provided by the government. The judge said he doesn’t expect to render a final decision on whether Sarsour will be deported until early September.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Scarborough calls on Congress to investigate activities at local ICE facility
description: Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month.  But residents who spoke at the town […]
text:
A Scarborough resident addresses the town council before they voted unanimously on a proclamation calling on Congress to investigate ICE activities in the town. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month. 
But residents who spoke at the town council meeting said the proclamation doesn’t go far enough.
“We’re not in charge of federal immigration policy, but all eyes in Maine are on us as the only town that hosts a facility,” said Mary Ellen Galante, a Scarborough resident and retired nurse midwife, who objected to the proclamation because it “places all of the responsibility for action on our federal delegation and not on our town.” 
Galante was among the roughly 70 people who attended the packed meeting, while more than 50 others braved the rain outside holding signs calling to get ICE out of Maine.
New restrictions on state involvement in immigration enforcement take effect Wednesday

The killing of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 has renewed scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in Maine and many residents have called for local and state leaders to do more to protect communities in the state. 
The question of how much power a community has to challenge federal activities within its jurisdiction is one that has wracked the state since President Donald Trump’s administration launched its enhanced enforcement operation in January. Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
ICE in Maine
Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells. Detainees have historically been held in local jails or transferred to detention centers in Massachusetts or New Hampshire, or as far as Texas.
But during the meeting, several speakers raised concerns that ICE was misrepresenting what was occurring at that location.
“I think there are legitimate questions about whether the ordinances and the plans that have been put into place are consistent with what is happening in practice there,” Maine Rep. Sophie Warren, a Democrat who represents Scarborough, told Maine Morning Star. Warren presented a petition signed by more than 370 Mainers, 175 of which are Scarborough residents, calling on the council to take specific actions, including formally investigating the operations at the ICE facility and enforcing local laws and other municipal tools to rein in unlawful activities, which she said has precedence in Oregon.  
The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC. According to the agency’s lease inventory, the current 15-year lease began in 2021. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly demonstrated outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts made an unannounced visit to the Scarborough facility on July 17, during which he confirmed that is where the officer who shot Guerrero works.
In December, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree also visited the Scarborough facility after concerns were raised about attorneys not being permitted to accompany their clients to routine check-ins. 
Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the building, said the GSA has the authority to sublease the facility to whichever agency they choose and that neither the state nor landlord has a say in who occupies the building.
Soley said he’s in support of the protests but believes the facility has nothing to do with what happened in Biddeford. He said people are “trying to find a place to put their voice, but I think it needs to be better targeted.” 
But Scarborough councilmember Jon Anderson said that he believes Soley “must be part of this conversation.” Anderson said residents should know whether the company intends to extend the lease when it expires, and said Soley should also explore whether there’s a “mutually agreeable path” to end the lease arrangement with GSA early, “given the tragedy that occurred from the ICE agent employed at that facility.”
GSA declined to comment on the proclamation or the terms of the current lease agreement. 
“I have a 20-page lease that I need to re-sign every single year and it asks me not to do unlawful activity,” Scarborough resident Sarah Lunt told the council. She added, “I would assume that that includes murdering someone in cold blood.” 
Dozens of people braved the rain outside the July 29 Scarborough town council meeting to protest the ICE facility in the town. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)
Proclamation details
The proclamation asks Maine’s congressional delegation to engage with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other agencies to review the facility and evaluate alternatives, “including the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.” 
It further asks for transparency and community engagement regarding federal immigration enforcement activities and for the delegation to “ensure that federal actions conducted within Maine respect human dignity, civil rights, public trust, due process, and community safety and commit to raising concerns with federal officials should evidence emerge that these standards are not being upheld.”
The town notes that proclamation should not be interpreted as opposition to lawful immigration enforcement but rather, the “expectation that such enforcement be conducted in a manner consistent with the values of safety, transparency, accountability, and respect for all people.”
While a handful of residents expressed concern that the resolution was beyond the purview of the council and would open the town to lawsuits from the federal government, the vast majority who spoke said they supported the proclamation as a first step for the town to take.
Congressional support
Ahead of the meeting, Pingree, who represents the southern Maine district that includes Biddeford and Scarborough, told the Scarborough council that the town “has every right to ask whether continuing to host this facility serves the interests of the community.”
“In my view, that question deserves serious consideration from the Department of Homeland Security,” Pingree wrote in a letter. “When a federal facility reaches the point where its very presence undermines the public confidence and leaves residents feeling less safe, the federal government has a responsibility to reconsider if that facility belongs there at all.”
Pingree added that she’s “exploring every available avenue to address enforcement operations and the continued presence of ICE in Scarborough.”
Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, and Rep. Jared Golden did not comment on the proclamation. They previously sent a joint letter to the DHS Inspector General calling for a full, transparent investigation into the shooting and King has called for a review of ICE protocol.
Emma Davis contributed reporting to this story.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Judicial selection amendment could ravage rural Kansas communities. School funding is at stake.
description: As former elected officials with 16 years of experience in the Kansas Legislature and more than 50 years working with parents and children in our public schools — from Belle Plaine to Stafford and from Haviland to Garden City — we want to highlight how Kansas school children and rural communities could be affected by […]
text:
The Kansas Supreme Court is the last bulwark defending our state's constitutional requirement that all kids receive an adequate and equitable education, write our columnists. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)



As former elected officials with 16 years of experience in the Kansas Legislature and more than 50 years working with parents and children in our public schools — from Belle Plaine to Stafford and from Haviland to Garden City — we want to highlight how Kansas school children and rural communities could be affected by the constitutional amendment on the ballot Aug. 4.

This amendment would establish direct elections of Kansas Supreme Court justices, without any limits on campaign funding, conflicts of interest, or political activity by the justices.
Discussions about changing judicial selection in Kansas started about 15 to 20 years ago because of court decisions requiring the Legislature to adopt constitutional funding for schools. The debate heated up again recently because the current school finance formula is set to expire next year.
Debate about the court’s makeup did not begin due to some lofty goal of promoting democracy, but because the Kansas Supreme Court is the last bulwark defending our state’s constitutional requirement that all Kansas kids receive an adequate and equitable education, regardless of where they grow up.
Over the years, legislators from both parties resisted overthrowing the state Supreme Court. Last year, legislative leaders twisted enough arms to put an amendment on the ballot. Instead of providing voters with a compromise such as adding more members to the vetting panel or Senate confirmation, Legislative leaders took the most extreme path — direct judicial elections with no limits other than what will be “provided by law” in the future, when the public no longer has a say.
The amendment explainer doesn’t mention it, but if you look closely, near the end of the struck-out language, the proposed amendment specifically removes prohibitions that prevented judges from wielding their position and influence to engage in political campaigns and partisan activities.
Kansas public school children could suffer if the next time a school finance case is decided, justices are more concerned about soliciting $1 million campaign checks from out-of-state special interests than protecting every kid’s right to an education.
When both of us were in the Legislature, the Supreme Court forced legislators from across the state and political spectrum to work together to achieve a school funding formula that provided every student a suitably funded education regardless of their ZIP code.
This was not an easy task. Legislators first had to fix our state’s budget after the disastrous tax experiment, which left schools reeling and considering major reductions in services. That could have meant cuts to school transportation funding and cuts to schools with lower enrollment, both of which would have devastated rural communities.
The current, merit-based selection method preserves the fairly good chance that lawyers who grow up and have experience working in rural communities are selected for Supreme Court seats. Right now, the primary qualifications for Supreme Court justices are lawyers’ reputation, their legal career and their judicial service record. Under these conditions, a lawyer with a rural Kansas background can compete with anybody.
And they have.
Since Kansas adopted merit-based selection in 1958, more than 30% of justices appointed under this system have had roots in Kansas towns with a population of less than 10,000 people, and more than 60% of justices have had roots in communities with a population of fewer than 50,000 people.
A recent opinion piece by a law professor criticized a decision the Kansas Supreme Court made in 2013, saying the court was “urban-dominated.” For most of the court’s history during the school finance cases — and for the past 20 years — the court has actually been “rural-dominated.” In 2013, the hometowns of five of the seven justices were Caldwell, Tipton, Goodland, El Dorado and Salina.
Salina and El Dorado may be getting pretty cosmopolitan, but the law professor may want to get out a little more before claiming Goodland, Tipton, or Caldwell are “urban-dominated.”
If the amendment becomes law, the No. 1 qualification for any candidate will not be their legal career or service, but rather how many “friends” can write $1 million checks for a statewide campaign. That will include a few big donors in Wichita and Kansas City, but mostly, that type of donor lives in New York City, California and wherever Elon Musk or George Soros call home for tax purposes.
In addition to rural justices’ service record, geographic representation is built into the current system. Every congressional district in the state is guaranteed two out of the nine seats on the vetting panel — one lawyer and one non-lawyer.
Regardless of the selection panel’s membership, Kansas governors have always made the ultimate selection under the current system, and governors of both parties have routinely spread out their appointments geographically because they know this will widen their appeal to voters.
The state lost two rural justices over the past 18 months due to unexpected health issues (Chief Justice Marla Luckert from Goodland and Justice Evelyn Wilson from Smith Center), but we retain K.J. Wall from Scott County, and the next governor will immediately have the opportunity to select two new justices because of the current system’s mandatory retirement provision.
The Legislature is going to be renegotiating our school finance formula next year. Over time, the current system has ensured we have rural Kansas voices on the court, and it has protected rural Kansas kids from severe funding cuts that would forever harm our rural communities.

John Doll served in the Kansas Senate from 2017 to 2025 and the Kansas House from 2013 to 2017. Before that, he taught government for 20 years at Garden City public schools. Mary Jo Taylor served in the Kansas Legislature from 2017 to 2021 and served as a teacher, principal and superintendent in Kansas public schools for 34 years. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Trump admin’s endangered species rule change could leave Georgia’s wild places unprotected
description: A federal rule change set to go into effect this fall could cause big changes to Georgia’s landscape, and environmental groups are sounding the alarm. “It’s probably the worst action that’s ever been taken in the history of the Endangered Species Act,” said Will Harlan, southeast director of the Center for Biological Diversity in Asheville, […]
text:
Female red-cockaded woodpecker at a nest cavity at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, Saturday, June 1, 2024. Experts worry a new rule change could put species like the red-cockaded woodpecker at risk of habitat loss. Larry Woodward/U.S. Fish and Wildlife ServiceA federal rule change set to go into effect this fall could cause big changes to Georgia’s landscape, and environmental groups are sounding the alarm.
“It’s probably the worst action that’s ever been taken in the history of the Endangered Species Act,” said Will Harlan, southeast director of the Center for Biological Diversity in Asheville, North Carolina. “It is absolutely devastating for not just listed species, but all wildlife. It will wreak havoc upon the ecosystems that both wildlife and humans depend upon.”
The change rescinds the definition of “harm” in the Endangered Species Act. Under the new rule, intentionally killing a protected species remains forbidden, but indirectly killing a species by altering or destroying its habitat is not.
The federal government describes the rule change, which is set to take effect Sept. 14, as aligning enforcement with the original intent of the 1973 Endangered Species Act.
But Georgia Wildlife Federation President Mike Worley said protecting species from only direct killing misses the point.
“The hazards to animals aren’t just the direct killing,” he said. “The hazard to a lot of our species today are indeed the habitat conversions, habitat destruction. We are at a place where roughly 80 to 90% of species that are on our endangered list aren’t there because people are shooting them or killing them intentionally.”
A unique woodpecker
Red-cockaded woodpecker. Chuck Hess/U.S. Forest Service
Worley said the red-cockaded woodpecker, a feathery critter who once was common throughout the southeast, could be emblematic of species under threat by the new rule.
“Nobody shoots a red-cockaded woodpecker – I doubt they’re very good table fare,” he said. “Nobody hunts them. Nobody does a direct take of them.”
But in the last century, their numbers dwindled as the longleaf pine forests they once thrived in were reduced to about 3% of their former area due to logging and development.
“That’s why the red-cockaded woodpecker was on the endangered species list, because we had done away with their habitat, not because we had killed too many of the individuals with a gun,” Worley said.
The longleaf pines of the Jones Center at Ichauway, a 29,000-acre research and conservation institute near the southwestern corner of the state, are home to about 200 red-cockaded woodpeckers, up from just one in 1999, thanks to relocation efforts from around the southeast and careful management.
The red-cockaded woodpecker was one of the first species to receive protection under the Endangered Species Act in 1973, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service changed its status from endangered to threatened in 2024 after conservation efforts led to its numbers starting to bounce back.
A North Atlantic right whale with propeller scars. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
Jones Center outreach and education coordinator Rachel McGuire said the birds are the only woodpeckers in North America that make their homes in living trees rather than dead ones.
One advantage of that is it allows them to bore holes around the tree, causing sticky resin to leak out and gum up the plans of snakes that climb up trees to eat woodpeckers. They also have a symbiotic relationship with a type of fungus that makes the core of the tree soft and easier to excavate.
Still, even in ideal circumstances, with help from other woodpeckers, it can take at least a year to build a nest, so the loss of an excavated tree can be devastating.
McGuire said highly adapted species like the red-cockaded woodpecker could be among the most vulnerable to the type of habitat loss conservationists worry the rule change will cause.
“The species that stand probably the most to lose are going to be those that need more specialized habitat, species that utilize larger home ranges, so they need simply more habitat, more connectivity,” she said, adding that it’s not unusual for red-cockaded woodpeckers to use up to a few hundred acres for foraging.
Harlan with the Center for Biological Diversity said he’s worried not just for the woodpeckers, but for species across the state, from humongous North Atlantic right whales that calve on protected sites off Georgia’s coast to credit card-sized bog turtles in the Blue Ridge Mountains.
“The protections for sea turtles and shorebirds protect a bunch of other marine species that maybe aren’t listed but are declining or need protections,” he said. “Same with endangered bats and forest birds and hellbenders and mussels and fish. They protect rivers that protect brook trout, which aren’t federally listed but are vital to the fly fishing trout industry of north Georgia, for example. So really all wildlife will be affected if habitat like rivers and forests are allowed to be degraded. Those Endangered Species Act protections were really umbrella protections for all of Georgia’s wildlife.”
Next steps
Red-cockaded woodpecker with bug snack. Photo credit: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
In a letter to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service during a public comment period, Georgia Department of Natural Resources Wildlife Division manager Ted Will criticized the change as contrary to the language of the Endangered Species Act and potentially harmful.
“We believe that the proposed interpretation of ‘harm’ is incorrect, and could do much to inhibit effective wildlife management and conservation. Habitat management is an integral part of Georgia DNR’s Strategic Plan, and permeates virtually every aspect of what we do as a state wildlife agency.”
Department of Natural Resources manager of external affairs Haley Chafin said in a statement that the department will continue to protect wildlife while following the law.
“Georgia has a reliable track record of conserving and preserving the state’s natural wonders and assets while also promoting greater opportunity for individuals and communities, and it will continue to balance those important objectives in the future,” the statement reads in part.
The Center for Biological Diversity is part of a lawsuit seeking to overturn the rule change. Harlan argues that the change exceeds the Trump administration’s authority.
“Congress passed the ESA, and they made it very clear in the language of the law itself that a species and its habitat are protected under the law,” he said. “Trump is trying to circumvent that by changing how the regulations are implemented, but that doesn’t change the law.”
The U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service did not respond to requests for comment.
Harlan said Georgia could decide to impose some of its own protections. The state Department of Natural Resources is reviewing recommended revisions to its own protected species list.
“It’s proposing to potentially add new species and maybe strengthen protections for state-listed species,” he said. “That’s different than the federal Endangered Species Act, but Georgia could put some more teeth in its state endangered species act to protect the habitat, to make up for what’s currently being lost federally, so that might be one path.”
But states don’t have the same authority – or the same budget – as the federal government.
“Georgia has in some ways laid a foundation, but the challenges of enacting an endangered species act and the resources that go into overseeing and managing that are enormous,” Worley said.
“I cannot imagine, as a national developer, having to face fifty different endangered species acts across the nation,” he added. “You’ve got to address each one individually and how that state effectively addresses those problems.”
Catherine Wannamaker, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is also suing over the proposed rules change, said the court actions are “hoping to keep this at bay until a new administration has a chance to revisit it.”
But she said the rule change could mean big changes to Georgia’s wild places before that has the chance to happen.
“This is a rule change that has landscape-scale impact, and everyone should care about it,” she said. “Not just for endangered species but because of habitat and common species we all see as we walk around our neighborhoods and drive through our back roads, and it’s just a really, really big deal.”
