name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Regulators cut $500 million from Eversource’s storm cost recovery
description: CT regulators agreed to allow Eversource to recover about $500 million less than the amount the utility requested last year for storm costs.
text:
Connecticut regulators agreed to allow Eversource to recover $861 million in deferred storms costs on Wednesday, cutting more than $500 million from the request filed by the company last year.
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority voted unanimously in favor of a final decision settling how much money was owed to the company for its response to a series of “catastrophic” storms between 2018 and 2023. Those storms, which each cost the company more than $4 million, are treated differently from smaller storms that are included in normal rates.
The decision also paves the way for Eversource to begin the process of recovering those costs through the use of long-term low-interest bonds. Eversource has estimated that the process, known as securitization, will save customers $6 to $7 a month compared to a shorter pay-back period.
The vast majority of the cuts — nearly $400 million — were the result of PURA’s rejection of Eversource’s request to collect interest on its previously incurred expenses until after regulators were able to review and approve those appropriateness of those expenditures. (The company is allowed to begin accruing interest on those costs moving forward, starting with the release of Wednesday’s decision).
PURA also found fault with other expenses Eversource sought to recover, cutting millions of dollars for things such combining several smaller storms into one event, excessive food and lodging costs and chartering a private plane to fly out a crew of workers to respond to one storm in 2023. 
Still, regulators approved nearly 90% of the actual costs that Eversource sought to recover from those storms, excluding interest payments. After accounting for about $191 million in payments that are already included within existing utility rates and a smaller amount of mutual aid from other utility companies, the total amount that will be collected through securitization is nearly $668 million, according to PURA. 
In his comments during Wednesday’s meeting, PURA Chair Thomas Wiehl said the decision is one that “may, ultimately, please no one,” but was based a painstaking review of thousands of pages of records submitted by Eversource and other stakeholders.
“We must evaluate whether Eversource’s decisions were reasonable in light of the circumstances at the time,” Wiehl said. “In other words, it isn’t as simple as just looking back with perfect hindsight and deciding that we’d rather not pay for performance that could have been better.”
In a statement responding to the decision, Eversource spokeswoman Jamie Ratliff said it represented an “important step” toward the recovery of past expenses while also providing the company with direction to shape its response to future storms.
“Storm response is a process of continual improvement, and we look forward to applying what we’ve learned from this outcome to improve our process,” Ratliff said. “With affordability a main focal point here in Connecticut and across the nation, the authorization to securitize these catastrophic storm costs will allow us to remove those hundreds of millions of dollars from our recently filed rate review, resulting in a lower bill impact for customers.”
The case was separate from Eversource’s request earlier this month to increase its base distribution rates by around 11% starting in 2027. Regulators are still reviewing that request.
However, company officials had asked that PURA complete its review of the storm costs in time for the securitization process to be completed and baked into customers’ bills around the same that new rates take effect next year. Without securitization, those officials argued, next year’s rate hikes would have to be much steeper. 
Critics of Eversource’s request praised PURA’s decision to reject Eversource’s request for retrospective interests payments, which they said would have set a bad precedent for future cases. 
“This is an important victory for Connecticut ratepayers. PURA has rejected Eversource’s attempt to make Connecticut families pay millions of dollars in interest payments on unvetted and unapproved costs,” Attorney General William Tong said in a statement. “We will continue to scrutinize every dollar Eversource requests from ratepayers, including in its upcoming rate case, to ensure ratepayers do not have to pay a penny more than they absolutely have to.”
The Office of Consumer Counsel, which represents utility customers in cases before PURA, had advocated for more than $171 million in additional cuts from Eversource’s request based on what it determined to be improper expenditures. 
“While today’s decision does not include our full list of disallowances and could have held Eversource to account in areas where OCC does not believe the company met its burden of proof, the decision appropriately denied Eversource retrospective carrying charges and adopted several of the adjustments identified through OCC’s prudency review related to storm eligibility, vendor oversight and management, excessive food, lodging, and transit spending, and duplicative cost recovery,” Consumer Counsel Claire Coleman said in a statement. “Overall, the ratepayer savings reflected in the final decision would not have been possible without OCC’s extensive investigation, legal analysis, and advocacy.”
During their public comments on Wednesday, several members of PURA’s board also lamented about the time that had passed since many of the storms in question occurred.
Wiehl, the chairman, noted that he and four other members of the board who were appointed by Gov. Ned Lamont last year inherited the case from the previous PURA regime under former chair Marissa Gillett. Gillett resigned in October, following a series of bitter disputes with Eversource and the state’s other major utility company, United Illuminating. 
Everett Smith, one of the new members on the board, also called for reforms that will allow for a more streamlined recovery of catastrophic storm costs, which he said would would be fairer for both the utilities and their customers.
“Storm costs recovery needs a fresh approach to ensure that this situation does not happen again,” Smith said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Gov. Shapiro faces calls to close youth detention center, end state collaboration with ICE
description: Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. Immigration advocates from across Pennsylvania called on Gov. Josh Shapiro to shut down a youth detention center in Berks County and end state collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Wednesday. Over 100 people from 15 Pennsylvania counties joined a rally [[...]
text:
Immigration advocates from across Pennsylvania gathered at the Capitol on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Emily Scolnick/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. 
Immigration advocates from across Pennsylvania called on Gov. Josh Shapiro to shut down a youth detention center in Berks County and end state collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Wednesday.
Over 100 people from 15 Pennsylvania counties joined a rally on the Capitol steps, urging Shapiro to protect immigrant communities, limit the enforcement of ICE detainers, and prevent ICE from accessing state databases and information from PennDOT that could lead to enforcement efforts. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Imagine waking up every day and knowing that going to work could separate you from your family,” said Vincent Nguyen, a youth leader with the Woori Center and intern with the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition (PIC), at a press conference Wednesday. “My generation is inheriting Pennsylvania, the United States, that today’s leaders are shaping. I want to inherit a commonwealth where every family can … live without fear.” 
The Shapiro administration said it is currently reviewing how ICE, Customs and Border Protection, and other federal agencies can access state  systems. Pennsylvania State Police officers are also not permitted to detain individuals due to their immigration status.
Several attendees said Shapiro’s response moving forward — or lack thereof — could determine how they vote in November’s election, where he is running for a second term against Republican and current state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. 
“You want our vote, you earn our vote,” Jasmine Rivera, PIC’s executive director, said at the rally. “You are not getting a dime of our money until you finally do something.” 
Vincent Nguyen, a youth leader with the Woori Center and intern with the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, speaks at a press conference on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Emily Scolnick/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Nguyen told the Capital-Star that he and many other young people “aren’t just voting for the party anymore. They’re voting for the person.” 
“I think it’s time that Josh Shapiro and many other politicians realize that they won’t get our support just because we may sort of agree with them on some things,” he said. 
Tammy Murphy, the public policy and advocacy manager for Make the Road PA, said politicians can’t hide from the immigration issue going into this year’s elections. She added that while she won’t vote for Garrity, that doesn’t mean Shapiro will get her vote if he does not act. 
“I’m an immigrant myself, formerly undocumented,” said Miguel Andrade, who is the communications director for PIC, but shared his personal views. “It’s a personal issue for me, and it does make me think about who are the elected officials I’m going to be supporting moving forward.” 
“I would not vote for Shapiro in this moment,” he added. 
Calls to close Abraxas
Many rally attendees displayed signs calling for Shapiro to issue an Emergency Removal Order to close Abraxas Academy, a youth detention center in Berks County that has faced several lawsuits alleging sexual abuse within the facility this year. 
Several rally attendees carried signs urging Gov. Josh Shapiro to close Abraxas Academy, a youth detention center in Berks County. (Photo by Emily Scolnick/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“A society is measured by how we treat our most vulnerable members, especially those who are in prison and children,” said David Wesley Cornish, an attorney representing multiple Abraxas victims. “Children are to be protected and cared for. They are to be nurtured. They are not to be harmed.” 
Rosie Lapowsky, a spokesperson for Shapiro, wrote in a statement that Pennsylvania’s Department of Human Services currently performs weekly unannounced visits to Abraxas to inspect living conditions and assess treatment of its youth.
“The Shapiro Administration has zero tolerance for any neglect, abuse or mistreatment of children in facilities it licenses,” she wrote. “Our priority is keeping these children safe — and we are mindful that if an Emergency Removal Order were to be issued for Abraxas Academy, non-citizen youth would be transferred back into the custody of the Trump Administration, at which point Pennsylvania would no longer have the oversight authority to ensure they are being cared for.” 
In November 2025, DHS revoked Abraxas’ license for its Secure Detention Unit — one of three licenses the facility maintains — for failure to report alleged instances of abuse. Lapowsky said there has been no new evidence that has prompted additional investigation. 
The other two licenses continue to be subject to increased monitoring from DHS, which has no role in placing non-citizen children, according to the Shapiro administration.
Immigration advocates posed after delivering a letter to Gov. Josh Shapiro on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Emily Scolnick/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Every leader, every lawmaker, every citizen of Pennsylvania should be demanding the immediate release of these youth and the immediate closure of the Abraxas facility,” said Leslie Mamas, a reverend at the United Church of Christ in Montgomery County. “This isn’t a political issue. It is a moral one.” 
Following the rally, Rivera led a group of organizers to Shapiro’s office to deliver a letter signed by immigrant rights advocates. The contents have not been released publicly.
She said up to this point, there have been no direct conversations with the governor about the coalition’s demands, “and it’s not for lack of asking.” 
“There’s been many, many, many conversations and research and reports sent over to his staff,” she added.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas suspends enforcement of law preventing limits on which pharmacies can sell medications
description: The Arkansas State Board of Pharmacy decided Tuesday to not enforce a 2025 law that would remove drugmakers’ power to limit which pharmacies can purchase their drugs after a federal judge called the measure unconstitutional. U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky in May granted Novartis Pharmaceuticals’ request to block the state from enforcing Act 630 of […]
text:
Medications are stored on shelves at a pharmacy in Los Angeles. (Photo by Eric Thayer/Getty Images)The Arkansas State Board of Pharmacy decided Tuesday to not enforce a 2025 law that would remove drugmakers’ power to limit which pharmacies can purchase their drugs after a federal judge called the measure unconstitutional.
U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky in May granted Novartis Pharmaceuticals’ request to block the state from enforcing Act 630 of 2025 against the New Jersey-based company. Rudofsky is presiding over similar suits filed by Bristol Myers Squibb and Accredo Health Group. The plaintiffs didn’t respond to requests for comment.
Act 630 is the second 2025 law related to prescription drug access that was blocked in federal court after Act 624, which would have banned pharmacy benefit managers from holding drugstore permits. Accredo Health Group is among the plaintiffs that sued over Act 624.

Act 630 injunction 
Both laws were found to violate the U.S. Constitution’s dormant commerce clause, which prohibits states from making laws that discriminate against interstate commerce.
The pharmacy board voted Tuesday to support settlements in the lawsuits against Act 630 and to not process any applications from pharmacies seeking limits on their distribution networks in Arkansas.
Republican Rep. Brandon Achor of Maumelle, a practicing pharmacist and Act 630’s sponsor, said the injunction was frustrating but provides guidance for how to amend the law in a future legislative session. Achor is running for a state Senate seat in November.
He said he found it disappointing that drug companies did not take the opportunity Act 630 gave them to “show their work and show cause for why their current network was necessary for patient care.”
“Rather than complying and taking on the opportunity to show why their process is for the good of the patient, they sued and said, ‘Stop asking us questions,’” said Achor, who also co-sponsored Act 624.
In addition to more legislative action, the state could come up with “a market-based solution, if the manufacturers would come to the table and listen and be open-minded,” Arkansas Pharmacists Association CEO John Vinson said.
“Until they do, I think there’s going to be a continued fight over it as long as patient lives and access are still at stake,” Vinson said.
He noted that a northeast Arkansas pharmacy has been unable to stock a specific life-saving cancer medication manufactured by Bristol Myers Squibb. Cancer patients’ mortality increases by 10% for every four weeks without treatment, Vinson said.

From left: Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin (fifth from left) announces a lawsuit against several prescription drug manufacturers on July 22, 2026. Supporters of the litigation include Arkansas Pharmacists Association CEO John Vinson (far left) and pharmacist and Republican state Rep. Brandon Achor of Maumelle (fourth from left). (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Achor and his wife, also a pharmacist, have both been through cancer treatment.
“I’ve seen that from the patient’s perspective, I’ve seen it from the provider’s perspective, and from my perspective as a legislator, I’m not willing to accept the current norm as something that is sustainable for Arkansas,” he said.
Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb are among 13 drug companies the state sued last week. Attorney General Tim Griffin alleged that the companies violated Arkansas’ 2021 law requiring drugmakers that participate in Medicaid to sell discounted drugs to contract pharmacies.
The 2021 law survived a federal court challenge when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of a lower court ruling that federal law does not preempt Arkansas law.
Both the 2021 law and Act 624 of 2025 were the first laws of their kind nationwide. Arkansas also sought to improve patient access to medication with another 2025 law allowing nonprofit hospitals to hold pharmacy permits.
The state appealed the Act 624 injunction, but an appeal in the Act 630 litigation “is very unlikely,” representatives from Griffin’s office told the pharmacy board Tuesday.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Trump hosts FCS Champion MSU Bobcats at White House
description: Members of the 2025 FCS Champion Montana State University Bobcat football team got a trip to Washington, D.C. and lunch on Wednesday as President Donald Trump met with students, coaches, the governor and members of Montana’s federal delegation. The Bobcats won the title on Jan. 5, 2026, in overtime against Illinois State, capping off a […]
text:
A football, Montana State Bobcats jersey and the 2025 FCS National Championship trophy are pictured on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. (Photo via X / Rep. Troy Downing's Office)Members of the 2025 FCS Champion Montana State University Bobcat football team got a trip to Washington, D.C. and lunch on Wednesday as President Donald Trump met with students, coaches, the governor and members of Montana’s federal delegation.
The Bobcats won the title on Jan. 5, 2026, in overtime against Illinois State, capping off a 14-2 season complete with a victory in a Cat-Griz rematch in the FCS semifinals. About 90 members of the Bobcat football team and Montana State head coach Brent Vigen attended the event in Washington, D.C., according to the Bozeman Daily Chronicle. 
Rep. Troy Downing, Sens. Tim Sheehy and Steve Daines and Gov. Greg Gianforte also attended the ceremony and took photos with the team. NBC Montana reported the team spent time in the Rose Garden and a photo from Daines’ office showed the team on the steps of the U.S. Capitol as well.
The Chronicle added the plan was for the team to dine on burgers and Wilcoxson’s Ice Cream on Capitol Hill.
“What a day celebrating the @MSUBobcats_FB National Championship at the White House,” Downing said in a post on X. “Thank you, @POTUS, for recognizing these outstanding student-athletes, coaches, and the entire Bobcat community. Montana is proud!”
The Bobcat football team has had a remarkable run of success during the past decade under former head coach Jeff Choate and Vigen, who has a 61-12 record at Montana State since taking over the team in 2021. Vigen’s base contract is $295,000 and he earned around $180,000 in bonuses for winning the title, according to the Montana Free Press.
The Bobcats have made the FCS playoffs all five years under Vigen. The 2025 football title was the university’s first national title in football since 1984.
“Our players will remember this trip for the rest of their lives, and they’ve earned it,” Vigen said in a press release.
MSU President Brock Tessman called it a “tremendous honor for our entire university and for the state of Montana.” 
Gov. Gianforte said in a press release it was great to join President Trump to congratulate the Bobcats on their “hard work, discipline, and a commitment to excellence.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico officials celebrate state bucking Obamacare enrollment trend
description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and state Health Care Authority officials on Wednesday celebrated a new analysis showing that New Mexico is the only state in the country in which Obamacare enrollment increased since Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire late last year.
text:
New Mexico officials, including Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, on July 29, 2026, celebrated the state’s increase in Affordable Care Act enrollment despite the expiration of federal subsidies. (Julia Goldberg/Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and state Health Care Authority officials on Wednesday celebrated a new analysis showing that New Mexico is the only state in the country in which Obamacare enrollment increased since Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire late last year. 
The Kaiser Family Foundation study published Tuesday evaluated recent enrollment trends for those who purchase coverage from exchanges established through the 2010 Affordable Care Act, aka Obamacare. The study found that New Mexico’s enrollment increased 14% since 2025. Nationally, enrollment dropped 12% in the same period.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kaiser’s study attributes the nationwide decline to the expiration of federal subsidies, known as the Enhanced Premium Tax Credit, that reduced premiums for certain Obamacare enrollees who made less than 400% of the federal poverty level ($128,600 for a family of four.) 
A 2021 federal law created the tax credits with a four-year expiration date, and Congress did not extend them, despite efforts from minority Democrats. 
But unlike other states, New Mexico used its own funds, both in an October 2025 special legislative session and during the regular legislative session earlier this year, to fully pay for the expiring tax credits with state funds.
Roughly 65,000 New Mexicans receive the tax credits. In some cases, the tax credit covers 90% or more of the premium. 
Obamacare enrollment declines in every state but New Mexico

The Kaiser study noted that New Mexico is the only state to fully fund the tax credits on its own. In the period the study analyzed, between late 2025 and May of this year, Obamacare enrollment increased from roughly 69,000 New Mexicans to more than 80,000.
In a statement Wednesday to Source NM, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said the enrollment increase shows that New Mexico was right to prioritize healthcare affordability. 
“Affordability is a top priority in New Mexico,” she said. “The results speak for themselves — people urgently need affordable health care. New Mexico is proving that it is possible, even in the face of Congress’s failure to extend these tax credits.” 
Health Care Authority spokesperson Marina Piña noted that the state’s Health Care Affordability Fund, which the Legislature established in 2021 and expanded during the 2026 session, “helped keep premiums and out-of-pocket costs low despite federal subsidy reductions.” 
The 2026 expansion transferred $91 million into the fund through July 1, 2027, along with an additional $162 million in the two fiscal years afterward. 
“We are grateful to the Legislature and the Governor for having the foresight to establish the fund in 2021 and support policies that protect the health and wellbeing of New Mexicans,” she said. 
New Mexico House of Representatives Majority Floor Leader Rep. Reena Szczepanski (D-Santa Fe), who championed state legislation funding the expiring subsidies, told Source NM in a text message Wednesday that maintaining New Mexicans’ access to healthcare during this tumultuous period will have lasting benefits. 
“If we can continue to increase access to healthcare, we will make gains in everything from education to public safety to economic development, because it all starts with good health,” she said. “It’s not too late for Republicans in Congress to act and restore the support that families need.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: US Sen. Lindsey Graham remembered by his ‘beloved’ South Carolina: ‘He was us’
description: The late Sen. Lindsey Graham was remembered Wednesday as a loyal friend who embodied the American Dream and the state he loved.
text:
The funeral service for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham at First Baptist Church in Columbia Wednesday, June 29, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The late Sen. Lindsey Graham was remembered Wednesday as a loyal friend who embodied the American Dream and the state he loved.
“The reason he resonated with us is because he was us,” former U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy of Spartanburg said Wednesday during Graham’s funeral at First Baptist Church.
“He wasn’t born with a silver spoon in his mouth, but a plastic fork,” he said. “It is the story of America. It is the story of South Carolina that we punch above our weight.”
Graham, 71, died late July 11 from a ruptured aorta, according to preliminary findings from the medical examiner’s office in Washington, D.C.
The two-hour public service in Columbia followed an invitation-only memorial at Washington National Cathedral, where President Donald Trump gave the eulogy.
Former U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy speaks during funeral services for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham Wednesday, June 29, 2026, at First Baptist Church in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“This kid from South Carolina … rose to be mourned by world leaders, friends with presidents,” Gowdy said, noting the small-town lawyer also ended up picking Supreme Court justices.
‘Least pretentious person’
And yet, Graham was the “least pretentious person I’ve ever seen in politics,” Gowdy told the more than 1,000 people gathered in the church for the funeral.
Those in attendance included current and former elected officials, state agency heads, college presidents, the senator’s family, and long-time employees he considered family.
Graham grew up in Central, in the back room of a restaurant and pool hall owned by his parents. He raised his sister, Darline, after both his parents died 15 months apart, while he was a student at the University of South Carolina.
“There are three things that matter to me,” Gowdy said Graham told him: the putter his father gave him, the class ring his mother bought for him just before she died, and his sister.
Giving an example of how unostentatious Graham was, Gowdy recalled how he showed up to fellow Sen. Tim Scott’s August 2024 wedding in Mount Pleasant.
Running late, as usual, Graham walked up wearing cargo pants and a Dale Earnhardt t-shirt. Asked by Gowdy’s wife whether he wanted them to wait while he changed, his response was: “Change what?”
Graham’s characteristic humor was also on display at Scott’s wedding.
As the vows began and the pastor asked the couple if they’d love each other “in sickness and in health,” Graham could no longer contain himself. He leaned over to Gowdy and asked: “How sick are we talking? Seasonal allergies?”
At the line for richer or for poorer, Graham quipped: “Tim, don’t do it. Negotiate.”
“You have no idea how hard it is to get kicked out of a wedding, but we managed to do it,” Gowdy joked, earning a chorus of laughter from the church.
Attendees laugh at stories told about the late Sen. Lindsey Graham during funeral services at First Baptist Church in Columbia Wednesday, June 29, 2026. Those in attendance included, left to right, Gov. Henry McMaster, U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn, U.S. Sen. Tim Scott, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
The hilarity continued at the reception, when Graham told a young child, “‘I’m so sorry, buddy. There will be no Social Security for you,'” Scott recalled.
An authentic man
But Graham wasn’t all jokes. He had a way of lifting people up, especially fellow South Carolinians.
Graham’s political career began in 1992, when he won a state House seat. Voters then elected him to the U.S. House in 1994 and the U.S. Senate in 2002 to replace retiring Strom Thurmond.
Graham had already been sworn in to the Senate in January 2003 when he came to Columbia for the inauguration of Gov. Mark Sanford. As part of the ceremony, Graham walked down the Statehouse steps with U.S. Sen. Fritz Hollings, who after 36 years in the Senate alongside Thurmond was finally South Carolina’s senior senator.
But Hollings, a Democrat, received only light applause at a ceremony where seven of the nine constitutional officers being sworn in were Republicans — including Henry McMaster, then newly elected attorney general. By comparison, thunderous applause came from the crowd when Graham’s name was called. He took Hollings’ hand and lifted it high, acknowledging the attention as a team rather than for himself.
It was a moment that stuck with McMaster.
“I believe that not many men would have done what Lindsey did,” the governor said.
Those who spoke about Graham also said he lived out his faith, even though he wasn’t a well-versed church-goer.
Asked at Scott’s annual prayer breakfast to share his favorite Bible verse, Graham gave a line that was actually a quote from the movie “Gladiator.”
“He did more for the cause of Christ, without being able to cite a Bible verse, just with the authentic way that he presented his relationship with Christ,” Gowdy said.
That down-to-earth, authenticity is something Maria Medanis and her mother Pat, both of Columbia, experienced firsthand.
Pallbearers carry the casket of late Sen. Lindsey Graham out of First Baptist Church in Columbia following funeral services held Wednesday, June 29, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Pat Medanis’ mother, who lived in London, was sick and didn’t have long to live. At the last minute, Pat Medanis learned her passport had expired. She contacted Graham at his Senate office. She didn’t have to say much. He just offered to help and got the job done.
“I got to hold my mother’s hand at the very last hour,” Pat Medanis said. “So, to me, that is a gift of a lifetime.”
“I think South Carolina lost a very important man,” she added. “Because he was all feelings, and he always wanted to help, no matter what area it was.”
That personal connection is what prompted the mother and daughter to pay their final respects at First Baptist Church.
Back home in South Carolina
Graham’s attention to constituent service continued the tradition of his predecessor, whose July 1, 2003, funeral was also at First Baptist Church. Thurmond, the only senator ever to turn 100 in office, died less than six months after retiring. His 47½ years in the U.S. Senate ranks fourth-longest in history.
It’s been 19 years since the church held the funeral for a statewide official. Former Gov. Robert McNair (1965-71), who was a member of the church, died in November 2007 at 83 years old.
In a final sendoff for Graham, the funeral attendees rose to sing the final chorus of “How Great Thou Art.”
Following the public funeral, a motorcade escorted Graham’s remains to his native Pickens County for a private family burial.
“You’re back in your beloved South Carolina,” Gowdy said, as attendees wiped back tears. ”And you will soon be laid the rest in your hometown.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey throws support behind conservation ballot question
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Asked if she has a position on any of the questions yet, Healey told GBH's Jim Braude and Margery Eagan, "Not on all of them, and you know, there are some that I've sort of taken a closer look at as a matter of priority," before mentioning the conservation measure.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY on Wednesday threw her support behind a ballot question that supporters say could unlock $100 million in new conservation dollars.
The measure, one of nine that will be before voters in November, will be listed as Question 6 on ballots. 
Asked if she has a position on any of the questions yet, Healey told GBH “Boston Public Radio” hosts Jim Braude and Margery Eagan, “Not on all of them, and you know, there are some that I’ve sort of taken a closer look at as a matter of priority,” before mentioning the conservation measure.
“It’s no new taxes, OK?” Healey said. “But what it does, is it takes the use of an existing sales tax on your recreational vehicles, golf equipment, other sporting goods — we get taxed when we buy that stuff. And it proposes that we take a piece of that and that we use it to fund land and water protection, park and trail restoration. And I think that’s a good thing.”
The tax revenues collected on the sales of sporting goods would be put into a new fund focused on conserving or restoring farms, forests and other lands, protecting drinking water, and creating or improving parks, green spaces, trails and outdoor recreation areas. 
Twenty-eight other states already have a dedicated funding source for conservation work, Mass Audubon CEO David O’Neill said Tuesday, when advocates kicked off the “Yes on 6” campaign on the Charles River Esplanade. The question is backed by a coalition of 95 groups. 
“I think that’s a good thing in Massachusetts to be supporting those things, and you know, we would be able to do it in a way that doesn’t raise fees or taxes on anyone,” Healey said.
After speaking to the conservation measure, Healey said that she thinks “we’ve got to continue the push on housing,” backing “any efforts that increase housing” and specifically naming the “yes in my backyard” housing proposal, alongside one that “looks at land that, you know, schools, that churches, religious institutions have that might be available for housing.” 
One housing-related ballot question will go before voters in the fall that would allow starter homes to be built on smaller lots, which proponents say would be a tool to alleviate housing shortages.

title: 86 Nebraska counties facing drought approved for USDA emergency loan assistance
description: LINCOLN — U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has approved another disaster declaration for 13 Nebraska counties due to drought, bringing the total number of counties covered by a USDA declaration for drought conditions this year to 86 of 93 counties. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced Rollins’ latest approval Wednesday, one day after she approved [[...]
text:
U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins speaks with officials who had been fighting Nebraska wildfires in March 2026. (Courtesy of USDA, via Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins' X post)LINCOLN — U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has approved another disaster declaration for 13 Nebraska counties due to drought, bringing the total number of counties covered by a USDA declaration for drought conditions this year to 86 of 93 counties.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced Rollins’ latest approval Wednesday, one day after she approved it. A secretarial designation frees up loan assistance for Nebraska farmers impacted by drought for up to eight months after the declaration is issued. Six counties are now covered for the first time in 2026.
Local USDA Farm Service Agency offices can provide affected farmers with additional information, according to Pillen’s office.
Rollins has approved similar drought-related orders for nearly all Nebraska counties since April. Some are listed multiple times, particularly those in western and north-central Nebraska. The eight-month deadline is restarted for any Nebraska county under a subsequent drought disaster declaration.
“I appreciate Sec. Rollins, her constant attention to the needs of [our] farmers and ag producers who might require this assistance as a result of the drought impact during this growing season,” Pillen said in a Wednesday statement.


Data from the U.S. Drought Monitor as of July 21, 2026. The service is produced through a partnership among the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, NOAA and NASA. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Drought Monitor)
The secretary also signed off on a disaster declaration for 21 counties affected by wildfires in early July. President Donald Trump issued a federal emergency for five of those counties, too.
Rollins’ latest drought-related declaration designates Lancaster and Saline Counties as primary counties plus any adjacent counties: Butler, Cass, Fillmore, Gage, Jefferson, Johnson, Otoe, Saunders, Seward, Thayer and York.
All but seven Nebraska counties on the eastern edge of the state are covered under recent declarations due to drought conditions: Burt, Douglas, Nemaha, Pawnee, Richardson, Sarpy and Washington, according to USDA data up through June 17, plus the latest declaration.
More than 76% of Nebraska faces at least “moderate” drought conditions, according to the most recent state-level data from the U.S. Drought Monitor, which is produced through a partnership among the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, the USDA, NOAA and NASA. That’s estimated to be 636,883 Nebraskans. Data is released each Thursday.
Nearly 94% of the state faces at least “abnormally dry” conditions, and over 24% of Nebraska is at the “extreme” or “exceptional” drought designation.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Democrats vow to fight Forbes’ ‘disingenuous’ lawsuit
description: Nebraska Democratic Party leaders called William Forbes a DINO – a Democrat in name only – while vowing to fight his lawsuit aiming to force them to find a replacement for former Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Cindy Burbank after she dropped out of the race.
text:
Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb speaks during a press conference in Lincoln on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Democratic Party leaders called William Forbes a DINO – a Democrat in name only – while vowing to fight his lawsuit aiming to force them to find a replacement for former Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Cindy Burbank after she dropped out of the race. 
Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb, and the party’s executive director, Precious McKesson, accused Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and state Republicans of being behind the lawsuit during a Wednesday press conference at the Democratic Party’s Lincoln headquarters. They pointed to Forbes’ support for President Donald Trump and his attendance at a training session earlier this year for conservative candidates, activists and staff, and called Forbes’ lawsuit “disingenuous.”
“He is no clear Democrat, at least no Democrat I can relate to,” McKesson said. “His sudden claim to care about Democratic voters being disenfranchised is clearly suspect considering a lawsuit of this kind could disenfranchise the very coalition that rejected Mr. Forbes.” 
The party leaders also pointed to him being represented by the same attorneys involved in the March lawsuit defending Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s decision to remove Burbank from the primary ballot. The Nebraska Republican Party released a statement saying the party has no affiliation with Forbes, “but it is his right to seek justice where he sees wrongdoing.” 
“This lawsuit says everything about Jane Kleeb’s leadership: a Democrat having to sue Democrats just to have a Democrat on the ballot,” part of the statement says. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This is just the latest drama in the Nebraska U.S. Senate race, primarily in the Democratic primary. There were allegations that each candidate was a “plant” to help either incumbent Ricketts or nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn. Both Ricketts and Osborn have denied any involvement with Forbes and Burbank. 
Forbes’ voting history and attendance at a conservative training session were reported by CNN during the primary. Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper, who declined to comment for the CNN story, told the Examiner earlier in the year that the party didn’t know Forbes, hasn’t had any relationship with him and has no knowledge of his motivations for entering the Democratic primary. 
Nebraska Democratic Party Executive Director Precious McKesson speaks during a press conference in Lincoln on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Kleeb said the state Democratic Party has been transparent about its plans to not actively recruit a Senate candidate, as Osborn is the “best path to defeat Pete Ricketts.”
“We believe that a strong coalition of voters, Democrats, independents and Republicans, are the best way to defeat Pete Ricketts and to end the corrupt Republican one-party rule across our state,” Kleeb said.
It wasn’t a secret that state Democrats were planning to clear the candidate field for Osborn, as the political strategy has been reported by the Examiner and multiple national outlets throughout this midterm cycle. 
In his lawsuit, Forbes is asking the court to grant an injunction requiring the party to find a replacement for Burbank, citing a state law that uses the word “shall” when addressing a vacancy.  He argues in the lawsuit that the word “shall” in the law means it must be done instead of an opinion to do so. Forbes argued that voters will be “disenfranchised.”
Brandon J. Johnson, an assistant professor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln College of Law who focuses on election law, said he can’t predict how a judge would rule, but it seems like the lawsuit doesn’t have a “terribly strong legal position.” 
“The argument is the provision that governs how to fill a vacancy uses mandatory language. …If this vacancy occurs, the party shall do X, Y, and Z,” Johnson said. “It’s hard to square that though with the statute that actually discusses the declination of nomination form.” 
The statute about declining the nomination said a vacancy caused by the candidate refusing the nomination “may be filled pursuant to section 32-627.” Johnson said the law cited in the lawsuit addresses the process that must be followed if a party chooses to replace a nominee. 
McKesson said the party is willing to take the case to the state Supreme Court if the ruling doesn’t go their way at the district level. 
This issue isn’t just a Nebraska one. Recently in Montana, the Secretary of State’s office told the national outlet Semafor that the Montana Democratic Party would be required to find a replacement if Democratic Senate candidate Alani Bankhead drops out — though she has said she doesn’t plan to drop out and a group of lawyers says the party couldn’t be forced to find a replacement. 
A hearing for the Nebraska case has been rescheduled for next week.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Shoreline, water quality improvements to West Okoboji Lake
description: The Iowa Department of Natural Resources announced Wednesday it had treated an area of West Okoboji Lake for Eurasian watermilfoil, an invasive aquatic plant, and that it will host a public meeting to discuss forthcoming shoreline restoration efforts. Nearly 100 segments of shoreline along the Iowa Great Lakes were damaged by flooding in 2024, including […]
text:
An excursion boat at sunset on West Okoboji Lake near Arnold's Park. (Photo by Kathie Obradovich/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Department of Natural Resources announced Wednesday it had treated an area of West Okoboji Lake for Eurasian watermilfoil, an invasive aquatic plant, and that it will host a public meeting to discuss forthcoming shoreline restoration efforts.
Nearly 100 segments of shoreline along the Iowa Great Lakes were damaged by flooding in 2024, including seven segments of Pillsbury Point’s shoreline on West Okoboji Lake. 
DNR said the construction along the small Pillsbury Point urban park will commence in the fall, primarily via barge, and take about a year to complete. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The public meeting, scheduled for Aug. 6 at 6 p.m. at Maser Monarch Lodge in Okoboji, will allow the public to share comments and ask questions about the restoration following a presentation about the project. 
A news release from the department said the shoreline work will regrade the slopes along the point, armor them with rock and seed native plants with deep roots, all to “stabilize and protect” nearly the 1,200 feet of “steep” public shoreline. 
According to a news release from DNR, the department has worked with local homeowners to repair and stabilize the toe of the slope and to develop a long-term plan to prevent future erosion and flooding issues at Pillsbury Point. 
DNR’s 2026 lake restoration plan noted the department has already restored shoreline at more than 30 sites in the Iowa Great Lakes and planned to work on additional sites in 2026. 
The department said lake users can expect increased boat traffic during the repairs around the point and at Gull Point State Park. 

Continued battle against Iowa Great Lakes invasive species

DNR and the Iowa Lakeside Laboratory – located along West Okoboji Lake – recently treated a “small, isolated population” of the invasive species Eurasian watermilfoil in the lake canals south of Miller’s Bay in West Okoboji Lake.
Eurasian watermilfoil forms a canopy that chokes out other aquatic plants. (Photo courtesy of Iowa DNR)
The department has found the tall-growing aquatic plant in the canals of West Okoboji Lake in the past, along with brittle naiad, another invasive plant species. DNR uses targeted herbicide applications to clear kill Eurasian watermilfoil before it spreads to the lake where it can choke out native species and impact lake recreation. 
Andrew Carlson, fisheries biologist for DNR, said the team “acted swiftly” to control the plant after it was discovered deep in the canals.
“With required permits already in place, we were in a prime position to respond rapidly to control this highly invasive plant and protect the aquatic ecosystem,” Carlson said in a news release. “We are thankful for community funding and staff at the Iowa Lakeside Laboratory for helping isolate the plants.”
DNR executed a $300,000 campaign to treat East Okoboji Lake, the Upper and Lower Gar Lakes and Minnewashta Lake in 2023 when the department discovered Eurasian watermilfoil was present in the waterbodies.
The department began treatments for the plant in Clear Lake — which is out of the Iowa Great Lakes system, but another popular recreational lake — in December.
According to the Wednesday news release, DNR did not find the invasive plant in the main body of West Okoboji Lake, nor in any of the other Iowa Great Lakes. 
Eurasian watermilfoil needs only a small fragment to take root, reproduce and form thick beds in a lake, which is why DNR said boaters need to follow the “clean, drain, dry” protocol when moving boats from one water body to another. 
The spread of Eurasian watermilfoil and other invasive species can be prevented by lake visitors who stop to clean their boats and equipment, drain all motors, live wells, bilges and bait buckets and dry anything that comes in contact with water, including dogs and clothing, before leaving the area. 
“The DNR is asking boaters and other users in these areas to be extra vigilant to help prevent the spread of these invasive aquatic plants elsewhere in West Okoboji or the other lakes in this chain,” the news release said. 
DNR said that since Eurasian watermilfoil was found in the canal, boat users should check their boat props for any vegetation fragments before moving into the main lake.

name: Daily Montanan
title: History is calling on Montana for courage, not divisions
description: I got involved in politics because I believed government could make life better for ordinary people. Growing up in rural southeastern Montana, I watched my father work as a truck driver and my mother wait tables while raising our family. They taught me that hard work matters, that opportunity isn’t guaranteed, and that public service […]
text:
I got involved in politics because I believed government could make life better for ordinary people. Growing up in rural southeastern Montana, I watched my father work as a truck driver and my mother wait tables while raising our family. They taught me that hard work matters, that opportunity isn’t guaranteed, and that public service is about fighting for people who don’t always have a voice.
Those values led me to serve in the Montana Legislature, as Montana’s state auditor, and later as executive director and vice chair of the Montana Democratic Party. Throughout those years, I always believed our party was strongest when we put principle ahead of politics and the people of Montana ahead of ourselves.
That is why I feel compelled to speak publicly today.
We have a real opportunity to defeat Kurt Alme and deny Donald Trump another reliable vote in the United States Senate. But this moment calls for selfless leadership. I believe Alani Bankhead can provide that leadership by withdrawing from the U.S. Senate race so Democrats and independents can unite behind the strongest candidate capable of winning.
I have spent my career encouraging women to run for office and supporting women in leadership. I wanted Bankhead to succeed. But after reflecting on the growing divisions within the Montana Democratic Party, I can no longer stay silent.
Bankhead’s public statements should serve as a red flag for all Democrats. On an episode of her podcast, “The (Humble) Warrior Podcast,” she said, “If you’re poor right now, it’s because you decided you wanted to be poor.”
Those were her own words, not AI-generated or deceptively edited. She later said the comments were directed at wealthy life-coaching clients, but that explanation doesn’t sit well with me.
There was a time when a statement like that would have been career-ending for a Democratic candidate seeking statewide office. These are challenging times, but our standards should not change.
For me, those words are deeply personal. I was raised by hardworking parents who did everything they could to provide for our family. They knew that hard work alone doesn’t erase every obstacle. Countless Montanans work two jobs, care for aging parents, or struggle with rising housing costs, grocery bills and health care expenses. Suggesting poverty is simply a choice dismisses their lived experience and contradicts the values Democrats have long fought to defend.
This election is about more than one campaign or one party. It is about protecting reproductive freedom, defending our public lands, supporting working families, and preserving our democracy. If Democrats remain divided, we risk losing not only this Senate race but also the momentum and resources Democratic candidates across the ballot need to compete.
Bankhead has served our country honorably in the Air Force, and I believe she could have a future in public service. But true leadership sometimes requires putting the cause ahead of personal ambition. Many who voted for her in the primary are deeply disappointed that she has failed to demonstrate a credible path to victory. I know the sheer volume of resources it takes to run and win a state-wide race in Montana and time has run out for Bankhead to generate what’s needed.
I urge Democratic leaders to unite behind independent Seth Bodnar, who offers the strongest opportunity to build the broad coalition needed to defeat Alme. Montana’s future is bigger than any one candidate, and this election demands the courage to do what is best for our state.
Monica Lindeen served in the Montana House of Representatives from 1999 to 2006, represented House District 43, was elected Montana State Auditor, served as vice chair and later executive director of the Montana Democratic Party, and was the Democratic nominee for Montana’s U.S House seat.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s Congressional delegation has abandoned U.S. veterans
description: It is a disgrace the way our congressional delegation has abandoned U.S. veterans. The Trump administration’s Big Beautiful Bill, which Murkowski, Sullivan and Begich all voted for, gave more tax breaks to billionaires and large corporations, while at the same time squeezing the middle class and the poor. Among the casualties are U.S. veterans.  In […]
text:
Nearly all abortions, except those to save a patient’s life, would be banned at U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals and would no longer be covered by VA medical benefits under a rule proposed by the Trump administration. The policy change comes from the Project 2025 playbook. (Getty Images)It is a disgrace the way our congressional delegation has abandoned U.S. veterans. The Trump administration’s Big Beautiful Bill, which Murkowski, Sullivan and Begich all voted for, gave more tax breaks to billionaires and large corporations, while at the same time squeezing the middle class and the poor. Among the casualties are U.S. veterans. 
In order to fund more tax breaks for the top 1%, government services to everyone else had to be cut. NPR reported that the Trump administration killed a Veterans’ Administration home loan program. Veterans are now losing their homes to foreclosure. The New York Times reported that the Veterans Affairs Department cut thousands of positions for doctors and nurses, and left vacant many unfilled positions. Furthermore, the Trump administration reversed expanded health benefits for women. The VA also pledged to end support for Housing First, the approach that was the VA’s greatest housing success. Huffington Post reported that mass firings at the VA — where many of the employees are veterans — will negatively impact its critical mission in healthcare, disability claims, services for transition to civilian life, suicide prevention and addiction treatment. 
The VA cut funding for research, including a promising study using electronic medical records to improve outcomes for veterans with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The New York Times reported that among the cuts at the VA was a collaborative research study with Harvard Medical School into veterans’ suicide. NPR further reported that the VA is making it harder for male veterans to get care for breast cancer — a rare disease for men, but just as deadly for them as it is for women. It has been widely reported, including in the Huffington Post, that ICE has arrested for deportation legal residents who served in the military with a promise of thereby obtaining US citizenship. Apparently, we are no longer a people of our word. 
The repercussions of the decimation of the staff and programs at the VA will last for years. It will not be easy for a new administration — one committed to honoring the service keeping the promises to our veterans — to undo the damage done by the Big Beautiful Bill by fully funding the agency and its programs. 
While all of our congressional delegation shares the responsibility for this disgraceful bill, I think it is Sen. Dan Sullivan who is the most to blame. He runs his campaigns in part on the fact that he is a former Marine and a champion of veterans’ causes. In a Congressional hearing, he went so far as referring to them as “my veterans.” Well, he has let them down and they are now our veterans. It is up to us to inform our congressional delegation that they will soon answer to us at the polls. Candidates now running for Senate and the House of Representatives should give voters specifics of how they will revitalize the VA.

title: Iowa Libertarian gubernatorial candidate plans to file appeal in ballot removal case
description: Iowa Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Nicholas Gluba said Wednesday his campaign plans to appeal a district court decision keeping him and his running mate off the ballot. Gluba and his running mate Jules Cutler, the Libertarian lieutenant governor candidate, were taken of the Nov. 3, 2026 general election ballot for Iowa governor by the State Objections[...]
text:
Libertarian candidate Nicholas Gluba, who is running for Iowa governor in 2026, spoke Aug. 10, 2024 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Jack O'Connor/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Nicholas Gluba said Wednesday his campaign plans to appeal a district court decision keeping him and his running mate off the ballot.
Gluba and his running mate Jules Cutler, the Libertarian lieutenant governor candidate, were taken of the Nov. 3, 2026 general election ballot for Iowa governor by the State Objections Panel in June. The panel found Cutler had not submitted an affidavit of candidacy for lieutenant governor before the deadline of 5 p.m., June 2, which disqualified their ticket. Cutler and her attorney, Jacob Heard had argued Dani Phillips, an elections support specialist at the secretary of state’s office told her she was not required to submit this paperwork when she accompanied Gluba to file for ballot access.
The gubernatorial ticket filed an appeal to the State Objection Panel’s decision in Polk County District Court. After hearing arguments for the case earlier in July, Polk County District Court Judge Joseph Seidlin released a decision in the case Monday, upholding the panel’s decision.
In a Wednesday interview, Gluba said this decision is not the end of the road for a Libertarian gubernatorial ticket. Gluba said he believed the judge’s decision reflects that “he decided he did not have the authority to change it,” but that a higher body — particularly, the Iowa Supreme Court — would be able to make a decision.
“So, we’ll be working on another appeal,” Gluba said.
The Monday decision addresses several of the Libertarian candidates’ claims about why the objection panel’s decision was not valid. The three-member panel typically consists of Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate, Attorney General Brenna Bird, and Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, but because Sand is running as the Democratic candidate for Iowa governor, he recused himself and was replaced by Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig. The candidates argued Sand should have been replaced by Gov. Kim Reynolds according to state law, and that Pate, who employs the elections support specialist, should have been recused from the panel.
Seidlin stated in the ruling he did not find that “the Panel’s decision to allow Secretary Naig to replace Auditor Sand on the Panel was unreasonable, arbitrary, or capricious,” and that “while the court can accept that Secretary Pate has an interest in having honest employees with good memories, there has to be more to trigger an obligation to recuse.”
However, the court decision also questions the State Objections Panel for affirming Phillips’ testimony at the June meeting without also considering Cutler’s account of the events. Phillips had told panel members she was not asked about filing an affidavit of candidacy, nor did she receive the paperwork from Cutler, but she also stated she did not know if Cutler had accompanied Gluba when he filed his paperwork.
“The court disagrees with the Panel’s finding that Cutler never offered and Phillips never declined or refused to receive Cutler’s affidavit of candidacy,” Seidlin wrote. “At best, the evidence appears to the court to be in equipoise. Nevertheless, the court cannot simply substitute its own findings for the Panel’s.”
While the decision upheld the panel removing Gluba and Cutler from the ballot, it still left a potential opening for a Libertarian ticket to appear on the ballot, if Cutler were to be replaced. The Libertarian candidates requested in court, as well as when they spoke to the panel, to be allowed to select a successor running mate for Gluba. Seidlin wrote this was not part of the objections process, and “the court should not give advisory opinions concerning a matter not before it.”
Gluba said he believes this decision opens the door for the Iowa Supreme Court to weigh in on these issues.
“If it goes to higher court, it would be the Iowa Supreme Court, which would therefore have supreme authority,” he said. “… So I believe that was his thought process was to refer to a higher court and establish case law throughout the state of Iowa as to how this will work in the future.”
Libertarian candidates’ challenges to State Objections Panel decisions have come before the Iowa Supreme Court before. In 2024, the state’s highest court upheld a State Objections Panel decision to remove three Libertarian candidates running for congressional offices in Iowa from the 2024 ballot because the state Libertarian party did not conduct its nominating process in accordance with state law.
Gluba said he believed the case being brought this year is significantly different from the issue brought up in 2024, related to the party nominating process.
“I feel fairly confident,” Gluba said. “Our case is actually pretty solid. The district court judge even agreed with us, that our case is good. He just did not, for reasons, decided to act in our favor.”
Gluba said the campaign has not yet filed an appeal. If reinstated by the court, Gluba and his running mate would appear on the ballot alongside Sand, the Democratic nominee, and Republican gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn.

description: The Montana Historical Society has been reaccredited by the American Alliance of Museums, which is the highest national recognition given to museums in the United States. text:
Scenes from America 250 Celebration at the Montana Heritage Center June 27th, 2026. The celebration was part of History Fest to celebrate the opening of the Montana Heritage Center. (Montana Historical Society photo)The Montana Historical Society has been reaccredited by the American Alliance of Museums, which is the highest national recognition given to museums in the United States.
The state’s historical society has been accredited by the national organization continuously since 1973, MHS said in a press release, adding the past year had been notable with the Montana Heritage Center overhaul complete and another award earlier this year from the national museum alliance.
Since the Heritage Center was reopened, it has seen more than 100,000 visitors, the historical society said in a press release.
“Reaccreditation affirms what our staff, board, and community partners work toward every day — a museum that holds itself to the highest standards of public service, ethical stewardship, and institutional integrity,” Molly Kruckenberg, director of the Montana Historical Society said in a press release. “After the extraordinary year we have had, this recognition means a great deal.”
Only eight museums in Montana — and about 3% of an estimated 33,000 American museums — are accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. The reaccreditation process is “rigorous” the press release says, involving site inspections during a multi-year process.
To maintain accreditation with the national alliance, museums must undergo the reaccreditation process at least every 10 years. The process recognizes the, “excellence, accountability, and continued institutional improvement,” a press release said.
“Accreditation is a monumental achievement,” Marilyn Jackson, AAM President and CEO, said in a press release. “The process demonstrates an institution’s commitment to best practice and is flexible enough to be accomplished by museums of any size.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: After state Supreme Court disbars him, former Hinds DA Jody Owens says his work isn’t over
description: Former HInds DA Jody Owens pleaded guilty last month, two weeks before he was to go on trial in a federal bribery case.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The Mississippi Supreme Court on Wednesday permanently disbarred Jody Owens, the former Hinds County District Attorney who recently resigned after pleading guilty to a federal charge conspiring to commit bribery. 
The move was expected after the Mississippi Bar sought to suspend Owens from practicing law by filing a complaint with the state’s high court earlier this month. Shortly after, Owens filed a motion indicating he would voluntarily resign. 
Owens pleaded guilty to the federal felony charge in June, two weeks before he was set to go on trial in a case stemming from an FBI operation that rocked Mississippi’s capital city.
Owens learned Wednesday afternoon that he was disbarred from a Mississippi Today reporter. He was working from his private downtown Jackson office, the space that prosecutors said Owens called his “War Room.” 
“In 20 years I did wonderful things with my law license and certainly impacted thousands of lives in Mississippi and I’ll always be proud of that,” he said, referring to the work he did as the former head of the Southern Poverty Law Center’s Mississippi branch.
“The problem right now is the world is so toxic,” he added. “You say ‘SPLC’ and people can’t wait to jump on you.”
The SPLC was recently indicted in Alabama on federal fraud charges.
A native of Terry in southern Hinds County, Owens was admitted to the Mississippi bar in 2006. He won election as Hinds County’s top prosecutor in 2019, besting two rivals in the Democratic primary, and avoided a runoff. 
A self-proclaimed “progressive prosecutor,” Owens eventually caught the eye of federal authorities. Beginning as early as 2023, two undercover FBI agents posed as real estate developers seeking to build a convention center hotel in downtown Jackson on a plot of land for which the city had previously obtained a federal loan to develop.
The agents enlisted an unsuspecting Owens, who has also worked in real estate, to connect them to powerful Jacksonians, including now-former Jackson City Council Member Aaron Banks and former Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba, according to a lengthy indictment unveiled in the fall of 2024. 
The two other elected officials also pleaded guilty in connection to the federal bribery case, one week after Owens. 
Owens’ sentencing is set for Oct. 15 before Judge Daniel P. Jordan III in the Southern District of Mississippi. He faces up to five years in prison. 
The now-former attorney isn’t quite ready to reveal what he plans to do next. But he’s recently been taking inspiration from the 1996 movie “The Preacher’s Wife.” 
“As the Whitney Houston song goes, ‘I believe in miracles,’” he said.

title: Diné community leaders protest Trump proposal to remove Chaco Canyon mining ban
text: WASHINGTON — A group of Diné allotment shareholders and community leaders called Wednesday for the Bureau of Land Management to continue enforcing oil and gas restrictions near New Mexico’s Chaco Culture National Historical Park.The delegation, gathered in front of the U.S. Department of the Interior headquarters that also houses BLM leadership offices, called on the agency to maintain a 2023 order that placed a 20-year ban on oil and gas extraction in public areas surrounding Chaco Canyon.The order applies to over 338,000 acres of federally managed lands that extend 10 miles beyond the park itself, creating a buffer zone around the site that holds great cultural and spiritual significance for Diné, Pueblo and other indigenous tribes. “It’s a beautiful area,” said Hazel James-Tohe, one of the community leaders who led Wednesday’s press conference. “It has so much history … everything that we hold sacred to us.” Revoking protected status For more than a year, the Trump administration has moved to potentially reverse the Biden-era BLM order and clear the way for mineral leasing in the Greater Chaco region. The BLM on July 15 opened a two-week public comment window on a draft environmental assessment of the proposal.According to the draft assessment, “the purpose and need for the proposed withdrawal revocation is to restore discretion over mineral leasing to the BLM and facilitate mineral development to meet the policies established by” a 2025 Trump executive order aimed at increasing U.S. mineral production. BLM did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment in time for publication.  Tribal leaders from the Greater Chaco region, along with advocates and New Mexico lawmakers, have organized on numerous occasions to protest the proposal to revoke the withdrawal. Effects of oil and gas development   Standing under the hot afternoon sun outside of the Interior building, the visiting delegation opened Wednesday’s press conference with a prayer before launching into their calls. “We came over here to Washington, D.C., to tell the leaders that we want to keep the buffer zone in place,” Diné allotment shareholder Mario Atencio said. “That’s what we’re here to do, to yell at buildings and yell at pictures of Donald Trump to tell them, ‘don’t frack around Chaco. It affects public health.”’ Nearly 40,000 oil and gas wells dot the Greater Chaco landscape, meaning the Diné people living in the region are already disproportionately exposed to environmental harms such as air pollution, oil spills, industrial traffic and land degradation even with the buffer zone in place, according to a press release from the group that organized Wednesday’s event. “The pollution does not recognize boundaries–it moves through air we breathe and water we depend on, placing the greatest burden on our elders, children,” said Wendy Atcitty, a member of the Eastern Navajo Huerfano community, in a separate release shared following the press conference. Atcitty and her fellow Diné representatives told firsthand accounts of what it's like to live near oil development.Growing up, she said, all she saw were “the different types of equipment scattered across the landscape,” and the sound of machinery was “louder than the birds.” Diné allotment shareholder and former Navajo National Council Delegate Daniel Tso also talked about witnessing large liquid waste leaks and exposure to methane gas in areas outside the protected withdrawal zone.“What you do to the land, you do to the people,” he said on Wednesday, quoting an old cultural saying. In a press release, he added that energy companies were “running amok” and he feared they would destroy the area’s land, air, water and sacred places.People who live near active mines often suffer from respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses, Atcitty said. Lawmakers respond After BLM announced the public comment window on July 15, members of New Mexico’s U.S. congressional delegation sent a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum urging him to extend the commentary period and condemning the Trump administration’s lack of communication with those who live in the Greater Chaco region. The administration has “been abdicating its responsibility for meaningful and complete Tribal consultation and continues to railroad communities through arbitrary deadlines and rushed decision-making,” Democratic U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich said in a July 16 press release. “Proposing to fully revoke protections for Chaco Canyon and only allowing 14 days to comment on this development is wrong, shameful, and a slap in the face to Tribes,” he added. Heinrich is the top Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.Diné and Pueblo community advocates, tribal members and allied organizations also conducted their own analysis of BLM’s draft environmental assessment. The document was shared with States Newsroom Wednesday. Among its findings, the analysis determined that “revoking the Chaco buffer zone would produce minimal additional energy production while imposing severe and irreversible harm on Indigenous communities, sacred cultural landscapes, and the environment.”The Diné group on Wednesday urged BLM to correct its environmental assessment.

title: City administrator denied jobless benefits after resigning amid dispute with the mayor
description: A city administrator who resigned after the mayor filed a police complaint against him is not entitled to unemployment benefits, an Iowa judge has ruled. State records indicate the former Fairfax city administrator, Chris Philipp, resigned in April 2026, eight months after accepting the job. At the time, Philipp alleged Mayor Jo Ann Beer had […]
text:
Iowa Workforce Development manages unemployment claims filed on behalf of Iowans. (Photo by Getty Images, logo courtesy the State of Iowa)A city administrator who resigned after the mayor filed a police complaint against him is not entitled to unemployment benefits, an Iowa judge has ruled.
State records indicate the former Fairfax city administrator, Chris Philipp, resigned in April 2026, eight months after accepting the job. At the time, Philipp alleged Mayor Jo Ann Beer had created a hostile, intolerable work environment.
The records show that in the months leading up to Philipp’s resignation, Beer had filed a complaint with the Linn County Sheriff’s Office alleging Philipp had shared with her a meme that consisted of a drawing of a bicyclist poking a stick into the wheels of the bike and falling down. The cartoon included the names of both Beer and Philipp. In her complaint, Beer allegedly suggested she felt threatened by the image.
After resigning, Philipp filed for unemployment benefits, which the city contested. That led to a July 15, 2026, hearing before Administrative Law Judge Elizabeth Johnson.
At the hearing, Philipp testified that his job had become much more difficult after Jan. 8, 2026, when the Fairfax City Council voted not to reappoint the city clerk and treasurer, Cynthia Stimpson, to her position. According to Johnson’s findings in the unemployment case, the city quickly contracted with Stimpson on a temporary basis from late January through early February, then agreed to have Stimpson remain as the “interim city clerk” through June 30, 2026.
In her findings, Johnson determined that after Feb. 9, 2026, Philipp “largely stopped reporting to work” in an effort to avoid dealing with Beer and the council members he perceived as being “in her camp.”
It was only later, Johnson found, that Philipp learned Beer had filed a police complaint against him that he deemed to be frivolous and part of an effort to drive him out of his job. On April 14, 2026, the city accepted Philipp’s resignation and agreed to pay him $30,000 as part of a formal separation agreement.
In a recent ruling denying Philipp unemployment benefits, Johnson agreed with Philipp that the meme he had shared with the mayor, which led to her police complaint, was “innocuous, particularly as (Beer) had asked to see it” and Philipp had not created it. “However,” Johnson added, “Mayor Beer overreacting to the meme and reporting it to the sheriff’s department does not create a hostile or intolerable work environment.”
Johnson concluded that while the mayor and several members of the Fairfax City Council “were challenging” for Philipp to work with, Philipp “became uncooperative and even non-communicative in the weeks after the city council voted not to renew Stimpson’s contract.”
Johnson also concluded that while Philipp contended he had left his job due to the effect it had on his health, he never saw a medical provider who advised him to quit and there was no evidence that he brought that specific issue to the attention of the city and asked for accommodations.
Philipp’s “stress level went up when the city was scrambling to cover Stimpson’s duties,” Johnson concluded, adding that she was “sympathetic to the position” in which the city had placed him. Philipp “presented a compelling personal argument for leaving his job,” Johnson ruled, but he had not met his burden of proving he quit for good cause that could be attributed to the city.
As a result, Philipp will be required to repay the $3,110 in unemployment benefits he has already collected, Johnson ruled. Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach Philipp for comment on Wednesday.
Beer declined to discuss the case when reached by the Iowa Capital Dispatch on Wednesday, describing it as “strictly a personnel matter” on which she could not comment.
