name: Florida Phoenix
title: U.S. appeals court revises Black-empowerment group’s discrimination claims against Pinellas
description: The Pinellas County Commission violated the First Amendment rights of a Black-empowerment group by withholding COVID-response grants for political and racial reasons, a federal appeals court ruled Tuesday. A unanimous opinion by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit rejected a trial judge’s ruling that the grant denials didn’t[...]
text:
Elbert P. Tuttle Courthouse in downtown Atlanta, home of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. (Photo by John McCosh/Georgia Recorder)The Pinellas County Commission violated the First Amendment rights of a Black-empowerment group by withholding COVID-response grants for political and racial reasons, a federal appeals court ruled Tuesday.
A unanimous opinion by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit rejected a trial judge’s ruling that the grant denials didn’t offend the African People’s Education and Defense Fund’s (APEDF) First Amendment and equal-protection rights.
“Giving it the benefit of all reasonable inferences, APEDF has plausibly alleged that the County intentionally discriminated against it on the basis of race when it revoked its previously awarded grant for radio equipment and then denied its second grant request,” Judge Kevin Newsom wrote for a three-judge panel, including Judge Andrew Brasher and Paul C. Huck, of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, sitting by designation.
“Accordingly, we reverse the district court’s dismissal of APEDF’s equal-protection claim and remand for further proceedings,” he continued.
Additionally, he wrote, the organization plausibly argued it was being punished for its relationship with the Uhuru Movement and its “goal of Black empowerment” in violation of First Amendment protections for speech and association.
The defense fund is a nonprofit that serves the South St. Petersburg community from a structure it calls Uhuru House (Swahili for “peace”), operating a gym, a licensed kitchen, a community center, and a Saturday school, and performing free HIV testing. It also operates a radio station called “Black Power 96,” according to the opinion.
The organization applied for grants under the COVID-era American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (ARPA), and was recommended by the Pinellas Community Foundation for $36,801 to buy radio equipment to keep its station on the air and $67,327 for a back-up power generator.
Chris Latvala, at the time a newly elected county commissioner, objected, accusing the organization of anti-semitism and asserting it shared its space with the African People’s Socialist Party (which the organization denies.) White-run groups conducting roughly the same activities were not penalized, according to the opinion.
The panel rejected the organization’s due-process claim, reasoning the government wasn’t obliged to award any grants.
Still, “[t]he essence of APEDF’s First Amendment claim here is that the County manipulated the ARPA grant program to suppress ideas that it viewed as dangerous — namely, those associated with the Uhuru Movement,” Newsom wrote.
“That, it seems to us, is the very kind of claim that [legal precedent] suggested might have merit. Though the government can deny funding to applicants for many reasons, it may not deny even a discretionary benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests — especially, his interest in freedom of speech.”
The case goes back to the trial court for further proceedings.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico House Republican leader urges county commission not to name replacement to vacant seat
description: A New Mexico House Republican leader is urging the Doña Ana County Commission to prevent a “blatant partisan power grab” and not name a replacement for House District 37, which Rep. Joanne Ferrary (D-Las Cruces) vacated earlier this week.
text:
New Mexico House Republican Leader Rep. Gail Armstrong (D-Magdalena) on July 28, 2026, urged the Doña Ana County Commission not to appoint a replacement to serve out the rest of state Rep. Joanne Ferrary’s term representing House District 37.A New Mexico House Republican leader is urging the Doña Ana County Commission to prevent a “blatant partisan power grab” and not name a replacement for House District 37, which Rep. Joanne Ferrary (D-Las Cruces) vacated earlier this week. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ferrary’s Monday retirement empowered the Doña Ana County Commission to name a candidate, subject to Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s approval, who would serve out the rest of Ferrary’s term, which ends at the end of this year.
But Ferrary’s departure comes several months before a November general election between Democrat Lori Martinez and Republican Isabella Solis for the HD37 seat. The winner of that race would take office in January and serve a two-year term. 
Ferrary previously told Source NM she hoped the county commission would name Martinez to give her a running start should she win the November election. 
House Republican Leader Rep. Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) issued a news release late Tuesday criticizing Ferrary for dropping out early and urging the commission to let the election play out without giving Martinez an advantage. 
Appointing Martinez to the seat before the election would provide her with benefits of incumbency like power, resources and visibility, Armstrong said, and would unfairly disadvantage Solis, she said. 
“The Democratic nominee should have to earn this seat from the voters, not receive it through a political appointment designed to tip the scales in her favor,” Armstrong said in a statement. 
She urged the commission to either leave the seat vacant until January, when the democratically elected candidate takes her rightful seat, or make a temporary appointment of someone who is neither Martinez nor Solis. 
“The voters of House District 37 should choose their next representative,” Armstrong said. “That decision should not be made for them in a backroom appointment that benefits one party and one candidate.”
Two New Mexico House members officially retire, teeing up Democratic primary winners to replace them

Doña Ana County Commission Chair Manuel Sanchez told Source NM on Wednesday that he is considering Armstrong’s suggestions. He had previously thought the county commission should appoint either Martinez or Solis, which would grant constituents of HD37 a “50/50 shot” of being represented by their eventual elected representative.
Still, Sanchez, a Democrat, said he is leaning toward appointing Martinez, because he thinks odds are already in her favor for the general election. He described the district as solidly Democratic and noted that Solis lost to Ferrary in the 2020 HD37 election. 
Appointing her now, which takes a majority vote from the commission, would let her “hit the ground running,” he said. 
Sanchez said he expects commissioners to take up the matter, with an application process and public input, sometime in August. 
Martinez did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Wednesday but said previously that she hopes the Doña Ana County Commission acts swiftly to name a replacement for the benefit of constituents in the district. 
Solis told Source NM on Monday that she thinks Ferrary’s retirement “put her finger on the scale” for Martinez, but she also said she’s not convinced being an incumbent will necessarily help Martinez come November. 
“It remains to be seen whether any political manipulation of the process will necessarily benefit them,” she said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah eyes applications for new independent medical cannabis pharmacy in ‘underserved’ area
description: Next week, Utah state officials will begin accepting applications to license a new independent medical cannabis pharmacy to be located in a “medically underserved” or rural area with a population that’s smaller than Salt Lake, Utah, Davis or Weber counties.  The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food announced in a news release Tuesday the application […]
text:
Buds of marijuana on display inside Mother Earth Wellness in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Next week, Utah state officials will begin accepting applications to license a new independent medical cannabis pharmacy to be located in a “medically underserved” or rural area with a population that’s smaller than Salt Lake, Utah, Davis or Weber counties. 
The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food announced in a news release Tuesday the application period will open on Aug. 3, and it will remain open until Sept. 2. 
The application is for the second of two independent medical cannabis pharmacies required to open under HB54, a bill passed by the Utah Legislature in 2025 that, among other measures, expanded the number of medical cannabis pharmacies allowed to operate in the state, including in “medically underserved” areas. It also aimed to create more opportunities for pharmacy operators that aren’t owned by large medical cannabis corporations. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The first independent medical cannabis pharmacy to open under the bill was Boojum in Moab. Before it opened, the nearest medical cannabis pharmacy was in Price, a nearly two-hour drive away. 
Before Boojum opened this year, its chief science officer Olivia Kulunder told Moab Sun News “we were awarded this license over a two billion dollar holdings corporation from Chicago.” 
“While we might not have over 150 dispensaries to our name, that means we will be pouring everything we have into this one pharmacy,” Kulunder told the outlet at the time. 
Kulunder, who grew up in Castle Valley, also said the licensing board cited Boojum’s local connection as a key reason for awarding its license. 
“We do know that this distance drives a lot of people to go out of state, which carries legal risks,” Kulander told Moab Sun News. “Having dependable local access to cannabis means that those who need it most will be able to access it safely and legally.”
Now it’s up to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food to decide where the next pharmacy will go. 
The independent medical cannabis pharmacy will be required to operate under Utah Department of Agriculture and Food regulations “to ensure patient safety and product quality,” the department said. 
To be eligible for the license, applications “must demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of medical cannabis regulations, possess the necessary financial resources, and propose a secure and compliant facility,” the department said. 
The following requirements must also be met:

Independence: The new licensee must not own a financial interest in a medical cannabis pharmacy or be owned by an entity that owns any interest in or operates a medical cannabis production establishment that is owned, partially or entirely, or operated by a medical cannabis production establishment.
Location: The new licensee shall be located in an area designated as medically underserved and in counties with populations smaller than 260,000. Eligible counties include Box Elder, Cache, Iron, Summit, Tooele, Uintah, Washington, Beaver, Carbon, Duchesne, Millard, San Juan, Sanpete, Sevier, Wasatch, Emery, Grand, Juab, Kane, Morgan, Piute, Daggett, Garfield, Rich and Wayne counties. 
Facility plan: Each applicant is required to provide a detailed layout and security plan for the proposed pharmacy.
Operational procedures: Each applicant must provide comprehensive standard operating procedures for dispensing, inventory management, and patient consultation.
Personnel Qualifications: Each applicant must provide information on key personnel, including pharmacists and technicians, and their qualifications.

After state officials review the applications, they’ll pick one proposed pharmacy to receive the license, which must be issued no later than Jan. 1, 2027. 
For more information on how to apply, visit the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food’s website.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Concern persists as former Three Mile Island nuclear plant progresses toward 2027 restart
description: In an otherwise dry public meeting Tuesday about emergency preparedness and environmental reviews, Nuclear Regulatory Commission officials also worked to assuage fears, some fueled by memories of the plant’s 1979 partial meltdown that upended life in the capital region.
text:
Unit 1 of the nuclear power plant at Three Mile Island will be renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center as part of an agreement between owner Constellation Energy and Microsoft to power artificial intelligence data centers. (Tim Lambert/Capital-Star) The former Three Mile Island nuclear power plant in Dauphin County is meeting milestones in its relicensing process and on track to begin producing electricity again by the middle of next year, federal regulators said.
But during a public meeting Tuesday about emergency preparedness and environmental reviews, Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) officials also worked to assuage fears, some fueled by memories of the plant’s 1979 partial meltdown that upended life in the capital region.
Daniel Rose, an emergency management specialist with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said the agency is conducting a detailed review of offsite radiological emergency plans (REP).
FEMA’s role, established after the Three Mile Island accident Rose noted, is to ensure that local officials have the preparedness and resources to adequately protect the public in the event of a nuclear accident.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We also inform and educate the public about radiological emergency preparedness, and we support and provide guidance to state and local governments in their emergency planning and preparedness activities that take place off-site,” he said, adding that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission oversees plans within the plant’s boundaries. 
FEMA will gather comments from other federal agencies and provide feedback. In February, the agency will lead plant owner Constellation Energy, the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency and county and local responders in a graded exercise followed by a public meeting, FERC’s Rose said.
Cumberland, Dauphin, Lancaster, Lebanon, and York counties and local governments, each in the 10-mile emergency planning zone around the plant, are participating along with the commonwealth, he said.
Now rebranded as the Crane Clean Energy Center, the former TMI 1 reactor slated to reopen next year was not affected by the accident that took its twin, TMI 2, permanently out of commission. TMI 1 continued operating until 2019, when Constellation Energy shut it down for economic reasons. The plant stands on an island in the Susquehanna River in Londonderry Township – about 10 miles south of Harrisburg.
Constellation is now undertaking a $1.6 billion effort to restart the reactor, which will supply 835 megawatts of electricity to the region’s electricity grid. It will offset an equivalent amount tech giant Microsoft has agreed to purchase from Constellation to power data centers elsewhere.
The company plans to permanently employ 600 people at the plant, including 150 “boomerang employees” returning from other sites and 450 new hires. Activity at the plant will also surge about every two years, as 1,500 to 2,000 workers spend weeks refueling the reactor, Constellation spokesman Dave Marcheskie said. 
The Crane Clean Energy Center, formerly the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant, in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The company is also training about 90 plant operators to be licensed by the NRC and new uranium fuel is set to be delivered to the plant by the end of 2026, he said.
With four currently operating nuclear power plants, the commonwealth has a robust REP program, FERC’s Rose said, adding that two exercises have been carried out this year with a third scheduled in October. He noted because the plant closed only seven years ago, many agencies are able to use their pre-existing plans as a starting point, streamlining the process.
One question from the audience of about 50 at Penn State’s Harrisburg campus centered on whether plans to evacuate schools, nursing homes and other facilities housing vulnerable would withstand the human instinct to flee an actual disaster.
NRC officials responded with uncharacteristic intensity, saying that they believe they and others responsible for public safety would stand by their posts in an emergency.
“If you’re asking me what I’m going to do. I’m going to be responding to the event to protect the people,” said Ray McKinley, director of the NRC’s division of reactor safety for the northeastern United States. “That’s our mission.”
Brett Klukan, an NRC attorney who moderated the meeting, conceded that the emergency preparedness plans depend on the selflessness of responders.
“There are moments every day where people rush into danger, rushing the fire to protect others, and we’re relying on that same greatest impulse within us to do their duty to protect the public in such a circumstance,” Klukan said.
And NRC spokesman Scott Burnell added that any danger at the plant is likely to develop over the course of hours, if not days, and the plans take that into account.
“They are based on realistic, evidence-based analysis of what could happen and how it will happen and how long it will take,” Burnell said. “And that is why there will be time for experts to examine what’s happening, and determine what could be necessary to protect the public.”
NRC officials also provided updates on inspection activities and the review of environmental impacts required under federal law. Erin Carfang, the engineering chief responsible for inspections throughout the northeast, said specialists are working to ensure the plant is restored to its pre-shut down specifications, while others are reviewing cybersecurity measures, the plant’s fire protection and its program to identify and correct safety issues. 
Officials from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission presented updates on the reopening of the former Three Mile Island nuclear power plant, now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, during a public meeting Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
Kevin Folk, senior environmental project manager for the NRC, said the agency is on course to issue its final environmental assessment, which covers more than a dozen resource areas, such as air quality and noise, surface and groundwater impacts and how the site will manage spent uranium fuel, which remains highly radioactive.
NRC staff determined that an exhaustive, in-depth study and environmental impact statement were not required and a less intensive environmental assessment was sufficient, Folk said. The draft assessment was published in June and public comment on the document closed July 8. The assessment found no significant effects on resources and a final Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) is expected to be issued in September, he said.
During the 21/2 hour meeting, speakers included a representative of the York County commissioners and Dauphin County Commissioner Mike Pries, both of whom spoke in favor of the project. Others expressed deep concern about the longer-term impact of nuclear energy and the storage of spent fuel at the site amid the flood-prone Susquehanna.
“I’m always seeking truth, and tonight I’m thankful that we heard some truths and some vagaries that you wonder, where are we getting this information tonight?” said Patricia Longenecker of West Donegal Township, Lancaster County,  noting there’s no plan to remove thousands of tons of radioactive waste left by the TMI 2 accident from the island.
Patricia Longenecker spoke at a public meeting in Middletown, Dauphin County, about the planned reopening of the former Three Mile Island nuclear plant. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)
Catherine Warner, a nuclear health physicist and lead decommissioning inspector for the damaged reactor, said 99% of the fuel was removed in dry cask containers for storage in Idaho. The remaining 1%, plus sludge and radioactive concrete from the reactor building, will also be removed but stored on site or sent to a burial site, depending on the level of radioactivity, she said. 
Warner said the waste stored on the island includes 46 spent fuel canisters from TMI 1 and one high-level waste container.
Dave Allard, the retired director of the Bureau of Radiation Protection in the state Department of Environmental protection, said his experience working with the plant’s former owner Exelon left him with no concerns about the emergency response plans. But Allard said he is worried about decreased staffing levels at the NRC and FEMA following efforts in the Trump administration to reduce the federal workforce. 
McKinley, the reactor safety director, said staffing levels have created challenges for the NRC in the last year. 
“We’re a leaner organization for sure, but we have quite a bit of depth in our talent and a very talented workforce,” he said. “We don’t foresee any difficulty with regards to being able to perform a very thorough and detailed licensing review.”
Allard also said he has deep concern about a rulemaking proposal the NRC filed earlier in July to scrap a decades old radiation safety principle requiring companies using radioactive materials to keep exposure “as low as reasonably possible.” The proposal is part of the agency’s response to President Donald Trump’s executive order demanding reform of the NRC. 
“These standards are basic standards for protection of workers,” Allard said, adding that he questions whether other federal agencies such as the Department of Energy and Occupational Safety and Health Administration should have been involved in the proposal. Burnell, the NRC spokesperson, noted the Crane restart would proceed under existing standards.
“I hope the public looks at this very hard,” Allard said, noting that the new rule would create different allowable radiation doses for the public and workers. “I think there’s going to be great confusion in the regulated community.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee picks up second teachers union endorsement
description: Gov. Dan McKee now boasts endorsements from Rhode Island’s two major statewide teachers unions, having secured the recommendation of the National Education Association of Rhode Island on Wednesday. The endorsement, made by a unanimous vote of the association’s political action committee, is not a surprise. The 12,000-member union also backed McKee in 2022, a[...]
text:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee visits students in a summer program in  2024. (Office of the Governor)Gov. Dan McKee now boasts endorsements from Rhode Island’s two major statewide teachers unions, having secured the recommendation of the National Education Association of Rhode Island on Wednesday.
The endorsement, made by a unanimous vote of the association’s political action committee, is not a surprise. The 12,000-member union also backed McKee in 2022, and donated $500 to his campaign in January. McKee’s decision to sign a contested charter school moratorium into law in June — prompting a federal lawsuit by a dual language charter school now blocked from opening — was widely viewed as a political move meant to win favor with the influential teachers unions. 
The other, equally sized state teachers union, the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals, endorsed McKee last week.
The National Education Association, led by Senate President Valarie Lawson, includes mostly suburban and rural school districts along with faculty and graduate workers at Roger Williams University and the University of Rhode Island. At least one representative from all of the association’s 76 locals participated in the endorsement vote, following interviews with Democratic gubernatorial candidates on Tuesday night. 
Stephanie Mandeville, an association spokesperson, declined to share the total number of members who voted in the endorsement decision. 
“Our endorsement is something our members take very seriously,” Amy Mullen, an elementary math intervention specialist in Tiverton who chairs the political action committee, said in a statement. “Committee members asked thoughtful, challenging questions and carefully considered not only the candidates’ positions, but also their willingness to engage in a meaningful dialogue and demonstrate a clear understanding of the issues affecting our members. We weren’t looking for talking points, we were looking for leadership, honesty, and a proven commitment to public education and working families.”
The association cited McKee’s “demonstrated understanding” of education issues and “detailed responses” to questions about his priorities as reasons for the endorsement.
Democratic primary challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Foulkes has said she would have vetoed the charter school moratorium bill if she was governor. 
Foulkes, who lost to McKee by 3 percentage points in the 2022 Democratic gubernatorial primary, leads McKee by double digits in the most recent public polling and has secured a majority of the municipal Democratic endorsements, including from McKee’s hometown of Cumberland.
Neither the Rhode Island Democratic Party nor the AFL-CIO made an endorsement in the gubernatorial primary in a decision seen as a snub for an incumbent Democratic governor.
But McKee has picked up several large union endorsements in recent weeks. In addition to both state teachers unions, he also received backing from the 10,000-member Rhode Island Council 94 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, the United Nurses and Allied Professionals and General Teamsters Local 251. Smaller labor groups, including local chapters of the Operative Plasterers’ and Cement Masons’ International Association and the International Union of Elevator Constructors have endorsed McKee, too.
He is expected to receive an endorsement from the Rhode Island Building & Construction Trades Council at a rally scheduled for tomorrow, as first reported by WPRI-TV 12
Foulkes has also won favor with labor groups, including the Rhode Island SEIU Council, UNITE Here hospitality workers, and the Rhode Island Troopers Association.
And she has a considerable cash advantage over McKee, helping her dominate the airwaves battles with more than $1.1 million spent on local TV commercials, according to the most recent filings with federal regulators. McKee’s campaign has spent just over $582,000 on political ads.
Second-quarter campaign reports for all state primary candidates are due to the Rhode Island Board of Elections by Friday night.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.
Reporter Christopher Shea contributed to this story.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine ACLU seeks $5 million in damages for wrongfully detained immigrants
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of Maine is seeking a total of more than $5 million from the federal government on behalf of three Maine residents it says were wrongfully detained. The five administrative claims filed by the local affiliate Wednesday are among 54 others filed in 17 states and Washington, D.C., under the Federal […]
text:
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota on Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The American Civil Liberties Union of Maine is seeking a total of more than $5 million from the federal government on behalf of three Maine residents it says were wrongfully detained.
The five administrative claims filed by the local affiliate Wednesday are among 54 others filed in 17 states and Washington, D.C., under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows people to seek financial compensation for harm caused by federal employees. The claims were filed with the U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The Maine claims stem from the large-scale immigration enforcement operation in January known as Operation Catch of the Day, during which roughly 200 people — the vast majority of whom were lawfully present in the U.S. — were detained.
“We’re participating in this … in part to get accountability for all of those individuals, but also to shed light on the widespread abuses that ICE is doing all over the country,” said Samuel Crankshaw, spokesperson for the Maine ACLU.  “And not just during big surges like Operation Catch of the Day, but happening on a daily basis, pretty much everywhere.”
The Maine ACLU filed five claims arising from three arrests during the operation. Three of the claims involve members of the same family, while the other two involve individual immigrants. All three people have since been released from federal detention, though the ACLU said they continue to live with the effects of the incident.
Whether the claims will result in compensation remains unclear. Federal agencies have six months to investigate an administrative claim and may choose to settle it or claimants can file a civil suit in federal court.
“The long-term trends are that the intent of that process under the law has not worked as well as it should,” Crankshaw said. “No matter what the outcome of the administrative complaint may be, it’s a required first step to get any kind of accountability.”
What the claims say
The first case involved an asylum seeker, who the ACLU identified as Mr. Diallo,who was detained while driving home with his family. The ACLU filed three separate claims on behalf of everyone in the car, Crankshaw said.
Years prior, Diallo had been detained and released. Despite complying with all conditions of release, ICE agents this winter stopped his car and detained him without a warrant, the ACLU said. During the stop, agents broke the driver’s side window, spraying broken glass over the entire family, including a baby, the claim reports. Diallo was detained for three weeks until he was able to obtain an attorney, who filed a successful challenge to his detention. 
Another of the claims is on behalf of  an immigrant who on Jan. 22 was dragged from his car after agents smashed his window. The civil rights organization did not disclose the identity of this person.
The third case involves Elias Tesfaye, who was taken from his home by masked agents on Jan. 20. Tesfaye had previously been in ICE custody but was released in 2013 and has been living and working in Maine for over a decade, where according to the ACLU he complied with all the terms of his release. Tesfaye was held in a detention facility for a month, during which he developed PTSD, had a panic attack, and was prescribed Prozac that he is still taking. After Tesfaye secured a lawyer, the government did not attempt to justify his arrest, releasing Tesfaye without responding to the legal challenge, the civil rights agency said.
A separate lawsuit filed by the ACLU on behalf of a Portland man in U.S. District Court rests on protections in the Maine Civil Rights Act — another approach the organization is taking to seek justice for wrongfully detained immigrants. The ACLU couldn’t confirm or deny if the same person was involved in one of the tort claims.
New laws limit ICE enforcement
Even after the end of the January enforcement surge, federal immigration agents have maintained a presence in Maine. Two weeks ago, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was killed by federal immigration agents in Biddeford, prompting renewed calls to investigate ICE operations, demand accountability and place additional limits on how and where agents can operate.
Several new Maine laws took effect Wednesday that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. One restricts local law enforcement from coordinating with federal immigration authorities, another prohibits landlords from sharing certain tenant information, and a third allows employees at certain schools and healthcare facilities to deny immigration agents access to nonpublic areas without a judicial warrant.
“These laws and the claims we’re bringing demonstrate our commitment to do everything possible to stop the ICE violence and chaos that led to the shocking killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero this month in Biddeford,” said ACLU of Maine Executive Director Molly Curren Rowles in a statement.
“Congress has refused to rein in ICE, but if the federal government won’t protect people in Maine, then Mainers will continue to take action and protect one another – just as we always have.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Senate approves judicial oversight measure despite warnings of politicization
description: The final version of H377 includes a provision giving the state Supreme Court the power to censure, publicly reprimand, suspend or remove judges at its discretion.
text:
A state flag flies outside the North Carolina Legislative Building on May 8, 2025. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)North Carolina Senate Democrats are concerned that a bill making changes to court processes will make the judicial branch more political. 
Presented by Sen. Warren Daniel, R-Burke, House Bill 377 passed the Senate 26-11 on party lines Wednesday. 
The final version of H377 gives the state Supreme Court the power to censure, publicly reprimand, suspend or remove judges at its discretion, even if the Judicial Standards Commission hasn’t recommended it. H377 also allows the chief justice of the Supreme Court to suspend a trial court judge without pay while the judge is under investigation, if the Judicial Standards Commission recommends it.
“It provides some due process elements for that,” Daniel said. 
Sen. Lisa Grafstein, D-Wake, said she’s worried about the increasing politicization of the courts.
She said the provision comes at a time when there’s low confidence among many people about the impartiality and fairness of the courts. In the current political climate, Grafstein said, there’s an “increasing use of power to intimidate and to enforce compliance with political preferences.” 
It also may give too much power to the chief justice, she said. 
“My concern about this provision specifically is that it invests a great deal of power in one individual to engage in suspension of judges who are supposed to be neutral arbiters, who are supposed to be outside of political influence,” Grafstein said. 
North Carolina judges are elected, not appointed for life, so the change may pressure them to make decisions that they believe the Judicial Standards Commission and the state Supreme Court, both controlled by Republican majorities, will approve, Grafstein argued. 
“We are on a really dangerous path in the way that we have vested power in fewer and fewer people, and that we’re doing that at a time when that power is being abused in so many ways,” she said. 
Sen. Jay Chaudhuri, D-Wake, asked why the provision was added to the bill. 
NC House Democrats call for changes to protect judicial independence, balance of powers

Daniel said it was requested by the North Carolina Administrative Office of the Courts.
“There’s currently a process for suspension without pay for clerk support and for assistant district attorneys,” he said. “There’s not one for judicial members, so it felt like this was conforming to those other officials.”
Daniel said there are guidelines in place to provide due process for a suspended judge.
If a chief justice decides to immediately remove or suspend a trial judge, it needs to be upon recommendation from the Judicial Standards Commission, he said, adding that that would only happen when there is “immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage to the public or the administration of justice.” 
“This is not a provision where somebody is going to just do a witch hunt based on ideology,” Sen. Amy Galey, R-Alamance, said, taking issue with Grafstein’s concerns.
“The position that this is some kind of boogeyman way that we’re going to have pretext to get rid of people based on politics, it’s really unfounded and does a lot to undermine our confidence in the integrity of the system and also in the deliberations of this body,” Galey said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Democrats re-introduce nine bills blocked by Hall and vetoed by Whitmer
description: Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July.  The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were […]
text:
Michigan House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said he was "skeptical" of the willingness of House Republican leadership to move forward with the progress of the nine bills, but that Democrats would re-introduce the bills as many times as necessary. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Legislative Democrats in the state House and Senate announced Wednesday they are re-introducing the nine bills that were the center of a lawsuit, a state Supreme Court decision and eventually a veto from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in mid-July. 
The bills, which passed both chambers of the legislature in 2024, when Democrats had a trifecta, were never transmitted to Whitmer’s desk for her signature prior to the end of that legislative session, and House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) refused to do so once he took control of the chamber at the start of 2025. That led to an 18-month legal battle between the leaders in both chambers, which culminated in the Supreme Court declining to take up the case, leaving a Court of Appeals decision in place that ruled it was unconstitutional for Hall not to transmit the bills to the governor’s desk.
Hours after the Supreme Court’s decision, Whitmer vetoed the bills, a decision that legislators and labor leaders alike called a betrayal. 
Now, legislators are bringing the bills back up, though they face an uphill battle in the Republican-controlled House. Hall’s refusal to transmit the initial versions of the bills leads most to expect that he will not push the legislation through his chamber while he remains at its helm.
House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said that, while he hopes to get these bills passed in the last five months of the current legislative session by “holding Republicans’ feet to the fire in the House,” he would join legislators in re-introducing the bills as many times as needed to — including next session, when Democrats hope to reclaim control of the House — in order to get them passed.
“I have not had conversations with the House Republicans on this, but the offer stands that we are willing to work in good faith to get this done,” Puri said. “I’m skeptical if that’s really going to happen in this year. But you know, the alternative to that is making sure that they don’t need to be a part of the equation in 2027.”
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) is surrounded by Democratic senators and representatives, as well as labor leaders, to announce the re-introduction of the nine bills that were the subject of a state court case and led to a veto from Gov. Whitmer. July 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren), who was one of the most vocal critics in the legislature of Whitmer’s decision to veto the bills, said she believes some rank-and-file House Republicans want to see these bills passed, and hopes that party leadership will be willing to work with them. 
“Anything is possible. We are all up for re-election,” Xiong said. “Certainly I look forward to hearing their response because now the ball is in their court, and if they want to take their ball home and not play, then they’re not doing the job that they were elected to do. That sends a very clear message to Michigan families.”
At a press conference on Wednesday morning, legislative Democrats were more focused on Hall’s role in keeping the bills from being passed, rather than Whitmer’s. 
Xiong noted that she hopes Whitmer will be willing to work with legislators on updated versions of the legislation. 
When asked if she believed that Whitmer would sign the bills, should they come to her desk, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said that she had been confident in the past and could not speculate on the Governor’s intentions. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“At this point, she is requesting those bills to come to her desk, and as we are introducing them today, we will make the necessary changes so that they meet the muster,” Brinks said. “We believe that they merit her signature. But that ultimately, as we all know, is a decision that she must make.”
A spokesperson for Whitmer’s office said in response to a question about whether or not she would sign the bills, should they make it to her desk again, “As the governor said, she stands ready to work with the legislature to consider new versions.”
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the frontrunner for the Democrats in the 2026 gubernatorial election, said in a press release following Whitmer’s veto that she would sign the bills into law if elected.
The importance of the bills, which include a shield for working families against debt collection practices that seize tax returns made possible by the Earned Income Tax Credit and a measure preventing massive healthcare costs for teachers and school employees, first responders, nurses and other public servants, was emphasized throughout the press conference. 
“For too long, the people of Michigan, the people who make Michigan run, the people who keep our children safe and educated, our communities healthy, and our state moving have been left to shoulder the burden of rising costs and economic uncertainty alone,” Michigan AFL-CIO President Ron Bieber said. “Michigan’s labor movement is committed to doing whatever is necessary to pass the bills reintroduced today by our friends in the House and Senate, these aren’t just pieces of legislation. These are lifelines for working families.”

title: Barack Obama tells Iowans ‘ball’s in your court’ to elect Josh Turek to U.S. Senate
description: Josh Turek picked up an endorsement for his U.S. Senate bid Wednesday from former President Barack Obama, announced in a video showing the two Democrats playing basketball together. Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympic gold medalist with 2016 and 2020 wins on the U.S. wheelchair basketball team, is the 2026 Democratic nominee for the […]
text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek shakes hands with former President Barack Obama, who offers his support for the Iowa U.S. Senate candidate as the two shoot hoops in a video released by Turek's campaign July 29, 2026. (Photo courtesy Turek for Iowa campaign)Josh Turek picked up an endorsement for his U.S. Senate bid Wednesday from former President Barack Obama, announced in a video showing the two Democrats playing basketball together.
Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympic gold medalist with 2016 and 2020 wins on the U.S. wheelchair basketball team, is the 2026 Democratic nominee for the seat currently held by U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, a Republican. He is facing a tough general election race against U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who has received support from national Republicans like President Donald Trump and campaigned alongside GOP leaders like U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Ted Cruz.
National Democratic leaders are also bringing high-power backers to the campaign. Turek’s campaign released the video “Who’s Got Next,” where the Democratic Senate candidate plays a game of horse, renamed “I-O-W-A,” against the former president at a gymnasium in Chicago. Obama, a well-known basketball fan, talks about his favorite players and Turek’s time on the Iowa campaign trail as they make shots.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The video doesn’t show who won the game, but Obama said at the end he’d been “whooped.”
Obama, who won the Iowa Democratic presidential caucus in 2008 and won the state in the 2008 and 2012 general elections, said, “of all the things I’ve done in politics, Iowa was my favorite thing.”
“There was just a magic about regular folks showing up in gyms like this, and just talk it out, ‘how do we move our state forward, how do we move the country forward,'” Obama said in the video.
Republicans have seen a stretch of victories in Iowa in recent election cycles — currently, Iowa has an all-Republican delegation in Washington D.C., and Republicans hold a trifecta of control at the Statehouse. Though political forecasters like Cook Political Report rate Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat as “leans Republican,” Democrats believe Turek — alongside other Democratic candidates on the ballot — will shift the political tides in Iowa.
National Democrats are investing significantly in the Senate race, with the Senate Majority PAC reserving $30 million for a fall ad campaign targeting Hinson’s voting record. Turek has also received endorsements from Democrats like former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, another previous Iowa caucus winner, as well as Iowans including former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin.
In the video, Turek said he believes Iowans are feeling optimistic about the midterms.
“I’ll tell you what, people all across Iowa are saying that they’re feeling that hope, that optimism for the first time in a long time,” Turek said.
After finishing the game, Obama said, “I’ve seen enough. Not only did I get whooped, but you’ve got here a man of character, somebody who knows how to win.”
“Now the ball’s in your court, Iowa,” the former president said. “Let’s make sure that we send Josh Turek to the United States Senate.”

title: Van Buren County files 34 charges of animal neglect against puppy mill operator
description: Van Buren County officials criminally charged a puppy mill operator Wednesday, alleging she committed 34 acts of animal neglect. Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington is charged with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal neglect with injury. In an affidavit attached to th[...]
text:
A dog at Wuanita Swedlund's kennels in Farmington, Iowa, as photographed by USDA inspectors in 2024. (USDA photo as reproduced in U.S. District Court records) Van Buren County officials criminally charged a puppy mill operator Wednesday, alleging she committed 34 acts of animal neglect.
Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington is charged with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal neglect with injury.
In an affidavit attached to the criminal complaints, Deputy Sheriff Spencer Rider alleges Swedlund failed to provide adequate food and water to the confined animals on her property, causing the animals unjustified distress and suffering.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During a June visit to Swedlund’s kennels, Rider alleges, officials observed water bowls containing no potable water for animals to drink; food bowls contaminated with feces; kennels with an excessive buildup of feces and organic matter, indicating the kennels had not been cleaned for a prolonged period of time; a flea infestation, and a Yorkshire terrier that was in need of dental care.
On June 30, 2026, deputies seized 32 dogs, plus one cat and one rabbit, from Swedlund’s property.
Swedlund could not be reached for comment Wednesday, although she told the Iowa Capital Dispatch on Tuesday that none of her animals were neglected. She has yet to enter a plea in the case, and an initial court appearance is now scheduled for Aug. 20, 2026.
Last month, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service sued Swedlund for allegedly barring federal officials from conducting “unannounced” inspections of her dog-breeding operations. The USDA asked the court to issue an injunction granting the agency access to the property.
On July 10, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher issued the injunction, stating that Swedlund’s noncompliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act “goes well beyond bureaucratic handwringing. The evidence shows that Swedlund has housed hundreds of dogs since acquiring her USDA license in 2023. She has consistently failed to provide her animals with adequate facilities, access to water, or access to medical care. It is evident that the animals in Swedlund’s care suffered needlessly — precisely the type of harm that the Animal Welfare Act sought to prevent.”
In separate state-court proceedings designed to determine to the fate of the 34 animals taken from Swedlund, District Court Judge Joel D. Yates transferred ownership of the animals to the PAW Animal Shelter in Fort Madison for eventual adoption.
In his ruling, Yates said the evidence showed the “animals were neglected by not having access to appropriate food, potable water, sanitary conditions, proper ventilated shelter and necessary veterinary care.”
Swedlund spoke to the Iowa Capital Dispatch Tuesday, about 20 hours before the charges were filed, and said she doesn’t believe any of the animals suffered from any type of neglect. She objected to the seizure of her family pets, which she said included a rottweiler, a Yorkshire terrier, a pug, a chihuahua, the cat and the rabbit. “All my animals were healthy,” she said Tuesday.
Court records indicate the USDA first issued Swedlund a license in July 2023. Since then, the records show, she has been cited for numerous violations of the Animal Welfare Act, some of which were tied to the death of eight puppies from three different litters.
In that case, the USDA alleged Swedlund told inspectors she had found three dead bulldog puppies after feeling a strong, cold draft at the front of their enclosure. Inspectors reported Swedlund had placed duct tape over the hole that caused the draft, but the tape was peeling away at the time of the inspection and the cold draft could still be felt.
Three more puppies from a litter of rottweilers were found dead, the USDA says, and one puppy was severely injured and later euthanized after a husky broke into an enclosure housing a sheepdog and her newborn litter. A week later, another of the puppies from that litter was apparently eaten by its mother.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Sing it loud, New Hampshire: ‘We’re No. 1! We’re No. 1!’ Oh, wait, we’re not?
description: Over the past three decades, New Hampshire Republicans have held trifecta power over the State House — or simultaneous control of the governor’s office, House, and Senate — for 11 years, including the past six. Democrats, meanwhile, have held trifecta power for just four years in that span.  And while Democrats had a decade-long run […]
text:
Gov. Kelly Ayotte celebrates the signing of a pair of bills at the State House in June 2025, one to broaden "parental rights" and the other to expand the voucher-like education freedom accounts program. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Over the past three decades, New Hampshire Republicans have held trifecta power over the State House — or simultaneous control of the governor’s office, House, and Senate — for 11 years, including the past six. Democrats, meanwhile, have held trifecta power for just four years in that span. 
And while Democrats had a decade-long run of success winning the governor’s seat starting in 2005, since 1995 Republicans have held majority control of both branches of the state Legislature at the same time for a staggering 22 years.
So, for better or worse, it’s fair to say the state of the state belongs to the Republican Party.
That’s why they get so excited when the U.S. News and World Report “Best States” rankings come out every year. The great thing about rankings as far as a Republican politician is concerned (and you may remember that I’ve written about their love of WalletHub lists, too) is that they can cherry-pick the good categories, deliver the news to voters without defining context or methodology, and essentially suggest that the ranking is more real than the reality of personal experience.
As Gov. Kelly Ayotte and other state Republicans proved this week, it can be a politically dangerous game to play. 
In separate press releases about the U.S. News and World Report rankings, Ayotte touted the state’s top rankings in a pair of subcategories, safety and economic opportunity. She did not, however, mention that on her watch New Hampshire dropped in the overall rankings from No. 2 in 2025 to No. 6 this year, most likely dragged down by a No. 41 ranking for affordability, No. 40 ranking for higher education, No. 39 ranking for fiscal stability, and a No. 32 ranking for the state’s economy (which also includes a No. 49 subcategory ranking for growth).
Even when you discount the latest lists and rankings, and we probably all should, July as a whole hasn’t been particularly kind to Republicans. A couple of weeks ago, the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute released a report outlining the toll of $51 million in back-of-the-budget cuts for the state Department of Health and Human Services in the 2026-2027 biennium. Among the programs most affected are: community mental health services, family intervention and prevention-related services, food assistance programs, and child and maternal health services.
Importantly, Health and Human Services was just one of 11 state departments hit with such cuts.  
“Policymakers faced significant expenditure needs, potential costs and federal policy shifts, and decreases in State revenue due in part to the previous choices of legislators,” wrote report author Jessica Williams, a senior policy analyst, “which resulted in more difficult funding tradeoffs for State Fiscal Years (SFYs) 2026 and 2027 than in the prior four budget cycles.” 
So purposeful self-sabotage, in other words.
The timing of the NHFPI report wasn’t great for Republicans. Days earlier Ayotte had vetoed the 10-year state transportation plan, upsetting lawmakers in both parties. The governor’s big beef was with a proposed toll increase aimed at out-of-state drivers, which was meant to help address a $400 million funding shortfall. See a pattern?
“You want your roads, we’ve got to do something about it,” said Republican Rep. David Milz, who called the toll increase “almost a no-brainer.”
That’s an important, and too rare, lightbulb for the state’s majority party. You see, if you want the things that make everybody’s life better, like roads, public education, childcare, healthcare, Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, etc., you do have to pay for them. And for that you need revenue. 
But the pattern keeps repeating. New Hampshire cuts off, reduces, or claws back funding for needed services and investments, calls it fiscal responsibility, and life gets a little harder not just for low-income residents but a middle class that can’t keep up with a deluge of higher prices, from gas and groceries to healthcare and housing.
I suspect that part of the slide under Republicans’ watch is due to the elevation of fringe voices with disparate axes to grind, with targets ranging from immigrants and LGBTQ+ people to vaccines and literature that offends them. But there has to be some responsibility taken by the Republican traditionalists who have not only embraced the anti-government dreams of the many Free Staters in their ranks but continue to peddle the idea that we don’t actually owe anything to each other. Low (or no) taxes, small government, and an unrestrained free market are all we need, and the resulting tide will raise all boats, they argue. 
Except it hasn’t, and it won’t. What has happened is that more and more boats sink every day, and just so a few more rich guys can buy super yachts. When you hear economists fret over the historic levels of wealth inequality, that’s precisely what they’re talking about.
Should a majority of the Republican Party ever come to disavow the presidency of Donald Trump, my guess is that they will try to paint him and his Cabinet as accidents of their movement, as outliers. The perfect crime was committed in broad daylight by a sitting president, they’ll say, and fully at the expense of the poor, innocent people he was elected to serve. If only we had had the ability then, they will lament, to see his actions for what they really were.
To that end, they could easily cite the obscene profits he and his family have collected while in power, or the way he greedily sabotaged the nation’s post-pandemic economic recovery through a thoughtless war, misguided tariffs, a violent and destabilizing mass deportation campaign, Elon Musk’s DOGE rampage, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which primarily exists to reward the rich at the expense of those below them on the wealth ladder.
But if you look at what’s happening in New Hampshire, in every red chamber in every red state, it’s clear that Trump was no accident, and he certainly is not an outlier. He is the fulfillment of what the right’s movement has long held as its primary, but often unspoken, tenet: The only way forward is to leave many behind.
Maybe that sounds just fine to a lot of Republican and independent voters in New Hampshire, as they peer back at the abandoned rabble in their dust. But what they’ll realize when they at last turn around is that the caravan has left without them, too. 
They will see that they were always among the “others” meant to be culled.
